findings.quote: by twenty-six with no university degree, and by thirty-two was publishing original mathematics
findings.problem: Both ages are too late, so the reader comes away with the wrong timeline. Boole opened his own school in Lincoln in 1834, at 19. His first paper appeared in the Cambridge Mathematical Journal in February 1840, at 24, and the Royal Society gave him its Royal Medal in 1844, at 28, for 'On a General Method in Analysis'. 'By thirty-two' points at 1847, so it reads as though The Mathematical Analysis of Logic was where his mathematics began.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Taught Latin by a local bookseller, he taught himself Greek, French and German, opened his own school at nineteen with no university degree, and at twenty-four was publishing original mathematics." Sources: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Boole/ (school in 1834 'although he was only 19'; Royal Medal November 1844); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Boole (first paper February 1840; own school at 19).

findings.quote: the output leaves on the right under its formula (· is AND, + is OR, ¬ is NOT)
findings.problem: The 'How it works' strip describes something the drawing does not have. The figure's outputs are labelled in words ('A and B', 'A or B', 'not A'), and no ·, + or ¬ appears anywhere in it, as the 375 px screenshot and the figure's own <desc> both show. A reader who looks for the formulas will not find them.
findings.fix: "*Reading a gate.* Inputs A and B enter on the left; the output leaves on the right, named in words; the table beside it lists every case. In formulas, · is AND, + is OR and ¬ is NOT."

findings.quote: He taught himself Latin, Greek and the major European languages by his late teens
findings.problem: He did not teach himself Latin. His father arranged lessons for him with a local bookseller (William Brooke). He did teach himself Greek (good enough by 14 to translate Meleager) and French and German.
findings.fix: This is folded into the M fix above: "Taught Latin by a local bookseller, he taught himself Greek, French and German..." Source: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Boole/ ('received instruction in Latin from a local bookseller').

findings.quote: a velocity value was converted to a 16-bit signed integer too small to hold it
findings.problem: The sentence sits inside a passage about silent wraparound (Fig 2.8, 'a silent wrap'), so readers will assume Ariane's value quietly wrapped to a wrong number. It did not wrap. The unprotected Ada conversion raised an Operand Error, which shut down both inertial reference computers. The flight computer then read their diagnostic bit pattern as flight data.
findings.fix: "...because a velocity value was too large for the 16-bit signed integer it was converted to, and the overflow shut down both of its guidance computers." Source: Ariane 5 Flight 501 Inquiry Board report (Lions), sections 2.1–2.2, mirrored at www-users.cse.umn.edu/~arnold/disasters/ariane5rep.html.

findings.quote: Before it, every CPU had its own format.
findings.problem: This is an overclaim. Before 1985 the formats belonged to makers and families, not to each CPU. IBM's hexadecimal format covered the whole System/360 line and its compatibles, DEC had its own, and Intel's 8087 (1980) already used the draft of 754.
findings.fix: "Before it, each computer maker had its own format." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754-1985 (history section).

findings.quote: in Python, JavaScript, C, Java and Rust alike
findings.problem: C computes the same double, but it does not show 0.30000000000000004 by default. printf("%f") prints 0.300000 and %g prints 0.3. You only see the long form if you ask for 17 digits. Python, JavaScript, Java and Rust print it unprompted. A reader who tries it in C will see 0.3.
findings.fix: "in Python, JavaScript, Java and Rust alike" (drop C), or "... Java and Rust alike, and in C when asked for 17 digits".

findings.quote: electricity reliably represents two states, but not many more
findings.problem: The reader will take away that more than two levels is impractical. In fact the flash in their own phone and laptop stores 3 or 4 bits per cell as 8 or 16 voltage levels (TLC/QLC), and PCIe 6.0, GDDR6X and 400G Ethernet send data on 4 levels (PAM4), paying for it with error correction. The claim holds for logic, which is what the section is about.
findings.fix: "*two voltage states are far easier to tell apart than three or more*", which keeps p3's margin argument and drops the false 'not many more'.

findings.quote: so gates are wired like Shannon's relays: two in series conduct only when both inputs are 1
findings.problem: Put next to the NOT description (a transistor that pulls the output to 0 volts), this suggests an AND gate is just two series transistors. In a real chip, a series pair in that position gives NAND. An AND is built as a NAND followed by a NOT, which is also why NAND, the next subsection's gate, is the one chips build most cheaply.
findings.fix: Add after the NOT sentence: "Put two transistors in series in that place and the output drops to 0 only when both inputs are 1: a NAND, the gate chips build most cheaply, so a chip's AND is a NAND followed by a NOT."

findings.quote: The three gates every circuit is built from
findings.problem: This contradicts the same section two paragraphs later, where NAND alone is enough and real CPUs use NAND, NOR, XOR and compound gates. AND, OR and NOT are what any circuit can be built from, not what every circuit is built from.
findings.fix: "The three gates any circuit can be built from: ..."

findings.quote: repeats forever; a double keeps 52 bits
findings.problem: The label is drawn directly under '0.0 0011 0011 ...', so it reads as if the double keeps the first 52 bits counted from the binary point. In fact the leading zeros go into the exponent, and the 52 stored bits start after the first 1, which is implied (Fig 2.10). A double therefore holds 53 significant bits of 0.1. The <desc> has the same wording: 'keeps only the first 52 bits'.
findings.fix: Drawn label: "repeats forever; a double keeps 52 bits after the first 1". <desc>: "so a double keeps the 52 bits after its first 1 and rounds".

findings.quote: DeMorgan's Laws
findings.problem: The math-callout heading misspells the name. The callout's own text, Fig 2.4's strip and the <desc> all say 'Augustus De Morgan' and 'De Morgan's law'.
findings.fix: "De Morgan's laws"

findings.quote: main's variables | main's rbp | return: main, next | main's rbp, saved
findings.problem: The name "main's rbp" labels two different values. The slot in main's frame is the rbp of main's caller, which main's own `push rbp` saved; add's slot holds main's rbp. In the listing, `push rbp` runs before any locals are made, so the saved value sits above main's variables, not below them. A reader trying to follow the strip's "each saved rbp points at the frame before it" finds main's rbp stored twice, in the wrong order.
findings.fix: Swap main's two slots and rename them: top slot (y=46) "caller's rbp, saved", next slot (y=86) "main's variables". Desc: "main's frame (its caller's saved rbp, then its variables) sits on the stack." Nothing else moves, because RSP still starts under main's frame.

findings.quote: one register, four names
findings.problem: The label, the SVG title and the caption all promise four names. The drawing and the caption show five: RAX, EAX, AX, AH and AL. Readers who count will stop.
findings.fix: Use "one register, five names" in the diagram-label and the SVG <title>, and start caption ch3-registers-p3 with "One register, five names: RAX (2003) contains EAX (1985), which contains AX (1978), split into AH and AL."

findings.quote: pop rsi | ; ret | // load 2nd arg | value: "/bin/sh" | [arg for system]
findings.problem: Fig 3.4, in this same chapter, teaches that a function's first argument goes in RDI. Here system()'s argument is loaded into RSI, and RDI gets an unexplained 0x68. The stack slot also holds the string itself where a pointer to the string belongs. Traced as drawn, the chain calls system(0x68). This is already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md, and it is still in the figure.
findings.fix: Owner-authorised redraw of the chain: addr of G1 (`pop rdi ; ret`), then "address of \"/bin/sh\"" [arg for system, into rdi], then addr of system(). Drop the 0x68 slot and the G2 (pop rsi) and G3 (xor rdx) gadgets.

findings.quote: "Tiger\0" + 11 unused bytes
findings.problem: "Tiger\0" is 6 bytes, so a 16-byte buffer has 10 bytes left, not 11 (6 + 11 = 17). The error sits in a figure whose whole point is counting bytes. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md and still present.
findings.fix: Change the label to "\"Tiger\\0\" + 10 unused bytes". It is a one-character SVG text change with no layout change.

findings.quote: Each region's base is shifted by ~16 bits of randomness on every launch
findings.problem: The figure says about 16 bits, the 32-bit PaX figure, on a 64-bit layout. Its own caption, directly below, says 28–30 bits for libraries, 24–28 for the heap and 30–32 for the stack. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md and still present.
findings.fix: Change the strip line to "Each region's base is shifted by about 28 bits of randomness on every launch".

findings.quote: DEP / NX bit | 2003 · non-exec stack | ASLR | 2001+ · randomisation
findings.problem: The axis runs from 1988 to today, but ASLR (2001+) is drawn after DEP (2003). That makes ASLR the defence just before ROP, and the caption says each red dot "broke the previous defence". So the figure tells the reader that ROP broke ASLR. The prose (ch3-defenses-p9) and the §4g row it came from say the opposite: "The leaks above undid the canary and ASLR, and ROP undid DEP." The figure brings back a corrected error.
findings.fix: Swap the DEP/NX and ASLR groups (translate x 280 and 380) so the timeline reads 1998 canaries, 2001+ ASLR, 2003 DEP/NX, 2007 ROP. ROP's previous defence is then DEP, which matches p9 and the dates.

findings.quote: ROP turned an entire field of defence (mark code non-executable) into a starting point.
findings.problem: DEP marks data pages (stack and heap) non-executable, not code. Code has to stay executable. ch3-defenses-p5 says correctly that the defence marks stack pages non-executable, so the locked caption contradicts the prose above it. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md.
findings.fix: "(mark data non-executable)" in place of "(mark code non-executable)".

findings.quote: RUN 1 · 09:14:22 / RUN 3 · 09:18:11 / within seconds of each other
findings.problem: The caption says the three launches were "within seconds of each other". The run stamps drawn above are 86 s and 143 s apart, about four minutes from first to last.
findings.fix: Restamp the runs seconds apart (09:14:22, 09:14:25, 09:14:29), or change the caption to "within minutes of each other".

findings.problem: Every column draws the heap above .text, which matches Fig 3.5: on Linux the heap starts just past the program's data. In Runs 1 and 2, though, the heap address is lower than the .text address (0x55A8… < 0x562B…, and 0x55C4… < 0x55F1…). Only Run 3 matches its own drawing.
findings.fix: Give Runs 1 and 2 heap bases above their .text bases, for example Run 1 heap 0x562B 4E00 ____ and Run 2 heap 0x55F1 9200 ____.

findings.quote: prologue stored canary == stack canary?
findings.problem: The canary the prologue stores is the stack canary, so as written the check compares a value with itself. The real check, which the caption describes as "checks that it has not changed", compares the copy on the stack with a master copy the program keeps elsewhere.
findings.fix: "canary on stack == master copy?" in both check boxes.

findings.quote: add, called by main | a=5 · b=3
findings.problem: The hero puts add's arguments in its stack frame. The chapter then teaches the opposite: the Fig 3.4 strip says six arguments or fewer "never touches memory", and the chapter's own listing keeps a and b in EDI and ESI. The hero's register row already shows "inputs 5 and 3". This is separate from the open hero call in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md, which is about the high and low address key and the stack-top pointer.
findings.fix: Change add's subline from "a=5 · b=3" to "its own values". The registers row keeps "inputs 5 and 3".

findings.quote: rbp, x29: an address · w8, w0: registers
findings.problem: The key sets rbp and x29 against registers, so it reads as if they are not registers. The very next figure (Fig 3.3) lists RBP among the sixteen registers. eax, which appears in the x86 code, is never glossed.
findings.fix: Two key lines: "rbp, x29: registers holding an address" and "eax, w8, w0: registers holding a number". Keep "dword: 4 bytes · #: a number" and add 20 to the viewBox height.

findings.quote: ARM must load, change and store, so storing 5 takes two lines
findings.problem: The "so" puts both counts down to load, change and store. That explains adding 3 taking three lines, but storing 5 has no load and no change. The actual reason is that ARM writes memory only from a register. A cold reader stopped at exactly this point in Pass 29.
findings.fix: "Square brackets mean memory: x86 changes it in place, but ARM reaches memory only through a register, so storing 5 takes two lines (put 5 in a register, then `stur`) and adding 3 takes three (`ldur`, add, `stur`)."

findings.quote: return: main, next | main, next line | main, next
findings.problem: One return address carries three labels. The slot says "return: main, next", the value flying to RIP says "main, next", and when it lands RIP reads "main, next line". The text changes at the moment the reader is matching the popped value to RIP.
findings.fix: Make the RIP text "main, next", the same as the value that flies into it.

findings.quote: 64-bit prefix | opcode | rax | 5 | in hex: 48 83 C0 05
findings.problem: The whole C0 byte is coloured and labelled "rax". Three of its bits (000) are actually what picks add: 83 on its own names a family of arithmetic operations (83 /5 is sub). So the "opcode" box alone does not mean add. The caption's "an opcode, a register and the number 5" still holds loosely, so this is minor.
findings.fix: Keep the drawing. Change the strip's x86 line to: "Here a prefix (64-bit), the opcode, a byte naming rax (three of its bits also pick add from the opcode's family), and the 5 itself...". Or accept it as a schematic.

findings.quote: The objective of this paper is to show how to write buffer overflow exploits
findings.problem: The pull-quote is attributed to Aleph One, "Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit", Phrack 49 (1996), but neither of its sentences appears in that article. The article's real introduction reads: "This paper attempts to explain what buffer overflows are, and how their exploits work. Basic knowledge of assembly is required." An exact-phrase web search finds the quoted words nowhere else either. It is a misattributed or invented quotation inside verbatim quote marks. Checked against phrack.org/issues/49/smashing-the-stack-for-fun-and-profit.html, archives.phrack.org/issues/49/14.txt and insecure.org/stf/smashstack.txt. The wording has been there since the initial commit, and no ledger row covers it.
findings.fix: Owner call: this is owner text, so it is not rewritten here. The precedent is Ch6, where both unverifiable Stroustrup pull-quotes were replaced with documented ones (UNDER.md, Part II fact pass). Verbatim text the owner could use: "This paper attempts to explain what buffer overflows are, and how their exploits work. Basic knowledge of assembly is required." (Aleph One, "Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit," Phrack 49, 1996). The source's own spelling should be kept.

findings.quote: value: "/bin/sh"
findings.problem: The gadget chain passes the argument in the wrong register. G1 (pop rdi) loads 0x68, and G2 (pop rsi, marked "load 2nd arg") loads the item labelled "[arg for system]". system() takes its one argument in RDI, which Fig 3.4 has just taught. As drawn, system() would receive 0x68. The stack also holds the string itself where a pointer to the string belongs. G3's "xor rdx, rdx // zero env" belongs to an execve chain, not to system(). A reader who has just learned Fig 3.4 will notice the contradiction. This is already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md and is still unfixed.
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original). Smallest correct chain: the slot under "addr of G1" reads 'addr of "/bin/sh"' with tag [arg for system, into rdi], followed directly by "addr of system()". Drop G2 and G3, or keep one plain '; ret' gadget for stack alignment.

findings.quote: ROP turned an entire field of defence (mark code non-executable) into a starting point.
findings.problem: DEP/NX marks data pages (stack, heap) non-executable. Code must stay executable. ch3-defenses-p5 and the Fig 3.5 strip both say so. Marking code non-executable would stop every program from running. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md.
findings.fix: "ROP turned an entire field of defence (mark data non-executable) into a starting point."

findings.quote: Each region's base is shifted by ~16 bits of randomness on every launch
findings.problem: The strip says ~16 bits, but the figure's own caption gives 28 to 32 bits on 64-bit Linux. Marco-Gisbert and Ripoll (Black Hat Asia 2016, Fig. 3b, Linux 4.5 x86_64) measured 30 bits for the stack and 28 each for glibc, heap and executable. 16 bits is far below any of these, so the reader gets two contradicting numbers inside one figure. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md.
findings.fix: "Each region's base is shifted by about 28 to 30 random bits on every launch" (source: blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Marco-Gisbert-Exploiting-Linux-And-PaX-ASLRS-Weaknesses-On-32-And-64-Bit-Systems-wp.pdf, Fig. 3b).

findings.quote: "Tiger\0" + 11 unused bytes
findings.problem: "Tiger" plus its null byte is 6 bytes, so a 16-byte buffer leaves 10 bytes unused. The label adds up to 17 bytes in buffer[16], which makes the normal case look like an overflow by one. The whole figure is about counting bytes up to the 16-byte edge. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md.
findings.fix: "\"Tiger\\0\" + 10 unused bytes".

findings.quote: RISC machines could clock faster, and the reason is decoding.
findings.problem: In the 1980s debate this paragraph describes, early RISC chips did not clock faster than x86. The 80386 (1985) ran at 16 to 33 MHz and the MIPS R2000 (1986) at about 8 to 16.7 MHz. RISC won on instructions per clock: simple, uniform instructions pipeline cleanly, so a RISC chip finished about one per cycle, while a 386 took several. Higher clocks came later (Alpha, 1992). Presenting decoding as the single reason, together with parallel "run of them at once" decode (a 1990s superscalar technique), leaves the reader with a false history. The decode mechanism itself is correct.
findings.fix: "RISC machines got more done per tick of the clock, and decoding is a large part of the reason." The rest of the paragraph stays as it is. Sources: Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture, ch. on pipelining (CPI near 1 for early RISC); Patterson and Ditzel, "The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer" (1980).

findings.quote: Three launches of the same executable, on the same machine, within seconds of each other.
findings.problem: The figure stamps the runs 09:14:22, 09:15:48 and 09:18:11, about four minutes apart in total, not seconds. In Runs 1 and 2 the heap address (0x55A8…, 0x55C4…) is also lower than the .text address (0x562B…, 0x55F1…). The column draws the heap above .text, as Fig 3.5 does, and Linux places the brk heap just above the executable. Neither point is in the existing owner-calls list.
findings.fix: In the caption: "Three launches of the same executable, on the same machine, minutes apart." In the figure (owner call): give each run a heap address just above its .text, e.g. Run 1 heap 0x562B 5200 ____, Run 2 heap 0x55F1 9600 ____.

findings.quote: a 16-bit chip whose instruction set no descendant has ever removed
findings.problem: This is literally false twice over. The 8086's POP CS (opcode 0F) was dropped from the 80186/80286 onward, and its byte was reused as the two-byte opcode escape. x86-64's 64-bit mode makes AAA, DAA, PUSH/POP of segment registers and other 8086 instructions invalid. It also turns the 8086's one-byte INC/DEC opcodes 40 to 4F into REX prefixes: the 48 that opens Fig 3.1 was DEC AX on the 8086. What is true is that every x86-64 chip can still run 8086 code in its legacy modes. Sources: felixcloutier.com/x86/aaa ("Invalid" in 64-bit mode); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64 (decimal arithmetic and segment push/pop not supported in 64-bit mode).
findings.fix: "In 1978, Intel released the 8086, a 16-bit chip whose programs every descendant can still run." The next sentence stays.

findings.quote: runs essentially every PC and most servers
findings.problem: Arm-based machines are roughly 13 to 14% of PC shipments (Mercury Research, Q1 2025; ABI Research about 13% for 2025), led by the Apple Silicon Macs this same paragraph credits to ARM. "Essentially every PC" conflicts with the paragraph's own ARM sentence.
findings.fix: "runs most PCs and most servers".

findings.quote: The chapter uses six rows
findings.problem: The registers it names (RAX; RDI and RSI; RSP; RBP; RIP) come from five table rows, because RDI and RSI share the single argument row "RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9". A reader who counts against the table finds five.
findings.fix: "The chapter uses six of these registers:".

findings.quote: The "rep" loop instruction implicitly uses RCX
findings.problem: rep is a prefix that repeats a string instruction (movs, stos), with RCX as the count. It is not a loop instruction. The separate LOOP instruction also counts down RCX.
findings.fix: "The rep prefix and the loop instruction count down RCX".

findings.quote: The CPU has no way to verify it is the same number that was pushed there originally.
findings.problem: This is stated without qualification, but ch3-defenses-p9 later says that Intel CET shadow stacks and ARM Pointer Authentication do exactly this check in hardware. A reader who reaches p9 meets a contradiction.
findings.fix: "Unless it has the extra hardware of Section 06, the CPU has no way to verify it is the same number that was pushed there originally."

findings.quote: For decades, memory-corruption bugs accounted for the majority of critical CVEs
findings.problem: No source is given, and across all software the claim is doubtful: web-application bug classes make up a large share of critical CVEs. The data that does exist is the next sentence's: about 70% for Microsoft's CVEs (MSRC, 2019) and for Chromium's serious security bugs, both C/C++ codebases. The first sentence generalises that to every CVE.
findings.fix: Cut that sentence and move the gloss into the next one: "Microsoft, Google, and others have published data showing that around 70% of severe security bugs (CVEs, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in their large C/C++ codebases trace back to memory unsafety."

findings.quote: 2017+ · hardware-signed
findings.problem: Of the three defences under this label, only ARM PAC signs anything. CFI is a compiler check (Microsoft CFG and Clang CFI, 2014 to 2015), and CET's shadow stack compares two copies. "Hardware-signed" misdescribes two of the three, as ch3-defenses-p9 makes clear.
findings.fix: "2017+ · hardware-checked".

findings.quote: SYSCALL or int 0x80
findings.problem: The SOURCE column draws SYSCALL as one of the three sources the IDT dispatches. §4g (system-call row, Pass 27) corrected exactly this: SYSCALL jumps through MSR_LSTAR and never touches the IDT. The figure contradicts chBridge-trap-p4, printed directly above it ('A system call made with SYSCALL skips that table'). This is already logged in STATE.md as BLOCKED ON TIGER and is reported here again so it is not lost.
findings.fix: Redraw the SYSCALLS source cell as 'int 0x80 (legacy)' and drop 'SYSCALL'. If the owner keeps the figure as drawn, accept the contradiction knowingly. Sources: §4g row 528; felixcloutier.com/x86/syscall.

findings.quote: 32 | timer (LAPIC) | apic_timer_interrupt | 33 | keyboard (IRQ 1) | do_IRQ
findings.problem: The rows mix Linux handler names with vector numbers from teaching kernels. On Linux the local APIC timer is vector 0xEC (236), not 32. §4g's Fig BR.6 row already corrected 'the timer raises IRQ at vector 32'. ISA IRQ 1 (keyboard) is vector 0x31 (49), not 33. The handler names (do_divide_error, do_page_fault, do_IRQ, apic_timer_interrupt) are also pre-5.8 names, now exc_* and sysvec_apic_timer_interrupt.
findings.fix: Either drop the Linux handler names and label the table 'a classic teaching layout (PIC remapped to 32)', or keep Linux and change the rows to '236 · timer (LAPIC)' and '49 · keyboard (IRQ 1)'. Source: linux arch/x86/include/asm/irq_vectors.h (LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR 0xec; ISA_IRQ_VECTOR(irq) = 0x30 + irq); §4g row 614.

findings.quote: When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register
findings.problem: The section calls system calls traps ('System calls are not the only traps'), and p4 says SYSCALL skips the IDT. 'Any trap' therefore repeats the §4g-corrected claim that system calls go through the IDT, in the caption right beside p4. docs/pass-29-part1-open.md lists this caption under the BR.3 kept-original items. If the owner treats captions as editable, it is a one-word fix.
findings.fix: 'When an exception or interrupt fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register, ...' (rest unchanged). Source: §4g system-call row.

findings.quote: drops back to Ring 3. No scheduling is involved.
findings.problem: Readers take this as a statement about system calls, and as that it is false. A call that must wait gives the CPU to another program before SYSRET: Fig BR.8 in this same chapter shows process A's read putting A to sleep while process B runs. Linux also checks need_resched on every syscall exit and calls schedule() if it is set. A reader would believe a system call never involves the scheduler.
findings.fix: Delete 'No scheduling is involved.' Or replace it with 'A call that has to wait, like process A's read in Fig BR.8, lets the kernel run another program first.' Source: Fig BR.8; Linux kernel/entry/common.c, exit_to_user_mode_loop (calls schedule() on _TIF_NEED_RESCHED).

findings.quote: Five small pieces of hardware are what separate a computer from a calculator.
findings.problem: Overclaim against the book's own Chapter 1. A computer is a universal machine whether or not it has these five features. An 8086 PC running MS-DOS had no privilege bit, no MMU and no protected device access, and it was a computer, not a calculator. The next sentence states the real claim (conditions under which one program can own the machine). If the chapter opener belongs to the owner's thesis set, this is an owner call.
findings.fix: 'Five small pieces of hardware separate a computer that runs one program at a time from one that can safely run many.' Or keep the sentence and treat it as owner text.

findings.quote: Then one instruction (SYSRET on x86-64, ERET on ARM) switches the CPU to Ring 3
findings.problem: Linux does not enter the first user program with SYSRET. ret_from_fork_asm jumps to swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode, which ends in IRETQ (ERETU on FRED machines). SYSRET is the fast return from a SYSCALL. The mechanism is right (one privileged return instruction drops to Ring 3); only the named instruction is wrong for x86-64 Linux. p8's 'SYSRET ... faults outside Ring 0' stays true.
findings.fix: 'Then one instruction (IRET or SYSRET on x86-64, ERET on ARM) switches the CPU to Ring 3 ...'. Source: linux arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S (ret_from_fork_asm → swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode → iretq).

findings.quote: Then a store to the next page up, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010
findings.problem: Arithmetic. With 4 KiB pages the page number is everything above the last three hex digits, so 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 is 0x10000 bytes above 0x7fff_a3c4_0010: 16 pages up, not the next page (that would be 0x7fff_a3c4_1010). The §4g row's point stands (the store goes to a different page, so it misses the TLB); only 'next' is wrong. The same shorthand puts Fig BR.5's 'page a3c?' labels one hex digit off the real page numbers (0x7fffa3c40, ...).
findings.fix: Smallest fix, in the desc: 'Then a store to another page, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010: ...'. Fuller fix that makes 'next page' and BR.5's labels exact: use 0x7fff_fa3c_4010 and 0x7fff_fa3c_5010 (page numbers ending a3c4, a3c5) with physical 0xa20_0010 (frame a200, offset 0x010 unchanged).

findings.quote: only the kernel maps device ranges into an address space, so a user program cannot reach a device's registers directly
findings.problem: The premise is true but the conclusion overclaims. The kernel can map a device's registers into a user process: VFIO and UIO for DPDK/SPDK user-space drivers, GPU doorbells for user-mode work submission, RDMA NICs, and historically X servers through /dev/mem. chBridge-io-p1's 'only the kernel gets to use it' has the same scope problem. A reader would believe user code can never touch device registers.
findings.fix: '... so a user program can reach a device's registers only if the kernel maps them into its address space.' Source: docs.kernel.org/driver-api/vfio.html (user-space device access with IOMMU protection).

findings.quote: network card | from 0xC010_0000 | GPU frame buffer | from 0xC000_0000
findings.problem: A map billed as 'typical' leaves the GPU frame buffer only 0xC000_0000 to 0xC00F_FFFF, which is 1 MiB. One 1920×1080 screen at 4 bytes a pixel needs about 7.9 MiB, and GPU frame-buffer apertures are typically 256 MiB or more. 'Not to scale' covers the drawn heights, not the printed addresses, which fix the sizes.
findings.fix: Move the network card to 'from 0xD000_0000' and its store to 'store x at 0xD000_0018', which leaves the frame buffer a 256 MiB window. Keep the frame buffer store at 0xC000_0400.

findings.quote: Operating systems use only two of those four levels
findings.problem: Too absolute. OS/2 used ring 2 for privileged I/O code, and pre-VT-x hypervisors (Xen PV on 32-bit x86, VMware binary translation) ran guest kernels in ring 1. Mainstream systems use only rings 0 and 3.
findings.fix: 'Almost every operating system uses only two of those four levels: ...'. Source: Wikipedia, Protection ring ('Even on x86, most operating systems only use ring 0 and 3'; 'OS/2 does, to some extent, use three rings').

findings.quote: (Linux's NO_HZ_IDLE and NO_HZ_FULL), saving power.
findings.problem: The strip gives both options the purpose of saving power. NO_HZ_IDLE saves power; NO_HZ_FULL exists for real-time latency and HPC throughput, and kernel docs list extra costs for it (dearer user/kernel transitions), not energy savings. chBridge-timer-p4 already states this correctly, so the strip contradicts the prose beside it.
findings.fix: 'Tickless. An idle core can skip ticks entirely to save power (Linux's NO_HZ_IDLE), and for real-time and HPC work a core running one task can almost stop them (NO_HZ_FULL).' Source: docs.kernel.org/timers/no_hz.html.

findings.quote: The instruction does not run and no error code comes back
findings.problem: #GP is one of the x86 exceptions that does push an error code (0 for a privileged-instruction violation) onto the kernel handler's stack. The intended meaning is that nothing returns to the program, but the literal reading is wrong, and a reader who knows x86 will stop on it.
findings.fix: 'The instruction does not run and nothing returns to the program; the CPU jumps to the handler ...'. Source: Intel SDM vol. 3A, 'Interrupt 13, General Protection Exception (#GP)': error code yes, 0 here.

findings.quote: under every forced switch from one process to another, a timer tick that took the CPU back
findings.problem: 'Every' overclaims. A forced switch also happens when a device interrupt wakes a task the scheduler prefers: a keyboard or disk interrupt wakes an interactive process and the kernel preempts the running one on the way out of that interrupt, with no tick involved. §4g settled who takes the CPU back (the tick, not a timer calling schedule()). The universal 'every' is a separate issue.
findings.fix: 'under every forced switch from one process to another, an interrupt, most often a timer tick, that took the CPU back; ...'. Source: Linux kernel/sched/fair.c wakeup preemption (resched_curr on wakeup).

findings.quote: between the CPU and the RAM sits a small piece of silicon called the memory management unit
findings.problem: Since the 386 the MMU has been part of the CPU, and today each core has its own, before the caches. The prose and Fig BR.4's title ('silicon between the CPU and the RAM') present it as a separate chip outside the CPU. That conflicts with ch3's 'the CPU's MMU' and leaves no place in the picture for the cache Chapter 1 taught.
findings.fix: 'It does, because inside the CPU, between each core and the memory, sits a small circuit called the memory management unit, and every memory access the core makes flows through it.' Fig BR.4 title: 'The MMU · silicon between the core and the RAM'.

findings.quote: pulls electrons up under the oxide until they form a thin channel between source and drain
findings.problem: In the off state the picture puts nine free electrons in the p-type body and none in the n-type source and drain. With voltage on, it raises those body electrons into the channel. ch1-transistor-p7 has just taught the opposite: p-type silicon has holes and almost no free electrons, the n-type regions are rich in free electrons (the figure's own How it works says so too), and the gate draws electrons out of the source and drain. The figure undoes the doping lesson the prose just gave. The caption ('pulls electrons up') and the desc ('pulls electrons ... up into a thin channel') follow the wrong drawing.
findings.fix: Redraw the states. Off: a few blue electrons sit inside each n-type region and the p-type body has no electrons (optionally a few hollow circles labelled 'hole'). On: electrons slide sideways out of the source and drain into the strip under the oxide, then flow source to drain. Caption: 'A positive voltage on the gate draws electrons in from the source and drain until they form a thin channel under the oxide, and current flows. The gate never touches them: its charge pulls through the insulator, as a rubbed balloon lifts hair, and that influence across a gap, an electric field, names the transistor.' In the desc, change 'pulls electrons (blue dots) up into a thin channel under it' to 'draws electrons (blue dots) from the source and drain into a thin channel under it'.

findings.quote: TRANSISTOR 1947 ... silicon
findings.problem: The picture dates the transistor 1947 and labels its body 'silicon'. The 1947 Bell Labs point-contact transistor was germanium. The first silicon transistor came in 1954 (Teal, Texas Instruments). The chapter itself says the first IC was germanium and that silicon later won over germanium (ch1-transistor-p9, p13), so the figure contradicts the timeline beside it.
findings.fix: Change the drawn label 'silicon' to 'semiconductor' and the desc's 'a small piece of silicon' to 'a small piece of semiconductor'. The caption's 'in a sliver of silicon' can stay, since it describes transistors today. Alternative: keep 'silicon' and drop '1947' from the TRANSISTOR header.

findings.quote: ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall with 17,468 vacuum tubes
findings.problem: On the drawing's own 10 m bar, the base of the U alone is 30 m and each arm adds about 7.5 m, so the cabinets total about 45 m in a hall 30 m wide. In life ENIAC's 40 panels stood in a U along three walls of a room about 30 × 50 ft (9 × 15 m). The figure of about 30 m (100 ft) is the total length of the cabinets laid end to end, not the length of the room (Smithsonian NMAH object record; ETHW ENIAC milestone: U-shape, about 80 ft across the front). The desc ('around a thirty-metre hall') and ch1-transistor-p1 ('filled a room thirty metres long') repeat the slip.
findings.fix: Redraw the U so its three sides together measure about 30 m on the 10 m bar, for example a base of about 15 m and two arms of about 7.5 m. Caption: 'ENIAC's cabinets ran thirty metres around three walls of a room and held 17,468 vacuum tubes; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip.' Desc: 'a U of cabinets thirty metres long in all'. In p1, 'It filled a room thirty metres long' becomes 'Its cabinets, thirty metres of them, lined the walls of a large room'.

findings.problem: The label 'M4 · 28 B' (text-anchor end at x=368) is centred under the 2017 Epyc dot (x=331, on the dashed line). The real M4 dot (x=372) is unlabelled at the right edge. A reader takes the on-line dot for the M4, which hides the point the caption makes: the M4 falls below the line. The label also shows for most of the loop while every dot after the 4004 is hidden, so it floats over empty space.
findings.fix: Anchor the label to the M4 dot: put it left of the dot and level with it (for example text-anchor end at x=362, y=34), or add a short leader line from the label to the 2024 dot. Fade the label in together with the M4 dot (keyTimes 0.6437 to 0.6625).

findings.quote: so in any column every stage is busy with a different instruction
findings.problem: The How it works strip says every stage is busy in any column. The grid shows that only cycle 5 has all five stages busy. Cycles 1 to 4 and 6 to 9 have empty rows, and the animation's own highlight on cycle 3 shows two of them. The caption says it correctly ('once the pipeline is full').
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Each instruction starts one cycle after the one before, so the instructions in a column are always in different stages; in cycle 5 all five stages are busy at once.'

findings.quote: bus: shared wires; data moves both ways
findings.problem: The hero draws three separate point-to-point links, each labelled 'bus' (CPU to RAM, CPU to I/O, CPU to disk). Fig 1.8 and its caption teach the opposite: one bus, shared wires that memory and the I/O devices all use, one transfer at a time, which is the bottleneck of ch1-vonneumann. A reader who comes back to the hero after section 03 finds three buses where the chapter says there is one. The disk is also drawn apart from 'I/O Devices', although the chapter treats it as an I/O device the kernel drives (Fig 1.14).
findings.fix: Draw one shared bus line, horizontal or vertical, that RAM, the CPU core and the I/O devices (disk among them) each tap into, with the single label 'bus' and the footer 'bus: one set of shared wires; data moves both ways'. Or put DISK inside the I/O group on one branch of that same bus.

findings.quote: KERNEL OS Core
findings.problem: The kernel is drawn as a box wired to the CPU core, in the same form as RAM, I/O and Disk, so it reads as a fourth piece of hardware. ch1-kernel-p4 defines it as 'the one program that stays loaded', which lives in RAM and runs on the CPU in Ring 0 (Fig 1.14). The dashed line is not explained anywhere in the picture.
findings.fix: Draw the kernel as software: a band inside the RAM box labelled 'KERNEL · the program that stays loaded', with a second band 'your programs' beside it, and drop the dashed line. If the box stays where it is, label the dashed line 'runs on' and subtitle the box 'software, kept in RAM' in place of 'OS Core'.

findings.quote: off
findings.problem: When the control signal is 'off', the tube's half of the control wire dims, but the segment into the transistor's base (path M 299 200 H 236 V 326, stroke #e8d0a2) stays bright cream. The off frame therefore shows the signal still reaching the base, which contradicts 'off' and the dark lamp.
findings.fix: Draw that segment in the same dim stroke as the rest of the control loop (rgba(212,168,83,0.35)), so that only the animated gold overlay lights the full wire when the signal is on.

findings.quote: filament, always hot
findings.problem: In the off state the tube contains no electrons at all, although the label says the filament is always hot and the How it works says the grid 'lets them through or holds them back'. The holding back is the switch's job, and it is never shown.
findings.fix: In the off state, keep two or three electrons hovering between the filament and the grid, below the dashed grid line, so the grid visibly holds them back. When the signal turns on, they cross to the plate.

findings.quote: In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the base is called the gate.
findings.problem: A field-effect transistor has no base. Its gate is a different structure that does the same job, so 'the base is called the gate' suggests the same part under a new name. It also leaves the reader to map collector and emitter onto the source and drain that p7 introduces without warning.
findings.fix: 'In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is the gate, and the current runs between the source and the drain (Fig 1.5).'

findings.quote: Every core runs this loop: fetch the instruction the program counter names, decode it, execute it
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch1-cpu-p1 and p2 almost word for word and says nothing about what only the picture shows: the counter stepping 0x00, 0x05, 0x08 by each instruction's length, and the jump setting it back to 0x00.
findings.fix: 'The counter steps from 0x00 to 0x05 to 0x08, moved on by each instruction's length. At 0x08 the jump sets it back to 0x00, so the three instructions run round forever.'

findings.quote: yours
findings.problem: As the time cursor sweeps the hour, jobs that have not run yet are dimmed, but 'yours' stays fully lit from the start (frame t2.667, cursor at about 9:14). It reads as if your job had already run before 9:30.
findings.fix: Dim 'yours' like the other future jobs until the cursor reaches 9:30, then light it in its brighter gold. The word 'yours' keeps it identifiable while it is dim.

findings.quote: right · ~95%
findings.problem: While the branch is still '?', the 'right' outcome box has a grey outline and the 'wrong' box has none. Cache slot 3 also carries a permanent cream outline before any load has run. Both make the outcome look decided before the check.
findings.fix: Give both outcome boxes the same neutral outline (stroke rgba(255,255,255,0.35)) until the check resolves. Give slot 3 the same grey outline as the other slots, and light it only when 'load from memory' runs.

findings.quote: KEY
findings.problem: The left column is headed 'KEY', but it also serves as the lampboard: lamps F, E and C light in that column. The title and caption speak of lamps, and nothing in the picture says the circles are lamps as well as keys.
findings.fix: Change the header to 'KEY · LAMP', or label the blue-filled circle 'lamp' on first lighting.

findings.quote: Fig 1.3 · Vacuum tube and transistor · the same switch
findings.problem: The SVG <title> (the accessible name, shown as a tooltip on hover) does not match the visible label 'Fig 1.3 · The replacement · the same switch, without the fire'. Every other ch1 figure's title matches its label.
findings.fix: Set the <title> text to 'Fig 1.3 · The replacement · the same switch, without the fire'.

findings.quote: the output leaves on the right under its formula (· is AND, + is OR, ¬ is NOT)
findings.problem: The How it works strip says each output sits under its formula and explains the symbols. The picture has no formulas: the outputs are labelled in words ("A and B", "A or B", "not A"), as the figure's own description says. A reader who opens the strip looks for ·, + and ¬ and finds none.
findings.fix: Reword item 1: "*Reading a gate.* Inputs A and B enter on the left, the output leaves on the right, named in words; the table beside it lists every case." Alternative: change the three drawn labels to "A · B", "A + B", "¬A" so they match the truth tables just above the figure and the strip as written.

findings.problem: The centre readout shows "+0" over 00000000 (keyTimes 0.339 to 0.438). Two's complement has exactly one zero. "+0" brings back the "positive zero" of signed magnitude, which ch2-twos-p3 names as that scheme's flaw. It also disagrees with the ring label "0" and the drawn "−1 + 1 = 0". The other readouts ("-128", "-127", "-2", "-1") use an ASCII hyphen, while the ring labels and equations use the true minus.
findings.fix: Change the readout text "+0" to "0" (neutral fill, like the ring's "0"). Replace the hyphens in the readouts "-128", "-127", "-2", "-1" with U+2212 so they match "−128" and "−1" on the ring.

findings.quote: A · B + ¬A · B
findings.problem: The hero circuit computes A·B + ¬A·B, which simplifies to (A + ¬A)·B = B: the A input cancels out and the circuit just passes B through. It looks like the XOR recipe from ch2-boole-p10, (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B), with one NOT missing. A reader who has just learned the algebra will spot that the chapter's emblem circuit does nothing.
findings.fix: Make it XOR, matching ch2-boole-p10. Formula: "A · ¬B + ¬A · B". Add a NOT on B before the top AND and label the top AND's output "A · ¬B". With A = 1 and B = 0 the top AND gives 1, so change the output from "0" to "1".

findings.quote: He died before electricity was understood, never imagining a circuit.
findings.problem: This contradicts the chapter's own careful version (ch2-boole-p5: he died thirty-three years before the electron was discovered). By 1864, Ohm's and Kirchhoff's circuit laws and the electric telegraph were decades old, so "before electricity was understood" and "never imagining a circuit" are both overstatements. "A century later" also clashes with Fig 2.2's "Ninety years apart" (1847 to 1937).
findings.fix: "In 1847, a self-taught English schoolteacher published a book reducing logic to algebra. He died thirty-three years before the electron was discovered, never imagining his algebra wired into a circuit. Ninety years later, it became the mathematics every machine computes with."

findings.quote: threshold
findings.problem: In the binary panel, the blue trace's rising edge (about x 123 to 131 in the viewBox) runs through the gold "threshold" label at x=70, cutting the "l" of "threshold". This is the chapter's first figure, and the overlap breaks law 3 (nothing overlapping).
findings.fix: Move the label to x="140" (y stays 84). It then sits above the threshold line over the flat top of the second bit (trace at y 43 to 61), clear of the rising edge near x≈128 and the falling edge near x≈252.

findings.quote: Both wires carry the same span and the same noise.
findings.problem: The drawn drifts are not the same. The binary fourth digit drifts at most 24 units from its 0 level (y 128 to 104). The ternary fourth digit drifts up to 33 units (y 258 to 225), almost onto the +1 level at 222, and it does so in a slightly smaller span (70 against 78). The drifted 0 therefore looks like a clean +1 rather than a near miss, and a careful reader may think the comparison is rigged.
findings.fix: Give the ternary fourth digit exactly the binary's offsets, so y = 257, 247, 246, 234, 234, 234, 242, 247, 254 at x 257.0 to 312.0. The read point (x 284.5, y 234) is still above the 240 threshold, so it still reads +1, and "same noise" becomes literally true.

findings.quote: sent 0, read +1
findings.problem: Unread digits dim to different levels: 0.2 for the first digit, 0.47 for the binary digits, and 0.74 for the ternary "+1" digits. Mid-scan (t≈2.3 s) the ternary +1s therefore look already read while the binary digits under the same scan line look unread. The "sent 0, read +1" note is never hidden, so it gives the verdict before the scan reaches the fourth digit.
findings.fix: Use one dim value (e.g. 0.35) for every unread digit in both rows. Give the "sent 0, read +1" text the same opacity animation as its red box (values 1;1;0;0;0;1;1, keyTimes as on the box) so it appears when digit 4 is read.

findings.quote: side by side they would be OR (Fig 2.3)
findings.problem: The reference sends the reader to Fig 2.3 for switches side by side, but Fig 2.3 draws the OR gate symbol and has no switches. A reader who follows the pointer finds a different picture.
findings.fix: "*Series and parallel.* Switches in series are AND; side by side they would be OR, the gate drawn in Fig 2.3."

findings.quote: Inside a full adder · two half adders and an OR
findings.problem: The title and caption build the explanation on "two half adders", but the picture never marks which gates form each one. The first half adder's XOR is at the top and its AND at the very bottom, with the second half adder's AND between them, so a newcomer has to reconstruct the pairing by tracing wires.
findings.fix: Draw a faint dashed outline around XOR1 + its AND (left column, roughly x 100 to 170, y 45 to 295 in the viewBox) labelled "half adder 1", and one around XOR2 + AND2 labelled "half adder 2", at 13 px and 0.5 opacity.

findings.quote: A full adder is two half adders and an OR. A and B meet in the first
findings.problem: The caption restates ch2-arithmetic-p5 almost clause for clause (the first adds A and B, the second adds that sum to the carry-in, the OR merges the carries), and the How it works strip says it a third time. It tells the reader nothing about how to read the picture.
findings.fix: "All eight cases in turn: follow the gold 1s from A, B and the carry-in to the sum and the carry-out, read below as carry-out, then sum."

findings.quote: tie its inputs together and it is NOT, follow it with that NOT and it is AND
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch2-gates-p4's three constructions and the picture's own row labels ("one NAND, inputs tied", "NAND, then NOT", "NOT both, then NAND"). The same content then appears a third time in How it works.
findings.fix: "Every gate drawn is a NAND; as the inputs step through each case, all three outputs match the plain NOT, AND and OR."

findings.quote: an 11-bit exponent stored 1023 too high so it can be negative
findings.problem: The caption and the How it works strip already give the 1023 bias (with 1025 meaning 2² and 1022 meaning 2⁻¹) and the never-stored leading 1. ch2-float-p6, directly after the figure, repeats both a third time.
findings.fix: Cut the first two sentences of ch2-float-p6 and open it at "A double rounds an endless expansion to the nearest binary fraction it can hold: 0.1 and 0.2 round up, 0.3 rounds down."

findings.quote: true sum: a tie, rounds up
findings.problem: The red sum dot slides in from cx=20, about one grid step below the stored 0.3, and passes through the blue dot to reach the tie. At t≈2.7 s it sits to the left of "0.3 as stored" with no labels, which suggests the sum is smaller than the stored 0.3.
findings.fix: Fade the red dot in at the tie (cx 154, keyTimes 0.30 to 0.36) instead of sliding from cx 20, hold it there, then slide it to 200 as it does now.

findings.quote: a double keeps only the first 52 bits and rounds
findings.problem: The description says "the first 52 bits" of 0.000110011…, and the drawn line says "a double keeps 52 bits". A double actually keeps 53 significant bits, starting at the first 1 (the hidden 1 that Fig 2.10 explains, plus 52 stored), not the first 52 bits after the point.
findings.fix: Drawn line: "repeats forever; a double must cut it off and round". Description: "so a double keeps its leading 1 and the next 52 bits and rounds the rest".

findings.quote: the only language electricity speaks
findings.problem: The tagline contradicts the chapter's own argument. ch2-binary-p3 says a transistor can hold a middle voltage and ternary machines were built, and Fig 2.1's strip ends "Engineering, not mathematics, decided it."
findings.fix: "two states: the easiest for electricity to tell apart"

findings.quote: Fig 2.1 · Why binary survives noise · one threshold against two
findings.problem: Fig 2.1's <title> has id svgt-part1-17, the same id as the Chapter 02 hero's <title>, which comes earlier in the page. aria-labelledby resolves to the first match, so screen readers announce Fig 2.1 as "Chapter 02 hero · The Algebra of Switches". The same id clash exists for svgt-part1-30 (ch3 hero / Fig 3.2), -39 (Fig 3.9 / Fig BR.1) and -40 (Fig 3.10 / Fig BR.2).
findings.fix: Give each hero's <title> its own id (e.g. svgt-part1-ch2-hero) and update its aria-labelledby. Renumber the duplicated BR.1/BR.2 ids. This is an id-only change: no visible text or kept-original content moves.

findings.quote: He died before electricity was understood, never imagining a circuit. A century later
findings.problem: Contradicts the chapter's own numbers and care. 1847 to 1937 is ninety years, and Fig 2.2's caption says "Ninety years apart". Circuits (telegraphs, and relays from 1835) existed in Boole's lifetime; ch2-boole-p5 is careful to say only that he "never saw electricity used in computing". "The only mathematics that machines can do" overclaims. The lead is three clipped dramatic sentences.
findings.fix: "In 1847 a self-taught English schoolteacher published a book that reduced logic to algebra. Ninety years later a student saw that switch circuits obey it, and it became the logic every chip is built from."

findings.quote: is the rounding error from cutting off
findings.problem: The code comments contradict the prose. ch2-float-p6 says 0.1 rounds UP, and the printed value 0.10000000000000000555 is above 0.1, which cutting off (truncation) cannot produce. The Patriot paragraph then uses "chopped" for exactly that truncation. "In binary, 0.1 is actually approximately:" introduces a decimal printout.
findings.fix: Comments: "# The double stored for 0.1, printed to 20 decimal places:" and "# The extra 555... is the rounding error: the endless binary fraction was rounded up to the nearest double."

findings.quote: the output leaves on the right under its formula (· is AND, + is OR, ¬ is NOT)
findings.problem: The How-it-works strip describes formula symbols that are not drawn. In the picture each output is labelled in words ("A and B", "A or B", "not A"). A reader looking for ·, + or ¬ finds none.
findings.fix: "Reading a gate. Inputs enter on the left; the output leaves on the right, named in words (A and B, A or B, not A); the table beside it lists every case."

findings.quote: A switch circuit computing one of the three operations is now called a gate
findings.problem: Gate is defined twice: here, and again as the key term in ch2-gates-p1 ("A logic gate is a small circuit of a few transistors..."). This first definition is also too narrow: section 03 calls NAND, NOR and XOR gates, and none of them is "one of the three operations".
findings.fix: boole-p7: "A switch circuit that computes a Boolean rule is now called a gate (not the transistor's gate terminal)." gates-p1: "In a chip, each **logic gate** is a few transistors: one or two input bits in, one output bit out. Only a handful of gate types are fundamental."

findings.quote: In 1996, an Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch because a velocity value was converted
findings.problem: Ariane comes straight after the silent wrap (two positives giving a negative, the bottom of Fig 2.8), so it reads as an example of that wrap. It was not one. Ariane 501's conversion of a 64-bit float to a 16-bit signed integer raised an unhandled Operand Error, which shut down both inertial reference computers. Nothing wrapped silently.
findings.fix: "In 1996 an Ariane 5 rocket broke up 37 seconds after launch when its guidance software converted a velocity too large for a 16-bit signed integer: the conversion failed, and the guidance computers shut down." (Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report, J. L. Lions, July 1996)

findings.quote: Binary's one threshold leaves each level a wide margin; ternary's two squeeze the bands until a drift
findings.problem: The caption repeats the last sentences of ch2-binary-p3 almost word for word (one threshold, wide margin, narrower bands, a drift binary shrugs off). The How-it-works strip then says it a third time.
findings.fix: Caption: "Two wires, the same span and the same noise: binary reads all five bits right, ternary misreads its fourth digit."

findings.quote: an 11-bit exponent stored 1023 too high so it can be negative
findings.problem: The exponent bias and the implicit leading 1 are explained three times in a row: this caption, the strip ("1025 means 2², 1022 means 2⁻¹") and ch2-float-p6 straight after ("stored 1023 too high... 1025 means 2^2, 1022 means 2^−1... never stored").
findings.fix: Caption: "6.5 and −0.75 as doubles, each read straight off its sign, exponent and mantissa bits." ch2-float-p6 keeps the explanation.

findings.quote: A and B meet in the first; its sum meets the carry-in in the second, which gives the sum bit
findings.problem: Repeats ch2-arithmetic-p5 ("the first adds A and B, the second adds that sum to the carry-in, and the OR merges their carry-outs"). The strip also repeats p5's point that the two half adders can never both carry.
findings.fix: Caption: "Inside one full adder of Fig 2.5: two half adders, each an XOR and an AND, and an OR, stepping through all eight inputs."

findings.quote: tie its inputs together and it is NOT, follow it with that NOT and it is AND
findings.problem: ch2-gates-p4 has just built all three (NOT, AND, OR from NAND) step by step. The caption restates them, and the strip does so a third time.
findings.fix: Caption: "NOT, AND and OR, each wired from NAND gates alone; the inputs step through every case."

findings.quote: The three gates every circuit is built from: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1
findings.problem: This is the third statement of the AND/OR/NOT rules in a few screens: ch2-boole-p3, the truth-table headings just above, and this caption. "Every circuit is built from" also clashes with p4 and p5, which say NAND alone suffices and that CPUs use NOR and XOR.
findings.fix: "AND, OR and NOT in their standard symbols, unchanged since the 1960s, each beside its truth table as the inputs step through every case."

findings.quote: The sum has a ninth bit the register cannot hold; it falls off
findings.problem: Repeats ch2-twos-p6 directly above ("Writing 256 takes a ninth place; the register has eight, so that 1 falls off the end and leaves exactly 2"). The strip also repeats p5 and p6.
findings.fix: Caption: "7 − 5 on the ordinary adder: 7 plus 11111011, with the ninth bit dropped."

findings.quote: Called with −1, the check passes, since −1 is not over 256
findings.problem: Retells the bug that ch2-twos-p10 has just told (the check passes, the length is read as unsigned, the copy runs past the buffer). The strip tells it a third time.
findings.fix: "The bug in three steps: the check, memcpy (the standard copy function) reading n as unsigned, and the copy running past the 256-byte buffer."

findings.quote: Shannon saw that two switches in series pass current only when both are closed
findings.problem: Repeats ch2-boole-p6 ("Wire two relays in series... current can reach the far end only if both are closed: that is AND").
findings.fix: "The same AND ninety years apart: Boole's overlap of two circles and Shannon's two switches in series light together only for A = 1 and B = 1."

findings.quote: In formulas, NOT is written ¬: ¬A means NOT A.
findings.problem: The NOT truth table above already heads its column "¬A" before this sentence defines ¬. The definition is also tacked onto the end of a paragraph about transistors.
findings.fix: Title the NOT table "NOT: flips the input (written ¬A)" and cut the sentence from p2.

findings.quote: DeMorgan's Laws
findings.problem: The callout label spells the name "DeMorgan". The next line, the Fig 2.4 strip and its desc all spell it "De Morgan".
findings.fix: "De Morgan's laws"

findings.problem: The wheel's centre readout uses ASCII hyphens ("-128", "-127", "-2", "-1"), while the rim labels in the same figure use the true minus (−128, −1). At zero it shows "+0". The section has just called "positive zero" a flaw of signed magnitude, so "+0" suggests two's complement has one too.
findings.fix: Use U+2212 in the four readouts, and show "0" (no sign) at zero.

findings.quote: Each gate is a few transistors (Fig 1.4), switching in well under a nanosecond.
findings.problem: Fig 1.4's own caption says it shows the older kind of transistor and that modern chips use the field-effect kind (Fig 1.5).

findings.quote: Switches in series are AND; side by side they would be OR (Fig 2.3).
findings.problem: Fig 2.3 draws no switches side by side, only the OR gate symbol, so a reader who looks there for parallel switches finds none.
findings.fix: "Switches in series are AND; side by side they are OR, whose gate symbol Fig 2.3 draws."

findings.quote: In 1985 the IEEE published standard 754
findings.problem: "IEEE" heads the section and is never expanded in Part I. The glossary cards send the reader forward: IEEE to Chapter 10 §02, and IEEE 754 to Chapter 12 §02, though this section is where IEEE 754 is taught.
findings.fix: "In 1985 the IEEE (the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) published standard 754...". Set the glossary home of "IEEE" and "IEEE 754" to ch2-float.

findings.quote: Boolean algebra works on statements that are either true or false
findings.problem: Boolean algebra is taught here, but its glossary entry's home is Chapter 18 §01, so tapping the term in Ch2 points the reader 16 chapters ahead.
findings.fix: Set the glossary first-use section of "Boolean algebra" to ch2-boole.

findings.quote: A program copying data into a buffer, a fixed block of memory, checks that a length it was handed
findings.problem: Three stacked appositives make the sentence hard to parse on a first read. It also re-defines "buffer", which ch1-memory-p11 already taught.
findings.fix: "A program that copies data into a buffer first checks that the length it was handed, perhaps by an attacker, is not more than the buffer holds; −1 passes."

findings.quote: came from the same endless 0.1, held in fixed point instead, a set number of binary places with no exponent
findings.problem: The definition of fixed point dangles as a second appositive, then a colon clause follows. Readers have to reread it. "The... failure, which killed 28" also makes the failure the killer.
findings.fix: "The 1991 Patriot missile failure, in which a Scud killed 28 American soldiers, came from the same endless 0.1. The system counted time in tenths of a second and held 0.1 in fixed point (a set number of binary places, no exponent), so it chopped off the digits that did not fit."

findings.quote: so that a calculation gone wrong keeps flowing instead of halting the machine
findings.problem: The paragraph's last sentence makes the same point ("instead of crashing the program where it arose"), so the paragraph says it twice.
findings.fix: Open with "IEEE 754 reserves some bit patterns for special values." and let the closing sentence carry the purpose.

findings.quote: Engineering, not mathematics, decided it.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer in the "X, not Y" reveal shape. It adds nothing to the margin argument just made.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence; the strip ends at "so the wider margin won."

findings.quote: even through electrical noise, voltage fluctuations and manufacturing variation
findings.problem: A reflexive triplet whose first two items overlap (noise is a voltage fluctuation). p3 then names the real drifts (ageing parts, temperature).
findings.fix: "even when noise and manufacturing variation nudge the voltage."

findings.quote: A computer is a machine for arithmetic, yet at the level of voltages and gates it has no idea
findings.problem: Sameness of shape: sections 04 and 05 both open on "A computer" lacking a notion ("no idea of 'five'", "no transistor that means 'minus'"). Section 01 already said that bits are all it has.
findings.fix: "Gates know only ones and zeros, yet a computer adds 5 + 3 the way you add on paper: one column at a time, carrying as it goes."

findings.quote: how the CPU actually executes a program, how function calls work at the metal, what a "stack" really is
findings.problem: The coda's handoff stacks intensifiers: "actually", "really", and then "actually" again at the end of the same sentence.
findings.fix: "We will look at how the CPU executes a program, how function calls work at the metal, what a "stack" is, and how attackers exploit the gap between what programmers intend and what their compiled code does."

findings.quote: He never saw electricity used in computing: he died thirty-three years before the electron was discovered.
findings.problem: The colon makes the electron's discovery the reason he never saw electrical computing. Relays and telegraphs ran on electricity long before the electron was known, so the reasoning does not hold.
findings.fix: "He never saw his algebra in a machine; he died thirty-three years before the electron was even discovered."

findings.quote: ran his own school by twenty-six with no university degree, and by thirty-two was publishing original mathematics
findings.problem: Both ages understate. Boole opened his own school in Lincoln at 19 (1834) and was publishing from 1841. In 1844, aged 28, he won the Royal Society's Royal Medal. As written, the sentence suggests he started late.
findings.fix: "opened his own school at nineteen with no university degree, and at twenty-eight won the Royal Society's Royal Medal for original mathematics." (MacTutor, "George Boole")

findings.quote: There is one more negative than positive because 0 takes a "positive" slot.
findings.problem: The wheel's strip repeats the last sentence of ch2-twos-p8 almost verbatim.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence from the strip; "The slots" ends at "from −1 to −128."

findings.quote: Flip every bit (0→1, 1→0). This is "one's complement."
findings.problem: Step 1 has no full stop while Steps 2 and 3 do. Steps 2 and 3 also put the full stop inside the quotation marks, the only place in the chapter that does. Elsewhere the chapter puts it outside ("it is raining". / "positive" slots.).
findings.fix: Step 1: "Take the binary representation of the positive number." Steps 2 and 3: This is "one's complement". / This is "two's complement".

findings.quote: It filled a room thirty metres long, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts
findings.problem: Thirty metres (100 ft) is the length of ENIAC's cabinets laid end to end, not the length of the room. The machine stood in a U along the walls of a room 30 by 50 feet, about 9 by 15 metres.
findings.fix: "Its cabinets, nearly thirty metres of them, lined a room fifteen metres long; it weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down..." Sources: IEEE Milestone, ethw.org/Milestones:Electronic_Numerical_Integrator_and_Computer,_1946 ("almost one hundred feet long", "filled a 30-by-50 foot room"); pbs.org/transistor/science/events/eniac.html ("Filling up a 30 X 50 foot room").

findings.quote: ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall with 17,468 vacuum tubes
findings.problem: This is the same room-versus-machine mix-up as in p1. The drawing makes it worse. Against its own 10 m scale bar, the back wall of the U is drawn 30 m long and the side arms add about 7 m each, so the cabinets total about 44 m: the real room was about 15 m and the real cabinets about 30 m. The caption's 'the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip' only works for the 30 m run of cabinets. With a die of about 13 mm (M4 about 166 mm²), a 15 m room is about 1,150 times the chip.
findings.fix: Redraw the U with a back wall of about 15 m (1.5 scale bars) and about 30 m of cabinets in total. Description: "a U of cabinets, nearly thirty metres of them, around a fifteen-metre room". Caption: "ENIAC's 17,468 vacuum tubes filled nearly thirty metres of cabinets; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's cabinets run some two thousand times longer than the chip." Sources: as for p1; the M4 die is 165.9 mm² per the MyDrivers die shot (wccftech.com/snapdragon-x-elite-die-shot-compared-with-apple-m4).

findings.quote: In the transistor the control goes to the base of a small piece of silicon
findings.problem: The figure dates the device 'TRANSISTOR 1947' and labels its body 'silicon'. The 1947 Bell Labs point-contact transistor was germanium, and every transistor stayed germanium until Tanenbaum's silicon transistor in January 1954. The book itself says germanium came first (p9 on Kilby, the p13 timeline), so the figure contradicts the prose.
findings.fix: Change the drawn word 'silicon' to 'germanium', and in the description write 'a small piece of germanium'. Make the caption's second sentence: "The transistor does it in a sliver of semiconductor (germanium in 1947, silicon today), with no glass, no glowing filament and nothing to burn out." Source: computerhistory.org/siliconengine/silicon-transistors-offer-superior-operating-characteristics/ ("For the first six years of their existence, transistors had all been made with germanium").

findings.quote: pulls electrons (blue dots) up into a thin channel under it
findings.problem: With the gate off, the drawing puts nine free electrons in the p-type body and none in the two n-type regions. When the gate turns on, the channel fills with electrons rising out of that body. This gets the doping backwards. The strip says n-type is 'rich in free electrons' and p-type is electron-accepting, and p7 says the gate 'draws free electrons out of the source and drain'. In a real MOSFET the channel electrons come from the source and drain, because the p-type body has almost none. The cold reader stumbled on exactly this point in Pass 29.
findings.fix: In the resting frame, put the free electrons inside the two n-type regions and at most one or two in the p-type body. When the gate turns on, animate them flowing in from the source and drain to fill the channel. Description: "A positive gate voltage acts through the oxide as a field and draws electrons (blue dots) out of the source and drain into a thin channel under it; they flow along it from source to drain."

findings.quote: formed in one piece of germanium (another semiconductor) instead of made separately and wired by hand
findings.problem: Kilby's 1958 parts were formed in one piece of germanium, but they were still connected by hand-bonded gold wires. Putting the wiring on the chip itself (aluminium laid over the oxide) was Noyce's planar step, and it is exactly why his process was 'more manufacturable'. Noyce's 'within months' was his notebook concept of 23 January 1959; the first working planar IC was tested on 27 September 1960. The glossary entry for 'integrated circuit' repeats 'within months'.
findings.fix: "...formed in one piece of germanium (another semiconductor), though its parts were still joined by hand with fine gold wires. Within months, Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor independently conceived the same on silicon, with the wiring laid on the chip itself, and his more manufacturable process became the basis of the entire industry." Update the glossary to match. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invention_of_the_integrated_circuit ("connected by gold wires"; Noyce 23 January 1959; first operational device 27 September 1960; aluminium metallization).

findings.quote: This is roughly what C's "int x = 5 + 3;" compiles to
findings.problem: The comment in the code block after p5 is false. Compilers fold constant expressions even with optimisation off: clang -O0 compiles `int x = 5 + 3;` to the single instruction `mov dword ptr [rbp - 4], 8` (checked locally). No compiler emits mov 5, mov 3, add for this line.
findings.fix: Replace the comment line with "; Adding 5 and 3 in registers, one step at a time". Or keep the C reference and say "; Roughly what C's "x = a + b;" becomes once a and b hold 5 and 3".

findings.quote: They called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor.
findings.problem: Bardeen and Brattain did not name it. Their Bell Labs colleague John R. Pierce coined 'transistor', and staff chose it from a list of candidates by ballot in May 1948.
findings.fix: "Bell Labs named it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor." Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Pierce; pbs.org/transistor/album1/pierce/naming.html.

findings.quote: ENIAC's 17,468 tubes failed about every two days
findings.problem: As written, the strip says all 17,468 tubes failed every two days. The source figure (and this book's p1 and Fig 1.7 strip) is one tube about every two days.
findings.fix: "A tube is hot, fragile and wears out: one of ENIAC's 17,468 tubes failed about every two days."

findings.quote: Assembly language is a human-readable label for these patterns, and the translation is one-to-one.
findings.problem: On x86 the mapping is not one-to-one. One mnemonic can assemble to several encodings: add eax, 3 is 83 C0 03 or 05 03 00 00 00, and the block's own add eax, ebx is 01 D8 or 03 C3. What does hold is that each assembly instruction becomes exactly one machine instruction.
findings.fix: "Assembly language is a human-readable label for these patterns: each line becomes one machine instruction."

findings.quote: L3 Cache | On the CPU package | 8–64 MB
findings.problem: Next to L1 and L2 'On the CPU die', the table makes L3 look like it sits off the die. In current Intel, AMD (on each core chiplet) and Apple chips the L3 or last-level cache is on the die, shared by the cores.
findings.fix: Change the L3 Location cell to "On the CPU die, shared by the cores".

findings.quote: L2 Cache | On the CPU die | 256 KB – 1 MB
findings.problem: This range is out of date for a 2026 'typical' value. Current cores carry 1 to 3 MB of L2 each (AMD Zen 4/5: 1 MB; Intel Raptor Cove: 2 MB; Lion Cove: 2.5 MB), and Apple M-series clusters share 16 MB.
findings.fix: Change the L2 Typical size cell to "512 KB – 3 MB".

findings.quote: If a register access took one second, L1 would take 3 seconds, L2 13, L3 43
findings.problem: The figure divides the table's rounded nanoseconds (1, 4, 13 ns) by 0.3 ns. Yet the same table gives the register as 1 cycle and L1, L2, L3 as 4, 12 and 40 cycles. A reader who scales by cycles gets 4 s, 12 s and 40 s and finds the figure disagrees with the table one screen above.
findings.fix: Make the table's nanoseconds exact at its own 0.3 ns per cycle ("~1.2 ns", "~3.6 ns", "~12 ns") and redraw the figure at 4 s, 12 s and 40 s. Or keep both and add to the figure's 'The scale' strip: "times use the nanosecond column".

findings.quote: will decide whether the statement is true or false?
findings.problem: Hilbert and Ackermann's Entscheidungsproblem asks whether a statement of logic is provable (universally valid), not whether it is true. Turing's paper states it that way: "no general process for determining whether a given formula ... is provable". Since Gödel 1931, true and provable are known to differ.
findings.fix: "is there a mechanical procedure that, given any mathematical statement, will decide whether the statement can be proved?" p4 still works unchanged. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem; Turing 1936, §11.

findings.quote: Von Neumann's insight: instructions are data
findings.problem: The section title (and the glossary entry 'von Neumann ... proposed storing the program') gives von Neumann sole credit for the stored-program idea. Eckert and Mauchly had proposed storing programs and data in one addressable memory by January 1944. The First Draft was built on their work and bore only von Neumann's name. The body text (p3, 'The report's central idea') is careful about this; the title is not.
findings.fix: Title: "The stored program: instructions are data". Glossary: "...whose 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, built on Eckert and Mauchly's design work, set out storing the program in memory alongside its data." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_architecture (Eckert, January 1944; the report "bore only von Neumann's name").

findings.quote: Defence four, and the attack that still beat it: ROP
findings.problem: The heading says ROP beat defence four. The section says the reverse. ROP (2007, p8) beat DEP, and defence four (CFI, shadow stacks, PAC in p9; 2017+ in Fig 3.11) came afterwards as the answer to ROP. The heading also puts defence four ahead of ROP, although the prose covers ROP first.
findings.fix: Heading: "ROP, and defence four" (or "The attack that beat DEP, and defence four").

findings.quote: The chapter uses six rows: RAX holds a function's result, RDI and RSI its first two arguments
findings.problem: It names six registers, but they fill only five of the table's eight rows: RDI and RSI share the arguments row with RDX, RCX, R8 and R9. The paragraph also says "(next section)" twice for RSP, and the table's RSP row says it a third time.
findings.fix: "The chapter needs six of these registers: RAX holds a function's result, RDI and RSI its first two arguments, RSP and RBP its place on the stack, and RIP the next instruction." This also drops the second "(next section)".

findings.quote: other encodings of the same operation run anywhere from two bytes to a dozen
findings.problem: Fig 3.1 is titled "Same operation", meaning add 5 to a register, and its strip says the longest form of that is 6 bytes. Adding 5 to a register never takes a dozen bytes. The 2-to-12 range in the ledger (01 C8 up to REX+SIB+disp32+imm32) is for x86's add in general, so a reader checking against the figure finds a contradiction.
findings.fix: "Fig 3.1's x86 add spent four bytes, but other forms of x86's add run anywhere from two bytes to a dozen, so the decoder..."

findings.quote: Pushes the address of the next instruction (main+19), then jumps. Neither function sees the handoff.
findings.problem: "main+19" appears nowhere else. Gate 2 changed the picture and desc to "main, next", and the listing shows no byte offsets, so the reader can't tell where 19 comes from. "Neither function sees the handoff" is a vague tag, and it sounds wrong: the return address sits in add's own frame.
findings.fix: "*call.* Pushes the address of the next instruction (`pop rbp` in main), then jumps to `add`."

findings.quote: If you control RIP, you control the program.
findings.problem: A bold aphorism closer, which the brief bans (the same kind of italic closer was flagged in ch2-arithmetic-p7). The sentence before it already says that a function call, a loop and a memory-corruption exploit all work by changing RIP.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence.

findings.quote: A processor doesn't run C, or Python, or JavaScript. It runs a sequence of binary patterns
findings.problem: A "Not X. Y." reveal, with a triplet inside it (another triplet closes the paragraph: "every compiler, every operating system, every program"). The same sentence also italicises the ISA as a new term, although ch1-cpu already defined it ("The mapping from bit patterns to operations is called the instruction set architecture, or ISA").
findings.fix: "Whatever language a program is written in, the processor runs it as a sequence of binary patterns drawn from a fixed menu, the instruction set architecture (ISA) that Chapter 1 named."

findings.quote: a contract between caller and callee about who puts arguments where, who saves which registers
