findings.problem: The reader meets the calling convention for the third time and is told here it is new (bold key-term). ch3-registers-p2 already explained it (conventions that let one function call another; which registers a callee may overwrite), and the Fig 3.4 caption already gave System V's argument registers and RAX for the result.
findings.fix: Name the term where the idea first appears, in ch3-registers-p2: "...the rest are conventions compilers share, together called the _calling convention_, so that one function can call another...". Then call-p2 reads: "The compiler must follow that calling convention: on Linux and macOS x86-64, the System V AMD64 ABI (application binary interface) drawn in Fig 3.4; on Windows, the Microsoft x64 calling convention." Record the moved glossary first-use.

findings.quote: call pushes the return address and jumps; add saves main's frame pointer and builds its own frame
findings.problem: The caption retells ch3-call-p4 step by step (call pushes and jumps, ret pops into RIP, main resumes at the next instruction), and the figure's strip tells call and ret a third time. The brief says that when prose and caption explain the same thing, the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: "The stack and RIP through one call of add, from call to ret."

findings.quote: Data that must outlive the call goes instead in a block of heap memory, taken with malloc
findings.problem: The Fig 3.5 caption just above already defines the heap ("memory taken with malloc while the program runs and kept until freed") and the frame ("one frame of local values per call, gone when the call returns"). p4 explains both again.
findings.fix: Keep the heap's definition in the caption, where the reader first sees the heap, and end p4 with: "Data that must outlive the call goes on the heap instead (Fig 3.5)." Optionally trim the caption's frame clause to "the stack growing down from just under the kernel".

findings.quote: To add two numbers from memory, it loads them into registers, adds, and stores the result back
findings.problem: The load-compute-store cycle has already been explained in ch3-isa-p6 ("reached memory only through separate loads and stores") and in the Fig 3.2 key and caption ("load, add, store"). Here it is told a third time, and the italics present loads and stores as new terms.
findings.fix: "Memory is too slow to compute on directly, so the CPU does its arithmetic in registers, loading and storing as Fig 3.2 showed; even x86's one-instruction add to memory takes those three steps inside the chip." Move the italics to the first use in ch3-isa-p6.

findings.quote: The compiler adds the check, and the program picks a random canary each time it starts
findings.problem: p3 repeats p2 (compiler-inserted check, random value). The kept-original Fig 3.8 caption that follows explains p2 and p3 again in full (random value placed by the compiler, checked before ret, abort, the leak assumption), so the reader gets the canary three times in a row. The kept captions of Fig 3.9, 3.10 and 3.11 do the same to p6, p8 and p1.
findings.fix: Because the captions are kept, trim the prose. Fold p3 into p2 as one sentence: "The program picks a fresh random canary each time it starts, so it cannot be guessed, though an attacker who can read the process's memory through a separate leak can sometimes recover it." Alias p3. Record the kept-caption duplication in owner-calls §B.

findings.quote: AMD added this to x86 in 2003
findings.problem: Defence three (ASLR, dated 2001 in p6) answers return-to-libc, an attack on defence two (DEP, dated 2003 here), and p1 says each defence followed the one before. The dates run backwards, and Fig 3.11 draws 2003 before 2001+. The missing step: software non-executable stacks came first.
findings.fix: "Software patches had made the stack non-executable since 1997 (Solar Designer's for Linux; PaX from 2000). AMD put it in hardware in 2003 as the \"NX bit\" (No-eXecute)..." Sources: Solar Designer, "Getting around non-executable stack (and fix)", Bugtraq, Aug 1997, where return-to-libc is introduced against that patch; PaX PAGEEXEC, 2000.

findings.quote: brought down roughly ten percent of every computer connected to the network
findings.problem: "ten percent of every computer" is ungrammatical (a percentage of a single computer).
findings.fix: "brought down roughly ten percent of all the computers connected to the network (about six thousand machines)". The "23-year-old" in the same paragraph is an owner ruling; leave it.

findings.quote: a program that runs whatever commands it is typed
findings.problem: Broken syntax; the reader has to read it twice.
findings.fix: "a program that runs whatever commands are typed into it"

findings.quote: One register, four names: RAX (2003) contains EAX (1985), which contains AX (1978), split into AH and AL.
findings.problem: It says four names, then lists five (RAX, EAX, AX, AH, AL). The title and label say "four names" too. Separately, the strip's "The quirk." bullet repeats the caption's second sentence word for word.
findings.fix: Caption, title and label: "One register, five names". Cut the strip's "The quirk." bullet.

findings.quote: Each red dot is an attack technique that broke the previous defence.
findings.problem: In the drawing, the defence just before ROP is ASLR, so the caption says ROP broke ASLR. That is the error §4g corrected in the prose (ch3-defenses-p9 row: ROP defeats DEP; ASLR falls to leaks). Other faults: the first red dot (Morris, 1988) broke no earlier defence; the timeline runs 2003 before 2001+; "CFI ... hardware-signed" contradicts p9, where CFI is the compiler plus the runtime; "1988 · stack overflow" is the name of a different bug.
findings.fix: Owner call, because the figure is kept. If the caption may change: "Attacks in red, the defences that answered them in green." Otherwise add Fig 3.11 to owner-calls §B next to Figs 3.7, 3.9 and 3.10.

findings.quote: pop rsi
findings.problem: Fig 3.4 teaches that the first argument goes in RDI, but the figure pops system()'s only argument, "/bin/sh", into RSI ("load 2nd arg"); this is known, in owner-calls §B. New: "RIP READS DOWN" is wrong, because RSP walks the stack, and upward in Fig 3.5's orientation. The caption calls CFI a hardware mitigation, against p9. Its "(mark code non-executable)" should be data pages (known).
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original). If allowed: G1 `pop rdi` loads the address of "/bin/sh"; the arrow reads "ret pops the next address"; the caption reads "(mark data non-executable)" and "Later mitigations (CFI in the compiler; shadow stacks, ARM PAC, Intel CET in hardware)".

findings.quote: Each region's base is shifted by ~16 bits of randomness on every launch
findings.problem: Contradicts its own caption (28–30, 24–28, 30–32 bits); this is known. New: in runs 1 and 2 the heap's address (0x55A8…, 0x55C4…) is lower than .text's (0x562B…, 0x55F1…), although the heap is drawn above .text and Fig 3.5 puts the heap above the program code.
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original). If allowed: "each region's base moves by 24 to 32 random bits on every launch", and heap addresses above .text in every run.

findings.quote: "Tiger\0" + 11 unused bytes
findings.problem: "Tiger\0" is 6 bytes, so 10 remain, not 11 (known, owner-calls §B). New: the frame is drawn with the buffer on top and the return address at the bottom, the reverse of Fig 3.5 and Fig 3.8 (high addresses up). p3 says the copy runs up into higher addresses, but here the overflow runs down the page.
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original). If allowed: "+ 10 unused bytes", and the frame flipped (return address on top) or labelled "higher addresses ↓".

findings.quote: The CPU has no way to verify it is the same number that was pushed there originally.
findings.problem: ch3-defenses-p9 later shows CPUs that do check it (shadow stack in CET, ARM pointer authentication), so the claim is too broad. The strip also repeats the Fig 3.6 strip's "ret" bullet ("If something has overwritten that slot, ret jumps there instead").
findings.fix: "A plain ret does not check that it is the number call pushed." Then cut the last sentence of the Fig 3.6 strip's "ret" bullet.

findings.quote: Rosetta 2 translated an Intel app's x86 code into ARM code once, on first launch, and cached it.
findings.problem: The picture ("translates once, on first launch", "CACHED"), the strip's "Ahead of time" bullet and p4 already say this. The caption's second sentence repeats the drawn key ("[ ] = memory", "ARM can't add in memory: load, add, store"), which p6 then explains again.
findings.fix: Caption: "Three lines of an Intel app and the six ARM lines Rosetta 2 turns them into: storing 5 takes two (mov, stur), adding 3 takes three (ldur, add, stur)."

findings.quote: What still divides x86 and ARM is the binary incompatibility
findings.problem: This is the fourth time the reader is told x86 and ARM can't run each other's code (ch1-cpu, the Fig 3.1 picture and caption, ch3-isa-p4), and the section ends on that summary.
findings.fix: Cut the last sentence.

findings.quote: Each pattern is meaningless to the other two chips.
findings.problem: It repeats the line drawn in the figure ("each pattern means nothing to the other chips") and ch3-isa-p4. "Meaningless" also contradicts p7's more accurate "mean different things on different chips".
findings.fix: Cut the caption's second sentence.

findings.quote: the OS reserves an area called the stack: a last-in-first-out buffer
findings.problem: Wrong word. ch1-memory-p11 defines a buffer as a fixed-size block for incoming data, and section 05 overflows one such buffer inside the stack. Calling the whole stack a buffer invites the reader to think a buffer overflow means the stack overflowing, a misreading Fig 3.11's "stack overflow" label supports.
findings.fix: "a last-in-first-out region"

findings.quote: When they're wrong, the corruption is silent
findings.problem: "they" grammatically points to the functions (strcpy, gets, scanf), but the one who is wrong is the programmer.
findings.fix: "When the programmer is wrong, the corruption is silent"

findings.quote: The CPU manages the stack with two instructions:
findings.problem: Two sentences later the same paragraph names four instructions that move RSP (push, pop, call, ret).
findings.fix: "Two instructions do the basic work:"

findings.quote: Modified by push/pop; we'll see this next section
findings.problem: push/pop, "stack frame" and "local variables ... at known offsets" are used before ch3-stack-p3 and p4 explain them. "we'll see this next section" is the third "next section" for RSP in a few lines.
findings.fix: RSP: "Moves as values go on and come off the stack (next section)". RBP: "Lets a function find its own values at fixed distances".

findings.quote: The "rep" loop instruction implicitly uses RCX
findings.problem: Wrong word: rep is a prefix that repeats a string instruction, not a loop instruction.
findings.fix: "The rep prefix and the loop instruction take their count from RCX" (Intel SDM vol. 2, REP and LOOP).

findings.quote: Base Pointer: points to current function's stack frame
findings.problem: The listing comments, the Fig 3.6 caption and the Fig 3.8 picture call RBP the "frame pointer", a name the table never links to RBP.
findings.fix: "Base Pointer (the frame pointer): points to the current function's stack frame"

findings.quote: RIP (the Program Counter, the address of the next instruction to execute) is itself a register
findings.problem: This is the third definition of RIP in this section (p2: "RIP the next instruction"; the table row), and the table already shows it is a register.
findings.fix: "RIP is Chapter 1's program counter, and because it is a register, changing it changes what the CPU does next."

findings.quote: which starts the shell, the program that runs whatever the attacker types
findings.problem: The shell was already defined in ch3-overflow-p5.
findings.fix: "which starts a shell"

findings.quote: The Blaster worm (2003, RPC).
findings.problem: A fourth example that adds nothing: no figure, and an unexplained acronym, after Code Red and Slammer have already shown the scale. Also "a buffer over-read rather than overflow" is missing "an".
findings.fix: Cut the Blaster sentence. Write "rather than an overflow".

findings.quote: For Rust this guarantee was the whole reason the language exists
findings.problem: Tenses clash (was ... exists).
findings.fix: "For Rust this guarantee was the whole reason the language was created"

findings.quote: refuses to execute instructions from a page marked NX
findings.problem: NX is used one sentence before it is expanded ("No-eXecute"), and ch3-overflow-p5 had already used "the NX bit" unexpanded.
findings.fix: Put the expansion first: "The defence is to mark stack pages No-eXecute (NX): the CPU's MMU refuses to execute instructions from such a page..."

findings.quote: the attacker chains together short fragments of existing code in the program
findings.problem: The sentence before already says "tiny fragments of existing code are enough".
findings.fix: "Instead of injecting new code, the attacker chains fragments that end in a ret instruction."

findings.quote: operating system kernels, web browsers, database engines, network stacks
findings.problem: In a chapter where "stack" always means the call stack, "network stacks" reads as that stack.
findings.fix: "networking code"

findings.quote: (the MMU of the Bridge maps it to real RAM)
findings.problem: "the MMU of the Bridge" reads like the name of a part. The MMU was introduced in ch1-memory; the Bridge is the chapter that opens it up.
findings.fix: "(the MMU from Chapter 1, opened up in the Bridge, maps it to real RAM)"

findings.quote: a library loads as one block, so one leaked address locates all of it
findings.problem: The argument depends on what a library is (shared, ready-made code loaded into the process). No page up to here defines it; earlier uses are "offered by a library" and "the C library's system()".
findings.fix: At the first use in p6: "the C library's system() (libc, the ready-made code every C program loads)".

findings.quote: RDI and RSI its first two arguments
findings.problem: "argument" is relied on here and in Fig 3.4 before any gloss. call-p2 shows it ("call add with 5 and 3") but never names it.
findings.fix: "RDI and RSI its first two arguments (the values handed to it)"

findings.quote: an x86 binary will not run on an ARM CPU
findings.problem: "binary" is used as a noun for a program, a sense never given. The reader knows it as the number system from Chapter 2.
findings.fix: "an x86 program will not run on an ARM CPU" and "rewrites x86 programs as ARM ones".

findings.quote: now licensed to the chip designers behind nearly every phone
findings.problem: The same sentence then makes the phone claim again ("every iPhone, every Apple Silicon Mac, and nearly every Android phone"), as a reflexive triplet.
findings.fix: Keep the §4g wording and drop the repeat: "...is the modern alternative: cleaner, more efficient, and also the chip of every Apple Silicon Mac."

findings.quote: whose instruction set no descendant has ever removed. Every x86-64 processor sold today still recognises
findings.problem: Two sentences make the same claim. The first needs a second read for its syntax.
findings.fix: "In 1978, Intel released the 8086, a 16-bit chip; every x86-64 processor sold today still recognises the core binary patterns Intel encoded that year."

findings.quote: so calling from one to the other needs a wrapper that moves each argument over
findings.problem: "from one to the other" is ambiguous: one OS, or one convention?
findings.fix: "so code built for one cannot call code built for the other without a wrapper that moves each argument over"

findings.quote: Below every Python script, every JavaScript framework, every neural network
findings.problem: A reflexive triplet with "truly" and "finally" as intensifiers. The ch2 closer just used the same shape ("a Python list to a TLS handshake to a neural network").
findings.fix: "Below every program, whatever language it is written in, lies a sequence of instructions in the only language a processor understands. This chapter follows your code down to them."

findings.quote: 1949 → present
findings.problem: Nothing in the chapter is dated before 1972 (C) and 1978 (the 8086), so a reader looks for 1949 and doesn't find it.
findings.fix: "1972 → present" (or "1978 → present").

findings.quote: Chapter 3 shows the defences, among them the stack canary, ASLR and DEP, at the assembly level.
findings.problem: A pointer into this chapter that promises something it doesn't deliver: ch3 shows the call and the overflow in assembly, but the defences only in prose and figures.
findings.fix: "Chapter 3 shows the attack at the assembly level, and the defences against it: the stack canary, DEP and ASLR."

findings.quote: The question after the war became how to build a machine that isn't purpose-built for a single problem
findings.problem: The next section opens with "The first general-purpose electronic computer, ENIAC (1945)". By the chapter's own account, a machine not built for a single problem already existed when the war ended, so the reader stops to ask whether ENIAC was the answer. What Section 03 actually answers is a machine that runs any program without being rewired (vonneumann-p1, p4). The §4g row for ch1-vonneumann-p4 fixed this same contradiction there, but this sentence still sets the question up the old way.
findings.fix: "The question after the war became how to build Turing's universal machine in actual hardware: one machine that runs any program without being rewired."

findings.quote: no current flows until a voltage on the gate, which rests on a thin insulating oxide over the p-type silicon
findings.problem: "the gate" arrives as if the reader already knows it. The prose so far has named only the base, collector and emitter (p4). The only place that says what a gate is, the Fig 1.4 strip, is closed by default. The sentence is also a read-twice: a relative clause separates "a voltage on the gate" from its verb "draws", and it ends on "under it", which the reader has to trace back to the gate.
findings.fix: Split after "nothing free to move": "...leave a thin barrier with nothing free to move, so no current flows. Over the p-type silicon, on a thin insulating oxide, sits the third terminal, the gate, which does the base's job; a voltage on it draws free electrons out of the source and drain and under the gate, where they form a bridge (Fig 1.5)."

findings.quote: In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the base is called the gate.
findings.problem: Wrong word, and this strip is the only place that introduces the gate. A field-effect transistor has no base. Its gate is a different part that does the same job, through an insulator (Fig 1.5). Read literally, the sentence says the same part was renamed, which Fig 1.5 then contradicts.
findings.fix: "In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is called the gate (Fig 1.5)."

findings.quote: Each stage takes one clock tick, or cycle.
findings.problem: p2 has just named the whole fetch-decode-execute-writeback loop "the instruction cycle" and said "Then the cycle starts over". Here "cycle" means one clock tick, and the Fig 1.11 caption then says each instruction "takes five cycles", so one instruction cycle lasts five cycles. Fig 1.9's desc ("One instruction goes round per cycle") uses the first meaning. A careful reader stops to work out which cycle is meant.
findings.fix: p2: "Then the loop starts over, on every core". p7: "Each stage takes one tick of the CPU's clock, a clock cycle." Fig 1.9 desc: "One instruction goes round per trip."

findings.quote: It filled a room thirty metres long, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts
findings.problem: Factual. Thirty metres (100 ft) is the length of ENIAC's cabinets laid end to end. They stood in a U along three walls of a room about 9 by 15 metres (30 by 50 ft). Fig 1.7 repeats the error: its caption and desc say "a thirty-metre hall", it draws one side of the U about 30 m long against its 10 m bar, and "in life the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip" rests on a 30 m hall. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENIAC ("100 ft (30 m) long"); engineering.upenn.edu/about/history-heritage/eniac ("a room 30 by 50 feet", 40 panels in a U); britannica.com/technology/ENIAC (50-by-30-foot basement, panels along three walls).
findings.fix: p1: "Its forty cabinets, some thirty metres of them end to end, lined three walls of a room; it weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down..." Fig 1.7 caption: "ENIAC's cabinets ran some thirty metres around its room, holding 17,468 vacuum tubes; ... in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip." Desc and drawing: a U whose three sides together make about 30 m (Pass 30 item). Add a §4g row.

findings.quote: there was a mathematician who died before seeing what he built
findings.problem: Factual, on the book's first page. Turing lived to see and use stored-program computers. The Pilot ACE, built from his ACE design, first ran in 1950, and at Manchester he wrote the programmers' manual for the Ferranti Mark 1 (1951). He died in 1954 (ch1-context-p11). A reader who knows this stops, and one who does not is misinformed. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_ACE; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing. Hero leads are agent-editable (the ch15 hero lead was corrected in Pass 27).
findings.fix: "Before there was the internet, there was a mathematician who described the computer before anyone had built one." This matches ch1-context-p5: "the first formal description of what we now call a computer".

findings.quote: The Bombe did not try every setting. It raced through the positions of Enigma's turning wheels, the rotors
findings.problem: A "Not X. Y." reveal, and it leaves a gap. Racing through every rotor position sounds like trying every setting, and the prose never says why the rotor positions are far fewer than the 158 quintillion settings: most of that count comes from the plugboard pairs, named only in Fig 1.2's closed strip. The owner could not explain the earlier version of this paragraph (§4ac, 2026-10-12), so this is where they are most likely to stop again.
findings.fix: "Instead of trying every setting, it raced through the positions of Enigma's turning wheels, the rotors, only 17,576 for each choice of three wheels (26 × 26 × 26), and threw out each one that could not have turned the guessed words into the scrambled text, leaving a handful for people to check." If no number is wanted, keep just "Instead of trying every setting, it raced through...".

findings.quote: enough such rules, wired together, add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's
findings.problem: Rules are not wired; circuits are. The chapter never names the circuit that applies such a rule, the logic gate, yet the chapter coda ("What you now understand") says "Transistors ... combine into logic gates", a term Chapter 1 never gives. The pointer "(Chapter 2 builds them)" also promises too much. Chapter 2 builds gates and an adder, but storing bits and running a program are only promised there ("Add memory to hold bits between steps, and gates build the CPU").
findings.fix: "Two switches in a row let current through only when both are on, a rule called AND, and a circuit that applies such a rule is a logic gate. Enough gates, wired together, add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's (Chapter 2 builds the gates and the adder)."

findings.quote: A round trip to main memory (RAM) takes 60 nanoseconds, two hundred times longer
findings.problem: The same thing is explained twice, in two sections. Section 03 (vonneumann-p6, p7) already taught it: the CPU takes under a nanosecond, main memory about sixty, and caches holding copies of recent data are the remedy. Section 06 teaches it again from scratch, with no link back: p1 says "Each level holds a copy", and p2 gives the same 60 ns and "Hiding these gaps is the job of the caches".
findings.fix: Open p2 from what the reader already has: "Section 03's bottleneck, in numbers: the CPU performs an arithmetic operation in roughly 0.3 nanoseconds; a round trip to main memory (RAM) takes 60, two hundred times longer, and a read from a fast SSD (solid-state drive) 50,000, about 167,000 times longer. The caches sit in three levels, L1 to L3, between the CPU and RAM."

findings.quote: One program had the whole machine: you handed in your cards, the operator ran the jobs one by one
findings.problem: The caption repeats p1, the one-sentence paragraph right above it ("you handed in your stack of punched cards, the machine ran it alone, and you came back later for the printout"), and the strip's "The queue" bullet says it a third time. Only the idle-machine half of the caption is new.
findings.fix: Caption: "Between jobs, while the operator loaded the next deck, the most expensive machine in the building sat idle."

findings.quote: At a branch the CPU guesses which way it will go and runs ahead; a right guess keeps the work
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence restates p9's last two sentences almost word for word ("guesses which way it will go and runs ahead ... A right guess keeps the work ...; a wrong one throws it away"). The cache-trace point is then told three times: in the caption, in the strip's "The catch" bullet and in insight strip p11 ("The work is thrown away but the location stays cached").
findings.fix: Caption: "The guessed path runs before the branch is decided. If the guess is wrong its work is thrown away, but the data it loaded stays in the cache: the trace Spectre and Meltdown read." Strip "The catch": "Throwing work away rolls back the registers, not the cache (the insight below shows what that leaks)."

findings.quote: Every core runs this loop: fetch the instruction the program counter names, decode it, execute it, write back the result
findings.problem: The caption restates all of p2 (the four steps, the counter moving on) and p1's "billions of times a second". It says nothing about what this figure adds, the program in the middle: the counter stepping 0x00, 0x05, 0x08 and the jump back.
findings.fix: "The counter steps from 0x00 to 0x05 to 0x08 as each instruction is written back; the jump at 0x08 sets it back to 0x00, so the program loops."

findings.quote: With no voltage on the base, no current flows between collector and emitter; with a small one, it does.
findings.problem: The caption repeats p4, two lines above ("A small voltage on its base ... lets a much larger current flow between ... the collector ... and the emitter; with no voltage there, nothing flows"), and the strip's "Three terminals" bullet repeats it again. The brief's rule is that the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: "Left, 0 V on the base: the lamp stays dark. Right, 0.7 V: it lights. This is the older kind of transistor; modern chips are built from the field-effect kind, opened in Fig 1.5."

findings.quote: so a program can ask but never choose where it lands
findings.problem: The strip's "The way in" bullet and p6 say the same thing almost verbatim ("so a program can ask but never pick where it lands"). The caption also explains the system call ("a controlled jump into the kernel in Ring 0, which does the work and returns the result") that p6 then explains in full. "The CPU itself" appears three times: caption, strip ("Enforced in silicon") and p7. Meanwhile p6 depends on the caption for what a ring is.
findings.fix: Strip "The way in": "The dotted path is a system call; the text below follows it." Caption: "The CPU runs each program at a privilege level, or ring: Ring 3 for programs, Ring 0 for the kernel. A program's direct reach for the disk is blocked; its system call is let through."

findings.quote: a running program (to the kernel, a process: on Linux, reading the file /proc/1234/status returns
findings.problem: A read-twice sentence. The subject is a list of four things with a long parenthesis inside it, which itself contains a colon, a second clause and a file path. The verb, "are all read and written", arrives about forty words after the subject starts.
findings.fix: "A file on disk, the keyboard and, in later versions, a network connection or even a running program are all read and written through file descriptors, so once a program holds one, the same read and write calls work on any of them. To the kernel a running program is a process: on Linux, reading the file /proc/1234/status returns process 1234's name and memory use as text." This keeps "process" in p8, its glossary first-use site.

findings.quote: or leave a file's pages unread until needed; when a program touches a page that is not in RAM
findings.problem: A read-twice sentence. One sentence holds three bolded benefits, and the middle one carries a parenthesis with a semicolon and the whole page-fault mechanism ("the MMU stops it and calls the kernel, which reads the page in, updates the table and lets the program carry on, none the wiser"). By the time "and protection" arrives, the reader has lost the list.
findings.fix: Three sentences: "Page tables give three things. Isolation: ... Flexibility: the kernel can move pages around in RAM, send little-used ones out to disk, or leave a file's pages unread until needed; when a program touches a page that is not in RAM, the MMU stops it and calls the kernel, which reads the page in, updates the table and lets the program carry on, none the wiser. Protection: the page tables also encode permissions for read, write and execute, and the MMU enforces them."

findings.quote: He called it an a-machine, for automatic machine; we now call it a Turing machine.
findings.problem: "it" points back past the whole proof. The nearest things it could refer to are the decider and "Hilbert's procedure", which p4 has just shown cannot exist. The device "it" means was described at the start of p4.
findings.fix: "He called his imagined device an a-machine, for automatic machine; we now call it a Turing machine."

findings.quote: A machine whose rules read another machine's rules from its tape can run any of them
findings.problem: The strip's "Universal" bullet restates p5 ("one machine ... can read any other machine's rules from its tape and do whatever that machine would do"), and the figure does not show universality. "One cell at a time" is said three times: p4, the caption and the strip's "Tape" bullet.
findings.fix: Cut the "Universal" bullet. Caption: "On a mark the head moves right; on an empty cell it writes a mark and stops. Following just these two rules, it has added one."

findings.quote: plugboard pairs gave about 158 × 10^18 possible settings, changed daily
findings.problem: The same number appears in two forms. The prose says "more than 158 quintillion", corrected on purpose because the exact count is 158.96 × 10^18 (§4ac). The strip still says "about 158", which rounds the wrong way.
findings.fix: "Rotor order, start positions and plugboard pairs gave more than 158 × 10^18 possible settings, changed daily."

findings.quote: They called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor.
findings.problem: Factual. "They" is Bardeen and Brattain, but the name was coined by John R. Pierce at Bell Labs and chosen in an internal vote in May 1948 (britannica.com, John R. Pierce; nap.nationalacademies.org/read/11172/chapter/15).
findings.fix: "Bell Labs called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor."

findings.quote: VACUUM TUBE 1906 ... TRANSISTOR 1947 ... silicon
findings.problem: "1906" (the triode) is never explained in the prose, caption or strip. "silicon" sits under "1947", but the 1947 transistor was germanium, and the chapter's own timeline (p13) says silicon won over germanium later. The visible label ("The replacement · the same switch, without the fire") also differs from the SVG title ("Vacuum tube and transistor · the same switch").
findings.fix: Drop the two years, or make the strip say "Tube. ... (the triode, 1906)" and label the 1947 device "germanium". Make the label and the title the same.

findings.quote: held for about fifty years, until around 2015
findings.problem: The Fig 1.6 caption beside it says the chips follow the line "for more than forty years". Both are right (one counts from 1965, the other from 1971), but a reader comparing "fifty" and "forty" stops. Timeline p16 then says Moore's Law "is slowing", while p10 says it held only "until around 2015".
findings.fix: Fig 1.6 caption: "The chips follow the dashed two-year line from 1971 until about 2015, then fall below it."

findings.quote: 28 billion transistors. 3-nanometre process. Each transistor smaller than the width of a flu virus.
findings.problem: Clipped fragments, the only timeline item written this way; every other item is a full sentence. "Physical limits are being reached" is vague and passive.
findings.fix: "Apple's M4 holds 28 billion transistors, made on a 3-nanometre process, each smaller than a flu virus; since about 2015 the doubling has slowed as physical limits near." ("3-nanometre" kept as ruled.)

findings.quote: Gordon Moore predicts the number of transistors per chip doubles every year (later revised to two years).
findings.problem: This timeline item restates p10, the paragraph just above it, almost word for word ("doubling about every year ... he later revised this to every two years").
findings.fix: Give the item something the prose lacks, or keep the title only: "Moore's Law stated: published in Electronics, April 1965." (Source this before using it.)

findings.quote: the distance between them is the history of the integrated circuit
findings.problem: An aphorism closer in the strip's "The same job" bullet. It sounds weighty but teaches nothing.
findings.fix: "Both machines flip switches according to instructions; the integrated circuit (above) is what shrank them."

findings.quote: The Von Neumann bottleneck
findings.problem: The capitalisation is inconsistent. p2 writes "John von Neumann", yet this sentence-case h3 and the chapter coda ("a design choice (Von Neumann's) that defines what a modern computer is") capitalise "Von" mid-phrase.
findings.fix: "The von Neumann bottleneck"; in the coda, "a design choice (von Neumann's)". The section title and the Fig 1.8 label start with the name, so "Von" can stay there.

findings.quote: Every CPU ever built does the same four things in a loop, today billions of times per second.
findings.problem: A one-sentence paragraph that announces without naming the four things, which only come in p2. The section title then names four different things ("Fetch. Decode. Execute. Repeat.": repeat is not a stage, and writeback is missing). "billions of times" comes back in the Fig 1.9 caption.
findings.fix: Merge into p2: "Every CPU runs the same four steps in a loop, billions of times a second: the instruction cycle." Optionally make the title "Fetch, decode, execute, write back".

findings.quote: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction.
findings.problem: The program counter is bolded here as if it were new, but vonneumann-p4 already taught it ("The CPU's program counter names the next cell to run"). "address" appears here for the first time, and nothing links it to the "number of the memory cell" of Section 03.
findings.fix: "The program counter, met in Section 03, holds the address (the cell's number) of the next instruction."

findings.quote: mov eax, 5
findings.problem: The figure's program is written in assembly, using register eax, before the text has said what assembly or eax is. Both come in p5 and the code block, one subsection later. The strip does not explain them.
findings.fix: Add a strip bullet: "The program. Three instructions in assembly, the CPU's own language written as words (next subsection); eax is one of its registers."

findings.quote: Assembly language is a human-readable label for these patterns
findings.problem: Wrong word: a language is not a label. "The mnemonic mov eax, 5" calls the whole instruction a mnemonic (only "mov" is one), and "the assembler" is used without saying what it is (only Fig 1.10's arrow shows it).
findings.fix: "Assembly language gives each pattern a human-readable name, one name per pattern, and a program called an assembler turns the names back into bits: mov eax, 5 assembles to 10111000 00000101 00000000 00000000 00000000 on x86."

findings.quote: They also use out-of-order execution.
findings.problem: "They" refers back to "modern CPUs" in p7, across all of Fig 1.11 (label, caption and strip). The nearest plural is the figure's instructions or stages.
findings.fix: "Modern CPUs also use out-of-order execution."

findings.quote: Chapter 15 returns to them.
findings.problem: Chapter 15 mentions Spectre and Meltdown only twice: in its opening list and in one sentence that files them under side channels. It explains nothing more, so a reader who follows the pointer for more finds nothing.
findings.fix: "Chapter 15 files them with the other side-channel attacks."

findings.quote: the machine stood idle in the gaps: the waste time-sharing set out to remove
findings.problem: The strip uses "time-sharing" before p4 defines it. The gaps between decks are also not what time-sharing addressed: p3 and p4 tie it to waiting on I/O and to several users at once.
findings.fix: "The cost. A bug meant new cards and another hour's wait, and the machine stood idle in the gaps."

findings.quote: when the data arrives, it reloads them and the first program carries on
findings.problem: "them" can be read as "the data". It means the program counter and registers, which were named only in a parenthesis earlier in the sentence.
findings.fix: "when the data arrives, it reloads that program's counter and registers and the program carries on"

findings.quote: driver | scheduler
findings.problem: Two labels drawn in the kernel layer that Chapter 1 never names. The scheduler is the turn-giver of p4, but the link is not made, and "driver" appears nowhere in the chapter.
findings.fix: Add a strip bullet: "Driver, scheduler. Parts of the kernel: the driver gives a device its orders; the scheduler decides whose turn it is (the turns of the text)."

findings.quote: without it, every program could read every other program's memory, every file and every network packet
findings.problem: p7 and the insight strip p10 in the same section make the same point twice: the boundary is the root of security, and breaking it gives the whole machine ("read any file and watch any keypress", "the most security-critical code"). p7's "every ... every ... every" is a reflexive triplet.
findings.fix: Fold p7 into p6's end: "...shows what the kernel does with the request. That boundary, enforced by the CPU itself, is what keeps one program out of another's memory and files." p10 keeps the attack.

findings.quote: Chapter 5 tells the story of the language it is written in.
findings.problem: A pointer that does no job in a paragraph about files and descriptors; the language is never named. It is one of four forward pointers in this section (fig 1.14 strip, p6 twice, p8, p10). p10 then names Chapter 4 as "Part II's kernel chapter", although p6 calls it "Chapter 4".
findings.fix: Cut the p8 sentence. p10: "Chapters 4 and 15 return to it."

findings.quote: 4 cycles (~1 ns)
findings.problem: Two numbers disagree. In the table, registers take "1 cycle (~0.3 ns)" and L1, L2 and L3 take 4, 12 and 40 cycles. Fig 1.15 says "If a register access took one second", then gives L1 3 s, L2 13 s and L3 43 s, because it scales the nanosecond column. A reader comparing them expects 4 s, 12 s and 40 s.
findings.fix: Fig 1.15 labels from the cycle column: L1 4 s, L2 12 s, L3 40 s (RAM's 200 cycles is still 3 min). Or table: L1 "4 cycles (~1.2 ns)", L2 "12 cycles (~3.6 ns)", L3 "40 cycles (~12 ns)".

findings.quote: made the idea rigorous for virtual memory (the next section)
findings.problem: Virtual memory is the next subheading inside this same section (06), not the next section. This is the chapter's last section, so the next section is Chapter 2's first.
findings.fix: "for virtual memory (below)"

findings.quote: the kernel does not give it a real physical address. It gives a virtual address
findings.problem: A "Not X. Y." reveal, coming straight after a heading that already promises "the lie the kernel tells".
findings.fix: "When your program asks for memory, the kernel gives it a virtual address instead of a physical one: every program sees its own private range of addresses..."

findings.quote: keeps its buffers, fixed-size blocks for incoming data, in that call's own memory (the stack)
findings.problem: The stack is not one call's own memory: it is shared by all calls, and each call has its own slot on it. The opening also says buffer overflows "pass the MMU's checks" right after p10 says the MMU enforces execute permission, which is exactly DEP, listed below as a defence. Only the write passes.
findings.fix: "The write itself passes the MMU's checks, because it lands in the program's own writable memory. Each call to a function (a reusable piece of the program) keeps its buffers, fixed-size blocks for incoming data, in its own slot on the stack, beside its return address..."

findings.quote: SYSCALLS · SYSCALL or int 0x80 · user request; 32 · timer (LAPIC) · apic_timer_interrupt
findings.problem: Two rows repeat errors §4g already corrected, right next to the corrected prose. (1) The SOURCE column lists SYSCALL as a way into the IDT, but chBridge-trap-p4 says 'A system call made with SYSCALL skips that table' (§4g, system-call row). (2) Vector 32 is drawn as the LAPIC timer with Linux's handler name, but Linux's local APIC timer uses its own vector, 0xEC (236) (§4g, Fig BR.6 row). This is already open as an owner call (STATE.md; docs/pass-29-owner-calls.md §C; pass-30-owner-calls §B), recommended 'redraw'. It remains the one place in the chapter where the picture states the opposite of the prose.
findings.fix: Redraw only those two rows (the owner's open call): change the SYSCALLS box to 'int 0x80 (legacy) · user request'; change row 32 to '236 · local timer (LAPIC) · apic_timer_interrupt' (or drop the number and keep the cause). If the drawing must stay as it is, the owner accepts it knowingly at the call.

findings.quote: When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register, indexes by vector number
findings.problem: chBridge-trap-p1 calls the system call a trap, and p4 says SYSCALL skips the IDT. So 'any trap' in this caption is false for the very trap Fig BR.2 just showed. The caption's third sentence ('every involuntary entry') then leaves out the voluntary int 0x80 that sentence two had just included. This is the caption of a kept-original figure, so it is reported here, not rewritten.
findings.fix: If the owner allows it: 'When an exception or interrupt fires (or a legacy int 0x80), the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register, indexes by vector number, and jumps to the handler the kernel registered for that vector.' Drop the third sentence.

findings.quote: store 0x7fff_a3c5_0010
findings.problem: The desc (and §4g row 615) call 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 'the next page up' from 0x7fff_a3c4_0010. With 4 KiB pages only the last three hex digits are the offset, so the two addresses are 0x10000 apart: 16 pages (64 KiB), not the neighbouring page. For the same reason Fig BR.5's 'page a3c4 → a200' is not a page number: the page number of 0x7fff_a3c4_0010 is …a3c40, and the frame of 0x4_a200_0010 is 0x4a2000. A reader who applies the 'last twelve bits are the offset' rule the section teaches (p2, How it works) gets a different page from the one the figures name.
findings.fix: Shift the addresses so that the four digits shown are the page number: BR.4 'load 0x7fff_fa3c_4010' → RAM '0x4a20_0010'; 'store 0x7fff_fa3c_5010' (now truly the next page up). The offset note '0x010' stays correct, and BR.5's 'a3c4 → a200', 'a3c5 → …' labels become true page and frame numbers. Update the desc and §4g row 615 to match.

findings.quote: offset 0x010 unchanged: only the page moves
findings.problem: At t=0, which is the still a reduced-motion reader sees, the figure shows only the second access: 'store 0x7fff_a3c5_0010', 'store to a read-only page: no', 'RAM not reached', 'page fault'. The successful translation never appears: no load, no 0x4_a200_0010, no TLB miss. The bottom note about the offset passing through unchanged then sits under 'RAM not reached' and refers to nothing on screen. In that state the picture does not show its title, 'silicon between the CPU and the RAM', translating an address.
findings.fix: Make the end and still state show both outcomes. Keep the load's '0x4_a200_0010' in the RAM box (the fault box already says the store never arrives) instead of 'not reached'. Give the CPU box one more line so it lists both 'load 0x7fff_a3c4_0010' and 'store 0x7fff_a3c5_0010'.

findings.quote: 1  kernel queues a command
findings.problem: No queue is drawn anywhere. Under step 1 the CPU box says 'kernel: doorbell' and a gold dot goes straight from the CPU to the SSD. Then the SSD reads blocks, without ever fetching a command from RAM. The prose (io-p4), the desc and How it works all say the command sits in a queue in RAM and the drive fetches it itself. The picture visually re-states the error §4g row 616 corrected: that the kernel hands the command to the SSD.
findings.fix: Turn the first cell of the RAM box into a small 'cmd' slot labelled 'queue' (leave 7 buffer blocks). Animate step 1 as a gold dot CPU → queue slot ('cmd' appears), then the doorbell dot CPU → SSD, then one dot queue slot → SSD (the drive fetches the command), then the data dots as now.

findings.quote: B | C while (1) | A
findings.problem: The process boxes are revealed left to right through a clip, but the labels B, C, 'while (1)' and the final A sit outside the clip group. Mid-animation (t3.667) they float over empty space at 1 to 4 ms, before those processes have run, so the frame announces C's endless loop ahead of time.
findings.fix: Move the five label <text> elements inside the clip-path group with the boxes, so each label appears as its slice is drawn.

findings.quote: level 3
findings.problem: During the load's walk, the level 3 highlight rect has fill="none", so level 3 gets only a thin outline while levels 4, 2 and 1 fill gold. The walk then reads as 4 → 2 → 1 with level 3 faint. The store's walk fills all four.
findings.fix: Give the load-pass level 3 highlight the same fill="#d4a853" fill-opacity="0.35" as the other levels.

findings.quote: The instruction does not run and no error code comes back
findings.problem: On x86 a #GP does push an error code for the handler (0 for a privilege violation). The strip means that the program gets no result, but it says the opposite of the SDM in x86's own vocabulary.
findings.fix: 'The instruction does not run and the program gets no result; the CPU jumps to the handler the kernel set up, and the kernel decides what happens to the program.'

findings.quote: Restores RIP and RFLAGS from RCX and R11 and drops back to Ring 3. No scheduling is involved.
findings.problem: A system call can block (a write to a full pipe, a slow disk), and the kernel may run other processes before it returns. 'No scheduling is involved' is true only of the SYSRET instruction itself, and it reads as a claim about the whole call.
findings.fix: Drop the sentence: 'Restores RIP and RFLAGS from RCX and R11 and drops back to Ring 3.'

findings.quote: no MMIO or DMA: no disk, no network
findings.problem: chBridge-io-p2 says x86 has a third channel, IN and OUT, and disks have long been driven through port I/O. 'No disk, no network' without MMIO or DMA conflicts with that. So does How it works' 'each row shows the feature its abstraction cannot do without'.
findings.fix: Label 'no device access: no disk, no network', and in the left column 'MMIO · DMA' → 'device access' (or keep the left label and change the strip to 'no way to reach devices: no disk, no network').

findings.quote: memory unit · own memory only
findings.problem: The hero has three names for one piece of hardware: the picture says 'memory unit', the lead says 'A page-table walker', and Topics says 'MMU'. 'Memory unit' is not the chapter's term ('memory management unit'), and a newcomer can read it as RAM, the opposite of what the line means.
findings.fix: 'MMU · own memory only' (the term Topics and Section 03 use), or 'page-table walker · own memory only' if the spelled-out form must stay and fits the 200-unit column.

findings.quote: C · 1972 · Bell Labs        2016
findings.problem: An amber year counter with no label sits inside the root C box. In the final and static state, which is also the t0 frame, the box reads 'C · 1972 · Bell Labs 2016'. Nothing in the picture, key or description explains the 2016, so a reader takes it as a second date for C. Mid-loop it shows 1984, 2000 and so on, still with no label.
findings.fix: Take the running year out of the C box. Either drop it, since every box already carries its own year, or move it outside the box with a label such as 'year: 1984'. In the final and static state, hide it or show the label 'now: 2016'.

findings.quote: double *d = 0x118
findings.problem: The double pointer stops at 0x118 after 3 steps and stays frozen for steps 4 to 7, while c moves on to 0x107 and p to 0x11C. That breaks the caption's 'take the same step' and the description's 'each is incremented together'. Nothing in the picture says why d stops (a fourth step would leave the 32 bytes shown), so the t2.667 and t5.333 frames show c and p at step 4 or 7 but d at step 3.
findings.fix: Stop all three pointers together after step 3 (c = 0x103, p = 0x10C, d = 0x118). Or keep d's step 4 and show it greyed past the end, with the label 'd + 4 = 0x120: past the 32 bytes'.

findings.quote: p = malloc(64)
findings.problem: The lower panel's step label 'p = malloc(64)' is visible from 0.07 to 0.51 of the loop, the whole time the leak half plays. During that time the chunk still reads 'free' and no line joins p to it (frame t4.333). The label says p has its chunk while the picture shows it does not.
findings.fix: Show the first 'p = malloc(64)' label only from 0.5077, when the chunk turns to "p's data" and the line appears. During the leak phase, leave the lower step label empty or dim the whole lower panel.

findings.quote: Before C, every operating system was rewritten from scratch for every machine.
findings.problem: The hero lead overstates the chapter's own opening: ch5-portability-p1 says 'usually'. It is also wrong in fact. Multics, which the chapter names in ch5-bell-labs-p2, was written in PL/I, and the Burroughs MCP (1961) was written in ESPOL, both before C.
findings.fix: Before C, an operating system was usually written in one machine's assembly and rewritten from scratch for the next.

findings.quote: a[2]   element 2 of a
findings.problem: Nothing in the book explains counting from zero before this figure (no earlier mention of zero-based indexing in parts 1 and 2). A newcomer reads 'element 2' as the second cell, 42, but the highlight lands on the third cell, 99. The arithmetic shows why, but only after the reader has already stumbled.
findings.fix: Change the label to 'element 2, counting from 0'. It fits the right-aligned slot at 13 px.

findings.quote: so `p + 1` always means the next element, never the next byte
findings.problem: 'Never the next byte' is false for the char pointer in this same figure, whose next element is the next byte. The second sentence also restates ch5-pointers-p3 ('not the next byte… The compiler scales the arithmetic for you').
findings.fix: Second sentence: 'The compiler scales pointer arithmetic by the size of the type, so `p + 1` always means the next element, whatever its size.'

findings.quote: The bracket under each pointer is the span a dereference loads
findings.problem: The picture has no bracket under a pointer. Each pointer has its own track, holding a filled block as wide as what it reads, which the description also calls a 'block'.
findings.fix: *What `*p` reads.* The block in each pointer's track is the span a dereference loads: one, four or eight bytes from its address.

findings.quote: where arguments arrive (`edi`/`esi`, `w0`/`w1`, `a0`/`a1`)
findings.problem: The picture and its description say 'a in rdi, b in rsi', but How it works names edi/esi for x86-64. Nothing tells the reader that these are the 32-bit halves of the same registers.
findings.fix: Change to '(`rdi`/`rsi`, `w0`/`w1`, `a0`/`a1`)' to match the picture.

findings.quote: 1971  First Edition: PDP-11 assembly
findings.problem: The 1971 row's opacity animation is '1;1;1;1;1;1;1;1', so it never dims like the other rows. During the walk it is already lit before the timeline reaches it: frame t3.333 shows 1971 lit while 1972 onwards are dim and the bar has only reached 1970.
findings.fix: Give the 1971 group the same opacity values as its neighbours: values="1;1;1;1;0.55;0.55;1;1" with its own keyTimes (lit at 0.395).

findings.quote: five mallocs
findings.problem: During the allocation phase (frame t4) the labels 32, 96 and 64 already float in the unallocated space with no boxes, and the tail already reads 'free 176'. At that moment the remaining free space is 432 bytes after p1, then 304 after p2, not 176. The frame shows sizes of chunks that do not exist yet next to a free tail of the wrong size.
findings.fix: Fade each size label in with its chunk (p3, p4, p5), and show the dashed 'free 176' tail only once p5 is allocated. Before that, leave the unallocated span unmarked or label it 'free'.

findings.quote: x86-64 most PCs … RISC-V open design
findings.problem: The hero colours x86-64 blue and RISC-V red. Fig 5.1, the chapter's first picture of the same three architectures, colours x86-64 amber and RISC-V blue, so blue means a different processor a few screens apart.
findings.fix: Recolour the hero boxes to Fig 5.1's key: x86-64 amber (#d4a853), ARM64 green, RISC-V blue (#86a8ff).

findings.quote: the MMU finds no mapping for address 0 and faults, and the kernel
findings.problem: The caption retells ch5-ub-p5 step by step (unmapped page, fault, kernel, SIGSEGV, process killed), and the picture already draws the same chain box by box. It adds nothing the reader has not just read and seen.
findings.fix: One bad write passes through five layers before anyone sees it; the programmer sees only the last line.

findings.quote: the allocator hands that chunk to the next caller, and every write through the old pointer overwrites their data
findings.problem: Both sentences restate ch5-malloc-p5, which already defines leak and use-after-free with the same consequences ('handed to a different malloc caller… writing it corrupts that data'). The caption does not guide the reader through the picture.
findings.fix: Top: each return without `free` strands a chunk no pointer reaches. Bottom: the chunk freed through `p` goes to `q`, so the write through `p` lands in `q`'s data.

findings.quote: steps by the size of what it points at: 1 byte for a character, 2 for an integer (Fig 5.3)
findings.problem: Fig 5.3 illustrates ch5-bell-labs-p5 under 'The PDP-11', but it sits after the 'K&R, 1978' heading, the K&R paragraph and the Ritchie pull-quote. A reader meets a PDP-7/PDP-11 memory picture inside the K&R subsection and has to scroll back to connect it.
findings.fix: Move the fig-5-3 block to directly after ch5-bell-labs-p5, before the 'K&R, 1978' heading. The ids are unchanged, so the anchor set stays identical.

findings.quote: 2005 a first fix, later undone | 2007 Linux 2.6.22: flaw ships
findings.problem: The timeline cannot be true in the order drawn: a 2005 fix for this race, then the flaw 'ships' two years later. Torvalds's fix commit 19be0eaffa3a calls it 'an ancient bug' that he tried to fix 'eleven years ago' (4ceb5db9757a, 2005-08-01). That fix was undone two days later (f33ea7f404e5, 2005-08-03, GitHub API dates), so the race was already in 2005 kernels. '2.6.22' is the advisories' estimate (dirtycow wiki: 'existed since around 2.6.22'). A careful reader will stop at 'fixed and undone, then shipped'. The same claim makes 'nine years' in ch4-vm-p17 and the caption a lower bound, not the length.
findings.fix: Figure labels: 2005 'a first fix, undone two days later'; 2007 'Linux 2.6.22: oldest kernel the advisories list'; bar 'nine years or more in every kernel'. ch4-vm-p17: 'For at least nine years a race...'. Caption ch4-vm-p18: 'It shipped in Linux for at least nine years, was patched...'. Sources: github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/19be0eaffa3a; commits 4ceb5db9757a and f33ea7f404e5; github.com/dirtycow/dirtycow.github.io/wiki/VulnerabilityDetails.

findings.quote: The earliest multi-tasking systems were cooperative
findings.problem: Time-sharing was preemptive from the start. CTSS was demonstrated in November 1961 and had a clock interrupt, a 200 ms quantum and a multilevel feedback queue (Wikipedia, Compatible_Time-Sharing_System). That is the MLFQ this chapter's own table lists. Ch1-kernel-p4 also says time-sharing used a hardware timer. Cooperative multitasking belongs to the personal-computer systems this paragraph names (Mac OS to 9, 16-bit Windows), not to the earliest systems. Together with p3's 'Modern systems are preemptive', it leaves the reader believing preemption came later.
findings.fix: 'Many early personal-computer systems were _cooperative_: each running program voluntarily yielded control...'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compatible_Time-Sharing_System (clock interrupt, 200 ms quantum, MLFQ, 1961).

findings.quote: a small, dedicated region of the disk where every intended modification is written first
findings.problem: This brings back in prose the error §4g corrected in Fig 4.13 ('A journaling filesystem does every write twice'). By default, ext4 (data=ordered) and NTFS journal only metadata. File contents go straight to their home blocks. The figure's own strip says so two screens later. 'Each change lands whole or not at all' is likewise true only of the structural (metadata) changes.
findings.fix: '...the **journal**, a small, dedicated region of the disk where each change to the filesystem's structure (inodes, free-block maps, directories) is written _first_, then applied...' and 'Each such change lands whole or not at all'. Source: §4g Fig 4.13 row; ext4 data=ordered default (docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/ext4.html).

findings.quote: From that moment, the kernel runs until the machine shuts down.
findings.problem: This echoes the error §4g corrected in the glossary 'kernel' entry ('the one program that always runs'). The ledger notes that the kernel is resident, not running, while a user process runs (OSTEP 6.3). Ch1-kernel-p4 and the glossary now say 'stays loaded'. This sentence says the opposite in the chapter that is about the kernel.
findings.fix: 'From that moment the kernel stays in memory, in charge of the machine, until it shuts down.' Source: §4g glossary 'kernel' row (OSTEP 6.3).

findings.quote: so work that must respond quickly runs on time rather than merely fairly
findings.problem: EEVDF's deadlines are virtual (eligible time plus requested slice over weight), not wall-clock deadlines. EEVDF stays a fair-share scheduler: tasks that ask for shorter slices are picked sooner, but no deadline is guaranteed (docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html). 'Runs on time rather than merely fairly' implies real-time behaviour that trades away fairness, which p12 then denies for general-purpose schedulers. Fig 4.4's strip repeats it: 'so latency-sensitive work runs on time'.
findings.fix: p5: '...but gives every task a virtual deadline set by the slice it asks for, so a task that asks for short slices gets the CPU sooner without taking more than its share.' Fig 4.4 strip: '...picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, so tasks that ask for short slices are served sooner.' Source: docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html.

findings.quote: For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).
findings.problem: The formula needs random (exponential) service times as well as random arrivals: that is what M/M/1 means. With random arrivals and fixed service times (M/D/1), W at 95% load is 10.5 service times, not 20. Fig 4.6's strip has the same gap: '(random arrivals, one server, called M/M/1)'.
findings.fix: p10: 'For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals and random service times, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).' Fig 4.6 strip: '(random arrivals and service times, one server, called M/M/1)'.

findings.quote: 10 requests a second, each inside for 2 seconds, keeps 20 inside at any moment
findings.problem: Little's Law gives the time-average number in the system, and the sentence before it says 'average'. 'At any moment' says the count is constant at 20, which no random queue does.
findings.fix: '10 requests a second, each inside for 2 seconds, keeps 20 inside on average.'

findings.quote: This is how databases and search engines handle large data
findings.problem: Overgeneralised. Some engines map their files (LMDB, Lucene/Elasticsearch). The major relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB, Oracle) deliberately avoid mmap and keep their own buffer pools (Crotty, Leis and Pavlo, 'Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?', CIDR 2022). The shared-library half of the sentence is right.
findings.fix: 'This is how some databases (LMDB) and search engines (Lucene) handle large data, and how every shared library loads on Linux.' Source: Crotty, Leis, Pavlo, CIDR 2022.

findings.quote: the kernel reads just that one page from disk
findings.problem: On Linux, a major fault on a file mapping triggers readahead: the kernel reads a window of neighbouring pages (typically 128 KB), not one page. Also, mmap() creates no page-table entries. It records the file-backed range in the process's list of regions (a VMA), and the entries stay empty until a fault. 'Sets up page table entries marking...as backed by that file' describes bookkeeping Linux does not keep in the page table.
findings.fix: 'It records that this range of addresses is backed by that file and leaves the page-table entries empty... The first time you touch a page, you take a page fault, and the kernel reads that page (and a few neighbours it expects you to want next) from disk.'

findings.quote: Every kernel-managed resource is exposed as a file
findings.problem: The italic 'Every' overclaims. The standard counterexample is network interfaces: Linux has no /dev/eth0, and they are reached through sockets and netlink. System V message queues and semaphores (in this chapter's own IPC table) are not files either. The bullets that follow are true. The universal claim is not.
findings.fix: '_Most_ kernel-managed resources are exposed as files:'

findings.quote: The idea is Edsger Dijkstra's, from his 1965 note "Cooperating Sequential Processes".
findings.problem: Dijkstra invented the semaphore in 1962 or 1963, for the Electrologica X8 operating system (his Dutch note EWD-35). The 1965 monograph EWD123 is its best-known exposition, not its origin. Fig 4.18's strip makes the date explicit: 'The idea is Dijkstra's, from 1965.'
findings.fix: p12: 'The idea is Edsger Dijkstra's, set out in his 1965 note "Cooperating Sequential Processes".' Fig 4.18 strip: 'The idea is Dijkstra's, from the early 1960s.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semaphore_(programming) (1962 or 1963, EWD-35).

findings.quote: Namespaces are translation tables, not copies
findings.problem: True of PID namespaces, which the second half of the sentence illustrates, but stated for all namespaces. A new mount namespace starts as a copy of the caller's mount list (mount_namespaces(7)). A network namespace is a separate instance of the network stack, with its own interfaces, routes and firewall rules (network_namespaces(7)).
findings.fix: 'A PID namespace is a translation table, not a copy: to the host, A's PID 1 is just process 8472.'

findings.quote: gives a new process (or, for PID, the caller's next children) a fresh namespace
findings.problem: This is right for clone(), which starts a new process in the new namespace. It is wrong for unshare(), which moves the calling process itself into the new namespace and creates no new process. The PID exception applies to unshare(): there, only the caller's next children enter it (unshare(2)).
findings.fix: '`clone()` with a flag such as `CLONE_NEWPID` starts a new process in a fresh namespace, which its children inherit; `unshare()` moves the caller itself (for PID, only its next children).' Source: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unshare.2.html.

findings.quote: The Linux kernel, as of 2025, is roughly 30 million lines, nearly all of it C.
findings.problem: In 2025 the tree passed 40 million lines: 40,063,856 at 6.14-rc1 (Heise, January 2025), 38.4 million at 6.16 by cloc. Roughly 30 million is right only for lines of code without comments and blanks (cloc 6.16: 28.9 million). A reader who saw 2025's 'Linux passes 40 million lines' headlines will stop here.
findings.fix: 'The Linux kernel, as of 2025, is roughly 30 million lines of code, nearly all of it C.' Sources: heise.de/-10250618; phoronix.com (Linux 6.16 cloc: 38.4M total, 28.9M code).

findings.quote: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a single fold with no loop in C++23
findings.problem: The fold with no loop is not new in C++23. C++98 already had std::accumulate (<numeric>, ISO 14882:1998 §26.4.1): `int total = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);` sums a vector in one call with no loop, and it is shorter than the C++23 fold_left line. The figure's C++98 panel and caption suggest C++98 forced a hand loop. The real C++23 gain is folding over the whole vector without naming two iterators.
findings.fix: Caption: "Seven standards in twenty-five years, and the same task keeps getting simpler: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a fold over the whole vector in C++23 (C++98's std::accumulate folded too, but between two iterators). The old forms still compile, so the language keeps growing while the recommended way to write it shrinks." The figure's C++23 gloss could also say "the whole of v, no iterators".

findings.quote: C offered no compiler-enforced way to wall parts off from one another
findings.problem: C does have compiler-enforced walls, but they are coarse. A file-scope `static` function or variable has internal linkage, so no other source file can reach it. An opaque struct (declared in the header, defined only in its .c file) makes the compiler reject `p->field` in client code. That pattern is the textbook C abstract data type (Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations, 1996). What C lacked was a wall around a type plus its functions inside one file, and access levels. p3's "nothing grouped functions" overstates in the same way.
findings.fix: Second caption sentence: "C's only walls were the source file and the opaque struct, too coarse to tie a type to its functions, and the classes and access rules of C++ were the answer." Optionally, in p3: "Functions could group statements; only the source file grouped functions."

findings.quote: Simula 67 was designed in 1967 ... expressly for writing simulations
findings.problem: That describes Simula I (1962–65). Dahl and Nygaard designed Simula 67 as a general-purpose language and moved simulation into a library class (SIMULATION). That generalisation is why its class and virtual mechanisms became the OO vocabulary. Source: Dahl and Nygaard, The Development of the SIMULA Languages (HOPL 1978), and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simula: "Simula 67 though was designed to be a general-purpose programming language".
findings.fix: "Simula 67 was designed in 1967 by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard at the Norwegian Computing Center, growing a simulation language into a general-purpose one."

findings.quote: Stroustrup's most original contribution was a rule for resources
findings.problem: RAII was worked out by Stroustrup and Andrew Koenig, 1984–89, as exception-safe resource management. Stroustrup coined the name. Source: Stroustrup, The Design and Evolution of C++ (1994), pp. 383–84 and 388–89, as cited at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization. Giving sole credit overstates it.
findings.fix: "Classes came from Simula, but the most original idea in C++ was a rule for resources: ..." (or "Stroustrup's most original contribution, worked out with Andrew Koenig, ...")

findings.quote: qsort vs std::sort, same algorithm, different cost
findings.problem: The C standard does not say which algorithm qsort uses. glibc's qsort, the common Linux one, is a merge sort with a heapsort fallback: introsort was tried in 2023 and the stable mergesort was put back on 2024-01-15 (libc-alpha patch "stdlib: Reinstate stable mergesort implementation on qsort"). libstdc++'s std::sort is introsort. So 'same algorithm' is often false. The figure's real point, the path of one comparison, does not need it. The caption repeats it: "Same algorithm, a shorter path per comparison".
findings.fix: Title: "qsort vs std::sort, same job, different cost"; caption: "Same sorting job, a shorter path per comparison, ..."

findings.quote: overflows for large values
findings.problem: Large values alone do not overflow the subtraction (2,000,000,000 − 1,000,000,000 is fine). It overflows when the two operands are far apart, for example a large positive minus a large negative. That is how the ledger row for Fig 6.6 states it (§4g: "when the operands are far apart").
findings.fix: "The usual comparator `return *(int*)a - *(int*)b;` overflows when the two values are far apart; `(x > y) - (x < y)` is safe."

findings.quote: `std::sort` takes the comparator as a _template argument_
findings.problem: std::sort takes the comparator as an ordinary function argument. Its type is the template parameter. The per-comparator copy and inlining follow from that type: a lambda or function object gets its own instantiation, while a plain function pointer only gets one for the pointer type. As written it reads as if the comparator itself is passed at compile time.
findings.fix: "`std::sort` takes the comparator's _type_ as a template argument: a template is a recipe the compiler fills in afresh for each type it is given. Here it builds a copy of `std::sort` for that comparator and inlines the comparison..."

findings.quote: Scott Meyers wrote _Effective Modern C++_ (2014) because C++11 had overtaken much of his _Effective C++_
findings.problem: Meyers chose not to revise Effective C++. He wrote a separate book with "42 all-new guidelines", which his site calls "a complement to Scott's existing books" (aristeia.com/books.html, GoingNative 2013 talk notes). Saying C++11 "overtook much of" Effective C++ invents a motive and suggests the older book was largely obsolete, which he did not say.
findings.fix: "*The books.* Rather than revise _Effective C++_, Scott Meyers wrote a new one for C++11 and C++14, _Effective Modern C++_ (2014)."

findings.quote: By the late 1980s these languages ran most systems that mattered
findings.problem: In the late 1980s C++ was barely out (Cfront 2.0 shipped in 1989). Much critical computing still ran on COBOL, Fortran, PL/I, assembly and Ada: banking, airlines, mainframe operating systems, defence. C was strong in UNIX, workstations and much PC software, but 'most systems that mattered' overclaims, especially for C++.
findings.fix: "By the late 1980s these languages ran much of the world's systems software, and many programmers took this as the trade every language must make."

findings.quote: lets the compiler refuse every touch that bypasses the interface
findings.problem: The Fig 6.1 strip ('The wall') says the compiler refuses every bypass. ch6-classes-p6 says private is compile-time only and 'a determined caller can cast their way to it'. The two statements contradict each other.
findings.fix: "*The wall.* A class with private members lets the compiler refuse every ordinary touch that bypasses the interface, cutting the lines that may exist."

findings.quote: When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register
findings.problem: Kept-original Fig BR.3 contradicts the prose beside it. trap-p4 says a SYSCALL system call skips the IDT, but the caption says every trap goes through it, and the SOURCE box draws 'SYSCALL or int 0x80' as an IDT source. The rows '32 · timer (LAPIC) · apic_timer_interrupt' and '33 · keyboard (IRQ 1)' mix hobby-OS/xv6 vector numbers with Linux handler names. In Linux the local APIC timer is vector 0xEC and ISA IRQ 1 is 0x31 (arch/x86/include/asm/irq_vectors.h). This is already open in STATE.md ('Fig BR.3, kept original, contradicts §4g', BLOCKED ON TIGER).
findings.fix: Owner call already queued. Recommended option: change the SOURCE label 'SYSCALL or int 0x80' to 'int 0x80 (legacy)', change the caption's 'When any trap fires' to 'When an exception, an interrupt or an int instruction fires', and remove the vector numbers from the timer and keyboard rows. Sources: Intel SDM vol. 2B, SYSCALL (RIP loaded from IA32_LSTAR); Linux irq_vectors.h (LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR 0xec, ISA_IRQ_VECTOR(irq) = 0x30 + irq).

findings.quote: Traps, interrupts, exceptions: the same mechanism, three names
findings.problem: The h3 above p4 presents trap, interrupt and exception as three names for one thing. The paragraph under it uses trap as the umbrella term, with three kinds (system calls, exceptions, interrupts), and says a SYSCALL system call skips the IDT, so the three do not even share one mechanism.
findings.fix: Change the heading to: "System calls, exceptions, interrupts: three kinds of trap".

findings.quote: No program can raise the bit itself: a trap raises it
findings.problem: p2 and Fig BR.1 say kernel mode is CPL 00 and user mode is 11. Read literally, 'raise the bit' to enter the kernel and 'SYSRET, which lowers it' are the wrong way round, so a reader comparing with the figure stops. The rest of the sentence ('keeps in registers and S pages that Ring 3 cannot change') is hard to parse and makes in advance the point that trap-p7's strip makes in full.
findings.fix: Replace the last two sentences with: "No program can switch the CPU into Ring 0 itself: only a trap does, always at an entry point the kernel chose (Section 02). And `SYSRET`, which returns the CPU to Ring 3, faults outside Ring 0."

findings.quote: it is the subject of Part II, which reads the kernel as a real program
findings.problem: Part II (The Software Layer) is Chapters 4 to 7. Only Chapter 4 reads the kernel, and the list given here (scheduling, virtual memory, files, IPC, bugs) is exactly Ch4's sections. Chapters 5 to 7 cover C, C++ and Python, so a reader is promised a Part II that does not exist. ch1-kernel-p6 already correctly says 'Chapter 4 shows what the kernel does'.
findings.fix: "Everything else is engineering, and it is the subject of Chapter 4, which opens Part II by reading the kernel as a real program: how it schedules processes, ..."

findings.quote: Five small pieces of hardware are what separate a computer from a calculator.
findings.problem: This contradicts ch1-kernel, where the 1950s machines are computers that had none of the five. The five pieces let one computer be shared safely, not make it a computer. After this sentence comes a run of clipped dramatic fragments ('A privilege bit. A trap. A page-table walker. ...'), one of the brief's listed tells. The fragments also name the MMU 'a page-table walker', while Section 03 and the synthesis call the feature the MMU.
findings.fix: "Five small pieces of hardware let one computer be shared safely by many programs: a privilege bit, a trap, a memory management unit, a timer and a way to talk to the world. Together they let one program, the kernel, own the machine, and Part I ends by naming them."

findings.quote: the program names the call in RAX and executes SYSCALL; the CPU saves where it was, switches to Ring 0
findings.problem: The caption retells p2 almost sentence for sentence: RAX, SYSCALL, saving the return address, Ring 0, the registered entry point, the work, SYSRET. The brief says the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: "One write system call, time running down: the program in Ring 3 on the left, the kernel in Ring 0 on the right, and below them the registers that carry the request and the way back. The round trip typically takes under a microsecond."

findings.quote: the device then copies it into RAM on its own while the CPU runs something else
findings.problem: The caption repeats p4's DMA walk-through (small command, device copies on its own, CPU runs other work, completion interrupt) straight after p4 gave it.
findings.fix: "One SSD read in the three steps drawn: the kernel queues a command and rings the doorbell, the drive fills the buffer while process B runs, and an interrupt wakes process A."

findings.quote: Each abstraction programs rely on needs one hardware feature above all
findings.problem: Garden-path syntax: 'abstraction programs' reads as a compound noun until the reader reaches 'needs'. The sentence also restates p2 ('Each rests, almost one to one, on one of the five features ... sets it up at boot').
findings.fix: "Each hardware feature on the left becomes, through the kernel, the abstraction on the right. Take the feature away and the abstraction goes with it: without the MMU there are no separate processes, and without the timer nothing can take the CPU from a program that never yields."

findings.quote: In Ring 3 the silicon itself refuses the privileged instructions and jumps to the kernel instead.
findings.problem: The caption restates p2 (two bits of CS, Ring 0 and Ring 3) and p3 (the CPU refuses the instruction and jumps to the kernel). The strip's CPL and #GP items say the same a third time.
findings.fix: "The same three instructions in each ring: add runs in both, while in Ring 3 the two privileged ones stop at #GP and the CPU jumps to the handler the kernel registered."

findings.quote: The kernel sets a hardware timer to interrupt it at a fixed rate
findings.problem: 'it' grammatically points to the kernel, which is not what gets interrupted. The second sentence repeats p1 and the figure's own label 'C never yielded; the tick took the CPU back'.
findings.fix: "Four milliseconds of one core at 1,000 ticks a second: at each tick the kernel's scheduler picks the next process, and C, stuck in an endless loop, loses the CPU like the others."

findings.quote: so the TLB, a small cache of recent translations, can answer most accesses at once
findings.problem: This is the TLB's third gloss in one section: the Fig BR.4 caption (p3), p5's full definition, and now this caption.
findings.fix: "Programs touch the same few pages again and again, so the TLB can answer most accesses at once. Only a miss pays for the four-read walk, and its translation then replaces the entry used longest ago."

findings.quote: between the CPU and the RAM sits a small piece of silicon called the memory management unit
findings.problem: This introduces the MMU as if it were new. Chapter 1 (ch1-memory-p9) defined it in nearly the same words ('Between the CPU and the RAM sits the Memory Management Unit'), and this chapter has used 'MMU' since mode-p4 and mode-p7.
