The step that explains the bytecode order is missing: the tree puts * under +, so the compiler emits b, c and * before +. A newcomer sees the multiplication run first with nothing to say why.
findings.fix: Draw the products in the strip. Under 'tokens', show five chips: a + b * c. Under 'AST', draw a three-node tree with + at the top, then a and *, with b and c under *. Keep the bytecode and stack below. If there is no room, retitle it 'Fig 7.6 · The eval loop runs a + b * c' and drop 'tokens, a syntax tree' from the desc.

findings.quote: back in Python: one array
findings.problem: The loop is rotated, so on first play the return comes before the call. Book.js unpauses the figure at t=0, about 300 px before it is in view. The first motion is the green climb from BLAS to NumPy to Python (1.8 to 3.1 s) with 'back in Python: one array' (2.6 to 4.8 s). The white descent from Python to the CPU starts only at 5.7 s. A reader arriving at normal speed sees the result before the call.
findings.fix: Rotate the timeline so the white descent starts soon after t=0 (about 0.6 s), with the green climb and 'back in Python: one array' after it. That is a −5.1 s shift on every keyTimes list. The t=0 still is unchanged: no layer lit.

findings.quote: 3.13 free-threaded build
findings.problem: In the default build, T1 computes for 10 ms (0–5 and 10–15) before its I/O wait at 15 ms. In the free-threaded rows it computes for 15 ms (0–15) and starts the same I/O at the same 15 ms. If the program is the same, T1 does 50% more work before an identical wait. The comparison then hides the real gain: without the lock, T1 would reach its I/O and finish sooner.
findings.fix: In the free-threaded T1 row, set runs 0–10 ms, waits on I/O 10–20 ms and runs 20–30 ms (or 20–25 ms and then nothing). Change the desc to match: '…both threads run at the same time, so thread 1 reaches its I/O wait at 10 ms instead of 15.'

findings.quote: class Duck
findings.problem: The 'thing' arrow points at boxes labelled 'class Duck' and 'class Robot', which means the classes themselves. The third box, '42, an int', is a value. announce receives an instance. Passing the class Duck would fail with TypeError (speak() is missing self), not print quack. The labels also mix classes with a value.
findings.fix: Label the three boxes the same way, as values: 'a Duck', 'a Robot', '42, an int' (or 'Duck()', 'Robot()', '42'). Keep 'speak()' and the returned string under each.

findings.quote: no shared parent class, no declared interface
findings.problem: Strictly false in Python 3. Every class, Duck and Robot included, inherits from object. The prose says it correctly: 'with no shared parent class required'. A reader who knows Python will stop at the drawn claim.
findings.fix: Change the drawn footer to 'no shared parent with speak(), no declared interface'.

findings.quote: Exact times vary with the machine; the ratio stays in the thousands.
findings.problem: The figure draws a ratio of 10,000. The bars, 0.012 s and 120 s, are exactly 4 decades apart, and the desc says 'roughly ten thousand times'. The How it works says the ratio 'stays in the thousands', which reads as 1,000 to 9,999.
findings.fix: Change it to: 'Exact times vary with the machine; the gap stays at three to four powers of ten.'

findings.quote: import dis; dis.dis("a + b * c") prints this bytecode.
findings.problem: On 3.11 and later, a reader who runs it sees two extra instructions the figure does not show: RESUME at the start and RETURN_VALUE at the end. The figure looks incomplete.
findings.fix: Change it to: 'import dis; dis.dis("a + b * c") prints this bytecode, between a RESUME and a RETURN_VALUE.'

findings.quote: 1 and 2
findings.problem: The legend keys only gold ('1 and 2') and green ('3'). A third, grey bar runs from above 1980s down to 1994 and has no key. It could be ABC, Python 0.x or the timeline spine.
findings.fix: Either add a grey key, 'before 1.0', after '3' in the legend, or remove the grey bar and start the gold bar at 1991 as Python 0.9.

findings.quote: Python grew from a project van Rossum began over Christmas 1989 into the everyday language of data science.
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p1 (Christmas 1989, then spread into data science). It also names something the picture does not show: data science is not on the timeline. Only the second sentence, the 2008–2020 split, describes the figure.
findings.fix: Cut the first sentence. The caption becomes: 'Python's defining event is the split: Python 3 broke compatibility in 2008, and Python 2 lived beside it for twelve years before it was retired in 2020.'

findings.quote: ABC, a teaching language at CWI
findings.problem: The picture and desc call ABC 'a teaching language'. Two paragraphs earlier, p1 calls it 'a research language called ABC'. On the same page the two labels read as a disagreement.
findings.fix: Use one label in both places. In p1, change it to 'a teaching language called ABC', which matches the figure and ABC's purpose.

findings.quote: 0.9.0 posted to Usenet
findings.problem: The figure and desc spell it 'Usenet'. The prose just above (p1) spells it 'USENET's discussion groups'. Two spellings of one name sit side by side.
findings.fix: Change p1 to 'In 1991 he posted it to Usenet's discussion groups', matching the figure.

findings.quote: print(x * x)
findings.problem: The source gives the loop body four leading spaces. SVG collapses them and the line is centred, so the indent shows as an accidental half-shift of about 2.5 characters, not a block. This is the opening picture of the chapter that teaches 'the layout you see is the structure the interpreter sees'.
findings.fix: Left-align both code lines at one x (text-anchor start, e.g. x=180). Write the indent as non-breaking spaces, as Fig 7.3 does: '    print(x * x)'.

findings.quote: slow but predictable
findings.problem: The chapter never claims or teaches that the interpreter is 'predictable', and the reader has nothing to connect it to. Its own GIL and garbage-collection story points the other way.
findings.fix: Change the third interpreter line to 'slow, one step at a time', or use a phrase the chapter teaches: 'checks types as it runs'.

findings.quote: copper | Ethernet, up to 100 m
findings.problem: This brings back an error the ledger already fixed (UNDER.md §4g, the 'Fig 8.2: the router-to-provider hop' row). The 100 m limit applies to an Ethernet run inside a building. The router-to-provider hop is DSL over telephone pair (a few km), cable coax or fibre. Pass 28 changed the label to 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km' and the desc to 'Ethernet to 100 m, DSL for a few kilometres' (bf00333). The Pass 30 Gate 2 repair (93184ba) put back 'Ethernet, up to 100 m', and the desc now reads 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run)'. Ledger law: re-introducing a corrected error is a failed pass.
findings.fix: Label under 'copper': 'DSL or coax, a few km' (or restore 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km'). Desc: 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (a telephone pair carrying DSL for a few kilometres, or cable coax) or on fibre.' The 'Copper' item in the How it works strip can stay as it is: it describes Ethernet runs in general.

findings.quote: The same voltage transition that switched a transistor in Chapter 1 ... now travels: ... across an ocean
findings.problem: Says a voltage transition crosses the ocean. §4g (the Fig 8.1 row) fixed this exact claim in the figure: today's transatlantic cables carry light in glass fibre, not voltage. Fig 8.1's caption now says 'in copper or in glass', so the opening paragraph contradicts its own figure and the corrected fact.
findings.fix: 'The same kind of transition that switched a transistor in Chapter 1 (...) now travels: across the motherboard, out a network interface, down a cable as voltage, across an ocean as light in glass, into another machine on the other side of the planet.' If the section title is not owner text, change 'the voltage on a continent' to match (e.g. 'The signal on a transistor extends to the signal across a continent').

findings.quote: How do you keep a voltage signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre?
findings.problem: Fibre carries no voltage signal. It carries light, as ch8-substrates-p3 and Fig 8.1 say. The paragraph's last sentence, 'The voltage on a wire is the substrate', repeats the copper-only framing for a chapter about copper, fibre and radio. This is the same error class as the corrected Fig 8.1 caption.
findings.fix: 'How do you keep a signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre? ...' and 'The signal on the medium is the substrate; everything else in the next five chapters is what we build on top of it.'

findings.quote: now in the Computer History Museum, is a hand-drawn diagram on a piece of yellow paper, dated "May 22, 1973" in the corner
findings.problem: No source found supports these specifics. The sketches are hand-drawn diagrams in Metcalfe's typed memo of 22 May 1973, written on an IBM Selectric with the subject 'Ether Acquisition' (CHM, This Day in History, May 22). The well-known reproduction is a composite of those sketches, credited to PARC (digibarn.com/collections/diagrams/ethernet-original). No source found mentions yellow paper, a date in the corner, or the museum holding the original. Also, 'the basic architecture of every wired LAN since' contradicts p4: switched stars replaced the shared cable it draws.
findings.fix: 'His first Ethernet memo, typed on 22 May 1973 and full of hand-drawn diagrams, shows the idea: many computers tapped onto one shared cable, the "ether".' Drop the museum, paper and corner details, and drop 'every wired LAN since' (or say 'every Ethernet frame since', which p4 supports).

findings.quote: Metcalfe analysed the math on the plane home
findings.problem: The documented sequence is different. Metcalfe read Abramson's 1970 ALOHA paper in spring 1972, and the thesis was rejected in June 1972. He then spent months in Hawaii modelling ALOHAnet with Abramson's students and presented the results at a University of Hawaii conference. He returned to PARC in late October 1972 and added the analysis to the thesis in May 1973 (historyofcomputercommunications.info, section 8.7). His main finding was that a realistic, finite-user ALOHA becomes unstable under heavy load unless stations back off. 'On the plane home' is an embellishment.
findings.fix: 'He spent the next months there modelling ALOHAnet, found that under heavy load its retransmissions could swamp the channel unless stations backed off and waited, wrote that analysis into a revised thesis, and got his doctorate in 1973.'

findings.quote: WPA2 (2004, broken 2017 by the KRACK attack) to WPA3 (2018, still standing)
findings.problem: The sentence calls WPA2 'broken' by KRACK, a flaw fixed by patches. By the same measure WPA3 did not stay unbroken: the 2019 Dragonblood attacks (Vanhoef and Ronen) recovered passwords from WPA3-SAE through timing and cache side channels and a transition-mode downgrade. Patches and a spec update followed (papers.mathyvanhoef.com/dragonblood.pdf).
findings.fix: '... to WPA3 (2018; the flaws found in it in 2019 were patched, and it still stands)', or simply 'WPA3 (2018)'.

findings.quote: Raspberry Pi devices begin `B8:27:EB`
findings.problem: Only boards up to the Pi 3 use B8:27:EB. The Pi 4 and 400 use the Raspberry Pi Ltd prefixes DC:A6:32 or E4:5F:01 (Raspberry Pi whitepaper RP-003474, 'Changing MAC addresses'), and the Pi 5 uses others again. A reader who checks a current Pi will see a different prefix.
findings.fix: 'older Raspberry Pi boards begin `B8:27:EB`, newer ones `DC:A6:32` and others; Apple's begin `00:03:93` or any of a few hundred other prefixes.' (Fig 8.9's 'B8:27:EB = Raspberry Pi Foundation' is correct and can stay.)

findings.quote: both directions on separate wire pairs (full duplex)
findings.problem: True of 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX only. Gigabit Ethernet (1000BASE-T), the usual link today, sends both directions on all four pairs at once and separates them by echo cancellation. Full duplex does not need separate pairs.
findings.fix: 'With one device per switch port and both ends able to send at the same time (full duplex), collision detection never fires.'

findings.quote: doubling the bandwidth doubles the capacity outright
findings.problem: This holds only if the SNR stays the same. With the same transmit power, doubling the bandwidth doubles the noise power, so the SNR drops by 3 dB. The capacity then grows by less than double (at low SNR, hardly at all). 'Outright' invites the false belief that bandwidth is a free doubling.
findings.fix: '...doubling the bandwidth at the same SNR doubles the capacity.'

findings.quote: cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
findings.problem: Contradicts the figure's own strip ('from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz') and the §4g Fig 8.2 correction ('cellular uses bands below 1 GHz as well as up to tens of GHz'). 5G millimetre-wave bands sit at 24 to 47 GHz, and 600 MHz bands (e.g. band 71) are in use.
findings.fix: 'cellular from about 600 MHz to tens of GHz'

findings.quote: TEMPEST, a US classification programme dating to the 1960s
findings.problem: TEMPEST is not a classification programme. It is the NSA codename for an emission-security specification, with a NATO certification alongside. The shielding standards date from the late 1950s: NAG-1 in 1958, then Directive 5200.19 in 1964 and NSA implementation in 1966 (Wikipedia, 'Tempest (codename)').
findings.fix: 'This is the basis of *TEMPEST*, the NSA codename for standards, set from the late 1950s, for shielding sensitive equipment against precisely this.'

findings.quote: By the 1990s, switches replaced the shared cable.
findings.problem: 'By the 1990s' puts the change at or before 1990. The first Ethernet switch, Kalpana's EtherSwitch, appeared in 1990. Early in the decade most LANs still shared one collision domain, first on coax and then on 10BASE-T hubs. Switching spread through the 1990s.
findings.fix: 'During the 1990s, switches replaced the shared cable.'

findings.quote: Ethernet, up to 100 m
findings.problem: This is a corrected error that came back, so the §4g fact law applies. The §4g row 'Fig 8.2: the router-to-provider hop labelled Ethernet runs up to 100 m' was fixed on 2026-10-11 to read 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km'. Pass 30 Gate 2 repair round 1 (commit 93184ba) put the old label back on the router-to-provider hop. It also changed the desc to 'twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run'. A 100 m Ethernet run cannot reach the provider: that hop is the phone line (DSL, a few km), coax or fibre. The picture also shows only copper, while its caption says 'copper or fibre'.
findings.fix: Change the drawn label to "phone line, a few km" (20 characters; fits the box). Change the desc to "From router to internet provider it travels on copper (the phone line, carrying DSL for a few kilometres) or on fibre." Keep the 100 m Ethernet limit only in the How it works copper bullet, where it describes cabling inside a building.

findings.quote: then B sends
findings.problem: The animation shows B transmitting while A's signal is still on the cable. A's second frame fills the cable from 0.40 to 0.674 of the cycle, but B's bar starts at 0.558. Frame t6.867 shows orange running from A to a third of the way along and blue from there to B. That is the same picture as the opening collision, minus the red block, shown under the label 'then B sends'. It contradicts the desc ('then sends once A has finished') and the carrier-sense rule the figure teaches.
findings.fix: Have A's frame end before B starts. Either sweep A's tail from A to B (x 66 to 334, width 268 to 0) and finish at the moment B's bar begins, or start B's bar (and the 'then B sends' label) at 0.674, when A's bar has cleared.

findings.quote: line busy: B waits
findings.problem: The label appears at 0.2765 of the cycle, but A's resent signal reaches B only at 0.4029. In frame t3.433, A's bar is less than halfway along the cable while B already says it hears a busy line. The figure's whole point is that a station hears another only after the signal arrives ('B has not heard it yet').
findings.fix: Start the 'line busy: B waits' label at keyTime 0.4029, when A's bar reaches B. Before that, B's line already reads 'B: wait 1 slot', which covers the gap.

findings.quote: Wi-Fi 6 · 6.7
findings.problem: Fig 8.4 labels a point 'Wi-Fi 6' and caps it at 6.7 bits per hertz. Three figures later, the Fig 8.7 caption says Wi-Fi 6 packs '10 in Wi-Fi 6' bits per symbol. The book never separates bits per symbol from bits per hertz, so a careful reader will ask whether Wi-Fi 6 beats Shannon's limit. It does not: 1024-QAM needs roughly 35 dB, where the limit is about 11.6. But the 20 dB point is drawn as if it were Wi-Fi 6 itself.
findings.fix: Change the drawn label to "Wi-Fi at 20 dB · 6.7" and the desc to "A Wi-Fi link at about 20 dB is allowed about 6.7 bits per hertz." In the Fig 8.7 caption, write "10 in Wi-Fi 6 on a strong, clean signal".

findings.quote: are the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart
findings.problem: The first caption sentence does not parse: 'the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart' reads as a garble, and a reader has to go back to work out that the two distances are what lie twelve orders apart.
findings.fix: "A bit crossing a micrometre of chip wiring and a bit crossing 5,600 km of ocean are the same thing, at scales more than twelve orders of magnitude apart: a signal guided along a line, in copper or in glass."

findings.quote: physical · wire
findings.problem: The hero's four-layer stack reads application / transport / network / physical · wire. That matches neither model the chapter teaches. Fig 8.12 gives TCP/IP's four layers as Application, Transport, Internet, Link, and OSI has seven. The stack also leaves out the link layer, where section 05's Ethernet, MAC addresses, ARP and switches all live. The chapter's closing line says it covered the physical and link layers.
findings.fix: Relabel the stack with the TCP/IP names from Fig 8.12: "application", "transport", "internet", "link · wire".

findings.quote: A sends; B has not heard it yet
findings.problem: This label disappears at 0.869 of the cycle. B's bar only starts at 0.927, and the collision label comes at 0.976. For about a second there is no step text, and B starting (the step that causes the collision, and that the desc names: 'B, which has not yet heard A, starts too') has no label.
findings.fix: Hold 'A sends; B has not heard it yet' until 0.927. Then show "B hears nothing and starts too" until the collision label at 0.976.

findings.quote: they reached 33.6 kbps, 9.8 bits per hertz
findings.problem: The caption and desc give the band as 3.4 kHz. A reader who divides gets 33.6 / 3.4 = 9.88, which rounds to 9.9, not the 9.8 drawn. The §4g row bases 9.8 on 3.43 kHz (33.6 / 3.43 = 9.80), but the text rounds that away.
findings.fix: Write "the 3.43 kHz band" in the caption and desc (30 dB over 3.43 kHz still gives about 34 kbps), and keep 9.8.

findings.quote: phone line · 10
findings.problem: The orange V.34 dot (9.8) sits 2.4 viewBox units below the cyan phone-line dot (10). At 375 px it almost covers it, leaving only a thin cyan sliver. The point the caption makes ('just under it') cannot be seen: V.34 looks as if it sits on the curve.
findings.fix: Draw V.34 as a hollow orange ring around the phone-line dot, or give it a short leader to a dot clearly below the curve. Keep both labels.

findings.quote: and the curve is symmetric between them
findings.problem: The curve is symmetric about p = 0.5, which is the fair coin. It is not symmetric 'between' a constant source and a fair coin. The phrasing blurs the symmetry the How it works strip states precisely.
findings.fix: "...a fair coin carries one full bit per flip, and the curve is symmetric about it."

findings.quote: its size (AM), how fast it oscillates (FM) or its phase (PSK)
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence and its QAM clause repeat ch8-encoding-p6, which sits directly above, almost word for word: size, how fast it oscillates, phase, and QAM changing size and phase together.
findings.fix: "The same four bits sent three ways: big or small, fast or slow, starting up or down; the receiver reads only the property its scheme changes. QAM changes size and phase at once, up to 10 bits per symbol in Wi-Fi 6."

findings.quote: TCP/IP folds OSI's top three layers into one Application layer
findings.problem: The first caption sentence repeats ch8-layers-p3: both folds, each with the same reason. The Fig 8.11 caption has already said it as well ('the top three blur into the application... four layers of TCP/IP'). The reader gets the same point three times in a row.
findings.fix: Keep only the new idea: "OSI's seven boxes collapse into TCP/IP's four; OSI says where a feature belongs, TCP/IP describes what is on the wire."

findings.quote: continent
findings.problem: The wire is cut by a square knockout (382 to 458), not by the globe circle, so it ends about 12 units short of the globe's edge. The pulse then crosses that empty gap into the globe with no wire under it, so the signal never visibly reaches the continent.
findings.fix: Use the circle (cx 420, cy 240, r 38) as the wire's knockout instead of the square, so the wire meets the globe's edge. Fade the pulse out at that edge.

findings.quote: copper, fiber, radio
findings.problem: The hero lead (and the Part III contents entry on line 78) spells it 'fiber', while every chapter paragraph, figure and caption uses 'fibre'. The first paragraph of the chapter breaks the book's own spelling.
findings.fix: Change it to "copper, fibre, radio" in ch8-hero-lead and in the toc-desc line of part-3.html.

findings.quote: works on _any_ object that has a `read()` method (a file, a network socket, a stand-in for testing)
findings.problem: A Python socket has no read() method. socket.socket offers recv() and send(); on CPython 3.14, hasattr(socket.socket(), 'read') is False. Only sock.makefile() and ssl.SSLSocket have read(). The example meant to show duck typing working names an object that would actually raise AttributeError, which is the exact failure Fig 7.3 shows.
findings.fix: "(a file, an HTTP response, a stand-in for testing)". http.client.HTTPResponse has read(). Checked locally on CPython 3.14.0: socket.socket has no read(); makefile() and SSLSocket do.

findings.quote: Dynamically typed languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby) check types at runtime.
findings.problem: The paragraph then says the same program "dies there with a `TypeError`". That is true for Python and Ruby but not for JavaScript, which usually converts the value and carries on: f("5") with n*2 returns 10, and f("abc") returns NaN, with no error. A reader comes away thinking JavaScript fails loudly the way Python does. JavaScript's silent coercion is the textbook counterexample, and Section 02 points at it when it calls Python's `1 + "a"` an error "rather than a guess".
findings.fix: Simplest: "Dynamically typed languages (Python, Ruby) check types at runtime." Or keep JavaScript and scope the next sentence: "The same Python program starts without complaint, runs until it reaches the mistake, and dies there with a `TypeError`; JavaScript often converts the value instead and carries on."

findings.quote: you give up an order of magnitude of performance
findings.problem: This understates the chapter's own numbers. Fig 7.9 shows 10,000 times (four orders of magnitude) for the matmul. Even pure C loops against pure Python loops typically differ by one to two orders of magnitude, not one. This is the still-open §4o hero-lead flag from Pass 20 (UNDER.md, item 2 of 'Flagged for the owner read'), parked for the punch-list pass. It is the first claim the reader meets in the chapter.
findings.fix: "you give up one to two orders of magnitude of performance in code that runs in Python itself". Sources: the Computer Language Benchmarks Game (CPython against C, typically 10 to 100 times or more), and the chapter's own Fig 7.9.

findings.quote: Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost nothing at run time
findings.problem: This misstates Stroustrup's zero-overhead principle and contradicts Chapter 6. Ch6 (ch6-zerocost-p1) gives the principle as "you do not pay for what you do not use, and what you do use is as fast as anything you could have written by hand" and calls the slogan "slightly misleading". ch6-stroustrup-p5 says a virtual method costs a hidden pointer and an indirect call. Stroustrup never held that abstractions cost nothing, only that they cost no more than hand-written code.
findings.fix: "Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost no more at run time than the code you would have written by hand". Source: Stroustrup, The Design and Evolution of C++ (1994): "What you don't use, you don't pay for. And further: What you do use, you couldn't hand code any better."

findings.quote: Every Python statement becomes hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop, plus the actual work.
findings.problem: This overstates simple statements by about two times on today's CPython, and "Every" makes it universal. Measured with /usr/bin/time -l (instructions retired) on CPython 3.14.0 on an Apple M4 Pro, taking the difference over 30M loop iterations with loop overhead subtracted: x = a + b is about 91 instructions including the add itself; x = o.v is about 70; x = f() is about 230. §4g already removed Fig 7.7's unsourced "~150 instructions" because 3.11+ specialises these paths.
findings.fix: "Every Python statement becomes dozens to hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop, plus the actual work."

findings.quote: The result was the first interpreter that mattered
findings.problem: This is an overclaim of 'first'. Interpreters were in production use years before Lisp: Mauchly's Short Code on UNIVAC (1950) and Backus's Speedcoding on the IBM 701 (1953), which was widely used and led directly to FORTRAN. The sentence implies those did not matter.
findings.fix: "The result was a working interpreter: a program that read each Lisp expression at runtime and executed it directly, without ever producing a separate binary." The paragraph's first sentence already says it was the first Lisp interpreter.

findings.quote: ran on an IBM 704 at MIT in 1959 ... who had been transcribing the paper
findings.problem: There are two problems. (1) Date: Russell's two firsthand accounts say McCarthy brought him the half-page eval in October or November 1958, he hand-compiled it for "probably six weeks", and "By December, I had a working interpreter" (Smithsonian NMAH AC1498, 2017). The 2008 CHM oral history says the same: "I got something working before Christmas". McCarthy's accounts put eval in the 1959 paper work, so the primary sources conflict; 1959 is not settled. (2) Neither oral history says Russell was transcribing the paper. Both say he had been hand-compiling Lisp functions into 704 code. Pass 20 declined this flag, citing "I'd been hand-compiling all sorts of things like that", but that quote supports hand-compiling, not transcribing.
findings.fix: "The first Lisp interpreter ran on an IBM 704 at MIT around the turn of 1959." Also replace "who had been transcribing the paper" with "who had spent months hand-translating Lisp functions into machine code". Sources: CHM oral history of Steve Russell, 2008, X4970.2009, pp. 8–9; Smithsonian transcript, 2017.

findings.quote: at 25 ms thread 1 takes the lock back
findings.problem: Fig 7.4 draws T1 running and T2 waiting from 25 ms, but CPython does not hand the GIL back that way. A thread returning from I/O waits for the GIL. Only after one full switch interval (5 ms) with no handoff does it set the drop request (take_gil in Python/ceval_gil.c, the 3.2+ GIL). So T2 keeps running until about 30 ms. The figure's own first three handoffs follow this rule; the fourth breaks it, and it hides the well-known I/O convoy cost.
findings.fix: Desc and drawing: "at 25 ms thread 1's I/O is done and it waits for the lock; thread 2 hands it over when the 5 ms interval runs out, at 30 ms." Draw T1 grey (waits for GIL) and T2 green from 25 to 30 ms.

findings.quote: in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs somewhat slower in it.
findings.problem: In 3.13 the overhead was about 40% on pyperformance. That is the same size the prose (ch7-gil-p2) calls a failure ("30–50%"), so "somewhat" understates it and blurs the 3.13 to 3.14 progress the prose describes.
findings.fix: "in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs about 40% slower in it (about 5–10% in 3.14)." Source: docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html ("In 3.13, this overhead is about 40% on the pyperformance suite").

findings.quote: Every Python object carries a count of how many names point to it
findings.problem: The reference count counts every reference: list slots, dict values, attributes and stack entries, not just names. Since ch7-types-p1 defines a variable as a name, a reader can conclude that an object held only in a list has a count of zero and would be freed.
findings.fix: "Every Python object carries a count of how many references point to it (names, list slots, attributes)"

findings.quote: Every web framework that accepted pickled session cookies has been bitten by this
findings.problem: This is a universal claim with no source. What is documented is narrower: Django's ticket #29708 says RCEs "continue to happen" despite MAC-signed pickled cookies once a key leaks (PickleSerializer was deprecated in 4.1; JSON has been the default since 1.6), and Pyramid 2.0 switched SignedCookieSessionFactory from pickle to JSON for the same RCE risk. The owner's register here is kept; only the quantifier overreaches.
findings.fix: "Web frameworks that kept sessions in pickled cookies were bitten by this, and moved to JSON;". Keep the rest of the sentence as is. Sources: code.djangoproject.com/ticket/29708; pyramid.readthedocs.io whatsnew-2.0.

findings.quote: it spread into data science, scientific computing and most of the world's introductory programming courses.
findings.problem: There is no global count of introductory courses behind "most". The usual source, Guo 2014 (CACM blog), covers top US CS departments only (8 of the top 10 taught Python first).
findings.fix: "and many of the world's introductory programming courses."

findings.quote: is ten thousand lines of C in a file called `ceval.c`, with a case for every bytecode instruction.
findings.problem: In 3.14, the release the chapter treats as current, ceval.c is 3,731 lines. Since 3.12 the instruction cases are written in bytecodes.c (5,557 lines) and generated into generated_cases.c.h (12,541 lines), which ceval.c includes at line 1127. Ten thousand matches neither the file nor the sum (about 16.3k). Pass 20 declined this flag by counting the include (3.13: about 9.4k), but by that reckoning 3.14 is about 16k. A reader who opens ceval.c finds no switch cases.
findings.fix: Drop the number: "is a loop in C, in a file called `ceval.c`, with a case for every bytecode instruction." Source: python/cpython 3.14 branch, line counts of Python/ceval.c, Python/bytecodes.c and Python/generated_cases.c.h.

findings.quote: Depending on how you count, between 35% and 45% of internet traffic is IPv6 in 2025.
findings.problem: No 2025 traffic measure gives that range. Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review counts 29% of dual-stack requests over IPv6 (28% in 2024). Google's user share peaked at 49.56% on 21 June 2025. Pass 28 replaced Fig 9.8's 'about 40% of traffic' with the Google user figure for exactly this reason, but the prose still says 'traffic', and its 35% floor leaves out Cloudflare's 29%.
findings.fix: "In 2025 close to half of Google's users reached it over IPv6, but only 29% of requests to Cloudflare did." Sources: blog.cloudflare.com/radar-2025-year-in-review ("29% of IPv6-capable requests ... up from 28% in 2024"); pulse.internetsociety.org/blog/18-years-later-ipv6-reaches-majority (49.56% on 21 June 2025).

findings.quote: A forger never sees the reply, so it cannot hold a TCP conversation
findings.problem: This contradicts the book's own Ch10 (ch10-attacks), which tells how Mitnick held exactly such a blind, spoofed TCP connection on Christmas Day 1994 by predicting the ISN, an attack Morris described in 1985. A reader of Ch10 meets the opposite claim one chapter later. It is hard only because sequence numbers are now random.
findings.fix: "A forger never sees the reply, so unless it can guess TCP's sequence numbers (Chapter 10's Mitnick story) it cannot hold a conversation; spoofing suits single packets, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood relies on it."

findings.quote: the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream, where PCCW passed its customer's announcement on without filtering it
findings.problem: This puts the whole mistake upstream. In the RIPE NCC RIS case study, Pakistan Telecom (AS 17557) itself started the unauthorised announcement of 208.65.153.0/24 to its upstream, and PCCW (AS 3491) then spread it. The chapter's own hero lead says the opposite ('a misconfigured router in Pakistan'), so the reader gets two different culprits.
findings.fix: "The block was a domestic order; the outage came from two configuration mistakes: Pakistan Telecom announced its block route to its upstream PCCW, and PCCW passed it on without filtering it." Source: ripe.net/publications/news/youtube-hijacking-a-ripe-ncc-ris-case-study.

findings.quote: take YouTube off the air for the whole world for two hours
findings.problem: Overclaim. Fig 9.11's caption says 'almost everywhere', and YouTube's /25s won most traffic back at 20:18, 91 minutes after 18:47. The /24 was withdrawn at 21:01. (The hero lead is not on the owner-text list; skip this if it counts as owner text.)
findings.fix: "take YouTube off the air for most of the world for about two hours."

findings.quote: somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (by rough estimates, about ten percent of the internet
findings.problem: The usual estimate is about 6,000 of the roughly 60,000 hosts then online (FBI 30th-anniversary account), and Stoll counted about 2,000. No source gives 10,000, and 10,000 would be a sixth of the internet, not 'about ten percent', so the sentence disagrees with itself.
findings.fix: "about six thousand machines (by the usual rough estimate, a tenth of the sixty thousand then online)". Sources: FBI, 'The Morris Worm' (2018): 'an estimated 6,000 of the approximately 60,000 computers'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_worm.

findings.quote: and weak passwords in rsh
findings.problem: The rsh/rexec route used trusted-host logins that needed no password. Weak passwords were a separate route: the worm cracked the password file and logged in with what it guessed. Passwords are not 'in rsh'.
findings.fix: "and the password-free trusted logins of rsh, helped by passwords it could guess". Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_worm (rexec/rsh 'with no password requirements'; dictionary attack on weak passwords).

findings.quote: Charley Kline, a graduate student in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA
findings.problem: UCLA's alumni history lists him as 'Charley Kline '70, M.S. '71, Ph.D. '80', a student assistant. A 1970 bachelor's means he was an undergraduate in October 1969. Primary accounts (UCLA, the ARPANET record) call him a 'student programmer'.
findings.fix: "Charley Kline, a student programmer in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA". Source: UCLA Alumni, 'UCLA History' (alumni.ucla.edu).

findings.quote: Those two letters, LO, were the network's first packets.
findings.problem: Claim of a 'first'. Before the host-to-host login attempt, the UCLA and SRI IMPs had already exchanged test and routing traffic over the line. LO was the first host-to-host message, which is how Kleinrock and the IMP log ('talked to SRI host to host') describe it.
findings.fix: "Those two letters, LO, were the network's first host-to-host message."

findings.quote: The "LO" message was packet switching going live
findings.problem: Two sentences earlier the same paragraph says Davies 'built a small working network at NPL by 1969'. The NPL Mark I was running in early 1969, before 29 October, so 'packet switching going live' contradicts the paragraph's own history.
findings.fix: "The "LO" message was the ARPANET's packet switching going live, though ARPA built it ..." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPL_network ('operational in early 1969 then fully operational in January 1970').

findings.quote: thousands of homes share one public address
findings.problem: Scale overclaim, by about ten times. One address has about 64,000 ports, and each outgoing connection takes one, as the figure itself shows. A home keeps hundreds of connections open, so CGNAT port blocks are typically 256 to 1,000+ ports per subscriber: tens to a few hundred homes per address. Thousands of homes share a CGNAT's pool of addresses, not one address.
findings.fix: "dozens or even hundreds of homes share one public address"

findings.quote: for almost exactly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice
findings.problem: 'Almost exactly' is more precise than the dates allow. The telephone was patented in 1876 and the first commercial exchange opened in 1878 (New Haven). That is 91 to 93 years before the 1969 ARPANET the chapter sets it against.
findings.fix: "for nearly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice"

findings.quote: set by the sender and verified nowhere along the path
findings.problem: Fig 9.4's strip ('no router checks it') says the same. Both clash with the chapter's next sentence (most ISPs filter, BCP 38) and with Fig 9.10, which shows edge routers checking sources by uRPF. What is true is that IP itself has no check.
findings.fix: ch9-security-p1: "is set by the sender and nothing in IP itself verifies it"; Fig 9.4 strip: "The sender writes it and IP itself never checks it, which is why a source address alone proves nothing."

findings.quote: For thousands of network waits, Python's asyncio shares one thread among many tasks
findings.problem: This paragraph explains why the GIL exists (reference counts, the lost update, PEP 703, 3.13/3.14). Its last sentence jumps to asyncio without any link to the GIL. The reader is never told why asyncio answers the problem: a waiting thread needs no core, so one thread is enough for work that mostly waits. The paragraph ends up doing two jobs, and the event-loop mechanism appears only in Fig 7.5's caption.
findings.fix: Take the sentence out of p2 and make it its own paragraph after Fig 7.4, with a new id (ch7-gil-p5). Give it the missing 'because': "A thread that is waiting needs no core, so a program that spends its time on network replies loses little to the GIL. For thousands of such waits, Python's asyncio shares one thread among many tasks, each handing it over only where it says await, as the Bridge's cooperative programs yielded (Fig 7.5)."

findings.quote: The parser assembles tokens into an abstract syntax tree.
findings.problem: Section 01 already walked the pipeline through tokens and an AST twice: for C in interpret-p2, then for Python (tokens, AST, bytecode, a C loop) in interpret-p3. cpython-p2 tells the same chain a third time and sets each stage in bold as if new. cpython-p1 also bolds CPython as a new term, although interpret-p3 already introduced it as 'the standard interpreter'. The only new material in p2 is the indentation tokens, the stack machine and ceval.c.
findings.fix: Keep the bold glossary sites (compiler, evaluator) and only the new material: "CPython names the four stages of Section 01's pipeline. The tokeniser also turns indentation changes into tokens; the parser builds the AST; the compiler emits bytecode for a stack machine, which computes on the values at the top of a stack (Fig 7.6); and the evaluator, the loop from Section 01, is ten thousand lines of C in a file called ceval.c, with a case for every bytecode instruction." In cpython-p1, take the bold off CPython.

findings.quote: The interpreter notices that a + keeps seeing ints and swaps in a specialised instruction
findings.problem: Fig 7.7's strip repeats two strips the reader has just opened. Its 'Since 3.11' bullet repeats Fig 7.6's 'Since 3.11' bullet in the same section (the interpreter specialises hot instructions once it has seen their types). Its 'JIT compilers' bullet repeats Fig 7.1's 'In between' bullet (PyPy turns hot code into machine code).
findings.fix: Build on the earlier strips rather than repeating them. "Since 3.11. The specialised instruction of Fig 7.6 (BINARY_OP_ADD_INT) skips step 3's lookup, though not the boxes." and "JIT compilers. PyPy, met in Fig 7.1, compiles hot loops with the types it has observed, removing most of the steps."

findings.quote: C pays for translation once, on the developer's machine, and every run executes native code
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p2 and p3, which sit just above it: in advance on the developer's machine, at runtime on the user's machine, the cached bytecode, interpretation on every run. The pass-29 rule says the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture. The caption's second sentence (portability) is new and is the only part that earns its place.
findings.fix: Replace the first sentence with one that points at the picture: "Each program runs three times; only Python's eval loop repeats its work on every run. Python ships source that runs wherever there is an interpreter, and pays in cycles each time it runs."

findings.quote: Python grew from a project van Rossum began over Christmas 1989 into the everyday language of data science.
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats vanrossum-p1 (Christmas 1989, the spread into data science). It also uses the exact phrase that ch7-datasci-p1 uses later ('the everyday language of data science'), so the same claim appears three times in the chapter.
findings.fix: Cut the first sentence and let the caption name what the timeline shows: "Python's defining event is the split: Python 3 broke compatibility in 2008, and Python 2 lived beside it for twelve years before it was retired in 2020."

findings.quote: Christmas 1989, at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica in Amsterdam, the Dutch programmer Guido van Rossum was bored.
findings.problem: The opening sentence places him at CWI over Christmas. Two sentences later he is 'working from home' over the same break. Van Rossum's own account (foreword to Programming Python, 1996) is that his office was closed that week and he had a home computer. Separately, 'outside CWI' uses an abbreviation the book never introduces. The van Rossum glossary entry repeats the 'hobby at the Centrum' wording.
findings.fix: "In December 1989 Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in Amsterdam, wanted a hobby project for the Christmas week, when his office would be closed." Later in the paragraph: "Working at home over the break, he started writing an interpreter ...". Bring the van Rossum entry in scripts/glossary-defs.json into line: "began Python at home over Christmas 1989 while working at CWI in Amsterdam ...".

findings.quote: There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it: the opposite of Perl's motto
findings.problem: The paragraph says Python's design choices trace to these Zen lines. The first two lines each get a Python mechanism (indentation; 1 + "a" and self). The third gets only a contrast with Perl, so it teaches nothing about Python. The same line then comes back word for word as the chapter's closing pull-quote (ch7-datasci-p6), so the reader meets it twice.
findings.fix: End p2 after the self clause ("... is spelled out as every method's first parameter."). The owner's closing pull-quote then carries the third line, and its 'unless you're Dutch' still lands because p1 already calls van Rossum Dutch.

findings.quote: The static side is safer; the dynamic side is quicker to write.
findings.problem: This sentence restates the trade p1 has just closed on (checks paid for in cycles, fewer declarations to get wrong). It also makes three paragraphs in a row end on a price/benefit pair (p1; p2; p3's 'The price is ...; the benefit is ...'). That is a summary closer and the same shape three times running.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. p3 then has no antecedent for 'the dynamic side', so open it with: "Python pushes dynamic typing to its logical limit with duck typing: ...".

findings.quote: would spend a hundred machine cycles to save a programmer five minutes
findings.problem: A hundred cycles is tens of nanoseconds at the clock speeds Part I taught. Read literally, the sentence describes no trade at all. The trade the chapter actually measures is a ratio: hundreds of instructions per statement where C uses one (interpret-p3, Fig 7.7).
findings.fix: "... and would let the machine do a hundred times the work to save a programmer five minutes."

findings.quote: The inheritance. From ABC, Python took indentation as structure
findings.problem: public/glossary.json points 'inheritance' (defined as 'Building one class on another; in memory, one struct embedded inside another.') to Chapter 7 §02. The extractor matched this strip label, which means what Python took from ABC. The OOP sense is taught in Ch6 (ch6-stroustrup, ch6-classes: 'Inheritance is one struct embedded inside another'). In the same way, 'compiler' points to ch7-cpython, although ch1-vonneumann defines it first ('a compiler, which turns code in a language such as C into the CPU's own instructions'). A reader who follows either entry from the glossary page lands on the wrong section.
findings.fix: Rename the strip label so the extractor stops matching it, e.g. "What ABC gave. Indentation as structure and a taste for being easy to read." Pin first-use to inheritance → ch6-classes and compiler → ch1-vonneumann. Then run npm run build:glossary and check both entries.

findings.quote: Shannon, Baran, Davies, Cerf, Berners-Lee, Eich
findings.problem: The glossary entries 'Baran' and 'Cerf' give their first use as 'Chapter 7 · §06 · Why Python won data science'. The extractor credited the End of Part Two tagline, which follows ch7-datasci, to that section. In the glossary, both names link to the Python data-science section, where neither person is taught. They are taught in ch9-arpanet (Paul Baran) and ch10-why (Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn).
findings.fix: Make scripts/build-glossary.js skip .part-opener text when it assigns first-use sections, or pin Baran → ch9-arpanet and Cerf → ch10-why. Then rebuild the glossary and confirm no other entry is credited to a part closer.

findings.quote: The contract "must have speak()" is checked by running the code, not by a compiler beforehand.
findings.problem: The strip's 'The strength' and 'The weakness' bullets repeat p3's last sentence (the fit is checked only at runtime; objects combine in ways their designers never anticipated). The caption's 'the mistake surfaces only when that call runs' says it a third time. Only 'The middle way' adds anything.
findings.fix: Cut 'The strength' and 'The weakness' and keep 'The middle way'. If three bullets are wanted, add one new fact rather than restating p3.

findings.quote: CPython's reference counts and internal structures were never safe to update from two threads at once
findings.problem: The 'Why one lock' bullet repeats the whole argument of ch7-gil-p2, which sits directly above the figure. 'Removing it' also repeats p2's PEP 703 and 3.13 sentences. Only 'The interval' and the per-object/biased-counting detail are new.
findings.fix: Cut 'Why one lock' and shorten 'Removing it' to the new detail: "Removing it. PEP 703's build replaces the one lock with per-object locks and biased reference counting."

findings.quote: One Python thread runs at a time. There are reasons. They are running out.
findings.problem: The section title uses clipped dramatic fragments, which the pass-29 brief lists as an AI tell. A heading is the most visible text in the section.
findings.fix: "One Python thread runs at a time, for reasons that are running out."

findings.quote: Imported modules keep their bytecode in a cache until their source changes; the interpretation is paid for on every run.
findings.problem: The previous sentence says the pipeline runs 'at runtime'. Here a semicolon sets a saving next to a cost without saying what the cache saves. The reader has to work out that the cache skips the translation but not the loop, and is likely to read the sentence twice.
findings.fix: "Imported modules keep their bytecode in a cache until their source changes, which saves the translation but not the interpretation: that is paid for on every run."

findings.quote: a program that read each Lisp expression at runtime and executed it directly, without ever producing a separate binary
findings.problem: This is the book's first use of 'binary' as a noun for a program file. Part I uses 'binary' only for base 2, and here the word carries the very contrast that defines an interpreter. 'Executable' is explained only in p2. 'ROM' in the next sentence also appears here for the first time in the book, unexplained.
findings.fix: "... without ever producing a separate machine-code program." In the next sentence: "an interpreter squeezed into the machine's read-only memory (ROM)".

findings.quote: In 1991 he posted it to USENET's discussion groups
findings.problem: Fig 7.2, directly below, reads '0.9.0 posted to Usenet', and Part III writes 'Usenet' too. Two spellings sit on the same screen.
findings.fix: "In 1991 he posted it to Usenet's discussion groups". ch4's 'a USENET newsgroup' should match.

findings.quote: He had spent three years on a research language called ABC
findings.problem: Fig 7.2 calls ABC 'a teaching language at CWI', and the strip says Python inherited its 'taste for being easy to read'. Prose and picture describe ABC differently.
findings.fix: Use one description in both places, e.g. "He had spent three years on ABC, a language CWI built for teaching and for non-programmers, which had failed to gain traction outside CWI."

findings.quote: Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost nothing at run time
findings.problem: The chapter writes 'at runtime' four times (interpret-p1, interpret-p3, types-p2, types-p3) and 'at run time' twice, here and in Fig 7.7's caption ('learns what they are only at run time'), all in the same sense. Part II otherwise uses 'at runtime' (10 times).
findings.fix: Use "at runtime" in ch7-datasci-p5 and ch7-cpython-p4.

findings.quote: The name. van Rossum (1996): "I chose Python as a working title for the project
findings.problem: 'van Rossum' starts a new sentence after the bold label but is lowercase. The section label itself correctly capitalises it ('02 · Van Rossum 1989–91').
findings.fix: "The name. Van Rossum (1996): ..."

findings.quote: With the GIL, two CPU-bound threads take turns, the lock passing between them every 5 ms
findings.problem: 'CPU-bound' is not explained anywhere before this. The prose describes the same idea in plain words ('a program whose threads all compute in Python').
findings.fix: "With the GIL, two threads that only compute take turns, the lock passing between them every 5 ms, ..."

findings.quote: you give up an order of magnitude of performance
findings.problem: The chapter's own numbers show more than one order: 'hundreds of CPU instructions' per statement (interpret-p3), and one instruction against nine steps of several each (Fig 7.7). The End of Part Two tagline, a few screens later, says 'slower than C by orders of magnitude'.
findings.fix: "you give up one or two orders of magnitude of performance"

findings.quote: The first twenty bytes of a packet on the wire are the IP header
findings.problem: Chapter 8 (ch8-layers, Fig 8.x) has just shown an Ethernet header going in front of the IP header before the bits reach the wire, so the first bytes on the wire belong to the Ethernet header. A reader who took in that wrapping stops here. The same sentence also says every router reads the header to learn 'what the higher-layer protocol is'. Forwarding does not need that field; the receiver does.
findings.fix: "The first twenty bytes of every IP packet (carried inside the Ethernet frame of Chapter 8) are the IP header, a fixed-format arrangement of fields that every router on the path reads to decide where the packet goes next, whether to fragment it and when to drop it; one field tells the receiver which higher-layer protocol the payload belongs to."

findings.quote: A 4000-byte packet meets a link that carries at most 1500
findings.problem: The picture says '4000 bytes of data', and its fragments carry 1480 + 1480 + 1040 = 4000 data bytes, so the original packet is 4020 bytes. The caption calls it a 4000-byte packet, while the prose and the figure title say '4 KB', which a Part I reader may take as 4096. A reader who checks the strip's arithmetic (a 20-byte header on each piece) gets 3980 data bytes and cannot reach 1040.
findings.fix: Caption: "A packet carrying 4000 bytes of data meets a link that carries at most 1500 bytes...". In ch9-ip-p3: "When a packet carrying 4000 bytes of data must traverse a 1500-byte link...". Figure title: "Fig 9.5 · 4000 bytes of data, fragmented onto a 1500-byte link".

findings.quote: A more dramatic attack exploits BGP itself.
findings.problem: The prose sets up hijacking as an attack ('the hijacker wins') and names Pakistan/YouTube as its canonical example. The Fig 9.11 strip then says 'No malice' and blames the spread on a leak upstream, and Fig 9.12 defines a route leak as 'nobody attacked anything'. The chapter never says what separates the two, so the reader cannot tell whether 2008 was a hijack, a leak or both.
findings.fix: Open p4 with: "BGP can also be misled, by malice or by mistake." End p4 with: "This is BGP hijacking: announcing addresses you do not hold, whether on purpose or by error. The canonical example happened on 24 February 2008." In the Fig 9.12 caption, after 'route leak:', put: "the routes were genuine, but they reached a neighbour that should never have heard them."

findings.quote: the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream, where PCCW passed its customer's announcement on
findings.problem: The chapter hero lead blames 'a misconfigured router in Pakistan' and says YouTube went off the air 'for the whole world'. The strip puts the only mistake at PCCW (Hong Kong), and the caption says 'almost everywhere'. Both companies erred: Pakistan Telecom sent its internal block route to PCCW, and PCCW passed it on unfiltered (RIPE NCC RIS case study, 2008).
findings.fix: Strip: "No malice. The block was a domestic order; Pakistan Telecom's mistake was announcing the route to its upstream PCCW, and PCCW's was passing it on to the world without filtering it." Hero lead: "...for a misconfigured route from Pakistan to take YouTube off the air across most of the world for two hours."

findings.quote: each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table
findings.problem: Ports first appear in Chapter 10 (ch10-udp). In Chapter 8 a 'port' was a physical socket on a switch (Fig 8.10), so a newcomer reads 'its own port' as a socket. NAT is never expanded, 'public address' is never set against a private one, and the prose of 05 never mentions CGNAT: the whole idea lives only in the caption.
findings.fix: Add one clause to ch9-v6-p1 after the 2011 sentence: "Most ISPs stretched the old pool by putting many customers behind one public address, a trick called network address translation (Fig 9.8)." Caption: "...thousands of homes share one public address, and the NAT tells their connections apart by a port number (the connection label Chapter 10 introduces, not a socket on a switch) kept in a translation table."

findings.quote: The internet is not one network. It is tens of thousands of independent networks
findings.problem: This is the 'Not X. Y.' reveal the brief bans, used as the section's opening line.
findings.fix: "The internet is tens of thousands of independent networks run by different organisations, glued together by a single protocol that lets them announce routes to one another."

findings.quote: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.
findings.problem: The h2 is three clipped dramatic fragments in a row. It also frames the ARPANET as a Cold War product, and the section's own last sentence denies that: ARPA built it 'to let universities share expensive computers, not to survive a war'. 'A Cold War' with the indefinite article reads oddly too.
findings.fix: "Two letters, then a crash."

findings.quote: was tasked in 1966 with building an experimental network, by 1967 he had read all three sets of work
findings.problem: The sentence starts 'When X was tasked in 1966...' and continues 'by 1967 he had read', which breaks the syntax. It then keeps going through two nested parentheticals to 'the network's first routers', so the reader has to read it twice.
findings.fix: "In 1966 ARPA (the US Advanced Research Projects Agency, not yet renamed DARPA) tasked Larry Roberts with building an experimental network. By 1967 he had read all three sets of work, and the design that emerged was Baran's mesh, Davies's terminology and Kleinrock's math. The firm Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) built its IMPs (Interface Message Processors), the network's first routers."

findings.quote: a packet network shares every link, and each packet finds its own way, sometimes arriving out of order
findings.problem: The caption says again what p2 and p3 just explained (circuits held through the silences, shared links, packets finding their own way and arriving out of order, computers talking in bursts). The strip's 'Putting it back' repeats p3's 'numbered chunks... reassembles them'. The brief says the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: "The same call both ways: a circuit held through every silence, and three packets crossing the mesh by three paths, arriving 2, 1, 3, that B puts back in order." Cut the strip item 'Putting it back', or keep only its Chapter 10 pointer.

findings.quote: Its first message, on 29 October, went from UCLA to SRI: L and O arrived, then the receiving system crashed.
findings.problem: The LO crash is told three times: in p1 at length, in this caption, and in the strip ('UCLA was typing LOGIN; the second try, an hour later'). The IMP is also explained three times: p3 ('BBN building the IMPs... the network's first routers'), the caption ('an IMP... built by BBN') and the strip.
findings.fix: Caption: "The ARPANET in December 1969: four computers on leased 50 kbps lines, each joined to the network by a refrigerator-sized IMP; below, how it grew until its retirement in 1990." Cut the strip item 'The message'. Keep 'The IMPs' (the DDP-516 detail is new) and 'Flag day'.

findings.quote: each with the same ID, its offset (in 8-byte units) and a more-fragments flag
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p3's list (same Identification field, its own Fragment Offset, a More Fragments flag). The strip item 'IPv6. Routers never fragment' repeats p3's last sentence ('IPv6 forbids router-side fragmentation entirely').
findings.fix: Caption: "One packet as three fragments, each a full IP packet with its own offset. Lose any one and the receiver must throw the whole packet away, since IP cannot ask for a single fragment again." Cut either the strip item 'IPv6' or the clause in p3, keeping one.

findings.quote: each network adds its own AS number before passing the route on
findings.problem: The caption restates p2's last sentence ('Each AS that hears the announcement adds itself to the path and re-announces'). The strip's 'such as 15169 for Google' repeats p2's 'Google is AS 15169'.
findings.fix: Caption: "Each AS adds its number as the announcement spreads (steps 1 to 3). When a copy comes back to AS 65001 carrying its own number, it knows the route has looped and drops it (step 4)." Strip: "real networks use public numbers, like the 174 and 15169 above."

findings.quote: IANA handed out its last blocks of IPv4 addresses on 3 February 2011
findings.problem: Section 05 has one paragraph of prose, and its two figures repeat it. The 2011 exhaustion appears three times: p1 (IANA, 3 February 2011, regional registries 'over the years that followed'), the caption ('ran out in 2011') and this strip (the same date and the same registries clause). The 2^32 count appears in p1 (4 294 967 296) and again in the Fig 9.9 strip ('about 4.3 billion').
findings.fix: Cut the strip item 'The dates'. Caption opening: "With the free pool gone, many ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade NAT...". Fig 9.9 strip 'Scale': "2^32 is fewer addresses than there are people alive; 2^128 is about 3.4 × 10^38...".

findings.quote: which is why, three decades on, the move is still unfinished
findings.problem: p1 says the migration is unfinished 'structurally': a v6-only and a v4-only machine cannot talk, so nobody can drop v4 until nearly everyone has v6. This strip restates the same conclusion with a different cause (every router and OS had to change). The reader gets two 'why's for one fact.
findings.fix: "The price. Every router, operating system, firewall and networking library had to change before IPv6 could carry real traffic."

findings.quote: The sender writes the source address itself and routers forward on the destination alone
findings.problem: The unchecked source field is explained three times: the Fig 9.4 strip ('The sender writes it and no router checks it'), p1, and this caption. The edge filter has three names (BCP 38 in p1, 'source address validation' here, uRPF in the strip) that are never tied together, so a newcomer may think there are three defences. 'Uneven' is said in p1 ('enforcement is uneven. Spoofed packets still flow.') and again in the strip ('Uneven deployment').
findings.fix: Caption: "The same forged packet twice: with no filter at the ISP's edge it gets through and any reply goes to 198.51.100.5; with the BCP 38 check on, the edge router drops it." Strip: "Automating the check. Routers can apply BCP 38 automatically (uRPF)...". Cut the strip item 'Uneven deployment' or cut p1's 'Spoofed packets still flow.' Cut the Fig 9.4 strip item 'The source', since section 06 teaches it.

findings.quote: somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (by rough estimates, about ten percent of the internet of the time)
findings.problem: Three hedges are stacked on one number: 'somewhere between', 'by rough estimates' and 'about'.
findings.fix: "Within hours between five and ten thousand machines, roughly a tenth of the internet of the time, were unusable."

findings.quote: The protocols of Chapter 9 had been built in an era of institutional trust
findings.problem: The strip names the chapter the reader is already in as if it were another one, then ends on an aphorism ('proved that era over'). It also ties the worm to 'the protocols of Chapter 9', yet the worm attacked host programs (fingerd, sendmail, rsh), not IP or BGP, so the reader asks what the link is.
findings.fix: "Like the source field and BGP in this section, the programs it attacked had been written for a community that trusted itself."

findings.quote: the first 16 of the 32 bits, two of the four numbers
findings.problem: Chapter 8 promised that IP addresses would be met in Chapter 9, but no passage introduces one before this sentence relies on an address being 32 bits written as four 8-bit numbers. That fact is first stated in the next section (ch9-v6-p1, 'IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long').
findings.fix: In ch9-ip-p1, after the first sentence: "The fields that matter most are the source and destination addresses, each 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 such as 198.51.100.7." Then ch9-v6-p1 can open: "Those 32 bits allow 4,294,967,296 addresses...".

findings.quote: With RPKI, a prefix holder signs a route origin authorisation (ROA)
findings.problem: RPKI is never expanded, and 'signs' relies on digital signatures, which arrive in Part IV. The Fig 9.12 strip adds 'the routing registries, RPKI and the newer ASPA records', and the Fig 9.10 strip adds uRPF with 'interface'. That is a run of expert acronyms the newcomer cannot use (law 4: never too deep).
findings.fix: Fig 9.11: "Origin validation. Prefix holders can now publish a signed record (RPKI) of which network may announce their addresses; a router that checks it drops a /24 like this one as invalid." Fig 9.12: "Defences. Route filters and signed routing records exist, and are only partly deployed."

findings.quote: ToS once meant priority and now carries DSCP and ECN
findings.problem: These are two acronyms that are never explained and never used again: expert detail the baseline reader cannot carry.
findings.fix: "ToS once meant priority and now carries traffic-class and congestion marks"

findings.quote: The TTL drops by one at every hop; if it reaches 0 the router drops the packet and reports back
findings.problem: The caption already says each router lowers the TTL by one and recomputes the checksum, and the strip says both again. Neither says why the field exists (so that a packet caught in a routing loop dies instead of circling forever), so the mechanism arrives without its purpose.
findings.fix: "Time to live. It exists so that a packet caught in a routing loop dies instead of circling forever: at 0 the router drops it and reports back, which is how traceroute maps a path... The checksum covers only the header, which is why changing the TTL forces a new one."

findings.quote: became the design argument of the ARPANET
findings.problem: The caption reads as if Baran's survivability case drove the ARPANET. p3 has just said the design was a synthesis of three people and that ARPA built it to share computers, 'not to survive a war'. The strip's 'The question' also repeats p2's account of Baran's problem.
findings.fix: "His case for the third, packets finding their own way through redundant links, became one of the arguments behind the ARPANET's mesh." Cut the strip item 'The question'.

findings.quote: The Cuban Missile Crisis had just shown the world how close to thermonuclear war it was
findings.problem: Baran's work is dated 1960 to 1964, and 'had just shown' puts the crisis before that work began. The crisis was October 1962, midway through it.
findings.fix: "In October 1962, midway through that work, the Cuban Missile Crisis showed the world how close to thermonuclear war it was;"

findings.quote: That is 4 294 967 296 possible addresses, which sounded like a lot in 1981, and fewer are usable
findings.problem: This is the only space-grouped number in the book (elsewhere 65,535 and 1,024), and its plain spaces can break the number across lines. The sentence also chains 'which..., and..., since..., so...' and has to be read twice.
findings.fix: "That is 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, which sounded like a lot in 1981. Fewer are usable: whole ranges are reserved, and blocks are handed out in fixed sizes, so part of each often sits idle."

findings.quote: Depending on how you count, between 35% and 45% of internet traffic is IPv6 in 2025.
findings.problem: The prose gives a hedged 35 to 45% of traffic, and the Fig 9.8 strip gives 'close to half of Google's users'. Two metrics a page apart read as figures that disagree. The strip's 'reached it over IPv6' is also ambiguous: 'it' could be Google or IPv6.
findings.fix: p1: "In 2025 close to half of Google's users reached it over IPv6." Strip: "The real fix. IPv6 gives every device its own public address."

findings.quote: There are no reservations, no setup phase, no central authority that has to grant a circuit before traffic flows.
findings.problem: This is a reflexive triplet: 'no reservations' and 'no setup phase' are the same fact. In circuit switching it is the switches, not a 'central authority', that set up the circuit.
findings.fix: "Nothing has to be reserved or set up before traffic flows."

findings.quote: the IMPs (Interface Message Processors), the network's first routers
findings.problem: 'Router' is never defined in Parts I to III. Chapter 8 used it only for the home Wi-Fi box, yet here and in ch9-ip-p1 the argument relies on routers as the computers that forward packets.
findings.fix: In ch9-circuits-p3: "The network's only job, done by computers called routers at each junction, is to get each chunk closer to its destination."

findings.quote: which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood relies on it
findings.problem: Chapter 10 (ch10-attacks) says the flood's sources are 'often spoofed', so a SYN flood uses spoofing but does not depend on it.
findings.fix: "which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood often uses it"

findings.quote: copper | Ethernet, up to 100 m
findings.problem: A corrected fact error has come back (§4g, UNDER.md line 582): the figure again puts a 100 m Ethernet run on the router-to-provider hop. The <desc> says the same ('twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run'). Commit 93184ba (Pass 30 Gate 2, repair round 1) swapped the corrected label 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km' for this one to get rid of the untaught abbreviation DSL. It also clashes with ch8-substrates-p2, which says a copper run stops at 100 m: the provider is kilometres away.
findings.fix: Change the label on the copper hop to 'phone line or cable, a few km'. Change the <desc> to: 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (a phone line or a cable-TV line, for a few kilometres) or on fibre.' Re-verify against the §4g row.

findings.quote: The same voltage transition that switched a transistor in Chapter 1 ... now travels: ... across an ocean
findings.problem: The prose says the voltage transition crosses the ocean. Fig 8.1 right below it, corrected under §4g row 552, shows light in glass fibre ('Today's transatlantic cables carry light in glass fibre, not voltage'). Section 02 then describes three substrates, and only one of them carries voltage. Two neighbouring passages disagree on what crosses the ocean.
findings.fix: 'The same kind of signal that switched a transistor in Chapter 1 (...) now travels: across the motherboard, out a network interface, down a cable, as light through glass fibre across an ocean, into another machine on the other side of the planet.' In p3 change 'The voltage on a wire is the substrate' to 'The signal on the medium is the substrate'.

findings.quote: are the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart
findings.problem: The caption's syntax is broken. 'The same thing ... apart' does not parse, so the reader has to read it twice.
findings.fix: '...are the same thing at scales more than twelve orders of magnitude apart: a signal guided along a line, in copper or in glass.'

findings.quote: How do you keep a voltage signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre?
findings.problem: Three rhetorical questions stand in for explanation, and the answer is a reflexive triplet that teaches nothing ('physics, mathematics, and practitioner cleverness'). The closing clause restates p1. 'The next five chapters' is ambiguous: read from inside Chapter 8, it seems to mean Ch9 to Ch13.
findings.fix: Replace the paragraph with: 'Keeping a signal readable over a kilometre of copper, a hundred kilometres of fibre or a radio link through rain is the work of this chapter; the rest of Part III is built on top of it.'

findings.quote: The voltage that flips a transistor inside a CPU is, at a different scale, the voltage that crosses a continent.
findings.problem: The chapter lead repeats, word for word, the first sentence of the Part III tagline the reader saw a moment earlier. The Part II closer, the ch8-bridge heading and ch8-bridge-p1 make the same point too, so the reader meets it four or five times in a row. The rest of the lead is a stack of clipped fragments ('The mathematics of how much... The encodings that... And the layer model...').
findings.fix: 'From the chip into the world: copper, fibre and radio; how much information each can carry; the encodings that turn ones and zeros into wave shapes; the rules that let many machines share one medium; and the layer model every conversation about networking refers back to.'

findings.quote: copper, fiber, radio
findings.problem: The hero lead and the Part III contents card for Chapter 8 spell it 'fiber'. The chapter's prose, captions and strips spell it 'fibre' 14 times.
findings.fix: Use 'fibre' in both the hero lead and the Part III toc-desc for Chapter 08.

findings.quote: Processor cores run at around 1 V; the older 3.3 V and 5 V levels survive only at the edges
findings.problem: This 'How it works' bullet is left over from the §4g 3.3 V correction. Nothing in the picture or the prose uses core voltages, so it explains nothing about the figure.
findings.fix: Delete the third bullet ('The voltage...'). The other two bullets cover the picture.

findings.quote: A one-metre USB cable inside a desk hides all of this.
findings.problem: Wrong word: a USB cable lies on a desk, not inside one.
findings.fix: 'A one-metre USB cable on a desk hides all of this.'

findings.quote: That is the trick behind the twist.
findings.problem: 'The twist' is used as if the reader already knew about it. The paragraph never says that the two wires are twisted around each other (a twisted pair). It also credits the twist with the trick, which is really the difference signal; the twist only supports it, as the paragraph's next-but-one sentence says.
findings.fix: 'The signal is the voltage difference between two wires twisted around each other (a twisted pair), and the receiver reads only that difference.' Then delete 'That is the trick behind the twist.' and keep 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer...'.

findings.quote: Cheap and easy to connect, but it loses signal quickly at high frequencies
findings.problem: The 'How it works' strip repeats p2 to p4 almost word for word: copper is cheap and loses 20 dB per 100 m so runs stop at 100 m, fibre loses 0.2 dB/km, and radio shares the air across the same bands. The same thing is explained twice, in the prose and in the strip.
findings.fix: Keep only what the strip adds. 'Copper. The 20 dB per 100 m is for Cat 6 cable at 100 MHz.' / 'Glass. The 0.2 dB per km is at 1550 nm, the wavelength long-haul fibre uses.' / 'Radio. Wi-Fi now also has a 6 GHz band.'

findings.quote: Each hop encodes the bits its own way, and the layers above see none of it.
findings.problem: 'The layers above' leans on the layer model, which this chapter only introduces in Section 06.
findings.fix: 'Each hop encodes the bits its own way, and nothing above the wire needs to know which.'

findings.quote: Wi-Fi runs around 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz; cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
findings.problem: These numbers disagree with Fig 8.2. Its <desc> and strip give Wi-Fi as 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and cellular as 'below 1 GHz to tens of GHz', the range §4g row 553 settled.
findings.fix: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.'

findings.quote: allowing tens to hundreds of kilometres between repeaters
findings.problem: Three different spacings appear in the chapter. p3 says 'tens to hundreds of kilometres', the Fig 8.1 caption says 'repeaters every 50 to 100 km', and the Fig 8.2 strip says 'tens of kilometres between amplifiers'.
findings.fix: Pick one figure and use it everywhere, e.g. p3: 'allowing 50 to 100 km between repeaters on an undersea cable', matching Fig 8.1. Drop the spacing from the Fig 8.2 strip.

findings.quote: an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed from across the street
findings.problem: Wrong words: what Van Eck reconstructed was the picture on the monitor, not the monitor. The earlier sentence also ends in a circular 'This is the basis of TEMPEST ... against precisely this'.
findings.fix: '(Van Eck showed in 1985 that the picture on an unshielded monitor could be rebuilt from its emissions across the street; ...)'. Earlier: 'TEMPEST, a US programme dating to the 1960s, sets the shielding standards that guard against it.'

findings.quote: At twenty-one, in his 1937 master's thesis at MIT, he showed that George Boole's nineteenth-century algebra
findings.problem: This paragraph retells the story that ch2-boole-p6 and p7 already tell in full: the 21-year-old at MIT in 1937, Boole's algebra as relay circuits, and the 'most important thesis' accolade (Goldstine there, Gardner here). It is explained twice in two sections. Its opening claim ('one of the strangest figures') is not what the paragraph goes on to show.
findings.fix: Shrink the paragraph to a recall clause: 'He was the Shannon of Chapter 2, whose 1937 master's thesis turned Boole's algebra into relay circuits (Howard Gardner later called it "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century").' Start p3 at 'At Bell Labs, ...' and drop 'He stayed strange.'

findings.quote: having given the mathematics to a networked world he could no longer quite see.
findings.problem: The paragraph is colour that teaches nothing about channels or entropy: the unicycle, Theseus, the chess and juggling papers, the illness. The brief cuts such detail (Harp and Mayer). It ends on an aphorism. Only 'he wrote the information theory paper on his own' supports the section.
findings.fix: Keep one sentence: 'At Bell Labs he wrote the information theory paper on his own, the whole field in one paper, more or less complete.' Cut the rest, or at least end on 'he died in 2001.'

findings.quote: A source that always sends the same symbol carries no information; a fair coin carries one full bit per flip
findings.problem: The caption restates p6: a fair coin gives 1 bit, a constant source gives 0, and entropy is the compression floor. It also brings a second biased example (90/10 gives 0.47) while the prose uses another (3/4, 1/4 gives 0.81). That is two examples where one works, and the prose's example is not in the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: 'Entropy of a two-symbol source against p, the chance of a 1; a 90/10 source is marked at 0.47 bits.' In p6, use the figure's example: 'A coin that lands heads nine times in ten gives H ≈ 0.47 bits: coded several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.47 bits per flip.'

findings.quote: coding several flips at a time, a long run of them can be stored in about 0.81 bits per flip
findings.problem: Dangling modifier: grammatically the 'long run' is what does the coding, so the reader has to reread the sentence.
findings.fix: '...: if you code several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.81 bits per flip.' (0.47 if the 90/10 example is adopted.)

findings.quote: sits somewhere on Shannon's curve, fighting for the last bit.
findings.problem: An aphorism closes the callout. 'Shannon's curve' points to a figure the reader has not yet reached, and that figure plots a two-symbol source, which no compressor sits on.
findings.fix: 'Every lossless compressor, ZIP and PNG included, is judged by how close it comes to that floor.'

findings.quote: Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz and signal-to-noise ratio SNR
findings.problem: 'Bandwidth' measured in hertz is never defined. The baseline reader knows 'bandwidth' as a data rate (Mbps), which here is exactly the wrong meaning. The formula and Fig 8.4 depend on it, and Section 04 then says 'double bandwidth'.
