findings.fix: 'Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz (the width of the range of frequencies it passes, not its bit rate) and signal-to-noise ratio SNR (signal power divided by noise power), ...'

findings.quote: the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N
findings.problem: A step is skipped. Nothing says why powers turn into square roots: a signal's voltage grows as the square root of its power. A reader with school maths stops here, and the rest of the derivation depends on it.
findings.fix: '...with signal power S and noise power N (a voltage grows as the square root of the power it carries), the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N, ...'

findings.quote: Bandwidth buys pulses per second; signal-to-noise buys bits per pulse; capacity is their product.
findings.problem: A reflexive triplet that only sums up the sentence before it ('Multiply the two, and the halves cancel').
findings.fix: Delete the sentence and keep 'Even the +1 earns its place...'.

findings.quote: there exists a coding scheme that achieves arbitrarily low error rate
findings.problem: The theorem rests on 'coding scheme', which is never explained. The reader cannot say how a code beats noise (by adding redundancy). Section 04 then uses 'encoding' for line codes, a different thing, which invites confusion. As written it is a slogan in place of the mechanism (law 4).
findings.fix: '...there exists a coding scheme (a way of adding redundant bits so the receiver can find and repair what the noise damaged) that achieves arbitrarily low error rate.'

findings.quote: Shannon–Hartley channel capacity
findings.problem: The callout label names Hartley, who appears nowhere in the chapter. p12 credits only Nyquist, and p1 says that before 1948 'amount of information' was only a metaphor, so the reader is left asking who Hartley was.
findings.fix: In p8: '...the channel capacity, named for Shannon and Ralph Hartley, a Bell Labs engineer who first counted distinguishable signal levels in 1928, is:' (source Hartley 1928, 'Transmission of Information', BSTJ, before adding it).

findings.quote: a channel of bandwidth B carries at most B · log₂(1 + SNR) bits per second, and above the curve errors cannot
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats the formula (p9) and the theorem (p10). The brief: the prose keeps the explanation, the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: 'Shannon's limit against signal-to-noise ratio, with two real links under it. A phone line at 30 dB allows about 10 bits per hertz, ... just under it.'

findings.quote: The signal sits at one of two levels and only changes when a new bit arrives.
findings.problem: Wrong: NRZ changes only when the next bit differs from the last one. As written it says the line changes on every bit, which contradicts the next sentence's flat line for a run of equal bits.
findings.fix: 'The signal sits at one of two levels and changes only when a bit differs from the one before it.'

findings.quote: Manchester code puts a transition in the middle of every bit: rising for a 1, falling for a 0.
findings.problem: The caption restates p3: mid-bit transition, rising for 1, clock recovered, the cost. The cost alone appears four times (p3 'double bandwidth', this caption, the Fig 8.5 strip '20 million signal changes', the Fig 8.6 caption 'up to twice the signal changes').
findings.fix: Fig 8.5 caption: 'The bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 in Manchester code; each mid-bit edge gives the bit and keeps the receiver's clock in step.' Fig 8.6 caption: drop ', at the cost of up to twice the signal changes'.

findings.quote: so it corrects its clock each time and reads all seven
findings.problem: 'All seven' right after 'four zeros ... reads five' can be read as seven zeros. The reader has to work out that it means the seven bits.
findings.fix: '...so it corrects its clock each time and reads all seven bits correctly.'

findings.quote: Non-return-to-zero simply holds the level for each bit: high for 1, low for 0.
findings.problem: The strip bullet repeats p2 ('High voltage means 1; low voltage means 0'). It also spells the name differently from the prose ('Non-Return to Zero').
findings.fix: Use the bullet to explain the name instead: 'The name. Non-Return to Zero: the line holds its level for the whole bit instead of dropping back to zero between bits.' Use one spelling of the name throughout.

findings.quote: The first standard Ethernet, 10BASE5 (10 Mbps over coaxial cable), used Manchester encoding
findings.problem: 10BASE5 is introduced here, before Section 05 introduces Ethernet. ch8-ethernet-p4 then introduces it again in key-term italics as if new, with its full details. The reader meets it twice.
findings.fix: 'The first standard Ethernet (Section 05) used Manchester encoding because it could not afford to lose synchronisation on a long run of zeros.' Keep the 10BASE5 details only in ch8-ethernet-p4.

findings.quote: A carrier wave has three things a transmitter can change: its size (AM), how fast it oscillates (FM)
findings.problem: The caption repeats p6 almost word for word: size/AM, how fast it oscillates/FM, phase/PSK, QAM changing size and phase together. The strip's 'The carrier' bullet repeats p6's 'a frequency the medium carries well' as well.
findings.fix: Caption: 'The bits 1 0 1 0 carried three ways: the wave's size, its speed or its starting direction changes with each bit.' Cut the strip's 'The carrier' bullet.

findings.quote: packing many bits into each symbol: 10 in Wi-Fi 6.
findings.problem: Fig 8.4 says Wi-Fi 6 at about 20 dB is allowed 6.7 bits per hertz. Here Wi-Fi 6 packs 10 bits per symbol, and nothing reconciles the two numbers. A careful reader will think the book has Wi-Fi beating Shannon's limit.
findings.fix: '...packing many bits into each symbol: up to 10 in Wi-Fi 6, on a strong clean signal well above the 20 dB that holds it to 6.7 in Fig 8.4.'

findings.quote: Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024, 10 bits, and Wi-Fi 7 4096, 12 bits, when the signal is clean
findings.problem: Too many commas: the numbers and bit counts run together, and the sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: 'Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024 combinations (10 bits) and Wi-Fi 7 uses 4096 (12 bits) when the signal is clean, dropping to fewer as it degrades.'

findings.quote: In ever faster versions of itself, it became the dominant local-area networking technology on the planet.
findings.problem: Grammatically 'it' is the CSMA/CD rule named just before. Read that way, the sentence contradicts p4, which says switches ended collisions and the collision machinery now sits unused.
findings.fix: 'In ever faster versions, Ethernet became the dominant local-area networking technology on the planet.'

findings.quote: Ethernet was the same insight on a wire, improved with carrier sensing ("listen before transmit").
findings.problem: This restates p1, which already says Ethernet carried the Hawaii radio idea onto a wire and gives the listen-first rule. 'With smarter timing' earlier in the paragraph is too vague to teach anything.
findings.fix: Delete the last sentence. Optionally replace 'with smarter timing' with what Metcalfe changed, once it is sourced.

findings.quote: But every Ethernet frame still carries the header structure invented for that shared cable, including the 48-bit MAC addresses.
findings.problem: 'Frame' and 'header' are never explained in this chapter or earlier, and MAC addresses only arrive three paragraphs later (p7). Frames are then relied on in Figs 8.9 and 8.10, p11 and ch8-layers-p2.
findings.fix: 'But every Ethernet frame (the block of bits a station sends in one go) still starts with the header designed for that shared cable: a few fields in front of the data, led by the address of the card it is for and the card it came from, the MAC addresses described below.'

findings.quote: When a host wants to send a packet to 192.168.1.5 on its own local network
findings.problem: 'Packet' is used here, and earlier in p2, but is only defined in ch9-circuits-p3. The brief names it as a term the baseline reader lacks. In the same exchange Fig 8.9 says 'frame' ('the next frame goes direct'), so the reader cannot tell whether these are two things.
findings.fix: 'When a host wants to send data to 192.168.1.5 on its own local network, ...; subsequent frames for that IP go straight to the matching MAC.'

findings.quote: With one device per switch port and both directions on separate wire pairs (full duplex), collision detection never fires.
findings.problem: That switches ended collisions is said three times in one section: p4, the Fig 8.8 strip ('Today. In switched Ethernet ... collisions no longer happen'), and this Fig 8.10 strip bullet.
findings.fix: In p4: 'Each device got its own cable to the switch, with each direction on its own wire pair, so collisions stopped happening...'. Cut this 'No more collisions' bullet. Shorten Fig 8.8's 'Today' to 'Wi-Fi uses the same random backoff but tries to avoid collisions rather than detect them.'

findings.quote: their signals collide, both notice, jam and stop. Each then waits a random number of slots
findings.problem: 'Jam' and 'slots' are explained nowhere in the prose or the caption. Only the closed strip says 'slot times', and only the invisible <desc> says 'jam signal'.
findings.fix: '...their signals collide; both notice, send a short jamming signal so every station knows, and stop. Each then waits a random number of slot times (a fixed short interval), so one goes first...'

findings.quote: Every Ethernet device has a MAC address, a 48-bit identifier burned into the network card
findings.problem: MAC is never spelled out in the chapter. Two sentences later 'Apple's begin 00:03:93', which invites the reader to read MAC as Apple's Mac.
findings.fix: 'Every Ethernet device has a MAC (Media Access Control) address, nothing to do with Apple's Mac: a 48-bit identifier burned into the network card at manufacture.'

findings.quote: A MAC address is 48 bits: the first half names the maker (B8:27:EB is the Raspberry Pi Foundation), the second the card.
findings.problem: The caption restates p7 (the two halves, the Raspberry Pi prefix) and p8 (broadcast 'who has 192.168.1.5?', reply, cache). The strip's 'The halves' bullet makes it a third time.
findings.fix: Caption: 'One MAC address split into maker and card, and the ARP exchange that finds it: broadcast, reply, cache.' Cut the strip's 'The halves' bullet.

findings.quote: the asker caches the answer for a few minutes
findings.problem: The Fig 8.9 strip says entries 'age out after seconds to minutes, depending on the system'. The two numbers disagree.
findings.fix: 'the asker caches the answer for a while (seconds to minutes, depending on the system)', and cut the strip's 'Expiry' bullet.

findings.quote: falls back to what it does when it does not know which port a destination MAC sits on: broadcast to every port
findings.problem: Fig 8.10 calls this 'flood' and its table 'SWITCH TABLE'. Here it is 'broadcast' and 'MAC table'. The Fig 8.10 strip uses 'broadcast' for something else, frames addressed to everyone. So the reader sees two words for one mechanism and one word for two.
findings.fix: 'A switch's table (Fig 8.10) has finite size...' and '...: flood the frame out of every port.'

findings.quote: the polite, table-based, learning-by-listening designs of the 1990s assumed every participant played fair
findings.problem: The strip ends on a moral built on a triplet of adjectives. 'This attack, called MAC flooding,' also repeats the strip's own heading.
findings.fix: 'It was packaged into a point-and-shoot tool...'. End with: 'ARP and the switch table both assume every station plays fair; Chapter 15 collects the attacks that exploit that assumption.'

findings.quote: Each layer is a customer of the layer below and a provider for the layer above.
findings.problem: The customer/provider analogy is never cashed out in prose. Encapsulation, the literal mechanism (each layer wraps its data in a header on the way down and removes it on the way up), appears only in the Fig 8.11 caption and strip. The section's central idea therefore lives outside the prose.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: 'On the way out, each layer hands its data to the layer below, which wraps it in a header of its own; on arrival each layer removes its header and hands the rest up.' The Fig 8.11 caption can then just name the picture.

findings.quote: TCP/IP folds OSI's top three layers into one Application layer, because protocols such as HTTP manage their own sessions
findings.problem: p3 already gives the collapse and both of its reasons. The Fig 8.11 caption repeats it ('the top three blur into the application, which is why...'), this caption repeats it with both reasons, and the Fig 8.12 strip ('HTTP as an example') makes it four times.
findings.fix: Fig 8.12 caption: 'The seven OSI layers beside the four TCP/IP layers that run the internet, with the protocols that live in each.' In the Fig 8.11 caption, cut 'In practice the top three blur ... four layers of TCP/IP.'

findings.quote: TLS around the request
findings.problem: TLS and 'GET /' carry the figure's first wrapping, but neither is glossed in any visible text. Only the closed Fig 8.12 strip says TLS encrypts. Both are taught in Chapter 11.
findings.fix: '...: TLS (the encryption Chapter 11 explains) around the request for a page (GET /), then a TCP header, ...'

findings.quote: Bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
findings.problem: The prose writes 'Data Link' but Figs 8.11 and 8.12 and the strip write 'Data link'. OSI is never spelled out. p3 calls TCP/IP's middle layer 'the IP layer' but Fig 8.12 calls it 'Internet'.
findings.fix: Use one capitalisation ('Data Link'). Expand on first use: 'the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) seven-layer model'. In p3 write 'the Internet layer, where IP lives'.

findings.quote: remains the teaching reference because its separations are cleaner to teach
findings.problem: Circular: it is the teaching reference because it is cleaner to teach.
findings.fix: 'Even so, the OSI model remains the reference for teaching, because it gives each job its own layer.'

findings.quote: Every diagram so far has assumed two devices on one wire, or a few on one Ethernet segment.
findings.problem: Not true of this chapter. Fig 8.1 crosses an ocean through repeaters, and Fig 8.2 follows one request from laptop to router to provider to data centre.
findings.fix: 'Every mechanism in this chapter has worked within one link: two devices on one wire, or a few on one Ethernet segment.'

findings.quote: on tens of thousands of independently-administered networks, none of them aware of most of the others, and packets that need
findings.problem: An -ly adverb takes no hyphen. The sentence also lists the internet as devices '... and packets that need to find their way', which forces a reread. 'That graph' refers to a graph the chapter never set up.
findings.fix: 'The internet is billions of devices on tens of thousands of independently administered networks, none aware of most of the others, and a packet must find its way across all of them from any source to any destination.'

findings.quote: The idea that made this work was small, strange, and explicitly Cold War.
findings.problem: The seam ends on a reflexive triplet and a teaser. The seam itself is a protected device; only this wording is the problem.
findings.fix: 'The idea that made this work came out of a Cold War question: how to build a network that keeps working when parts of it are destroyed.' (This matches ch9-arpanet's Baran account.)

findings.quote: Money flows the other way: each network pays the one above it for transit
findings.problem: Fig 9.7 draws 'pays' arrows pointing up on both sides. On the left the packet also climbs, so there the money goes the same way as the packet, not the other way. The caption is true only for the right half of its own picture. The <desc> repeats it ('Money flows the other way up each side').
findings.fix: Caption: "Money flows up both sides: each network pays the one above it for transit, while the dozen or so Tier 1s exchange traffic with each other for free." Desc: "Money flows up each side: your ISP pays the regional network for transit, and the regional network pays the Tier 1."

findings.quote: network · 64 bits
findings.problem: The 64/64 bar is drawn with unequal halves: the network line runs x=20 to 170 (150 units) and the device line x=182 to 372 (190 units). It sits right under the step-3 short form, where the 'network' half covers '2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:3'. That puts 8a2e, a device group, on the network side. The device line also runs 48 units past the end of the step-1 address.
findings.fix: Draw equal halves tied to the full address: network line x=20 to 168, exactly under '2001:0db8:85a3:0000' of step 1; device line x=176 to 324, under '0000:8a2e:0370:7334'; device label text-anchor end at x=324. Move the bar directly under the step-1 box (or repeat the full address above it) so nobody reads it against the shortened '2001:db8:85a3::8a2e…'.

findings.quote: 65030 picks one by policy, adds itself
findings.problem: The thick highlight lines (.fx, stroke 4) run from box centre to box centre. The base links stop at the box edges with knock-out clips, but these do not. In steps 2 to 4 they strike through the AS numbers: the step-3 line crosses the middle of '65030' and '65099' like a strikethrough, step 2 cuts through '65010', '65020' and '65030', and the red step-4 line crosses '65010' and '65001'. Checked at t=4.5 s, 6.0 s and 7.33 s.
findings.fix: Give each .fx highlight line the same knock-out clip-path as its base link (clip-path="url(#ko-fig-9-6-N)", the clip already used on the matching thin line). The highlights then stop at the box edges and never cross a number.

findings.quote: A 4000-byte packet meets a link that carries at most 1500
findings.problem: The picture and desc show a packet carrying 4000 bytes of data, and the fragments carry 1480 + 1480 + 1040 = 4000 data bytes. That makes the original packet 4020 bytes with its header. A '4000-byte packet' would leave 3980 data bytes and a last fragment of 1020. Anyone checking against the How it works arithmetic finds a 20-byte mismatch.
findings.fix: "A packet carrying 4000 bytes of data meets a link that carries at most 1500, so it is cut into three fragments, each with the same ID, its offset (in 8-byte units) and a more-fragments flag."

findings.quote: thousands of homes share one public address
findings.problem: One IPv4 address has 65,535 ports. Carrier-grade NAT usually hands each subscriber a block of several hundred to a few thousand ports, so one public address serves dozens of customers (often 16 to 64), not thousands. A reader who knows networking stops here.
findings.fix: "many ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT): dozens of homes share one public address, each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table."

findings.quote: IPv6 · 128 bits · about 3.4 × 10³⁸
findings.problem: The exponent uses Unicode superscripts. At 375 px it renders as '10³ ⁸': the ³ comes from Space Mono and the ⁸ from a fallback font. The two glyphs differ in size, sit a gap apart, and are about 5 CSS px tall, below the 11 px floor in law 3. This is the figure's key number.
findings.fix: Draw the exponent as a tspan in the figure font: `about 3.4 × 10<tspan dy="-5" font-size="12.5">38</tspan>` (12.5 × 357/400 ≈ 11.2 px rendered). Or write "about 3.4 × 10^38", the form the How it works strip uses.

findings.quote: Identification 7238 | Flags 010
findings.problem: The header is drawn on a '0 bits 31' ruler, and the desc says 'laid out 32 bits to a row as in RFC 791'. The widths do not match that scale (352 units = 11 per bit). Version (4 bits) is drawn 66 units, as wide as ToS (8 bits, also 66). Identification (16 bits) is drawn 156, so it stops short of the midline that Total length and Header checksum share. Flags (3 bits) is drawn 53, about 5 bits, and straddles that midline.
findings.fix: Use the true widths: Version 44, IHL 44, ToS 88, Total length 176; Identification 176, Flags 33, Fragment offset 143. Abbreviate the labels that no longer fit ('Ver'; set 'Flags' above its box).

findings.quote: Flags 010
findings.problem: The value 010 (the don't-fragment bit set) is shown, but nothing in the figure, its strip or the chapter decodes it. Part 3 never mentions don't-fragment. A newcomer is left holding a mark they cannot read. Fig 9.5 explains only the more-fragments flag.
findings.fix: Draw the value as "010 DF" (or "DF"), and add to the How it works 'small fields' item: "**Flags** 010 sets don't-fragment, the bit path MTU discovery relies on."

findings.quote: silence: still reserved
findings.problem: The 'silence: still reserved' label shows from 4.2 to 6.2 s. Voice dots are still running along the wire until 5.3 s, and the next voice dot leaves A at 5.8 s while the label still says silence (checked at t=4.5 s and 6.0 s). The reserved but empty wire, which is the point of the label, is on screen for only about 0.5 s.
findings.fix: Show the label only while the wire is empty. Start it when the last voice dot reaches B (keyTime 0.6625), and delay dots 7 and 8 until it ends. Or end the label at 0.725 and widen the gap between dots 6 and 7, so the still-reserved empty wire stays up for about 2 s.

findings.quote: pays
findings.problem: The four 'pays' labels touch the vertical links. The right-hand labels, end-anchored at x=354, start at about 323 against the link at x=322, so the 'p' sits on the line. The left-hand labels end at about 77 against the link at 78. The moving packet (r 7) passes over the left-hand 'pays' as it climbs.
findings.fix: Move the dashed arrows and labels outward: left arrows at x=28 with labels starting at x=34; right arrows at x=372 with labels ending at x=366. Each label then clears its link by about 13 units, and clears the passing packet.

findings.quote: became the design argument of the ARPANET
findings.problem: The caption says Baran's survivability case became the ARPANET's design argument. The prose around it says the design was a synthesis (Baran's mesh, Davies's terminology, Kleinrock's math), and that ARPA built it 'to let universities share expensive computers, not to survive a war'. The caption half-revives the survive-a-nuclear-war story that the section corrects.
findings.fix: "His case for the third, packets finding their own way through redundant links, became the shape of the ARPANET's mesh."

findings.quote: The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs
findings.problem: The path the paragraph gives is only the client's: it opens the connection and closes first. The states left off it are LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK and CLOSING. The first four are the normal path of every server that answers a connection and closes second, and Fig 10.3 and its caption draw them that way. Only CLOSING is kept for a simultaneous close. No state exists for lost FINs: retransmission timers handle them (RFC 793, Fig. 6). As written, a reader learns that the server's ordinary states are failure handlers.
findings.fix: Replace the last two sentences with: "A client usually walks CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the server it talks to walks LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The remaining rules handle simultaneous opens and closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send) and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive."

findings.quote: It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs.
findings.problem: Measurement says otherwise. The 2019 census (Mishra et al., "The Great Internet TCP Congestion Control Census", Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst. 3(3), 2019) found CUBIC on about 36% of the Alexa top 20,000 sites. BBR was on 22% of sites, but its estimated share of traffic volume was "larger than 40%". So CUBIC runs on the most servers, not on the great majority of traffic.
findings.fix: "It is the most common TCP algorithm on web servers (about a third of the top 20,000 sites in a 2019 census), though BBR, next, already carried an estimated two-fifths of the traffic."

findings.quote: BBR can be two to ten times faster than CUBIC
findings.problem: No source gives this range. Google's own figures (Google Cloud blog, July 2017) are: 2,700 times CUBIC's throughput on a 10 Gbit/s, 100 ms path with 1% loss, a microbenchmark; 4% more throughput across YouTube; and, behind an oversized queue, 25 times less queueing delay (43 ms against 1,090 ms) with no throughput gain. Behind home routers with oversized queues BBR's win is lower delay, not speed, because CUBIC fills those links too.
findings.fix: "On long paths with random loss BBR can move many times more data than CUBIC; behind home routers with oversized queues its gain is delay, not speed, keeping round trips short where CUBIC fills the queue. Across YouTube it raised throughput by 4 percent and cut round-trip time by a third." (source: cloud.google.com/blog/products/networking/tcp-bbr-congestion-control-comes-to-gcp-your-internet-just-got-faster)

findings.quote: By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests, and the share is growing.
findings.problem: Cloudflare Radar's Year in Review puts HTTP/3, and so QUIC, at 20% of requests in 2023, 20.5% in 2024 and about 21% in 2025: one request in five, not well over a quarter, and almost flat. The paragraph also disagrees with Ch11's "roughly a third of web traffic by volume" (a different measure; Ch11's checker should confirm it).
findings.fix: "By 2024 about one web request in five used it (20.5 percent of those Cloudflare saw), and the share is creeping up." (source: blog.cloudflare.com/radar-2024-year-in-review)

findings.quote: when an attacker can predict the sequence numbers of an existing connection, they can inject data into it
findings.problem: The definition does not fit the story it introduces. Morris's 1985 report (Bell Labs CSTR 117) described opening a new connection in a trusted host's name by guessing the server's next ISN. Mitnick's attack in p7 does the same: a new spoofed connection, not injection into an open one. In Shimomura's own account (Jan 1995), the takeover of an existing session came later and used a kernel STREAMS module on a machine already broken into, not sequence prediction.
findings.fix: "*TCP hijacking*: an attacker who can predict the sequence numbers a host will use can forge segments in another machine's name, opening a connection that seems to come from a trusted host or injecting data into one already open." (keep the key-term span on "TCP hijacking")

findings.quote: The random ISN requirement (Bellovin's RFC 1948)
findings.problem: RFC 1948 (May 1996) is Informational ("does not specify an Internet standard"), so it is not a requirement. It says outright that "simple randomization ... will not work well". What it proposed was the cryptographic scheme the next sentence credits to 2012: ISN = clock + F(four-tuple), where F is a keyed cryptographic hash such as MD5. RFC 6528 (2012) made that same scheme the standard. The paragraph splits one fix into a random step and a later cryptographic step. The ledger's timing (about a year, stacks took the decade) stays.
findings.fix: "Bellovin's RFC 1948, about a year after Mitnick's arrest, proposed the cure: start each connection's sequence numbers at a clock plus a keyed cryptographic hash of its addresses and ports, so no connection's numbers reveal another's. Stacks took the rest of the decade to adopt it, and RFC 6528 made it the standard in 2012." Keep "random ISN" (or say "unpredictable ISNs") wherever the glossary term needs it.

findings.quote: Predicting the ISN, Mitnick blind-sent the third ACK
findings.problem: p6 and p7 state as settled that Mitnick ran the Christmas Day spoofing attack himself. That is Shimomura and Markoff's account in Takedown. In his memoir Ghost in the Wires (2011), Mitnick says an associate ("JSZ") made the Christmas break-in ("I have a Christmas present for you. My friend, I got into ariel tonight") and that Mitnick then came in "using the backdoor that JSZ had set up". The attribution is disputed, and the book presents it as fact.
findings.fix: After the Takedown sentence, add: "Mitnick, in his 2011 memoir Ghost in the Wires, says an associate made the Christmas break-in and handed him the access." Optionally in p6: "until, on Christmas Day 1994, it was used on the live internet for the highest-profile intrusion of the era, the one pinned on Kevin Mitnick." (excerpt: gizmodo.com/how-to-become-the-most-wanted-hacker-in-the-world-5834494)

findings.quote: Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals.
findings.problem: Congestion control serves none of the four 1974 goals. Section 04 says flow control "does nothing to prevent the sender from outrunning the network" and dates congestion control to 1988, yet p3 of this section lists congestion-control state in the TCB. A careful reader hits the contradiction two sections later.
findings.fix: "Almost every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals; the big exception, congestion control, came fourteen years later (Section 04)."

findings.quote: DNS, every video call, every game, every connection over QUIC
findings.problem: "Every game" is false: many games run over TCP (World of Warcraft, most turn-based and mobile games over HTTP or WebSockets). Video calls fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.
findings.fix: "(DNS, most video calls and fast-paced games, every connection over QUIC, the newer transport of Section 05)"

findings.quote: with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment
findings.problem: The present tense says TCP starts at one segment today. Modern stacks start at ten (RFC 6928, 2013; Linux since 2011). One segment is right for the 1988 algorithm and after a timeout.
findings.fix: "with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment (ten in today's stacks)"

findings.quote: collapsed from its design capacity of 32 kilobits per second
findings.problem: Jacobson and Karels say only that throughput "dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps". 32 kbit/s was the link's normal throughput, not a design capacity: the ARPANET IMP lines ran at 56 kbit/s.
findings.fix: "collapsed from its usual 32 kilobits per second to roughly 40 bits per second"

findings.quote: some of it through cellular networks Shimomura himself had earlier helped secure
findings.problem: No source found says Shimomura helped secure the cellular networks Mitnick used. His cellular work was research into phones' weak privacy (1992 congressional testimony). The final trace was a cellular modem in Raleigh, found with Sprint technicians and direction-finding gear.
findings.fix: "(the last leg through a cellular modem, which he and Sprint technicians tracked by radio)", or drop the parenthesis.

findings.quote: opened a TCP connection to Shimomura's main workstation
findings.problem: Shimomura's technical account names the spoofed connection's target "x-terminal": "a diskless SPARCstation running Solaris 1" that he used as an X terminal. It was not his main workstation.
findings.fix: "opened a TCP connection to a diskless workstation Shimomura used as an X terminal" (source: Shimomura's Jan 1995 post, mirrored at pld.cs.luc.edu/courses/447/sum08/class7/shimomura.text)

findings.quote: the reason every modern OS ships with SYN cookie support
findings.problem: Windows' documented SYN-flood defence is SynAttackProtect: fewer SYN-ACK retransmissions and half-open handshakes held in a hash table. Microsoft documents no SYN cookies. Linux and FreeBSD do ship them. Also, "the reason cloud DDoS protection ... exists" overclaims: those services absorb many kinds of flood.
findings.fix: Owner text, so report only. A true version would say "the reason Linux and the BSDs ship SYN cookies, and one of the floods cloud DDoS protection (Cloudflare, AWS Shield) absorbs".

findings.quote: the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second
findings.problem: The animation plays the server's whole life first (listen, SYN in, ACK in, FIN in, close(): send FIN, ACK in, about 2 to 8.5 s), then the client's (connect, SYN-ACK in, close(): send FIN, ..., about 10.4 to 15.6 s). So 'server: FIN in: send ACK' and 'server: close(): send FIN' light up before the client has even connected, let alone sent its FIN. That puts cause after effect and contradicts the caption's 'client ... closes first, the server ... closes second'.
findings.fix: Interleave the twelve steps in causal order, keeping both rings visible and the same 16 s loop: server: listen() → client: connect(): send SYN → server: SYN in: send SYN-ACK → client: SYN-ACK in: send ACK → server: ACK in → client: close(): send FIN → server: FIN in: send ACK → client: ACK in → server: close(): send FIN → client: FIN in: send ACK → server: ACK in → client: wait 2 × max segment lifetime.

findings.quote: a returning client can send its request in its very first packet
findings.problem: This clause appears word for word in ch10-modern-p6, the paragraph right above the figure. The caption's second sentence ('QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it and runs over UDP, in the application rather than the kernel') restates p6's 'runs over UDP ... inside the application, not the kernel'. The reader gets the same words twice in a row (law 2).
findings.fix: Make the caption read the picture: "Over TCP a browser spends one round trip on TCP's handshake and another on TLS's before it can ask for the page: three in all. QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it, so one handshake does both jobs (two), and a resumed connection gets the page after one."

findings.quote: The result is a sawtooth around a capacity TCP never measures directly
findings.problem: The picture shows the window hanging below the capacity line: it touches the line only at the peaks (25 against 24) and falls to 12, half of it. 'Around' (also in ch10-aimd-p6, 'oscillates around the true capacity', and in the desc) suggests swings above and below by about the same amount. The caption's first sentence also repeats p6 almost clause for clause.
findings.fix: Caption: "After slow start's first loss, TCP adds one segment per round trip and halves at each loss: a sawtooth that climbs to the capacity and falls to half of it. TCP never measures the limit; it finds it by overshooting." In p6: "so the window swings between half the capacity and just above it in a sawtooth pattern".

findings.quote: TCP's eleven states, as RFC 793 defined them in 1981
findings.problem: The picture draws twelve boxes, because CLOSED appears twice (top and bottom) and nothing says the two are the same state. A reader who counts the boxes against the caption's 'eleven' gets twelve.
findings.fix: Label the bottom box "CLOSED (again)", or add to the key line: "CLOSED is drawn twice: where a connection starts and where it ends".

findings.quote: ACK 109: it slides on
findings.problem: At 5.8 to 6.1 s the window frame glides backwards from 109–114 to 100–105 while the label still reads 'ACK 109: it slides on' and every cell is still acked. A TCP window never moves back. At 2.2 to 2.5 s and 9.0 to 9.3 s the frame starts sliding forward before the ACK label and the cell colours change, so for 0.3 s orange in-flight bytes sit outside the window while the label says 'sent 106 to 108: full again' or 'window full: wait for an ACK'.
findings.fix: Make the loop reset a cut: hold translate 216 until 0.6095, then jump to 0. Start each forward slide only after the ACK label and the cell colours have switched, moving the slides from 0.22–0.25 to 0.25–0.28 and from 0.90–0.93 to 0.93–0.96, or switch the label and cells at 0.22 and 0.90.

findings.quote: each ACK names the next byte expected, the window's left edge moves up to it, and room opens on the right
findings.problem: The caption retells ch10-aimd-p2 in other words: in flight means sent but not acknowledged, the trailing edge advances, room opens at the leading edge, the receiver sets the window in every ACK, flow control. It never points at what the picture shows.
findings.fix: Tie it to the drawn values: "ACK 103 says bytes 100 to 102 arrived, so the six-byte window moves up to 103 and three new bytes may go; ACK 109 moves it on by six. The receiver restates that six in every ACK, so a slow reader throttles a fast writer with no extra messages."

findings.quote: BBR aims here
findings.problem: One white dot plays both senders. It climbs to 'buffer full', 'loss' flashes, then it glides back to the knee and rests there while the queue drains. The loop therefore reads as one sender that settles at the knee after a loss. Neither sender behaves like that: loss-based TCP halves and climbs again, and BBR never fills the buffer.
findings.fix: After the loss flash, cut the dot back to the start instead of gliding it to the knee. Or recolour the returning dot blue (BBR's colour) and tag it "BBR" while it moves, so the glide reads as BBR's target, not as loss-based TCP's recovery.

findings.quote: the second is lost on the way
findings.problem: After datagram 2 vanishes, the red X stays on the wire and datagram 3 runs straight across it (around 5.8 s, just as 'sender: no idea' appears), then arrives. For a moment the loss mark looks like a spot that kills packets, and 3 seems to pass through it unharmed.
findings.fix: Drop datagram 2 below the line at the loss point and put the X there, under the wire, so datagram 3 travels clear of it. Alternatively, hide the X while datagram 3 passes (about 0.70 to 0.75 of the loop).

findings.quote: SYN · let's connect, I count from X
findings.problem: The travelling dots follow two colour rules at once. The SYN-ACK dot is the server's red and the ACK dot is the client's green, but the SYN dot, also sent by the client, is the arrow blue. A reader who notices the colours cannot tell what they mean.
findings.fix: Colour the SYN dot the client's green (rgba(150,216,150,0.95)) to match the ACK dot, or make all three dots the arrow blue.

findings.quote: The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs
findings.problem: The 'well-trodden path' the paragraph gives is only the client's end. Fig 10.3, directly below, shows every server taking LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED on an ordinary connection. So four of the 'off-path' states are the normal server path, not failure handling, and the prose and the figure contradict each other. This overlaps the open owner call on Fig 10.3 (option a, which would add how a connection closes).
findings.fix: Replace from 'Most connections take one well-trodden path' to the end of the paragraph with: 'A client's end usually runs CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; a server's runs CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The remaining state, CLOSING, and the extra moves handle simultaneous opens and closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send) and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive.' This also settles owner call Fig 10.3 (a).

findings.quote: Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals.
findings.problem: This is untrue of today's TCP, and the chapter itself shows it. Congestion control (Section 04) serves none of the four goals: flow control protects only the receiver (ch10-aimd-p4), and ch10-why-p3 lists 'the congestion-control state' in every TCB. The section title ('still in force') makes the same claim.
findings.fix: 'Every piece of machinery TCP carried in 1974 served one of those four goals; a fifth, congestion control, was added in 1988 (Section 04).'

findings.quote: UDP carries an enormous fraction of modern internet traffic (DNS, every video call, every game
findings.problem: DNS is the chapter's main UDP example (p1, p2, Fig 10.1's '53 · DNS' and 'payload: the DNS query', the strip), yet no earlier chapter teaches it. Ch8 and Ch9 only name it in a layer list. The only gloss in this chapter is in the seam at its very end ('DNS for finding servers by name'). The baseline reader cannot see why a DNS lookup is one small question and one small answer.
findings.fix: At first use: '(DNS, the lookup that turns a name like example.com into an address; every video call, every game, ...)'. Alternatively, in p2: 'A DNS lookup (asking which address a name like example.com stands for, Chapter 11) is a single small request...'

findings.quote: eight bytes of header with two ports, a length and a checksum, and nothing else
findings.problem: A port in the networking sense (a number that names the program at each end) is never taught. The book's only earlier 'port' is a socket on a switch (ch8-ethernet). Fig 10.1 ('source port 51234', 'destination port 53') and ch10-attacks-p4 ('source IP, source port, ...') rely on it. Without it the reader misses the one thing UDP adds to IP: delivery to the right program.
findings.fix: In ch10-udp-p1: 'an eight-byte header on top of IP, mostly two port numbers that name the program at each end (53 means a DNS server).'

findings.quote: The paper's fix centred on two pieces, explained next: slow start and AIMD
findings.problem: AIMD is named here, as a key-term chip, and then never expanded or named in the prose. p6 describes halving and linear growth without saying that this is AIMD. The expansion appears only in Fig 10.5's closed strip and in the math callout p8, which then expands it a second time.
findings.fix: In p6, after 'in a sawtooth pattern': 'Adding a constant and halving is AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease.' Then drop the parenthetical expansion at the start of p8.

findings.quote: begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment
findings.problem: The congestion window gets a name and nothing more. The prose never says it is a second limit the sender sets for itself and obeys alongside the receiver's window. That step exists only in Fig 10.4's closed strip ('The sender obeys the smaller'). A reader who knows only the receive window cannot tell whose window is being halved.
findings.fix: 'Slow start begins cautiously, with a congestion window (cwnd), a second limit the sender sets for itself and obeys alongside the receiver's window, of one segment, and doubles it on every successful round trip.'

findings.quote: In every ACK, the receiver advertises how much of its receive buffer remains free: the receive window.
findings.problem: Section 02 (ch10-why-p2) already taught the window and 'in flight' ('Receivers periodically advertise a window ... senders never have more than that many in flight'). This paragraph teaches both from scratch again, and caption p3 defines 'in flight' a third time. The two passages also disagree: 'periodically' in why-p2, 'in every ACK' here and in caption p3.
findings.fix: In ch10-why-p2, change 'Receivers periodically advertise' to 'Every acknowledgement also carries'. In ch10-aimd-p2, start from what the reader has: 'The first piece is the sliding window, built on the window from Section 02, which every ACK carries: the sender never has more than that many bytes in flight. As ACKs arrive, ...'

findings.quote: The receiver sets the window size in every ACK, so a slow reader throttles a fast writer
findings.problem: The caption teaches p2 again: 'in flight' defined again, the window set in every ACK, and flow control restated as 'a slow reader throttles a fast writer'. It should name the picture instead.
findings.fix: 'Bytes 100 to 114 with a six-byte window: each ACK moves the left edge up to the byte it names, and as many cells open on the right.'

findings.quote: Slow start doubles the window every round trip until the first loss; after that TCP adds one segment
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p6 almost word for word.
findings.fix: 'One connection on a path that carries 24 segments: slow start overshoots to 32, then the window saws between about 12 and 25. TCP never measures the capacity; it finds the limit by overshooting it.'

findings.quote: the server answers with its own and acknowledges the client's plus one; the client acknowledges the server's plus one
findings.problem: The caption retells p1's SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK sequence, and the strip explains 'plus one' again. Only the round-trip cost is new.
findings.fix: 'Each side starts counting from its own number, 4170 and 9012, and each acknowledges the other's plus one. The client's first byte of data waits a full round trip, the tax QUIC (Section 05) sets out to cut.'

findings.quote: When it ends, both sides know each other's starting sequence numbers
findings.problem: 'it' comes right after 'A TCP connection begins...', so it reads as the connection ending. The sentence means the handshake ending. A reader has to go back to sort this out.
findings.fix: 'When the third arrives, both sides know each other's starting sequence numbers, ...'

findings.quote: a returning client can send its request in its very first packet
findings.problem: The caption repeats p6 word for word. Its second sentence ('QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it and runs over UDP, in the application rather than the kernel') repeats both p6 and the strip's 'The stacks' item, so the same point is made three times.
findings.fix: Caption: 'Over TCP and TLS 1.3 the page arrives after three round trips; QUIC's combined handshake makes it two, and a resumed connection one.' In the strip, cut the first sentence of 'The stacks' and keep the iterability point.

findings.quote: over TCP, one lost packet stalls every request queued behind it: "head-of-line blocking"
findings.problem: Ch11 §06 (ch11-modern-p2, p4–p6, Fig 11.15) teaches head-of-line blocking, HTTP/2 streams and QUIC's per-stream ordering in full. This parenthesis, plus 'many independent streams per connection', teaches them early in compressed form, before the reader knows what an HTTP stream is. The two chapters also give QUIC's share differently: 'By 2024 ... well over a quarter of web requests' here, 'As of 2026 ... roughly a third of web traffic by volume' in ch11-modern-p5.
findings.fix: Replace from 'Loss in one HTTP request stream' to the end with: 'It also stops one lost packet from stalling unrelated requests, which Chapter 11 shows with HTTP/2. QUIC is what HTTP/3 runs on.' Drop the share sentence; Ch11 carries the 2026 figure.

findings.quote: No connection, no order, no retransmission: a lost datagram is simply missing
findings.problem: The caption restates p1 (eight-byte header; no connection, no order, no retransmission). The strip restates p1 ('RFC 768 ... three pages long') and p2 (DNS fits in one datagram; voice and games would rather lose than wait). The figure's text adds nothing the prose has not just said.
findings.fix: Caption: 'Port 51234 asks port 53 a DNS question with eight bytes of header. Datagram 2 is lost and nothing notices; retrying, if anyone does, is the application's job.' Strip: cut 'is three pages long' and the 'Where it wins' item.

findings.quote: UDP's strength is that it has no state. TCP's strength is that it has all the state that reliability requires.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer built on a parallel pair. It repeats Section 01 ('no state' in Fig 10.1's title), and Section 06 opens with the same antithesis ('TCP's strength is ... TCP's weakness is the same'), so two sections share one shape.
findings.fix: Cut both sentences. The paragraph ends on the million TCBs, and Section 06 picks up the cost.

findings.quote: is not merely a combination that works; it is the only one that does
findings.problem: The callout opens with a 'Not X; Y' reveal and closes on an aphorism ('forced by the mathematics, not chosen by taste') that restates the proof's claim.
findings.fix: Open with: 'Chiu and Jain proved in 1989 that AIMD is the only one of the four combinations of additive or multiplicative increase and decrease that converges to both efficiency ... and fairness ...'. Cut the last sentence.

findings.quote: the network can never authenticate who you are, only what you say
findings.problem: An aphorism closer that is also wrong as written. The network does not authenticate what you say either. It delivers whatever a packet claims, source address included, which is the point of the Mitnick story.
findings.fix: 'The deeper lesson is that a packet's source address is only a claim, which the network carries but never checks, so applications must authenticate cryptographically on top.'

findings.quote: The defences are nearly all about making the protocol stateless under attack
findings.problem: Two of the three examples it gives keep state (random ISNs, TLS). The strip's own last sentence says patches 'push state into harder places', which contradicts 'stateless'. 'state in the unguessable' does not name anything concrete.
findings.fix: 'The defences mostly move state where an attacker cannot reach or forge it: SYN cookies (state in the wire), random ISNs (state an outsider cannot guess), TLS (state cryptographically authenticated).'

findings.quote: TCP hijacking
findings.problem: The glossary key-term chip wraps 'TCP' alone inside the bold 'TCP hijacking'. It renders as a cyan mono chip followed by bold 'hijacking', in the last section of the TCP chapter, and makes the glossary send TCP to Section 06. 'three-way handshake' is chipped in ch10-attacks-p2, so its glossary entry also lands in Section 06, not Section 03 (glossary.json: tcp → ch10-attacks, three-way handshake → ch10-attacks).
findings.fix: Make 'TCP hijacking' plain bold. Move the TCP chip to 'TCP' in ch10-why-p1 and the three-way-handshake chip to ch10-handshake-p1. Then run npm run build:glossary.

findings.quote: TCP's strength is that the kernel remembers every connection. TCP's weakness is the same:
findings.problem: This is the same strength/weakness antithesis that closes Section 02, so it reads as a template.
findings.fix: 'The TCB that makes TCP reliable (Section 02) is also its weakness: an attacker who can make the kernel allocate one without ever completing a connection can, ...'

findings.quote: No connection. No retransmission. No ordering. No way for the receiver to say slow down.
findings.problem: Four clipped fragments in a row, the dramatic-fragment tell, and the caption repeats three of them. 'to say slow down' has no quotation marks and reads awkwardly.
findings.fix: 'just send packets, with no connection, no retransmission, no ordering and no way for the receiver to ask the sender to slow down.'

findings.quote: Most applications find this terrifying; a few find it liberating.
findings.problem: A balanced antithesis that teaches nothing. The next sentences already show which applications want UDP.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence.

findings.quote: A factor of eight hundred.
findings.problem: A clipped dramatic fragment after the numbers have already been given.
findings.fix: '...collapsed from its design capacity of 32 kilobits per second to roughly 40 bits per second, a factor of eight hundred.'

findings.quote: the receive window accounted for the receiver but said nothing about the network in between
findings.problem: This restates p4 ('prevents the sender from outrunning the receiver. It does nothing to prevent ... outrunning the network').
findings.fix: 'Their diagnosis, published in 1988 as "Congestion Avoidance and Control", was that a network without explicit congestion feedback would always, eventually, congest itself to death.'

findings.quote: The trick: the source IP could be forged
findings.problem: The emphasis covers 'the source IP could' instead of the one contrasted word, so the stress lands wrongly. 'The trick:' is also a clipped opener.
findings.fix: 'But the source IP could be forged, if you also knew TCP's sequence numbers.'

findings.quote: ISN generator was barely random at all
findings.problem: A mixed idiom. The same sentence says each ISN stepped up by a fixed 128,000, which means not random at all.
findings.fix: 'And Shimomura's machines' ISN generator was not random at all: minutes of probing ... showed each new connection's ISN stepping up by a fixed 128,000, ...'

findings.quote: A book (Shimomura and Markoff's Takedown) and, later, a film based on it followed.
findings.problem: The chase, the apartment in Raleigh and the book and film teach nothing about sequence numbers; the brief says colour that teaches nothing goes. Only the arrest is used later (p8).
findings.fix: Cut the last sentence. Shorten the chase to: 'Shimomura traced the intrusion, and the FBI arrested Mitnick on 15 February 1995.'

findings.quote: It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs.
findings.problem: Traffic does not 'run' an algorithm, and the sentence reads as if a word is missing.
findings.fix: 'Most of the internet's TCP traffic uses it.'

findings.quote: where round-trip times were tens of milliseconds and bandwidths a few megabits
findings.problem: Section 04 has just told the reader that the 1986 LBL–Berkeley link was designed for 32 kilobits per second. 'a few megabits' for the same era is a hundred times more, and nothing reconciles the two.
findings.fix: 'where round-trip times were tens of milliseconds and links ran at kilobits to a few megabits per second.'

findings.quote: Its protocol, which they called simply TCP
findings.problem: TCP is never expanded anywhere in the book (the glossary says Transmission Control Protocol), while TCB is expanded two paragraphs later. 'simply' implies there is nothing to expand. In 1974 the letters stood for Transmission Control Program.
findings.fix: 'Its protocol, the Transmission Control Program (TCP; the P later became Protocol), was designed to do four things...'

findings.quote: Three segments. Two synchronised counters. One conversation.
findings.problem: The section title is a countdown triplet of clipped fragments, and the hero's 'three messages. one connection.' repeats the shape.
findings.fix: 'Three segments synchronise two counters.'

findings.quote: (TCP calls each one a segment)
findings.problem: 'Segment' was already defined in ch10-why-p1 ('manageable chunks, called segments').
findings.fix: 'A TCP connection begins with three segments: SYN (...), SYN-ACK (...) and ACK (...).'

findings.quote: Four would be redundant.
findings.problem: A clipped closer that asserts without saying why. The reason is that the server's acknowledgement and its own SYN ride in one segment.
findings.fix: 'A fourth is not needed because the server's acknowledgement and its own starting number travel together in the SYN-ACK.'

findings.quote: each move triggered by an arriving segment, a program call or a timer
findings.problem: This repeats p3 ('A segment arriving, a call from the program or a timer running out moves it').
findings.fix: 'TCP's eleven states, as RFC 793 defined them in 1981: the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second. The side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT ...'

findings.quote: The result is distributed feedback control.
findings.problem: A label closer. The term is never used again and adds nothing to the sentence before it.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence.

findings.quote: The last two decades produced three answers.
findings.problem: It announces what the section title has just said ('Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis').
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. p2 opens on CUBIC directly.

findings.quote: Classic Reno halves on a loss signalled by repeated ACKs
findings.problem: Reno is first introduced in ch10-modern-p1 ('Classic TCP (Tahoe, Reno, NewReno)'), a section later.
findings.fix: 'Classic TCP halves on a loss signalled by repeated ACKs and falls back to one segment on a timeout.'

findings.quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
findings.problem: Hashes are first taught in Ch11 §04 (ch11-crypto); nothing earlier in the book mentions them. The SYN cookie mechanism relies on what a keyed hash guarantees.
findings.fix: 'a keyed hash (a scrambled 32-bit fingerprint that only the holder of the secret key can compute) of the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and a time bucket, ...'

findings.quote: racing back, slowing near the old peak, then probing past it
findings.problem: This repeats p2's description of the curve ('climbs fast at first, then eases into a plateau ... accelerates past it').
findings.fix: 'After one loss on a 1 Gbit/s, 100 ms path, Reno halves its window and adds a segment per round trip; CUBIC cuts to 0.7 and is back at the old peak in 19 seconds, where Reno needs seven minutes.'

findings.quote: keeps the gap between them; halving both on a loss halves it
findings.problem: The caption and the strip's 'The two moves' item say the same thing (additive keeps the gap, multiplicative halves it), and p8 has just said it for AIAD.
findings.fix: Caption: 'From A 22, B 4 on a link of 32, the gap goes 18, 9, 4.5, 2.25: every loss brings the pair closer to equal shares while each peak still fills the link, though neither flow knows the other exists.'

findings.quote: the W_max both flows had reached when the loss came
findings.problem: The underscore from code notation shows as text ('W_max'), while the figure's desc says 'W max' and the drawing says 'the last peak'.
findings.fix: Write W<sub>max</sub> in the strip and its formula: W(t) = C(t − K)³ + W<sub>max</sub>, K = ∛(W<sub>max</sub> × 0.3 / C).

findings.quote: The signature, made with the certificate's private key, proves the server is who the certificate says
findings.problem: Section 04 promises everything TLS needs ('enough to read the TLS handshake') but never teaches digital signatures. It teaches only 'public key locks, only private unlocks'. Yet TLS p2, p4, Fig 11.12 and its caption all depend on a signature being made with a private key and checked with a public key ('checks each signature with the public key of the certificate above it'). To the reader that is the operation just learned, run backwards. Also, a certificate holds no private key.
findings.fix: In ch11-crypto-p7, after 'can only be decrypted with the matching private key.', add: 'The pair also works the other way round: a value computed from a message with the private key, which anyone can check with the public key but only the key's owner could have made, is a digital signature.' In tls-p2: 'The signature, made with the private key that matches the certificate's public key, proves...'. To stay net-zero, pay for it by cutting the repeated Fig 11.10 strip items (see fig-11-10).

findings.quote: Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows.
findings.problem: Until now, the only MAC this book has taught is the Ethernet MAC address (Ch8), so the reader will read this as a hardware address. The strip also contradicts tls-p2, which says the closing messages 'each carry a hash of the entire transcript'.
findings.fix: 'Each Finished carries a keyed hash of the whole transcript, so any tampering shows.'

findings.quote: if the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it
findings.problem: As written, links break in Xanadu as well as on the web, so the contrast falls apart. Two sentences later Xanadu is the system that 'demands a working link to every published target'. The reader is left asking what the difference is.
findings.fix: 'In Project Xanadu, every link was known to the system at both ends and every document kept a permanent address, so the system itself guaranteed that no link ever broke.'

findings.quote: The trade was correct. The web exists; Xanadu does not.
findings.problem: A clipped aphorism closer that does no job. p9 has just made the argument, and p3 already says Xanadu 'never shipped'.
findings.fix: Cut ch11-bernerslee-p10 and alias its anchor to ch11-bernerslee-p9 in ANCHOR_ALIASES.

findings.quote: Each by itself was uninteresting. Together they made the web.
findings.problem: Clipped dramatic fragments that work as an aphorism and teach nothing. p8 explains why the three together mattered.
findings.fix: Cut both sentences, so that p5 opens 'He wrote both ends himself: ...'.

findings.quote: the long empty stretch is the quiet, the cluster at the bottom is the take-off
findings.problem: In the drawing, the shaded band labelled '2½ quiet years, one machine' runs from Mar 1989 to Aug 1991. The long empty stretch on the line is Dec 1991 to Apr 1993, a different period. The strip points the reader at the wrong stretch. Also, from Mar 1989 to Dec 1990 no machine was serving the web at all.
findings.fix: Strip: '*The scale.* Each dot sits at its date: the shaded band is the quiet, from proposal to announcement; the green cluster at the bottom is the take-off.' Caption: 'For two and a half years the web was one project at CERN: ...' (drop 'on one machine').

findings.quote: three protocols invented in 1989 at a particle physics lab
findings.problem: The title just above reads 'HTTP · DNS · TLS', so the reader maps 'three protocols' onto those three. But DNS dates from 1983 and TLS from 1999, and neither came from CERN. The three meant here are URL, HTTP and HTML, and two of those are not protocols: ch11-bernerslee-p3 rightly calls them 'conventions'. ch11-bernerslee-p8 repeats the slip: 'None of the three protocols required anyone else's permission.'
findings.fix: Hero: 'three inventions from a particle physics lab in 1989 (an address, a request, a page format)'. bernerslee-p8: 'None of the three required anyone else's permission.'

findings.quote: read every byte of an HTTPS request from voltage to JSON
findings.problem: The book has not explained JSON anywhere up to here, and the chapter never deals with it (it appears only in 'JSON Merge Patch' in a strip). The promise names something the chapter does not deliver.
findings.fix: '...read every byte of an HTTPS request, from voltage to the page's HTML.'

findings.quote: a little hypertext program Berners-Lee had written years earlier for himself
findings.problem: ENQUIRE is introduced twice: p1 has 'the linked-notes program he had already built for himself at CERN' and p2 repeats it with its name. p2 also uses 'hypertext' one paragraph before p3 defines it ('This is the idea of hypertext').
findings.fix: p1: 'generalising ENQUIRE, the linked-notes program he had already built for himself at CERN.' p2: '...design notes in ENQUIRE.' 'Hypertext' then first appears at its definition in p3.

findings.quote: (AOL, MSN, Compuserve in their walled-garden phases)
findings.problem: The proper name is spelled wrong.
findings.fix: 'CompuServe'.

findings.quote: CERN released the entire web (code, protocols, specifications) into the public domain
findings.problem: Nobody can release 'the entire web'. The caption and Fig 11.1 say, correctly, that CERN gave the software away (the 30 April 1993 statement covered the W3 code).
findings.fix: 'On 30 April 1993 CERN put the web's software into the public domain, with a one-page document...'

findings.quote: a first line, the headers, a blank line, then the body
findings.problem: The caption retells ch11-http-p2, which sits right beside it: request line, headers, blank line, body, and a response of the same shape with a status code. Brief: the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: 'One request and its response, byte for byte; every line ends in a carriage return and a line feed, drawn as \r\n.'

findings.quote: Statefulness scales with engineering effort; statelessness scales with money.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer. The sentence before it has already explained why stateless servers scale.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence.

findings.quote: it performs about twenty separate operations across four layers
findings.problem: Ch8 taught 'the four layers of TCP/IP' (link, internet, transport, application). DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP are not those layers: DNS and HTTP both sit in the application layer. The 'twenty operations' are never shown. The figure and its caption show four exchanges.
findings.fix: 'The browser does not simply open the page: it runs four exchanges in a row, and the page appears only at the end.'

findings.quote: Fig 11.3 · One curl, fully traced
findings.problem: curl appears nowhere earlier in the book. The prose has just asked the reader to type the address into a browser, and the figure and strip ('curl prints the body') switch to curl without a word.
findings.fix: Retitle it 'Fig 11.3 · One page fetch, fully traced', and in the strip say 'The browser reads the body as it arrives, then closes the connection or keeps it for the next request.' Alternatively, add to p6: '(or run curl, a command-line program that fetches one URL and prints the reply)'.

findings.quote: The TLS ClientHello rides in the same flight as TCP's final ACK, and the GET rides with TLS's Finished
findings.problem: This strip, in Section 02, depends on 'ClientHello' and 'Finished' (taught in Section 05) and on 'resolver' (defined in Section 03). The newcomer cannot follow the overlap.
findings.fix: 'The opening message of TLS rides with TCP's final ACK, and the GET rides with TLS's last message, so each handshake costs one round trip, not more.' In 'The setting', use 'A DNS server a 10 ms round trip away...'.

findings.quote: A POST that should have been a PUT will, on a flaky network, occasionally charge a credit card twice.
findings.problem: The section tells the double-charge four times: here, in Fig 11.4's lower panel and caption, in the strip ('a POST only with an Idempotency-Key'), and in full in insight strip p10.
findings.fix: Cut this sentence from p8, since p10 tells the case in full. Also trim the caption (see ch11-http-p9).

findings.quote: a safe one changes nothing, an idempotent one has the same effect sent once or twice
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats the definitions of safety and idempotency that p8 has just given.
findings.fix: Keep only the second sentence: 'When a reply is lost and the client sends again, a PUT leaves the quantity at 3, but a POST places a second order.'

findings.quote: because HTTP itself does not guarantee what its method properties promise
findings.problem: The case is a POST, and HTTP promises nothing about idempotency for a POST. As written, the reason contradicts the method table just shown, and the reader stops.
findings.fix: '...runs through some version of this dance, because nothing in HTTP makes a POST safe to resend, and any reply can be lost on the way back.'

findings.quote: HTTP is the simplest protocol in this book, simple enough to speak by hand.
findings.problem: Chapter 10 has just presented UDP as 'the simplest thing you can do with IP' (eight-byte header, three-page RFC), so the superlative contradicts the book.
findings.fix: 'HTTP is simple enough to speak by hand.'

findings.quote: Humans do not remember 93.184.216.34. Humans remember example.com.
findings.problem: The sentence presents 93.184.216.34 as example.com's address. Fact ledger §4g (row for Fig 11.3) records that example.com has moved to other addresses and dropped this one from the figure, so the prose brings the corrected claim back. The two clipped sentences are also an AI-style tell.
findings.fix: 'Humans do not remember an address like 203.0.113.7; they remember a name like example.com.' (203.0.113.7 is a documentation address, RFC 5737, already used in Fig 11.7.)

findings.quote: and copied and cached everywhere, designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983
findings.problem: 'designed by' hangs off a list that has already closed with 'and', so the reader has to read the sentence twice.
findings.fix: 'That something is the Domain Name System: a database spread across thousands of servers, arranged as a tree, and copied and cached everywhere. Paul Mockapetris designed it in 1983 (RFC 882 and 883, refined in 1987 as RFC 1034 and 1035).'

findings.quote: Twelve organisations run it as thirteen named servers
findings.problem: The strip repeats ch11-dns-p3 almost word for word: twelve organisations, thirteen servers a to m, anycast, well over a thousand instances, VeriSign for com, the owner's own zone or a CDN. The caption also repeats p3's 'read right to left, root to com to example to www'.
findings.fix: Cut the 'The root' item, and cut the VeriSign/registrant overlap from 'The levels', keeping what is new (org by PIR, fi by Traficom, 360 million names, the trust point). Caption: 'One branch of the tree: each step down hands authority to a different operator, and www is one host in the last zone.'

findings.quote: on a cold cache the resolver walks the tree, asking the root, then the com servers
findings.problem: The caption retells ch11-dns-p5, the walk and the TTL cache, and the strip's 'Referrals' item repeats p5's 'I don't know, but the com servers do'.
findings.fix: Caption: 'A cold lookup: one question from the laptop, three for the resolver, two of them answered with a referral.' Cut the 'Referrals' strip item.

findings.quote: If a forged reply with a matching ID arrives before the real one, the resolver caches the lie
findings.problem: Fig 11.7's caption retells all of ch11-dns-p7: the race, caching for the TTL, Kaminsky 2008, source-port randomisation, 65,000-fold, minutes to years. Only the DNSSEC sentences are new. Fig 11.7 is kept original, so this is the owner's call.
findings.fix: Owner call. If the caption may be touched: 'The attacker races the real answer with forged replies; source-port randomisation multiplies the guesses needed about 65,000-fold. DNSSEC, which signs every record, is the deeper fix but still covers under half the namespace.'

findings.quote: (duplicate response, wrong source)
findings.problem: This note sits under 'ignores real answer', but the real answer comes from the right source. It is dropped because it arrives second, as a duplicate. The box label 'NS' (name server) is never expanded in the chapter.
findings.fix: Owner call: '(arrives second: treated as a duplicate)'. 'real bank.com NS' could become 'real bank.com name server'.

findings.quote: Below that, the registrant runs its own zone or hands it to a host or CDN.
findings.problem: The prose never defines 'zone', yet the caption ('a host in the last zone') and the drawing ('one host in that zone') depend on it. The same strip names DNSSEC before caption p8 explains it.
findings.fix: In ch11-dns-p3: '...then a host called www inside example.com's zone, the part of the tree its owner answers for.' In the strip, drop 'unless DNSSEC signatures are added' (p8 covers it).

findings.quote: (512 bytes without EDNS)
findings.problem: EDNS is never explained. This is expert detail the reader cannot carry (law 4). Cutting it does not bring back the corrected '~512 bytes' claim, because the sentence still ties truncation to 'the UDP size the asker offered'.
findings.fix: 'If an answer is too big for the UDP size the asker offered, the server marks it truncated and the asker repeats the query over TCP.'

findings.quote: The phone book of the internet.
findings.problem: The section title's analogy is never paid off. The section's own point is that DNS replaced the single list everyone copied (HOSTS.TXT, the real phone book) with a delegated tree, so the analogy stops being true exactly where the mechanism starts.
findings.fix: In p2, after the HOSTS.TXT sentence: 'That file was the internet's phone book, one list everyone copied. DNS keeps the lookup but splits the book: ...'

findings.quote: was edited by hand, and was copied out over the network
findings.problem: Restates the previous sentence ('every machine on the network downloaded it periodically').
findings.fix: 'By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries and was edited by hand.'

findings.quote: The hash is, in effect, a fingerprint of the data, uniquely identifying it without revealing it.
findings.problem: A fixed 256-bit output for inputs of any size cannot be unique. The property that makes it unique in practice, collision resistance, is missing from the 'three properties' just listed. Ch14 then lists a different three (preimage, second-preimage, collision), so the reader meets two clashing 'three properties' sets.
findings.fix: '...a fingerprint of the data: in practice no two inputs share one (no SHA-256 collision has ever been found), and it reveals nothing of the data.'

findings.quote: (Git is the exception: it still fingerprints its commits with the older SHA-1.)
findings.problem: It is unclear what Git is the exception to: the sentence before is about certificates and TLS handshakes. The Fig 11.9 strip repeats the same fact ('Git's commit IDs (still SHA-1 by default)').
findings.fix: Cut the parenthesis. The strip keeps the fact.

findings.quote: one bit changed, all 256 bits scrambled
findings.problem: The figure title says all 256 bits are scrambled, but the caption and the grid show 124 of 256 bits differing, 'about half'. The numbers appear to disagree.
findings.fix: 'Fig 11.9 · SHA-256 avalanche · one bit changed, half the output flipped'.

findings.quote: That is what makes a hash a fingerprint: any change at all, however small, gives a completely different one.
findings.problem: Restates p4's avalanche property and its fingerprint line.
findings.fix: Cut the second sentence of the caption.

findings.quote: With a key pair the public half locks and only the private half unlocks
findings.problem: Fig 11.10 retells p6 and p7 three times: the caption (one key for both, key pair, TLS agrees a symmetric key), the 'Symmetric' strip item (AES, CPU instructions, gigabytes per second, all in p6) and the 'In TLS' item (Diffie–Hellman halves, all in p7).
findings.fix: Caption: 'Left, one key K that must somehow reach Bob; right, Bob's key pair, whose public half can cross openly.' Cut the 'Symmetric' and 'In TLS' strip items and keep 'Asymmetric' (the link to Fig 11.8).

findings.quote: The client's hello already carries its half of a Diffie–Hellman exchange, so the server can derive the keys at once
findings.problem: The caption repeats tls-p2 almost word for word ('The client's hello already carries its half of a fresh Diffie–Hellman exchange...'). The strip's 'The cost' item repeats p2's '(TLS 1.2 needed two)'.
findings.fix: Caption: 'The handshake as a ladder: after one round trip both sides hold the keys (gold), and the request already travels encrypted.' In the strip, cut 'One round trip before data, against two in TLS 1.2;'.

findings.quote: Its lineage starts with SSL 1.0 (Netscape, 1994, found broken before it was ever released), through SSL 2.0
findings.problem: 'starts with ... through' does not parse.
findings.fix: 'Its lineage runs from SSL 1.0 (...) through SSL 2.0 (...), SSL 3.0 (...), then, renamed TLS, 1.0 (1999), 1.1, 1.2 (2008, dominant for a decade) and finally TLS 1.3 (...)'.

findings.quote: encrypted under keys derived (with HKDF) from the shared Diffie–Hellman secret
findings.problem: HKDF, and in the next item 'AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305', are never explained. This is expert detail the reader cannot use (law 4).
findings.fix: Drop '(with HKDF)'. In 'The cost': 'the hellos also settle the cipher suite, the symmetric cipher that will carry the data.'

findings.quote: With ephemeral Diffie–Hellman the long-term key only signs, and each session's secret is erased when it ends
findings.problem: The caption's second sentence restates tls-p6. Only its first sentence, on RSA key transport, is new.
findings.fix: Caption: 'Top row: the session key crossed the wire sealed with the long-term key, so stealing that key later opens every recorded session. Bottom row: nothing to unseal.'

findings.quote: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections, RFC 9000, 2021) replaces TCP entirely for HTTP traffic.
findings.problem: ch10-modern-p6 and Fig 10.9 have already taught QUIC: over UDP, reliability, independent streams, TLS 1.3 inside, 'QUIC is what HTTP/3 runs on', and head-of-line blocking. Ch11 teaches it again as new (and p2 introduces 'head-of-line blocking' in italics as a new term) without pointing back. The brief: never explain twice what the book has already explained.
findings.fix: p2: 'The headline problem with HTTP/1.1 was head-of-line blocking (Chapter 10 §05): ...'. p5: 'QUIC, the transport Chapter 10 §05 introduced (RFC 9000, 2021), replaces TCP for HTTP traffic. What matters here: each stream is ordered independently, so ...'. Cut the re-listing of what it rebuilds.

findings.quote: Sixty parallel requests now share one connection
findings.problem: The same paragraph lists HTML, 10 stylesheets, 30 JavaScript files and 50 images: 91 resources. It is not clear where 'sixty' comes from.
findings.fix: 'All ninety-odd requests now share one connection, with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.'

findings.quote: Neither is a new HTTP: the headers, methods, and status codes you saw in Section 02 are unchanged.
findings.problem: The Fig 11.2 strip item 'HTTP/2 and HTTP/3' already says the same thing in Section 02, so the book says it twice.
findings.fix: Keep it here, in its place, and cut the 'HTTP/2 and HTTP/3' strip item from Fig 11.2. This does not bring back the old 'every request has this exact shape' error, because the caption no longer claims that.

findings.quote: Then mobile networks happened, JavaScript-heavy sites happened
findings.problem: A reflexive anaphoric triplet ('X happened, Y happened, ...').
findings.fix: 'Then came mobile networks and JavaScript-heavy sites; the average web page grew from 50 KB to 3 MB, and the protocol's one-request-at-a-time model started costing real time.'

findings.quote: HTTP/2 makes no byte faster, it only fills idle time.
findings.problem: A comma splice. The 'The workaround' item in the same strip also repeats p2's parenthesis about six connections per host.
findings.fix: 'HTTP/2 makes no byte faster; it only fills idle time.' Cut 'The workaround' or the parenthesis in p2.

findings.quote: and is climbing toward HTTP/2's share everywhere else
findings.problem: It is unclear what 'everywhere else' is set against, and what reaching 'HTTP/2's share' means. The reader has to read it twice.
findings.fix: '...Cloudflare's and Meta's), and elsewhere it is gaining on HTTP/2.'

findings.quote: escaping TCP at the protocol layer
findings.problem: Every layer is a protocol layer. The prose says the fix had to happen 'at the transport layer itself'.
findings.fix: 'Fig 11.15 · HTTP/3 over QUIC · escaping TCP at the transport layer'.

findings.quote: This is especially true of network protocols, because their designers cannot iterate quickly
findings.problem: Every protocol in the chapter is a network protocol, so 'especially' compares them with nothing. The strip also says all of them were shaped by 'attacks and patches', but HTTP's changes in Section 06 came from load and latency, not attacks.
findings.fix: 'Every protocol in this chapter was patched into its present shape rather than designed into it: HTTP by load, DNS and TLS by attacks. And slowly, because a network protocol cannot iterate quickly: every change has to be deployed across millions of independently operated machines without breaking the existing ones.'

findings.quote: minimal, text-based, perfect for 1991
findings.problem: The strip stacks reflexive triplets ('minimal, text-based, perfect'; 'denser, harder, more cryptographic'; 'port randomisation, DNSSEC and encrypted DNS').
