It also recaps what earlier sections said: SSL 1.0 never released because it was broken (tls-p1), and the Kaminsky patch (dns-p7).
findings.fix: Replace the recap sentences with the two-sentence version given for the other ch11-modern-p7 finding.

findings.quote: hi
findings.problem: In both rows the message box turns back into plaintext "hi" while it is still on the open dashed wire. Per the SVG, the box travels x 96 to 260 (wire 96 to 304, Bob's box starts at 308). It is ciphertext only for the middle half of the trip: plaintext for the first quarter after leaving Alice, and plaintext again for the last quarter before reaching Bob. In the asymmetric row the "hi" also comes back before Bob's prv highlight (0.70 to 0.76). Frame t6.667 shows a plaintext "hi" in mid-wire on the public channel, the opposite of what the figure says encryption does.
findings.fix: Keep the ciphertext (x7f / x9q) for the whole crossing. Swap to it while the box still sits at Alice, before it moves. Reveal the decrypted "hi" only once the box has arrived: extend the translate so the box ends inside or under Bob's box (x ≥ 308), and switch x9q to hi at keyTime ≥ 0.70, timed with the prv highlight. Time the symmetric row the same way against Bob's K.

findings.quote: The client's hello already carries its half of a Diffie–Hellman exchange
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch11-tls-p2, which sits just above the figure, almost word for word ("The client's hello already carries its half of a fresh Diffie–Hellman exchange ... so the server can encrypt the rest of its very first reply: certificate, signature and all"). The reader reads the same sentence twice in a row, and the caption never points at what the picture adds, the gold lanes that show who holds the keys when.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The gold lanes show who holds the keys: the server as soon as the ClientHello lands, the client one round trip later, when it checks the certificate and sends its request already encrypted."

findings.quote: One curl, fully traced
findings.problem: ch11-http-p6 sets the scene in a browser ("Type https://example.com/ into a browser and press Enter"), but the figure title and How it works switch to curl, and no word drawn in the picture says curl. "Fully traced" also overclaims: the picture shows four bars.
findings.fix: Retitle "Fig 11.3 · One HTTPS fetch · four exchanges in a row". In How it works, change "curl prints the body as it arrives" to "The browser reads the body as it arrives", and change "curl" in the desc to "a browser". Alternatively, make ch11-http-p6 open with `curl https://example.com/`.

findings.quote: one bit changed, all 256 bits scrambled
findings.problem: The figure title says all 256 bits are scrambled, but the picture and caption show that 124 of 256 bits differ (recomputed: correct), "about half". A reader comparing the title with the red grid sees two different claims.
findings.fix: Retitle "Fig 11.9 · SHA-256 avalanche · one bit changed, half of the 256 bits flipped".

findings.quote: cache keeps
findings.problem: The table gives POST "rarely" and PATCH "no" in the cache column, but the rule is the same for both. RFC 5789 §2 makes a PATCH response cacheable only with explicit freshness and a matching Content-Location, the condition RFC 9110 sets for POST (the condition the §4g ledger row for Fig 11.4 cites for "rarely").
findings.fix: Set PATCH's "cache keeps" cell to "rarely", with the same neutral colour as POST's (source: RFC 5789 §2; RFC 9110 §9.3.3).

findings.quote: check with key
findings.problem: Both "check with key" arrows hang off one continuous vertical spine at x≈575, from the root's edge down to the leaf. R11 gets only an incoming arrowhead, with no tail leaving it, so in the still picture (and with reduced motion) the arrow into the leaf seems to come from the root. That contradicts the caption ("with the public key of the certificate above it"). Only the animation's lighting order separates the two checks.
findings.fix: Split the spine: end the root's arrow at R11 (y 123 to 297), and draw the second arrow as its own line starting at R11's right edge, offset (for example x 590, from y ≈ 310 down to the leaf at y ≈ 470), so the leaf's check visibly leaves R11.

findings.quote: A domain name is a path through one tree, written leaf first
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch11-dns-p3 step for step: read right to left, the same name www.example.com., root then com then example then www, and a different operator at each level. It says nothing the prose has not just said.
findings.fix: Point it at the picture: "The bold path is the name read from the right; each box on it belongs to the operator listed beside it, and www is just one host inside example.com's zone."

findings.quote: The laptop asks its resolver once; on a cold cache the resolver walks the tree
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch11-dns-p5, which walks the same example.com lookup through root, com and the authoritative servers, then caching for the TTL. It adds nothing that the paragraph just above it has not said.
findings.fix: "Only the resolver walks the tree; the laptop sends one question and gets one answer. Once the resolver holds the answer for an hour, the next asker never reaches the root or com servers."

findings.quote: 2½ quiet years, one machine
findings.problem: The bar labelled "one machine" runs from March 1989, but the NeXT cube only arrived in autumn 1990 (WorldWideWeb was written October to December 1990). For about 18 of the 29 months there was no web machine at all. In 1991 the line-mode browser also ran on other CERN machines. The caption (ch11-bernerslee-p6) repeats "one project on one machine".
findings.fix: Label: "2½ quiet years at CERN". Caption: "For two and a half years the web was one project at CERN: a proposal, a server running by December 1990, an announcement in August 1991."

findings.quote: GET /index.html HTTP/1.1 \r\n
findings.problem: The figure is titled "byte for byte", yet every line has a literal space before \r\n (the tspans read " \r\n"). On the request line a trailing space is not valid HTTP (RFC 9112: request-line = method SP request-target SP HTTP-version CRLF), so a reader who takes the title at its word learns an extra byte that is not there.
findings.fix: Drop the leading space from each \r\n tspan, so the dim \r\n sits right after the text, or retitle "request and response, line by line".

findings.quote: A2 lost
findings.problem: A static knockout clip (ko-fig-11-15-1/-2) cuts holes in stream A's lane where the X and the hollow A3 square will appear later. In the early frames (t3.333), before any loss has happened, both A lanes show two unexplained breaks at those spots, giving away the loss before it is drawn.
findings.fix: Fade the knockout in with the X and the hollow square (or drop it and draw those marks with a background-coloured fill), so stream A's lane stays unbroken until the loss appears.

findings.quote: (duplicate response, wrong source)
findings.problem: The note explains why the real answer is ignored, but "wrong source" is factually wrong. The real reply comes from the real name server's address, the right source. The attacker spoofed that same address. The resolver drops the real reply only because the query was already answered.
findings.fix: If the owner ever allows a label change: "(late duplicate, query already answered)". Otherwise leave the figure as it is and note the error in the kept-original list.

findings.quote: SHIPPED IN 10 days
findings.problem: The badge says JavaScript shipped in ten days. The chapter says ten days bought a prototype: Eich 'had ten working days to produce a prototype' (ch12-eich-p1), Mocha was a working interpreter by mid-May (p2), it went out in the Netscape 2.0 beta that September (p3, ch12-browser-p3), and Fig 12.2 reads 'written in 10 days'. A careful reader sees the chapter's opening picture contradict its second section.
findings.fix: Change the badge's small line from 'SHIPPED IN' to 'WRITTEN IN' (the hero's line 4583) so it matches Fig 12.2. '10 days' stays.

findings.quote: copies the part of the URL after the `?` into the page unsafely
findings.problem: The prose says DOM-based XSS copies the part of the URL after the '?'. Fig 12.9 (a kept original) shows it with location.hash, the part after '#', and says the attack 'never touches the server'. Text after '?' is sent to the server, so prose and figure describe different attacks. Pass 29's law-4 rewrite (537eb28) brought this in; the earlier text said 'URL parameters'.
findings.fix: Fix the prose, not the kept figure: "*DOM-based XSS*: a similar attack carried out entirely in the browser, by page JavaScript that copies the part of the URL after the `#` (which the browser never sends to the server) into the page unsafely."

findings.quote: browser executes the injected script as same-origin with example.com
findings.problem: The attack URL in row 1 is https://search.example.com/. By the book's own rule (ch12-security-p2: a.example.com and b.example.com are different origins; Fig 12.8: shop vs www is 'other'), the injected script runs with the origin of search.example.com, not example.com. A reader who has just learned that subdomains are separate origins, two figures earlier, will stop here.
findings.fix: Report only (kept original). Correct claim: '③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com'.

findings.quote: render(await getInvoice(orders));
findings.problem: The colour key does not match across the three blocks. The callbacks and promises blocks light four matching lines (blue getUser, green getOrders, yellow getInvoice, orange render). The async/await block lights only three, because render is folded into the yellow getInvoice line, so the orange step disappears. The caption also counts 'three steps (the user, then the orders, then the invoice)' while two blocks show four colours.
findings.fix: Split the async line into `const invoice = await getInvoice(orders);` (yellow outline) and `render(invoice);` (orange outline), growing the third box by one 18-unit row. Or, if the box must not grow, change the caption to 'The same job (the user, the orders, the invoice, then render) spelled three ways: …'.

findings.quote: five stages, one ~16 ms frame
findings.problem: The label promises one ~16 ms frame, but nothing in the picture shows time or a frame budget. The figure's own How it works keeps parse out of the frame ('parse runs when HTML or CSS arrives'), and a first load, which runs all five stages, takes far more than one frame.
findings.fix: Label: 'Fig 12.7 · Critical rendering path · five stages, and which ones a change re-runs' (also in the SVG <title>).

findings.quote: new colour
findings.problem: Cells waiting to run are drawn two ways. Every pending style cell has a full-strength yellow outline (stroke-opacity 0.95), while pending layout, paint and composite cells are dim (0.35). In the 4 s frame, the style cells of both 'new width' and 'new colour' look active before either has run, while their other cells look idle. The one stage that is 'on' is otherwise shown by a white ring.
findings.fix: Give every pending cell the same outline strength: one value that passes 3:1 for all five hues (for example 0.6 on all, or the yellow's 0.95 matched by the other four). Keep the white ring as the only 'running now' mark.

findings.quote: then a decade's stall when the ambitious ES4 was abandoned
findings.problem: Read literally, the stall starts when ES4 is abandoned. The picture shows the opposite order: ES3 in 1999, nothing for a decade while ES4 was fought over, ES4 abandoned in 2008, ES5 in 2009. Abandoning ES4 ended the stall.
findings.fix: "JavaScript was written in ten days in 1995 and renamed twice for marketing; a standard followed in 1997, then a decade's stall over the ambitious ES4 until it was abandoned in 2008. ES2015 finally brought classes and modules, and since then the language has shipped one edition a year."

findings.quote: event loop
findings.problem: The caption's last step ('libuv's event loop queues the callback and V8 runs it') is never actually shown. Coming back from the pool thread, the dot reaches the event-loop spot at 6.6 s and leaves straight away, nothing lights, and its diagonal path to V8 runs through the 'event loop' text (the 6.667 s frame shows 'event l●p'). The loop's job is the one moment a reader cannot see.
findings.fix: Draw a small slot under 'event loop' (e.g. a chip 'callback queued') that lights when the dot arrives. Hold the dot there about 0.6 s, then move it down and left under the label into the V8 box, so it never crosses the text.

findings.quote: static documents and a tab-out to Java
findings.problem: 'Tab-out' is not a term the book or the field uses, and it suggests leaving the page. The picture, the caption ('hand a box to a Java applet') and the prose all show an applet that sits in a box on the page and cannot reach the page around it.
findings.fix: Label (and SVG <title>): 'Fig 12.1 · The web of 1994–95 · static pages and a walled-off Java box'.

findings.quote: The same fetch · three eras of async syntax
findings.problem: The label says 'fetch', but none of the three blocks calls fetch. They call getUser, getOrders and getInvoice. The prose just above uses `fetch(url)`, so a reader looks for that call in the picture and does not find it.
findings.fix: Label (and SVG <title>): 'Fig 12.4 · The same job · three eras of async syntax'.

findings.quote: XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10
findings.problem: This is a factual error in the locked caption. The OWASP Top 10 is not yearly: editions came out in 2003, 2004, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2017, 2021 and 2025. Since 2021, XSS no longer has its own entry; it is folded into the Injection category.
findings.fix: Report only (locked caption of a kept original). Correct claim: 'XSS is still on the OWASP Top 10, folded into its Injection category since the 2021 edition.'

findings.quote: pushing the attack from "a few minutes" to "years."
findings.problem: Port randomisation made forging about 65,000 times harder, but it did not push the attack out to years. Kaminsky's attack on an unpatched resolver took about 10 seconds. In August 2008 Evgeniy Polyakov poisoned a patched BIND 9.5.0-P2, with about 64,000 random ports, in a little under 10 hours, using two machines on a gigabit link; the estimate before his demonstration was about a week. The reader is left thinking the patched attack is out of reach, which the sentence before ('did not fix the underlying weakness') rightly denies.
findings.fix: "...multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to 2³² and turning seconds of flooding into hours or days of it." Sources: Polyakov's write-up (exploit-db.com/raw/6236, "a bit less than 10 hours"); Slashdot/NYT (Markoff), 9 Aug 2008, "BIND Still Susceptible To DNS Cache Poisoning".

findings.quote: pushed the practical attack from minutes to years
findings.problem: This is the same overclaim as ch11-dns-p7, in the kept-original caption. A patched BIND was poisoned in under 10 hours in August 2008 (Polyakov), and the unpatched attack took seconds, not minutes. The figure is owner-kept, so this is reported only. If the prose is fixed, the caption will contradict it.
findings.fix: If the owner allows a caption edit: "...showed how to make this practical against unpatched resolvers in seconds... multiplied the attacker's search space ~65,000-fold and pushed the practical attack from seconds to hours or days." Source: exploit-db.com/raw/6236.

findings.quote: if the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it
findings.problem: This gets Xanadu backwards. Nelson's design made links visible and followable from every endpoint (rule 7), gave every document a unique permanent identity (rule 10), let documents be found without knowing where they were stored (rule 12) and kept them redundantly (rule 14), all so that links could not break. Links breaking when a target moves is the web's behaviour (Xanadu attacks the web for its 'one-way ever-breaking links'). As written, the sentence takes away the very contrast the paragraph is drawing.
findings.fix: "In Project Xanadu, links ran both ways and every document kept a permanent address that the system itself maintained, so no link could ever break; keeping that promise needed one system that tracked every link." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Xanadu (Nelson's 17 rules; xanadu.com critique of the web).

findings.quote: released the entire web (code, protocols, specifications) into the public domain, with a one-page document declaring no royalties
findings.problem: The 30 April 1993 statement put three pieces of software into the public domain: the line-mode browser, the basic server and the library of common code. It says CERN 'relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code' and lets anyone 'use, duplicate, modify and distribute it'. It does not cover protocols or specifications, and it says nothing about patents. The 'royalty-free' wording belongs to CERN's later 1994 licence.
findings.fix: "On 30 April 1993 CERN put the web's software (the line-mode browser, the basic server and the library of common code) into the public domain, giving up all intellectual property rights so that anyone could use, copy, modify and redistribute it." Sources: home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/licensing-web/; Berners-Lee to www-talk, May 1993 (ksi.cpsc.ucalgary.ca/archives/WWW-TALK/www-talk-1993q2.messages/257.html).

findings.quote: By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries
findings.problem: The host table listed 213 hosts in August 1981, 235 in May 1982 and 562 in August 1983, the year DNS was designed. It passed 1,000 only in October 1984 and reached about 2,000 in 1985. The book's own Fig 9.2 draws '1981 · 213 hosts', so the two figures contradict each other.
findings.fix: "By 1983 the file listed more than 500 hosts, roughly doubling each year, was edited by hand, and was copied out over the network." Source: RFC 1296 (Lottor, 1992), host-count table taken from the NIC host tables.

findings.quote: Humans do not remember 93.184.216.34.
findings.problem: With 'Something has to translate the second into the first', this says example.com resolves to 93.184.216.34. The §4g ledger (Fig 11.3 row) recorded that example.com has moved off that address and removed it from the figure. The prose brings the stale address back. On 15 Oct 2026, dig gives 104.20.23.154 and 172.66.147.243.
findings.fix: "Humans do not remember a number like 203.0.113.7. Humans remember `example.com`. Something has to translate the name into its number..." (203.0.113.7 is a documentation address, RFC 5737, already used in Fig 11.7).

findings.quote: the certificates of Section 05 rely on it, and so does every TLS handshake
findings.problem: TLS 1.3 handshakes negotiated with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 use SHA-384 for the transcript hash and HKDF, not SHA-256. The §4g row for Fig 14.11 already corrected this point in Ch14 ('HKDF uses SHA-256 or SHA-384 by cipher suite').
findings.fix: "...the certificates of Section 05 rely on it, and so do most TLS handshakes (the rest use its longer sibling, SHA-384)." Source: RFC 8446 §B.4 (cipher suites TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384).

findings.quote: a fingerprint of the data, uniquely identifying it without revealing it
findings.problem: A 256-bit hash cannot identify inputs uniquely: inputs are unlimited, so collisions must exist. A hash works as a fingerprint because of collision resistance (nobody can find two inputs with the same hash), and the paragraph's list of 'three properties' leaves that out. Yet it is the property that certificates and Git IDs depend on, and why SHA-1 ('the older SHA-1', mentioned in the next sentence) was retired.
findings.fix: "The hash is, in effect, a fingerprint of the data, identifying it because nobody can find two inputs with the same hash (collision resistance), and revealing nothing of it."

findings.quote: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections, RFC 9000, 2021)
findings.problem: RFC 9000 says explicitly: 'QUIC is a name, not an acronym.' The expansion was Google's name for its original protocol, so pairing it with the IETF standard is inaccurate.
findings.fix: "*QUIC* (RFC 9000, 2021, a name that began at Google as Quick UDP Internet Connections)". Source: RFC 9000 §1.2 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html).

findings.quote: HTTP/1.1 from 1999 was good enough for nearly two decades.
findings.problem: HTTP/1.1 was first standardised in RFC 2068 in January 1997. RFC 2616 (June 1999) was a revision. This also sits oddly next to 'HTTP/1.0 from 1996' in Section 02.
findings.fix: "HTTP/1.1, from 1997, was good enough for nearly two decades." Source: RFC 2068 (January 1997), obsoleted by RFC 2616 (June 1999).

findings.quote: submitted a 17-page document to his manager
findings.problem: CERN's archived copy of the March 1989 proposal (the one Sendall annotated) is a cover plus pages numbered 1 to 14, with one handwritten comment page: 16 scanned pages, 15 typed. The May 1990 reissue runs to 20 pages. I found no source for 17.
findings.fix: Drop the count: "submitted a document to his manager titled _Information Management: A Proposal_." Source: repository.cern/records/6kxvc-v6203 (ARCH-WWW-4-010.pdf, 16 pages; dd-89-001.pdf, 20 pages).

findings.quote: the server will reply with a status line, a few headers, and the document
findings.problem: Today most servers on port 80 answer a bare GET with a redirect to HTTPS, and name-based virtual hosts need a Host header. Tested 15 Oct 2026: wikipedia.org returned 301, info.cern.ch 302, neverssl.com 403. A reader who tries this, as the sentence invites, will usually not get the document.
findings.fix: "...and the server will reply with a status line, a few headers and, unless it sends you on to HTTPS, the document."

findings.quote: (Project Xanadu, which never shipped)
findings.problem: Xanadu never shipped as designed, but parts of it did: Udanax, an incomplete implementation, was released in 1998, XanaduSpace 1.0 in 2007, and OpenXanadu, described as 'a working deliverable', went online in 2014. 'Never shipped' (and 'Xanadu does not' [exist] in p10) is stronger than the record supports.
findings.fix: "(Project Xanadu, which never shipped as he designed it)"; p10 could read "The web exists; Xanadu, as designed, does not." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Xanadu.

findings.quote: the dozen earlier hypertext systems that never caught on
findings.problem: Not every earlier hypertext system failed to catch on. HyperCard (1987) came free with every Macintosh and was very widely used. What it lacked was links between computers.
findings.fix: "One decision separates the web from the hypertext systems before it."

findings.quote: URL: Uniform Resource Locator.
findings.problem: Berners-Lee called his addresses Universal Document Identifiers (UDIs). The name 'Uniform Resource Locator' came from the IETF and was fixed in RFC 1738 (December 1994). 'He defined three: URL...' credits him with a name he did not coin.
findings.fix: "*URL*: an address, later named the Uniform Resource Locator." Sources: RFC 1630 (1994, Berners-Lee, on the UDI/URI history); RFC 1738 (December 1994).

findings.quote: and it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished
findings.problem: The paragraph puts closures and object-to-object inheritance into 'the first version, internally called Mocha'. Neither was in it. Wirfs-Brock & Eich, 'JavaScript: The First 20 Years' (HOPL IV, 2020), says: 'In JavaScript 1.0/1.1 function declarations may occur only at the top level of a script and may not contain nested function declarations' (§3.1). Function expressions were also put off (§2.2), so closures were impossible. Nested functions and function expressions arrived with SpiderMonkey in JavaScript 1.2 (Netscape 4, 1997; §5, Fig 10). The paper also says 'JavaScript 1.0 has no concept of object inheritance' (§3.3). The prototype property came in JavaScript 1.1 (Netscape 3, August 1996). Eich had planned Self-style delegation but 'lacked sufficient time to expose that mechanism in the Mocha prototype' (§2.2). Only first-class functions were there from the start.
findings.fix: "Under the C-like syntax sat Scheme's ideas, some of them finished only in the next two releases: a function was a value that could be stored and passed around like a number, and, once functions could nest (1997), it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished (a _closure_). Objects inherited straight from other objects (from 1996), an idea taken from David Ungar and Randall Smith's language _Self_." Source: Wirfs-Brock & Eich, HOPL IV, doi 10.1145/3386327, §2.2, §3.1, §3.3, §5 (https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/brendan-eich/js-hopl.pdf).

findings.quote: What he got in his first week was a different brief: Marc Andreessen and Bill Joy
findings.problem: This credits Andreessen and Joy with asking for 'the dynamic, interpreted, untyped flexibility of Scheme underneath'. They asked for a 'little language' to go alongside Java. It had to 'look like Java', be object-based without classes, and be easy enough for anyone writing HTML. HOPL §2.2: 'Other than looking like Java, Brendan Eich was free to select most language design details.' The Scheme-style functions and Self-style prototypes were Eich's own choice (Eich, 'Popularity', 2008: 'the diktat ... was that the language must look like Java'). 'In his first week' is also unsupported: Eich 'spent his first month at Netscape officially working in the server group' (HOPL §2.2, note 10).
findings.fix: "What he got instead was a different brief: Marc Andreessen and Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership) wanted a small companion to Java that looked like Java, so that it seemed familiar to working programmers. What went underneath was left to him, and he chose the dynamic, untyped flexibility of Scheme." Source: HOPL IV §2.1–2.2.

findings.quote: In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems and renamed it again
findings.problem: The partnership did not begin in December. On 23 May 1995, at Sun's public announcement of Java, Netscape announced it would license Java (HOPL §2.1), and p1 already has Bill Joy in the Netscape-Sun partnership that spring. What happened on 4 December 1995 was a joint Netscape-Sun press release announcing the language as JavaScript (HOPL §3, Appendix F). A careful reader sees p1 and p3 contradict each other.
findings.fix: "On 4 December 1995 Netscape and Sun announced it jointly under a new name, *JavaScript*, the Java name licensed from Sun." Source: HOPL IV §2.1, §3.

findings.quote: JavaScript was originally interpreted a statement at a time by Netscape's engine
findings.problem: Mocha never ran source statement by statement. 'The parser emitted bytecoded instructions rather than a parse tree. The bytecode interpreter was simple and slow' (HOPL §2.2). Bytecode was in fact a requirement of Netscape's LiveWire server team. 'Statement at a time' gives the reader the wrong mechanism, and it clashes with the bytecode interpreter that Fig 12.5 describes for V8.
findings.fix: "JavaScript was originally compiled to simple bytecode and interpreted, slowly, by Netscape's engine: Eich's Mocha, soon rewritten as the engine still called _SpiderMonkey_ today." Source: HOPL IV §2.2.

findings.quote: By 2008, when Google released V8 alongside the first Chrome browser, JavaScript engines had become aggressive optimising compilers
findings.problem: This dates the change too early. When Chrome shipped in September 2008, no shipping engine had an optimising compiler. V8 1.0 compiled straight to machine code without optimising, as the next sentence and the Fig 12.5 strip say. V8's first optimising compiler, Crankshaft, was announced on 7 December 2010 (Chromium blog, 'A New Crankshaft for V8'). TraceMonkey first shipped in Firefox 3.5 in June 2009. 2008 is when the move to compilers began, not when it was done.
findings.fix: "In 2008, when Google released *V8* alongside the first Chrome browser, JavaScript engines began turning into compilers. V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code, and its first optimising compiler (Crankshaft) followed in 2010; today's engines, V8 included, run a tiered pipeline..." Source: Chromium blog, 7 Dec 2010 (repost: https://jmesnil.net/weblog/2010/12/07/chromium-blog-a-new-crankshaft-for-v8/).

findings.quote: exported from the browser to the server fourteen years after birth
findings.problem: JavaScript ran on servers from its first release. Netscape Enterprise Server 2.0 shipped in March 1996 with JavaScript 1.0 in its LiveWire server-side scripting, and LiveWire's needs shaped Mocha's bytecode design (HOPL §2.2, §3). Microsoft's IIS also ran JScript in Active Server Pages from 1996 (HOPL §4). Node.js in 2009 was the server JavaScript that took hold, not the first.
findings.fix: "...and carried to the server for good, by Node.js, fourteen years after birth." Source: HOPL IV §3 ('Netscape Enterprise Server 2.0 also shipped in March and incorporated JavaScript 1.0 within its LiveWire server-side scripting component'), §4.

findings.quote: given an unrelated marketing name to ride a competitor's hype
findings.problem: Sun was Netscape's partner, not its competitor. Netscape licensed Java in May 1995, Andreessen's rallying cry was 'Netscape plus Java kills Windows', and the two companies announced JavaScript together on 4 December 1995 (HOPL §2.1, §3). The chapter's own p3 calls it a partnership, so the closing paragraph contradicts it.
findings.fix: "given an unrelated marketing name to ride a partner's hype"

findings.quote: by page JavaScript that copies the part of the URL after the `?` into the page unsafely
findings.problem: Fig 12.9, right below, shows DOM-based XSS through location.hash, the part after #, and says it 'never touches the server'. The part after ? is the query string, which the browser sends to the server, so 'carried out entirely in the browser' fits the fragment, not the query. The reader sees ? in the prose and # in the figure, and may wrongly think the query string never reaches the server.
findings.fix: "*DOM-based XSS*: a similar attack carried out entirely in the browser, by page JavaScript that copies the part of the URL after the `#` (which the browser never sends to the server) into the page unsafely."

findings.quote: do not attach this cookie to cross-site POST requests; only to top-level navigations
findings.problem: This is the caption (ch12-security-p7). SameSite=Lax sends the cookie only on top-level navigations that use a safe method such as GET (following a link). A cross-site form POST, which is exactly the attack the figure draws, is also a top-level navigation and gets no Lax cookie. As written, 'only to top-level navigations' suggests Lax would let the figure's auto-submitted POST through.
findings.fix: "`SameSite=Lax` means: attach this cookie to a cross-site request only when it is a top-level navigation that uses GET, such as following a link; never to a cross-site POST." Source: MDN Set-Cookie SameSite (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie#samesitesamesite-value); RFC 6265bis 'Lax' enforcement (safe methods only).

findings.quote: a niche by 2000, obsolete by 2010, removed from browsers entirely by 2017
findings.problem: Not all browsers had dropped it by 2017. Chrome dropped NPAPI in 2015 and Firefox 52 in March 2017, but Firefox ESR 52 kept it into 2018. Safari dropped all NPAPI plug-ins except Flash only in Safari 12 (September 2018), and Internet Explorer 11 kept running the Java plug-in. Oracle deprecated the plug-in in JDK 9 (2017) and removed it in JDK 11 (2018). The Fig 12.1 strip repeats the claim: 'browsers had dropped the plugin interface they needed by 2017'.
findings.fix: Prose: "a niche by 2000, obsolete by 2010, and cut loose by Java itself in 2018, when Oracle removed the browser plug-in." Strip: "Applets faded, and Java removed its browser plug-in in 2018." Sources: https://www.java.com/en/download/help/jdk9_plugin.html; Oracle JDK 11 'Removed Tools and Components' (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/migrate/removed-tools-and-components.html); Safari 12 NPAPI removal (Wikipedia NPAPI).

findings.quote: Eich had ten working days to produce a prototype.
findings.problem: Eich's own dating is 'ten contiguous days in May, 1995', which he believes was May 6–15 (HOPL §2.2 and note 8). That runs from a Saturday to a Monday: ten calendar days, about six of them working days. The chapter hero lead (ch12-hero-lead) says 'ten working days' too.
findings.fix: "Eich had ten days to produce a prototype." In ch12-hero-lead: "Brendan Eich was given ten days, in May 1995, to design..." Source: HOPL IV §2.2.

findings.quote: microtasks arrived with Promises
findings.problem: The microtask queue entered the HTML/DOM specs for Mutation Observers in about 2011–12. Promises were moved onto it in 2013, 'for pretty much the same reasons as with MutationObserver' (W3C bug 22296; W3C bug 24725 'Use the microtask queue for MutationObserver'). Promises are now the main user of microtasks, but they did not bring them.
findings.fix: "...microtasks arrived in the 2010s, and Promises are their main user."

findings.quote: Within five years Node had become the default backend for Silicon Valley startups
findings.problem: This overclaims. By 2014 Node was popular, but nothing supports calling it 'the default': Rails, Python and Java stacks were at least as common among startups. As it stands it is an unsourced superlative.
findings.fix: "Within five years Node had become a common backend for startups; within ten it had taken a large share of server-side work."

findings.quote: the framework computes the minimum set of DOM mutations and applies them together
findings.problem: No mainstream framework computes the minimum. React's reconciliation is an O(n) heuristic, chosen because a truly minimal tree diff is O(n³) (React docs, 'Reconciliation'). Svelte compiles direct updates and does no diffing at all.
findings.fix: "the framework works out a small set of DOM mutations and applies them together"

findings.quote: it runs a hundred kilobytes of code on your machine
findings.problem: This understates by about five times. The median page ships 558 KB of JavaScript on mobile and 613 KB on desktop (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024, Page Weight), and news sites usually ship more.
findings.fix: "it runs hundreds of kilobytes of code on your machine" Source: https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/page-weight.

findings.quote: A typical strict policy
findings.problem: In current usage (web.dev 'Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP'; the CSP Level 3 spec), 'strict' means a policy built on nonces or hashes. An allowlist of hosts like this example is the kind the Google study 'CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!' (CCS 2016) found bypassable in most deployments. The chapter's own Fig 12.11 strip says 'A strict policy admits chosen inline scripts by a fresh random nonce', so the two passages use 'strict' for different things.
findings.fix: "A typical allowlist policy: `script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; style-src 'self'` means..."

findings.quote: If an attacker injects a `<script src="evil.com/x.js">`
findings.problem: In HTML, src="evil.com/x.js" is a relative path. It resolves to /evil.com/x.js on the page's own origin, which 'self' would allow, so the worked example does not show what the sentence claims. In a section that teaches origins, a programmer reading closely will catch this.
findings.fix: "If an attacker injects a `<script src="https://evil.com/x.js">`, the browser sees that `evil.com` is not in the policy..."

findings.quote: were retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked
findings.problem: The same-origin policy appears in this list of retrofits, but p2 says it was 'introduced in Netscape 2.0, the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'. It was there from day one, not retrofitted after attacks.
findings.fix: "The security mechanisms that surround it (the same-origin policy from the first release, then CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were added over thirty years, most of them in response to attacks that worked."

findings.quote: whose browser had become the market-share leader through 1994 and 1995
findings.problem: Netscape was not the leader through 1994. Navigator was first widely distributed in October 1994, and 'by early 1995 Netscape Navigator had achieved its initial goal and was rapidly displacing Mosaic' (HOPL §2).
findings.fix: "Netscape, whose browser had overtaken Mosaic as the market leader by early 1995, wanted something different."

findings.quote: XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10
findings.problem: This is the caption (ch12-security-p5). The OWASP Top 10 is not yearly: it is revised every three to four years (2003, 2004, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2017, 2021, 2025). Since 2021 XSS has had no entry of its own; it sits inside Injection (A03:2021, A05:2025).
findings.fix: "Even so, XSS is still on the OWASP Top 10, inside its Injection category." Source: https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A05_2025-Injection/.

findings.quote: browser executes the injected script as same-origin with example.com
findings.problem: The attacked URL in the same panel is search.example.com. By the rule Fig 12.8 has just taught (shop.example.com is not www.example.com), that is a different origin from example.com, so the label contradicts the lesson before it.
findings.fix: "③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com"

findings.quote: which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, minutes of work.
findings.problem: A trillion row comparisons takes hours in a real database engine, not minutes. I timed a SQLite nested-loop join (10,000 x 10,000 rows, in memory, automatic index off) at about 20 ns per comparison, which extrapolates to about 5.7 hours for 10^12. Even a bare C loop at 1 ns per comparison needs about 17 minutes. The chapter's own rate also disagrees: ch13-indexes-p1 says a 10-million-row scan takes 'seconds', which puts 10^12 row visits at roughly a day.
findings.fix: "which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, hours of work."

findings.quote: He spent his last decade increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model
findings.problem: This puts the frustration in the wrong period. Codd died in April 2003, and during the 1990s his health declined and he stopped working (Wikipedia, Edgar F. Codd). His fight over the word 'relational' was in the 1980s: the 1985 Computerworld rules named in the next sentence and RM/V2 in 1990. Read together, the two sentences place 1985 inside his 'last decade'.
findings.fix: "From the 1980s on he grew increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model ..."

findings.quote: Serializable also tracks which transactions read data that others wrote
findings.problem: This names the wrong conflict. PostgreSQL's Serializable Snapshot Isolation watches for read-write antidependencies: a transaction reads a row version that a concurrent transaction is overwriting, so the reader never sees that write. Reading data that another transaction wrote and committed is normal and harmless. As worded, the sentence suggests the opposite case is the one being tracked.
findings.fix: "Serializable also tracks which transactions read data that a concurrent transaction was changing, and aborts ..."

findings.quote: Called Ingres, it became the basis for the open-source Postgres (1986)
findings.problem: 'Basis' implies Postgres was built from Ingres's code. It was not. Postgres was Stonebraker's new 'post-Ingres' project, begun after he returned to Berkeley in 1985, with implementation starting in 1986. It was a fresh code base that took ideas, not code, from Ingres, and its query language was PostQUEL until Postgres95 (PostgreSQL docs, 'A Brief History of PostgreSQL'; Wikipedia, PostgreSQL). Fig 13.1's 'Ingres led to Postgres' is accurate; the prose goes further than the figure.
findings.fix: "Called Ingres, it led to Stonebraker's successor project, Postgres (1986), which became PostgreSQL (1996), and indirectly to Sybase ..."

findings.quote: DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
findings.problem: SELECT reads data and changes nothing, so it cannot be an example of a statement that 'changes the data'. The DDL half of the sentence is right ('changes the schema').
findings.fix: "DML (Data Manipulation Language) reads and changes the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE."

findings.quote: the 2011 Sony PlayStation Network breach (77 million)
findings.problem: The 77 million were PlayStation Network accounts, not payment cards. Placed straight after 'Heartland breach (130 million payment cards)', the bare number reads as 77 million cards. Sony said card data was on file for far fewer accounts. This is only about the unit. The owner's ruling to keep PSN in the SQL injection list is not touched.
findings.fix: "the 2011 Sony PlayStation Network breach (77 million accounts)"

findings.quote: it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished (a closure)
findings.problem: The closure matches the glossary key "closure", whose entry is relational-algebra closure (ch13-algebra). book.js therefore attaches a hover/tap tooltip here that shows "The property of relational algebra that every operation returns a relation..." and links forward to Chapter 13. The reader is shown the wrong definition on the spot where the right one is taught.
findings.fix: Keep the word but stop it matching: write the term in plain text, e.g. "(this is called a closure)" with no <em>. Or rename the ch13 glossary key to "closure (relational)" and add a function-closure entry for ch12-eich. Rebuild the glossary afterwards.

findings.quote: copies the part of the URL after the ? into the page unsafely
findings.problem: DOM-based XSS is described as using the part after the `?`, the query string, which is sent to the server. Fig 12.9 shows the same attack through `location.hash`, the part after `#`, and says it "never touches the server". The prose and the figure disagree, and the `?` version undercuts "carried out entirely in the browser".
findings.fix: "...by page JavaScript that copies the part of the URL after the `#` (which the browser never sends to the server) into the page unsafely."

findings.quote: with .then() and .catch() chained horizontally
findings.problem: Wrong word. In Fig 12.4 the promise chain runs down the page, one `.then` per line. The thing that marches sideways is the callback pyramid this sentence is contrasting with. "Horizontally" says the opposite of the picture.
findings.fix: "...with `.then()` and `.catch()` chained one after another in a flat list instead of nested."

findings.quote: In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems and renamed it again
findings.problem: p1 already has Bill Joy "brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership" in April–May 1995, so the partnership exists before p3 announces it in December. The reader cannot tell whether there were two deals.
findings.fix: "In December 1995, in a joint announcement with Sun Microsystems, Netscape renamed it again, to *JavaScript*."

findings.quote: given an unrelated marketing name to ride a competitor's hype
findings.problem: §02 presents Sun as Netscape's partner: a joint deal, and Sun held the Java trademark that Netscape licensed. The closing paragraph now calls Sun a competitor.
findings.fix: "given an unrelated marketing name to ride a partner's hype" (or "to ride Java's hype").

findings.quote: It should run instantly, fail loudly without crashing the browser
findings.problem: §02 and the insight strip make JavaScript's defining quirk implicit coercion, "silently turning one type into another". The language was built to forgive, not to fail loudly. A careful reader sees the contradiction two sections later.
findings.fix: "It should run instantly, fail without taking the browser down with it, and be easy enough..."

findings.quote: meant JavaScript could never expose the difference
findings.problem: "The difference" has no referent: between what and what? The sentence has to be read twice and still does not land. It also repeats p2's "no integers (only floating-point numbers...)", so the no-integer point is made twice.
findings.fix: "`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` is just IEEE 754 (Chapter 2's floating-point section), but because every number is a 64-bit float, JavaScript has no exact integer type to fall back on."

findings.quote: It was genuine elegance underneath surprising syntactic awkwardness
findings.problem: This is an aphorism closer ("the shape of any language born in ten days under the wrong brief"), and "syntactic" is the wrong word. None of the listed flaws is syntax: missing classes, no integers and implicit coercion are semantics. The C-like syntax is presented as the familiar part.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. The paragraph ends on the coercion clause, and the insight strip (p6) already draws the ten-day lesson.

findings.quote: None of this was inevitable. All of it became, by accumulation, the shape of the modern web.
findings.problem: The paragraph closes on a two-fragment aphorism. It also reuses p1's phrase "over thirty years in response to attacks that worked" almost word for word, summarising what was just said.
findings.fix: End the paragraph at "...in response to attacks that worked." and drop the two closing sentences. Or vary the p1 echo: "were added one attack at a time."

findings.quote: Part IV turns to where information lives at rest, and how it stays trustworthy
findings.problem: The End of Part III closer, which sits directly below, says the same thing again: "every layer from copper to pixels. Part IV turns to where information lives at rest: the relational database, real cryptography, and the unified security chapter...". The Part IV preview is read twice in a row. p11's version also ends in clipped fragments ("The relational database. The cryptographic primitives in mathematical depth. And...").
findings.fix: End p11 at "...rendering at 60 frames per second." and let the part closer, the arc device that names the next part, carry the Part IV preview.

findings.quote: An origin is a scheme, a host and a port, and two URLs share one only if all three match
findings.problem: The definition and the three one-change examples appear three times: p2 (a./b.example.com, http/https, :80/:8080), the picture, and the caption ("http for https, shop for www, 8443 for 443"). Per the brief, the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: "One origin split into its three parts, and three URLs that each change one of them; the path never counts, so only the first is the same origin."

findings.quote: The CSS is parsed into another tree (the CSSOM).
findings.problem: CSS is never explained anywhere before this point. Ch11 only mentions "stylesheets" once, in passing. The style and layout stages, and the caption's width and colour changes, all lean on it.
findings.fix: "The CSS (the style rules that set each element's size, colour and position) is parsed into another tree (the CSSOM)."

findings.quote: watched the progress bar on a file upload in a browser and realised
findings.problem: The story image is never cashed out. Nothing says why a progress bar would show that thread-per-connection servers are the wrong shape: the browser had to keep asking a busy server how much had arrived. The reader stops at the leap.
findings.fix: Cash it out with one clause: "watched a browser's upload progress bar, which could only learn how far the upload had got by asking the server again and again, and realised...". Or cut the image: "In 2009 a developer named Ryan Dahl realised..."

findings.quote: ③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with example.com
findings.problem: The reflected example's URL is https://search.example.com. Its origin is search.example.com, not example.com. p2 has just taught that a.example.com and b.example.com are different origins, so the figure contradicts the section.
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original): "③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com".

findings.quote: Take one task, run it to the end, run every microtask, render if a frame is due
findings.problem: The strip's first bullet repeats the last sentence of p2 ("pull one task off the macrotask queue, run it to completion, drain the microtask queue completely, optionally render, repeat"). Only the 16 ms figure is new.
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with "*The render step.* The browser renders only when a frame is due, about every 16 ms on a 60 Hz screen."

findings.quote: Parse turns HTML and CSS into the DOM and CSSOM; style matches rules to elements
findings.problem: The "The stages" bullet walks through the five stages that p1 has just walked through, one by one.
findings.fix: Drop the bullet. If "style matches rules to elements" is wanted, put it in p1: "the style stage then matches the CSS rules to the elements, giving a render tree...".

findings.quote: Composite assembles the painted layers into the frame you see.
findings.problem: "Layers" are never explained, yet the caption's key claim depends on them ("an animated transform on its own layer needs only composite"). So do the strip's compositor-thread fast path.
findings.fix: "Paint draws the pixels, often into several separate layers; composite stacks those layers into the frame you see."

findings.quote: Understanding this pipeline is the difference between a page that holds 60 frames per second and a page that stutters.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer. The paragraph also opens with a "Not X. Y." reveal ("Loading a web page does not 'show' the HTML. The browser runs...").
findings.fix: Open: "When a page loads, the browser runs the fetched bytes through a five-stage pipeline...". Close by handing to the figure: "Which stages a change re-runs decides whether the page holds 60 frames per second (Fig 12.7)."

findings.quote: Changing a DOM node makes the browser redo the pipeline from the stage the change touches onward.
findings.problem: This repeats the caption just above it ("A change re-runs only the stages it touches").
findings.fix: "Each DOM change re-runs the stages of Fig 12.7, and the browser batches that work: ..."

findings.quote: is just IEEE 754 (Chapter 2.6)
findings.problem: "Chapter 2.6" is the only decimal section reference in the book; elsewhere sections are "06 · Floating point". The link covers only "Chapter 2" (href part-1#ch2), and the ".6" sits outside it.
findings.fix: "(Chapter 2's floating-point section)", linked to part-1#ch2-float.

findings.quote: The XSS attack from Fig 12.9 is neutralised even though the injection succeeded.
findings.problem: p8 explains only the origin allowlist, with an external `<script src>`. Every attack in Fig 12.9 is inline (`<script>steal()</script>`, an `onerror` handler), and those are stopped by the no-inline rule, which p8 never states.
findings.fix: "Inline injections like those in Fig 12.9 are refused as well, because the policy allows no inline code (Fig 12.11)."

findings.quote: A typical strict policy
findings.problem: The p8 example (an origin allowlist) is called "strict", while Fig 12.11's strip uses "a strict policy" for the nonce-or-hash kind. One word, two meanings in one section.
findings.fix: "A typical allowlist policy:"

findings.quote: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port)
findings.problem: "Scheme" in the URL sense is never glossed. The reader last met Scheme as the Lisp dialect in §02, and the URL meaning has to be inferred from the examples.
findings.fix: "An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port), the scheme being the `https` or `http` at the front of the URL, and..."

findings.quote: Change any one, `http` for `https`, `shop` for `www`, 8443 for 443
findings.problem: The caption gives http-for-https as a change to one part. The picture and the strip say that URL "differs in two places" (scheme and default port).
findings.fix: Covered by the caption rewrite above. Otherwise: "(`http` for `https` changes the default port too)".

findings.quote: even when an XSS injection has already put it in the page
findings.problem: The key-term highlight (span.key-term) sits on "XSS" in this caption, its fourth appearance. The term is defined in p4, where it carries only <strong> on "cross-site scripting". The new-term styling lands in the wrong place.
findings.fix: Move the key-term span to the first "XSS" in p4 and make the caption's "XSS" plain text.

findings.quote: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.
findings.problem: The section delivers one boundary (same-origin), two attacks (XSS, CSRF) and one defence (CSP). A reader counting "four boundaries" cannot find them.
findings.fix: "One wall, two ways around it, and the defences that close them." Or keep the shape: "Four lessons that keep the web from being one big shared computer."

findings.quote: is not magic; it is a few specific, layered defences
findings.problem: A "Not X; Y" reveal.
findings.fix: "That visiting a webpage does not compromise everything else you care about is the work of a few specific, layered defences, invented over thirty years in response to attacks that worked."

findings.quote: An interpreter that pretended to be a compiler
findings.problem: The section says engines really became optimising compilers, and the first V8 had no interpreter at all (Fig 12.5 strip). The title's "interpreter that pretended" has to be decoded and contradicts both.
findings.fix: "An engine that became a compiler · then a runtime that escaped the browser."

findings.quote: Break the bet, a string where only numbers came, and the optimised code is thrown away
findings.problem: The appositive inside an imperative clause has to be read twice for its syntax.
findings.fix: "If a string arrives where only numbers came before, the bet fails: the optimised code is thrown away and the function goes back to the interpreter."

findings.quote: as the function gets hotter it moves on to compilers
findings.problem: "Hotter" (also drawn in Fig 12.5) is never tied to p1's "which functions run most often".
findings.fix: "as it runs more often (gets 'hotter'), it moves on to compilers..."

findings.quote: Why not move that model to the server?
findings.problem: A rhetorical question stands in for the statement of Dahl's idea.
findings.fix: "Dahl's idea was to move that model to the server."

findings.quote: servers such as Apache, which gave each connection its own process or thread, which then sat waiting on the disk
findings.problem: Two stacked "which" clauses inside a parenthesis. The second "which" could refer to Apache or to the thread, so the sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: "(servers such as Apache gave each connection its own process or thread, and that thread sat idle while it waited for the disk or the network)"

findings.quote: within ten it had eaten enormous amounts of the server-side language landscape
findings.problem: Mixed metaphor (eating a landscape) and a vague quantity.
findings.fix: "within ten it was one of the most widely used server-side platforms."

findings.quote: The first V8, in 2008, had no interpreter and compiled everything straight to machine code.
findings.problem: p1 says the same ("V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code").
findings.fix: Under law 4, history goes in the strip, so cut the clause from p1: "...aggressive optimising compilers. Today's engines, V8 included, run a tiered pipeline...".

findings.quote: Ryan Dahl showed Node at JSConf EU in November 2009
findings.problem: This repeats p3 ("showed it at JSConf EU in Berlin that November").
findings.fix: Keep only the new fact in the strip: "*History.* libuv was written for Node in 2011, to bring it to Windows."

findings.quote: The policy arrived with JavaScript itself, in Netscape Navigator 2.0.
findings.problem: This repeats p2 ("introduced in Netscape 2.0, the same release that shipped JavaScript itself").
findings.fix: "*Cookies.* Cookies follow older, looser rules than the same-origin policy: they ignore the port, for one."

findings.quote: Mocha in May, LiveScript in September, JavaScript in December 1995
findings.problem: The names-and-months bullet repeats p2 and p3. Only the trademark point is new.
findings.fix: "*The names.* Sun held the Java trademark, which is why the 1997 standard had to be called ECMAScript."

findings.quote: What was missing was a small language that ran inside the page itself, at once.
findings.problem: The caption retells p1–p3 (forms round-trip, applets slow and walled off, a page language was needed) instead of naming the picture.
findings.fix: "Two pages of 1995: a form that must ask the server whether "abc" is a number, and a Java applet that starts slowly inside a box it cannot leave."

findings.quote: The event loop underneath is the same; only the shape on the page changed.
findings.problem: This repeats p4's framing ("What has changed... is the way JavaScript code spells...").
findings.fix: Drop the second sentence. The caption ends at "...async/await that reads like straight-line code."

findings.quote: pass a function to whoever does the work, and it will call your function back when finished
findings.problem: The callback is defined a second time in the same section. p1 already said "you hand it a function, a callback, to run when the work is done".
findings.fix: "The first era was plain *callbacks*: simple, and the source of the famous callback pyramid of doom..."

findings.quote: because legacy never dies
findings.problem: An aphorism closer used as the reason.
findings.fix: "All three coexist in any modern codebase, because code written in each era is still running."

findings.quote: The event loop's shape has been the same since 1995; microtasks arrived with Promises.
findings.problem: p2 makes the microtask queue one of the model's four parts, so a part arriving in 2015 means the shape did change. The clause contradicts itself.
findings.fix: "The event loop has kept its shape since 1995, apart from the microtask queue that arrived with Promises."

findings.quote: standardised in ES6, the 2015 edition of the language's ECMAScript standard
findings.problem: Figs 12.2 and 12.4 call this edition ES2015. The prose adds a second name, ES6, that is used nowhere else in the chapter.
findings.fix: "(standardised in ES2015, the 2015 edition of the ECMAScript standard, Fig 12.2)"

findings.quote: optionally render, repeat. Forever.
findings.problem: A clipped dramatic fragment.
findings.fix: "...optionally render, and repeat for as long as the page is open."

findings.quote: He delivered.
findings.problem: A clipped dramatic fragment as the paragraph opener.
findings.fix: Cut it. Open with "The first version, internally called *Mocha*, was a working interpreter by mid-May 1995."

findings.quote: The language should look enough like Java that the buzzword "Java" could be used in marketing
findings.problem: This gives away §02's point ("The name change was pure marketing: Netscape wanted to ride Sun's Java publicity"). The look-like-Java brief is also given again in eich-p1 ("C-like syntax, so that it looked familiar"), so the marketing idea arrives twice as news.
findings.fix: "The language should be far simpler than Java. It should run instantly..." and leave the look-alike and the marketing to §02.

findings.quote: applets were hard to write in small pieces
findings.problem: Unclear phrase: what is a "small piece" of an applet? The intended point (Java was too heavy for a few lines of page logic) does not come through.
findings.fix: "even a few lines of page logic needed a whole compiled Java program"

findings.quote: static documents and a tab-out to Java
findings.problem: "Tab-out" is not a recognisable term. The reader has to guess it means a box handed over to Java.
findings.fix: "Fig 12.1 · The web of 1994–95 · static documents and a box for Java"

findings.quote: V8 + libuv + a JavaScript stdlib
findings.problem: "stdlib" is jargon shorthand in a visible title. The prose and the picture both say "standard library".
findings.fix: "Fig 12.6 · Node.js · V8 + libuv + a JavaScript standard library"

findings.quote: Even so, XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10.
findings.problem: The OWASP Top 10 is not annual (editions 2003, 2004, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2017, 2021, 2025). Since 2021 XSS has been folded into the Injection category rather than listed on its own.
findings.fix: Owner call (kept original): "Even so, XSS has stayed in every edition of the OWASP Top 10, since 2021 as part of Injection."

findings.quote: consistent: T42 kept, T43 gone
findings.problem: Fig 13.6 uses Fig 13.5's people and amounts but splits the transfer into two transactions: T42 debits Alice 100, T43 pays Bob 100. Its end state, Alice €100 and Bob €50 (total €150), is exactly the state Fig 13.5, two figures earlier, marks in red as '€100 has vanished'. Here that state is labelled 'consistent'. A reader who has just learned that a transfer is one atomic transaction sees money vanish and be called correct.
findings.fix: Redraw T43 on a third account so neither transaction is half of the Alice-to-Bob transfer. For example: 'T43 Cara 80 → 30', Cara's page written early and undone back to €80. Alternatively, let T42 carry both halves of the transfer (Alice 200 → 100, Bob 50 → 150, commit) and make T43 an uncommitted second transfer. Update the <desc> and the caption to match.

findings.quote: O(|R| × |S|), yet the right choice when one side is tiny
findings.problem: The strip writes all three costs in Big-O with |R| and |S| bars: O(|R| × |S|), O(|R| + |S|), O(|R| + |S|). Big-O is first explained two sections later, in ch13-indexes-p1, and the bar notation is never explained. Pass 30's handover listed this (docs/pass-30-figures.md) and it is still open.
findings.fix: Nested loop: "Work grows with the product of the two table sizes, yet the right choice when one side is tiny or …". Hash join: "Work grows with the sum of the two sizes, for equality joins, if …". Merge join: "Also the sum, after sorting, so it wins when …".

findings.quote: a result that running them one after the other, in any order, could not
findings.problem: The sentence on Serializable stacks two parentheticals and ends on an elliptical 'could not' (could not produce). It has to be read twice for its syntax, in a paragraph the owner-read map sends him to (ch13-acid-p8).
findings.fix: "…Repeatable Read one per transaction. Serializable also watches which transactions read data that others wrote: when two overlap in a way no one-after-the-other order could reproduce, it aborts (cancels and rolls back) one of them, sometimes more often than strictly needed."

findings.quote: a manager's manager's manager, which SQL later adds, sit outside it
findings.problem: In 'That is what relationally complete means (counting, totals and queries that follow a chain of any length, a manager's manager's manager, which SQL later adds, sit outside it)', the parenthetical has its own subject, an appositive and a relative clause, all set off by commas. The reader cannot find the verb on the first pass.
findings.fix: "That is what relationally complete means. Counting, totals and chains of any length (a manager's manager's manager) sit outside it; SQL added them later." Then end the paragraph there (see the next finding).

findings.quote: the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection.
findings.problem: 'Join = product + selection' is said four times in one section: p1 ('the last of them derived from the others'), the Fig 13.2 strip ('a join is a product followed by a selection'), p3 itself ('bolt a selection onto it and you have rebuilt the join from parts') and again at the end of p3. The strip also calls it 'Cartesian product' where p3 says 'cross product'.
findings.fix: Cut p3's closing clause '; the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection'. Cut the Fig 13.2 strip bullet 'The rest of the algebra': p3 names all six operators and rebuilds the join.

findings.quote: so the output of one can feed the next: that closure is what lets SQL queries nest.
findings.problem: Closure is explained three times in one section: p1 ('the result of any operation is itself a relation, and so can be the input to the next'), this caption, and p5 ('Because every expression yields a relation, the algebra is compositional: expressions nest without bound').
findings.fix: Caption: "Selection keeps the rows that pass a test, projection keeps the columns you name, and a join pairs the rows of two tables that agree on a value; each result is a new table." In p5, replace the second sentence and the opening of the third with: "Closure is what lets a query optimiser parse a complex SQL statement into a tree of relational operators and rewrite …".

findings.quote: A relation is a set of tuples that all share the same structure: a table, in everyday language
findings.problem: 'Relation' is defined three times. Section 01 gives it in ch13-codd-p1 ('a table of rows in no fixed order (to a mathematician, a set of tuples)') and again in ch13-codd-p4 ('a row (tuple) in a table (relation)'), and here it is defined from scratch a third time. codd-p1 also uses 'tuples' before any gloss.
findings.fix: Open algebra-p1 from what the reader has: "In a relation, Section 01's table of rows, each row is a tuple and each column an attribute." In codd-p4, shorten the data model to "every piece of data is a row in a relation, and there is no other structure (…)".

findings.quote: Filtering first gives the same answer with fewer rows to join: σ(R ⨝ S) = σ(R) ⨝ S
findings.problem: Selection pushdown is explained twice, in two sections. ch13-algebra-p6 states the rule with the same formula and points to Fig 13.3. Here the caption ('moves the age filter below the join, so only adults are joined') and this strip bullet repeat it.
findings.fix: Cut the 'The rewrite' bullet. The caption and ch13-algebra-p6 already carry the rule.

findings.quote: the major relational databases still running descend from one or the other
findings.problem: The lineage is said three times: ch13-codd-p6 ('the major databases in production in 2026 either descend from one of two 1970s prototypes…'), this caption, and the strip ('MySQL and SQLite were written fresh, but speak the same SQL'). The brief says the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Caption: "Two family trees from one paper, System R at IBM and Ingres at Berkeley; the dashed lines mark Oracle borrowing IBM's published SQL and Ingres alumni founding Sybase." Cut the strip's last sentence ('MySQL and SQLite were written fresh, but speak the same SQL').

findings.quote: committed changes the pages missed are redone, and uncommitted ones that reached them are undone
findings.problem: The caption retells ch13-acid-p4 just above it: log first and forced to disk, pages lazily, then redo committed and undo uncommitted. The undo of uncommitted work has already been stated in the Fig 13.5 caption, the Fig 13.5 strip and p4, so this is the fourth time.
findings.fix: Name the picture instead: "T42 committed, so recovery redoes it although Alice's page was stale; T43 never committed, so recovery undoes it although Bob's page was written early." Adjust if Fig 13.6 is redrawn per the H finding.

findings.quote: the scan then walks the linked leaves left to right, emitting keys until one passes the end.
findings.problem: The range-scan mechanism (one descent, then a walk along the linked leaves) is explained three times: ch13-indexes-p2 ('one descent to the first key plus a walk … because the leaves are linked'), this caption, and the strip bullet 'Why the links' ('turns a range into one descent plus a walk').
findings.fix: Caption: "Three page reads down to the leaf holding 22, then two along the links: 22, 30 and 38 are found, and 45 stops the scan." Strip: cut 'Why the links', or keep only "Only the leaves hold row pointers."

findings.quote: Since a value never reaches the parser, nothing in it can change what the query does
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch13-injection-p4 ('Whatever the attacker sends as a value … stays data and is never parsed as code'). p4 itself then restates the point a second time, 'The predicate is always exactly what the developer wrote.', using 'predicate', a word this chapter's prose never explains.
findings.fix: Cut p4's last sentence. Caption: "The SQL text, with a slot for the value, is parsed once into a plan; O'Brien, then Smith, is bound into the slot without passing the parser, its apostrophe only a letter."

findings.quote: None of these alone is sufficient; together they make SQL injection rare even when one layer fails.
findings.problem: The heading says 'The fix · parameterised queries · and only that' and p4 calls the defence 'clean and absolute'. This closing line then says 'none of these alone is sufficient', which a reader can take to include parameterised queries. 'Rare even when one layer fails' is also muddled: the extra layers limit the damage, they do not make injection rarer.
findings.fix: "None of these replaces parameterised queries; they limit what an attacker gets when a query somewhere was built by concatenation after all."

findings.quote: each permitting more anomalies in exchange for more concurrency
findings.problem: The prose never says what the anomalies are. Dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom are defined only in the Fig 13.7 caption, yet ch13-acid-p8 leans on them ('locks on ranges of rows that stop phantoms appearing'). Law 3 says the explanation lives in the prose.
findings.fix: Move the definitions into p6: "…in exchange for more concurrency: a dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted change, a non-repeatable read sees a row change between two reads, and a phantom sees new rows appear." Caption: "Which anomalies each level allows, and one re-read run: 50 under read committed, 100 under repeatable read."

findings.quote: was invented for IBM's System R by Patricia Selinger and described in a 1979 paper at SIGMOD
findings.problem: A 33-word relative clause separates the subject ('The optimiser-as-component') from its verb. 'that is among the most cited' then attaches to 'conference' rather than 'paper'. The next sentence restates the first ('choose the plan by its estimated cost, using statistics about the data'). The owner-read map sends him here.
findings.fix: "Patricia Selinger invented the optimiser as a component, for IBM's System R. It estimates each plan's cost from statistics about the tables and finds the cheapest join order by working out the best way to join each small group of tables, then building up. Her 1979 paper at SIGMOD, the main database research conference ("Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System"), is among the most cited on query optimisation. Every cost-based optimiser since (…) builds on that idea."

findings.quote: the optimisation tooling (Selinger's planner, the WAL, the B-tree) has had fifty years of battle-testing
findings.problem: Section 04 taught the WAL as the durability and atomicity mechanism, not optimisation. ARIES dates from 1992, so 'fifty years' does not hold for it. The sentence also opens on a 'The reasons are not nostalgia:' reveal.
findings.fix: "Its reasons: relational algebra is relationally complete and composes without limit, the transaction model is precise, and its machinery (Selinger's planner, the write-ahead log, the B-tree) has had decades of battle-testing."

findings.quote: Every change goes to the write-ahead log before the table (Fig 13.6)
findings.problem: The 'How recovery knows' bullet explains undo at restart, which the caption beside it already says and ch13-acid-p4 and the Fig 13.6 caption say again. The 'Who.' bullet repeats ch13-acid-p1's 'Jim Gray in a 1981 paper'.
findings.fix: Cut 'How recovery knows'. 'Who.' becomes: "Jim Gray, Turing Award 1998; Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter named it ACID in 1983."

findings.quote: PostgreSQL's hash indexes are crash-safe (WAL-logged) since version 10, yet almost every index people create is a B-tree.
findings.problem: The strip repeats ch13-indexes-p4 ('PostgreSQL has hash indexes, but they are rarely used'). 'nothing for ranges' is said a third time after p4 and the caption. The bullet 'The cost of any index' repeats ch13-indexes-p1 ('slower writes (each insert or update has to keep the index in sync)').
findings.fix: Hash bullet: "O(1) on average for equality (the toy hash here is 37 × id mod 8; real ones scramble harder)." Cut 'The cost of any index'.

findings.quote: In the algebra a relation is a set, so π drops duplicate rows
findings.problem: The 'Sets and bags' bullet is explained in full by ch13-algebra-p4, two paragraphs later in the same section.
findings.fix: Cut the 'Sets and bags' bullet.

findings.quote: snapshot isolation still allows write skew, which only serializable prevents.
findings.problem: 'Write skew' is never explained anywhere in the chapter. 'Snapshot isolation' appears before ch13-acid-p8 explains what a snapshot is.
findings.fix: "PostgreSQL's repeatable read gives each transaction one snapshot (below) and blocks phantoms too." Drop the write-skew clause, or explain it: "two transactions each check a rule, then make changes that together break it (write skew); only serializable prevents that."

findings.quote: Engines either lock what a transaction reads, or keep old versions of rows
findings.problem: The 'How.' bullet summarises ch13-acid-p8, which follows the figure and explains both families in full.
findings.fix: Cut the 'How.' bullet.

findings.quote: PostgreSQL's log is redo-only: an aborted transaction's row versions simply stay invisible.
findings.problem: 'Row versions' depends on MVCC, which is explained only in ch13-acid-p8, two figures later.
findings.fix: "PostgreSQL's log is redo-only: it keeps old and new versions of each row (MVCC, below), so an aborted transaction's versions simply stay invisible."

findings.quote: SELECT name, product
findings.problem: Fig 13.2 draws the same users/orders join with the orders column 'item' (lamp, desk, pen); Fig 13.3 selects 'product'. The strip's 'here nearly everyone is an adult' also clashes with Fig 13.2's users table, where two of four are minors.
findings.fix: Use 'item' in Fig 13.3 (SELECT name, item; 'π keep name, item'). Strip: "(if nearly everyone is an adult, scanning wins)".

findings.quote: He spent his last decade increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model
findings.problem: Codd died in 2003, but the next sentence dates his rules to 1985, 18 years earlier. Read together, the two sentences put 1985 in his last decade.
findings.fix: "He spent his later years increasingly frustrated…"

findings.quote: (thirteen, counting rule 0, in two Computerworld pieces, the first asking
findings.problem: One parenthetical holds two unrelated facts, the rule count and where the rules were published, so the sentence has to be reread.
findings.fix: "In 1985, in two Computerworld pieces (the first asking "Is Your DBMS Really Relational?"), he published twelve rules, thirteen counting rule 0, listing properties any system claiming the title must satisfy."

findings.quote: System R at IBM San Jose or Ingres at Berkeley (DB2, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server), or, like MySQL
findings.problem: The parenthetical list of databases lands after 'Berkeley', so it reads as a list of Berkeley products. The either/or frame is split across 50 words.
findings.fix: "So DB2, Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, the major databases in production in 2026, descend from one of two 1970s prototypes, System R at IBM San Jose or Ingres at Berkeley; others, like MySQL, SQLite, Snowflake and ClickHouse, were written fresh to speak the SQL that System R introduced."

findings.quote: read Codd's paper and founded a company to build a relational database before IBM did
findings.problem: The prose gives Codd's paper as Oracle's source. Fig 13.1 draws Oracle hanging off System R by 'IBM's SQL', and its strip says Oracle was 'built from IBM's published papers'. The reader meets two origins.
findings.fix: "read Codd's paper and IBM's published papers on System R's SQL, and founded a company to build a relational database before IBM did".

findings.quote: Codd's complaint was not that they were slow but that they were brittle
findings.problem: A 'not X but Y' reveal. The sentence before ('Both worked well enough') already says they were not slow.
findings.fix: "Codd's complaint was that they were brittle: the schema, the queries, and the storage layout were entangled, and changing any one broke the others."

findings.quote: Find one user out of ten million by name? Read all ten million rows.
findings.problem: A question used as a clipped dramatic device, answered by a fragment.
findings.fix: "To find one user out of ten million by name, the engine reads all ten million rows."

findings.quote: one more step each time the table multiplies in size
findings.problem: 'Multiplies in size' does not say by what, and this phrase is the whole of the O(log N) definition the newcomer gets.
findings.fix: "one more step each time the table grows by a fixed factor (about a hundredfold, for the B-tree below)".

findings.quote: most working SQL is built almost entirely from three operations
findings.problem: Two hedges stacked: 'most' plus 'almost entirely'.
findings.fix: "and most working SQL is built from three operations: …"

findings.quote: Each of the other operators buys a specific question.
findings.problem: 'Buys a question' is the wrong verb, and the reader stops on it.
findings.fix: "Each of the other operators answers one kind of question."

findings.quote: The English is the contract; the plan is private to the engine.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer that restates ch13-codd-p4's independence principle. 'The English' for the SQL text reads oddly. The Fig 13.3 caption in the same section closes the same way ('The plan, not the SQL, decides how fast the query is').
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. The one before it already says the engine turns the SQL into its own plan.

findings.quote: which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, minutes of work
findings.problem: 'Two million-row tables' also reads as tables of two million rows, which would give four trillion comparisons, not one.
findings.fix: "which for two tables of a million rows each is a trillion of them, minutes of work".

findings.quote: a million a side: a trillion against a few million.
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch13-sql-p4's trillion comparisons for million-row tables.
findings.fix: End the caption at "Five rows a side: 25 comparisons against about ten."

findings.quote: The SQL standard defines four isolation levels in decreasing order of strictness
findings.problem: The prose announces the levels in decreasing strictness; Fig 13.7, directly below, lists them weakest first.
