findings.fix: "The SQL standard defines four isolation levels; each step down from serializable permits more anomalies in exchange for more concurrency."

findings.quote: Read Committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement, Repeatable Read one per transaction, and Serializable
findings.problem: The level names are capitalised here. Everywhere else in the section (p6, the Fig 13.7 caption, strip and labels) they are lowercase.
findings.fix: "read committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement, repeatable read one per transaction, and serializable …"

findings.quote: once a transaction has been told it committed
findings.problem: A transaction is not told anything; the application is.
findings.fix: "once the application has been told its transaction committed".

findings.quote: let code read and write rows as ordinary objects while they write the SQL
findings.problem: 'They' could mean the code or the libraries.
findings.fix: "libraries such as Django ORM and ActiveRecord, which write the SQL themselves and hand the code its rows as ordinary objects".

findings.quote: The theory is set theory; the practice is fifty years of refinement; the surface area is small enough
findings.problem: A three-clause semicolon run in the chapter opener (the reflexive triplet the brief lists). The middle clause carries nothing.
findings.fix: "Its theory is set theory, and its surface is small enough that a working programmer can master it in weeks."

findings.quote: ' UNION SELECT pw FROM users-- exfiltrates every password hash
findings.problem: The vulnerable code compares pw directly with what the user types (pw='" + input_pw + "'), so the column holds plaintext passwords. The payload would steal passwords, not hashes. Owner's figure: reported only.
findings.fix: Label: "exfiltrates every stored password" (owner call).

findings.quote: Add one bit to the key and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.
findings.problem: This sentence describes exponential O(2^n) work, but it now comes straight after the sentence inserted in Pass 29 that says factoring is sub-exponential: 'each extra bit costs less than a doubling'. In this order it reads as more about factoring, so the paragraph contradicts itself two sentences apart. The p7 formula line ('inverse time = exp(n)') repeats the mix-up.
findings.fix: Move the sentence up to follow the exponential definition: "*Hard*, in the cryptographic sense, means _exponential_: roughly _O(2^n)_. Add one bit to the key and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares. Factoring is kinder, called _sub-exponential_: each extra bit costs less than a doubling, ... yet its cost still outgrows any power of _n_."

findings.quote: in ECDSA and Ed25519 (the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses)
findings.problem: TLS 1.3 also signs with RSA-PSS. RFC 8446 §4.2.3 makes rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 mandatory to implement, and most web servers still present RSA certificates. The chapter says so itself in the Fig 14.11 strip ('Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS'), the Fig 14.8 strip and ch14-publickey-p6. Read as written, the parenthesis tells the reader RSA plays no part in TLS 1.3.
findings.fix: "in ECDSA and Ed25519 (which TLS 1.3 offers beside RSA-PSS) it is a different curve computation with the same shape."

findings.quote: was settled soon after in the Bernstein and Junger appeals, and it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source
findings.problem: Neither case 'settled' the point. The Ninth Circuit withdrew the 1999 Bernstein panel opinion when it ordered an en banc rehearing, and in 2003 the case was dismissed without a ruling (Wikipedia, Bernstein v. United States). Only Junger v. Daley (6th Cir., 2000) still holds that source code is speech, and only in that circuit. Crypto libraries can be distributed openly today because of the January 2000 export rule (License Exception TSU for publicly available source code), not because of a settled ruling.
findings.fix: "...that source code is protected speech, was upheld by appeals courts in the Bernstein (1999) and Junger (2000) cases, and together with the 2000 export rules it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source and globally distributed."

findings.quote: several orders of magnitude beyond the entire computational capacity of Earth running until the heat death of the universe
findings.problem: The arithmetic does not hold. 2^256 is about 1.2×10^77. Heat death is usually put at about 10^100 years (about 3×10^107 s), so even 10^21 operations per second for that long gives about 3×10^128 operations, far more than 2^256. The claim is true for the age of the universe: 4.4×10^17 s × about 10^22 ops/s ≈ 10^40, so 2^256 is about 37 orders of magnitude beyond. Also, the sentence follows 'an elliptic-curve key needs 256', but breaking a 256-bit curve key costs only about 2^128.
findings.fix: "Trying every 256-bit key would take every computer on Earth far longer than the age of the universe." (This also matches ch14-primer-p3.)

findings.quote: When a machine of that size exists, it breaks all current public-key cryptography.
findings.problem: ML-KEM is current public-key cryptography too: Chrome has used it by default since 2024, and the next paragraph and Fig 14.13 present it as the scheme that survives Shor. Caption ch14-tls-pqc-p8 says 'would break every public-key scheme in use today' and then 'browsers already pair X25519 with ML-KEM', which contradicts itself in the same way.
findings.fix: p6: "When a machine of that size exists, it breaks every one of these systems." Caption p8: "Shor's algorithm would break every classical public-key scheme in use today, so NIST's 2024 standards replace them..."

findings.quote: in the same performance class as RSA (a few milliseconds per handshake)
findings.problem: This overstates the cost by about ten times and contradicts p1 ('takes microseconds'). Measured on this Mac with OpenSSL 3.6.2: X25519 about 18 µs per operation, 2048-bit finite-field DH (ffdhe2048) about 134 µs, RSA-2048 signing about 0.34 ms.
findings.fix: "in the same performance class as RSA (well under a millisecond per operation on a modern server)"

findings.quote: broken: Babbage, Kasiski 1863
findings.problem: Every other label gives each breaker their own year ('Rejewski 1932, Bombe 1940'), so this one reads as if both broke it in 1863. Babbage broke it in 1854, as ch14-history-p1 says. The desc says the same wrong thing: 'broken by Babbage and by Kasiski in 1863'.
findings.fix: Drawn: "broken: Babbage 1854, Kasiski 1863" (same length as the Enigma line). Desc: "broken by Babbage in 1854 and by Kasiski, who published the method, in 1863".

findings.quote: Your disk encryption, your VPN tunnel, and your iMessage and Signal messages are AES too.
findings.problem: WireGuard, which ch14-ecc-p1 names as a modern protocol, encrypts only with ChaCha20-Poly1305, and many consumer VPNs are now built on it. A reader whose VPN runs WireGuard is told something false.
findings.fix: "Your disk encryption, most VPN tunnels, and your iMessage and Signal messages are AES too."

findings.quote: so that a certificate authority's (CA's) log of issued certificates can be publicly audited
findings.problem: CT logs do not belong to the CA. They are independent public logs, run by operators such as Google and Cloudflare, and they accept certificates from every CA. That independence is what lets them catch a misbehaving CA, which ch14-tls-pqc-p4 describes correctly.
findings.fix: "uses Merkle trees so that the public logs of every certificate the certificate authorities (CAs) issue can be audited without downloading every certificate."

findings.quote: remained classified until 1997, by which time the patents on the public re-inventions
findings.problem: The timing is off for one patent. The Diffie–Hellman patent (US 4,200,770, filed 6 September 1977) expired on 6 September 1997. GCHQ disclosed the work in December 1997, so by then only MIT's RSA patent still stood. Source: cr.yp.to/patents/us/4200770.html and the 1997 cypherpunks archive.
findings.fix: "...remained classified until 1997, by which time the public re-inventions (patented by Stanford for Diffie–Hellman and by MIT for RSA, licensed to RSA Data Security) stood beneath a billion-dollar security industry."

findings.quote: The hour after 11 o'clock is not 12; it is 0.
findings.problem: On a real 12-hour clock the hour after 11 is 12, so the sentence states something false about clocks before it makes the modular point. A careful reader stops on it.
findings.fix: "On a clock the hour after 11 wraps back to the top, 12, which arithmetic modulo 12 writes as 0."

findings.quote: would have to pull one secret exponent back out to finish the multiplication, and that is the discrete logarithm
findings.problem: Nobody has proven that getting g^ab from g^a and g^b requires the discrete log (this is the computational Diffie–Hellman problem). What is true is that no faster way is known. As written, it presents an assumption as a proven fact.
findings.fix: "The eavesdropper, holding only _g^a_ and _g^b_, knows no faster way to finish than pulling one secret exponent back out, and that is the discrete logarithm."

findings.quote: from the silicon (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III)
findings.problem: Part II is 'The Software Layer' (the kernel, C, objects, Python), not silicon. The reader has just read it, so the description of the book's own map will jar.
findings.fix: "from the silicon and the software on it (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III)..."

findings.quote: row by row, 64 MB of memory per guess
findings.problem: The drawn label says MB, but the desc and the generator use 64 MiB (argon2id m = 65536 KiB), and the strip gives OWASP's minimum as '19 MiB'. One figure uses two units for the same quantity.
findings.fix: "row by row, 64 MiB of memory per guess"

findings.quote: Alice €100? Bob €50 total €250
findings.problem: In the BEGIN … COMMIT row, from 1.6 s to 4.8 s of the 10 s loop (seen at 1.2 to 3.3 s), Alice reads '€100?' and Bob '€50', but the total still says '€250'. That sum is wrong. In the no-transaction row above, the total drops to '€150' at the same moment, so the two rows count 'total' in two different ways and a reader stops to add it up.
findings.fix: While the debit is uncommitted, show this row's total as '€150?' in the same muted style as '€100?'. Switch it back to '€250' (green) at the undo, at the same moment Alice returns to €200.

findings.quote: debit Alice power cut restart
findings.problem: The three step pills are supposed to light up in order, but only 'debit Alice' has a dimmed waiting state (opacity 0.3). 'power cut' starts at full strength (its waiting group has opacity 1, with the same stroke as the lit one), and 'restart' starts at 0.74. At 1.2 s, before anything has happened, 'power cut' is already lit next to a dim 'debit Alice'. At 2.8 s it looks as if the power has already failed, though the cut comes at 3.2 s.
findings.fix: Give 'power cut' and 'restart' the same waiting style as 'debit Alice': dim (group opacity 0.3), or a dashed muted outline that still passes contrast. Light each one when its event happens: power cut at 3.2 s, restart at 4.8 s.

findings.quote: power cut … running: log first, pages later
findings.problem: The 'power cut' pill looks the same before and after the crash (waiting stroke #b8372f at opacity 1, lit stroke #bb3f37). At 2.0 s and 3.3 s it is fully lit beside 'running: log first, pages later', and the crash at 4.2 s has no visible moment of its own. Only the status line changes. This is the same cause as the Fig 13.5 pills.
findings.fix: Draw the pill dim until 4.2 s, then light it with a brief red flash, the same 'fx' outline the figure already uses for changed values.

findings.problem: Recovery's reading cursor is a green outline (#a9bf8e), and it lands on the uncommitted T43 record that is about to be undone. Everywhere else in this figure green means committed or kept ('T42 commit', 'T42: OK', 'consistent: T42 kept'). At 6.67 s, T43 glows green next to Bob's red undo flash, so it looks as if T43 is being kept.
findings.fix: Draw the reading cursor in a neutral colour, the cream #e6d9bd or the amber of 'data pages', and keep green for commits only.

findings.quote: IBM shipped it as SQL/DS (1981) and DB2 (1983)
findings.problem: DB2 was announced in June 1983 and became generally available in April 1985, so 'shipped … DB2 (1983)' is wrong. Pass 29 handed this over in docs/pass-30-figures.md ('DB2 "1983" is the announcement; it shipped in 1985'), and it has not been fixed in the strip or logged in §4g.
findings.fix: Strip: 'System R produced SQL; IBM shipped it as SQL/DS (1981) and announced DB2 in 1983 (on sale 1985), after Oracle had shipped its own version, built from IBM's published papers, in 1979.' The DB2 box can keep 1983 once the strip says 'announced'. Log the fix in §4g.

findings.quote: Codd 1970 to PostgreSQL 18 · two lineages, fifty years
findings.problem: The label promises a timeline that ends at PostgreSQL 18, but the picture ends at 'PostgreSQL 1996'. The number 18 appears only in the closed How it works strip, left over from the earlier drawing.
findings.fix: Add a small second line under the PostgreSQL box, 'v18 · 2025', or retitle it 'Fig 13.1 · Codd 1970 to today · two lineages, fifty years'.

findings.quote: IBM, San Jose … Oracle 1979
findings.problem: Oracle sits in IBM's band, right under the 'IBM, San Jose' heading, drawn in a red close to IBM's salmon. Berkeley's outside offshoots (Sybase, SQL Server) get their own green. So the colours mark Sybase as outside Berkeley but make Oracle look like an IBM product.
findings.fix: Draw the Oracle box in the same 'outside company' green as Sybase and SQL Server, so both dashed offshoots follow one colour rule.

findings.quote: the major relational databases still running descend from one or the other
findings.problem: The caption restates ch13-codd-p6 (two prototypes, and which databases descend from each) and says nothing about how to read the drawing: what a solid arrow means against a dashed one, or why the boxes light up in sequence.
findings.fix: 'Solid arrows are one product line becoming the next; a dashed line carries only ideas or people across: Oracle built from IBM's published SQL, and Ingres alumni founded Sybase. The boxes light in year order, and four of them are still running.'

findings.quote: σ filter age > 18 … ⨝ join on id = user_id
findings.problem: While the optimiser pushes σ down (about 2.2 to 3.7 s), the σ box slides straight down through the join node. For about a second the two labels sit on top of each other and neither can be read (seen at 2.5, 3.0 and 3.3 s). This is the step the figure exists to show.
findings.fix: Route σ around the join: slide it left onto the users branch, then down. Or fade it out above the join and back in above users.

findings.quote: SELECT name, product
findings.problem: Fig 13.2 drew the same orders table, joined on id = user_id, with the columns user_id and item (lamp, desk, pen). Two figures later the same query asks for a column 'product', which that table does not have.
findings.fix: Use 'SELECT name, item' in the SQL box and 'π keep name, item' in the tree, and update the desc to match.

findings.quote: here nearly everyone is an adult, so scanning wins
findings.problem: The strip says 'here', but the chapter's own users table has two adults out of four (Fig 13.2) and three out of five (hero). A reader who has just seen those tables will not find 'nearly everyone is an adult' in the book's data.
findings.fix: '(in a typical users table most rows pass, so scanning wins)'.

findings.quote: name item Alice lamp Cara desk Alice pen
findings.problem: The join's result table shows only name and item. A join keeps every column of both rows it pairs (id, name, user_id, item). Dropping id and user_id is the projection drawn just above it, which blurs the line between the two operators. Fig 13.3 needs a separate π after its join for exactly this reason.
findings.fix: Show the result as 'id · name · user_id · item' (1 Alice 1 lamp; 3 Cara 3 desk; 1 Alice 1 pen). If that is too wide at 375 px, label the result 'a new table (id, user_id not shown)'.

findings.quote: 4 Dan 9
findings.problem: The hero's users table has the same ids and names as Fig 13.2's table (Alice 31, Bob 14, Cara 42), but gives Dan age 9. Fig 13.2 gives him 17.
findings.fix: Change Dan's age in the hero to 17. He stays dimmed, since 17 is not over 18.

findings.quote: SQL is shorthand for set mathematics
findings.problem: The hero's tagline says the opposite of the chapter. ch13-algebra-p4 and Fig 13.2's strip say SQL works on bags and keeps duplicate rows unless you write DISTINCT. ch13-codd-p8 names that as the gap Codd objected to. 'Shorthand' claims an exact match the chapter denies.
findings.fix: 'SQL is built on set mathematics'. This also matches the committed intended message ('the theory under SQL is set theory').

findings.quote: Parameterised queries · code and data on separate wires
findings.problem: Neither route is drawn. The SQL text's path through the parser into the plan, and the value's path past 'never parsed' into the slot, exist only as moving dots. The still frame (t=0, also what reduced-motion readers see) shows no wire at all, and 'never parsed' floats unconnected, although the label promises two separate wires.
findings.fix: Draw two faint fixed lines: amber from 'the SQL text' through 'parser' to the plan, and green from 'the value' past 'never parsed' to the dashed slot. Keep the dots running along them.

findings.quote: After a crash, recovery replays the log: committed changes the pages missed are redone
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch13-acid-p4 almost clause for clause (log forced first, pages lazily later, committed changes replayed, uncommitted rolled back) and never points at what the picture shows: T42's stale page and T43's dirty one.
findings.fix: 'T42 is in the log, commit and all, before the OK, yet Alice's page still says €200; T43 never committed, yet its €150 reached Bob's page. Recovery redoes the first from the log and undoes the second.'

findings.quote: Add one bit to the key and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.
findings.problem: The sentence sits right after the factoring aside, so it reads as describing RSA. But the clause before it says that for factoring each extra bit costs less than a doubling. The two sentences contradict each other, and the callout exists to make exactly this point (why RSA keys are long). The formula line right after it (p7, 'inverse time = exp(n)') then ignores the sub-exponential case.
findings.fix: Move the sentence up to the exponential definition: "*Hard*, in the cryptographic sense, means _exponential_: roughly _O(2^n)_, so one more bit of key doubles the work and twice the bits squares it. Factoring is kinder, called _sub-exponential_: each extra bit costs less than a doubling, which is why an RSA key needs thousands of bits where an elliptic-curve key needs 256, yet its cost still outgrows any power of _n_. At 256 bits of key, ..."

findings.quote: SLH-DSA rests only on the hash functions of Section 02.
findings.problem: One paragraph says three times that SLH-DSA is built only on hash functions: 'built only on hash functions', then 'rests only on the hash functions of Section 02', then 'needs nothing but a hash function'. The first two are in a single sentence of about 70 words, with the lattice definition wedged between them, so the reader has to read it twice to see which scheme rests on what.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "*SLH-DSA* (formerly "SPHINCS+") is a signature built only on the hash functions of Section 02. The first two rest on lattice problems: a lattice is a regular grid of points extended to hundreds of dimensions, and finding the grid point nearest to a given point is easy in two dimensions and believed infeasible in hundreds, even for a quantum computer. Neither basis is factoring or discrete log, and no polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for either. SLH-DSA is the conservative hedge: if lattices turn out to hide a weakness, a signature that needs nothing but a hash function still stands."

findings.quote: from the silicon (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III)
findings.problem: Part II is 'The Software Layer' (the kernel, C, the languages), not silicon. As written, the chapter's last sentence gives a wrong map of the book.
findings.fix: "from the silicon and the software on it (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III) to the data and cryptography (Chapters 13 and 14)"

findings.quote: in ECDSA and Ed25519 (the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses) it is a different curve computation
findings.problem: Other places in the chapter say TLS 1.3 signs with RSA too. The Fig 14.11 strip names 'Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS'. ch14-publickey-p6 and the Fig 14.8 strip say RSA 'only signs' in TLS 1.3. This parenthesis implies RSA signatures are not used.
findings.fix: Drop the parenthesis: "In RSA this is literally "decrypting" the hash with the private exponent; in ECDSA and Ed25519 it is a different curve computation with the same shape."

findings.quote: uses the long-term RSA or ECDSA key only for signing the handshake
findings.problem: Within this one section, three things are each said several times. (1) A signature, not Diffie–Hellman, proves identity: said in the Fig 14.7 strip, the Fig 14.8 strip, p6's second sentence, and again in p6's last sentence. (2) Forward secrecy: explained in the Fig 14.7 strip and again in p6, cited two different ways for the same place ('Part III, Fig 11.13' and 'Chapter 11, Section 05'). (3) 'RSA is roughly 1000× slower than AES ... TLS does not use RSA for the actual data' repeats ch11-crypto-p7 almost word for word, with no recall clause.
findings.fix: Cut p6's last sentence ("TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral key exchange ... signing the handshake."). Cut the third item of the Fig 14.7 strip ("In TLS. ..."), since p6 carries forward secrecy. Open p6 with a recall: "As Chapter 11 showed, RSA is roughly 1000× slower than AES per byte, so ...".

findings.quote: The secret is safe not because it was hidden, but because the one step needed to reconstruct it runs backward
findings.problem: A 'not X, but Y' reveal used as an aphorism closer. It restates the sentence before it, which already says the eavesdropper would have to take the discrete logarithm.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The paragraph ends on "...and that is the discrete logarithm."

findings.quote: cryptographic engineering is the discipline of keeping ahead of whoever is computing more cleverly than you
findings.problem: An aphorism closer stacked on a 'comes not from X but from Y' construction. The strip as a whole also restates ch14-primer-p4: 'hard' is contingent, and when the algorithm changes the assumption dies.
findings.fix: End at the migration point: "The system's resilience comes from migrating to the next primitive before the current one fails." Delete the colon clause.

findings.quote: In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor, working at Bell Labs, published an algorithm
findings.problem: Shor's algorithm is introduced as new here, but ch14-primer-p4 already introduced it: 1994, factoring and discrete log, polynomial time, a large quantum computer. The primer's last sentence also already gave Section 06's answer: replacements on lattice problems, for which no efficient quantum algorithm is known. That answer is repeated in p7.
findings.fix: Here: "Shor's algorithm, met in the primer (Peter Shor, Bell Labs, 1994), solves both integer factoring and discrete logarithm in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer." In ch14-primer-p4, shorten the last sentence to: "That is why Section 06 of this chapter is about post-quantum migration."

findings.quote: In ECB mode every 16-byte block is encrypted on its own, so equal plaintext blocks come out as equal ciphertext
findings.problem: The caption explains ECB and CBC again, after p4 explained both. 'AES is sound, but the mode decides what leaks' repeats p4's 'the mode is more often the source of cryptographic bugs than the cipher itself'. Two strip items also repeat p4: 'What to use' (GCM is counter mode plus a tamper tag) and 'The famous one' (Tux).
findings.fix: Caption: "The same padlock encrypted with AES-128 twice: in ECB mode it is still there to see; in **CBC** mode it becomes noise." Then either cut the strip items "What to use" and "The famous one", or cut the GCM and Tux sentences from p4. Keep each in one place.

findings.quote: by drawing the line through P and Q, finding where it meets the curve a third time
findings.problem: The prose teaches only the rule for two different points. Yet the caption ('Adding a point to itself k times is fast'), Fig 14.2 ('k × point G') and Fig 14.11 ('x·G') all depend on adding a point to itself many times. There is no line through P and P (it is the tangent), and the chapter never says why k·G is fast. A careful reader stops at the caption.
findings.fix: Add one clause to p2 after the reflection: "To add a point to itself, the line becomes the tangent at that point; doubling again and again (2P, 4P, 8P, …) reaches k·P in about as many steps as k has bits, the trick repeated squaring plays in Section 04."

findings.quote: To add two points on the curve, draw the line through them, find where it meets the curve
findings.problem: The caption repeats p2's point-addition procedure almost word for word. Two strip items also repeat the prose: 'A real group' repeats p2 (associative, point at infinity as zero) and p4 (finite field), and 'In use' repeats p4's curve list.
findings.fix: Caption: "P + Q on y² = x³ − 3x + 5: the line through P and Q, its third meeting point, and that point's reflection. Repeating the addition k times is fast; recovering k from the result is the elliptic-curve discrete log ECC rests on." Keep only the strip's "The numbers" item, plus "a 256-bit key gives about 128 bits of security" if it is wanted there rather than in p1.

findings.quote: At GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson found public-key cryptography between 1969 and 1974
findings.problem: The Fig 14.1 strip item 'First, in secret' tells the same story as the insight strip ch14-history-p6 (same three names, same years, classified until 1997). It also uses 'GCHQ' before p6 explains it as Britain's signals-intelligence agency.
findings.fix: Cut the strip item "First, in secret." The insight strip p6 carries the story.

findings.quote: The episode is a recurring lesson about classified research: discoveries kept secret are functionally non-discoveries.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer that states the moral the previous sentence already showed (a footnote for the hidden inventors, the Turing Award for the public ones).
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The strip ends on "...the public inventors got the Turing Award (Diffie and Hellman, 2015) and patents."

findings.quote: The previous sections took the primitives one at a time. A real protocol composes them.
findings.problem: Two clipped sentences that only fill space as a transition, then an announcement that ends in a reflexive triplet ('which operations happen, which keys derive from which, which security property each piece contributes'). The figure and strip deliver those three things right after.
findings.fix: "TLS 1.3, sketched in Chapter 11, Section 05, uses these primitives in one fixed sequence, and with the math in hand its handshake can now be read at full depth (Fig 14.11)."

findings.quote: A function f(x) = y is one-way if computing y from x is fast
findings.problem: The section defines a one-way function twice: in p1 ('easy to run forward and infeasible to run backward') and again here. It also gives 'infeasible' three different yardsticks: the age of the universe (p3), longer than civilization is likely to last (p4), and the heat death of the universe (p6). Chapter 11 §04 already taught one-way functions with the same 61 × 53 example and the same 'age of the universe' phrase (Fig 11.8), but the primer presents the idea as new.
findings.fix: In p1, make the definition a recall: "...is built on a different **one-way function**, the easy-forward, hard-backward asymmetry Chapter 11 showed with 61 × 53 (Fig 11.8)." In p3, delete "(longer than the age of the universe, with every algorithm currently known)", since p4 defines "hard".

findings.quote: The hour after 11 o'clock is not 12; it is 0.
findings.problem: On every clock the reader has seen, the hour after 11 is 12. The sentence states something the reader knows to be false, as a 'not X; Y' reveal, before the convention (0 at the top) has been explained.
findings.fix: "Nine hours after 5 o'clock is 2, not 14: the count wraps around at 12. Arithmetic modulo 12 writes the top of the clock as 0, so every result lies between 0 and 11." The §4w punch-list callback to Ch2's wheel can share this sentence.

findings.quote: Most mathematical operations are symmetric: addition has subtraction, multiplication has division
findings.problem: 'Symmetric' already has a set meaning in this chapter: one shared key (ch14-history-p2 italicises it, and Section 03 is titled 'Symmetric encryption'). Here it means 'as easy to undo as to do', so the same word names two different ideas within a few screens.
findings.fix: "Most mathematical operations undo as easily as they run: addition has subtraction, multiplication has division, squaring has square root."

findings.quote: was unbreakable for three hundred years. Then Charles Babbage broke it in 1854
findings.problem: A cipher that was broken was not unbreakable. The word says the opposite of what the sentence means (unbroken, or thought unbreakable).
findings.fix: "...was thought unbreakable for three hundred years, until Charles Babbage broke it in 1854 and Friedrich Kasiski published the method in 1863."

findings.quote: Modern Chrome and Safari refuse to trust certificates that are not in at least two CT logs.
findings.problem: Browser enforcement is stated three times: in p4's opening parenthesis ('mandatory in Chrome since 2018'), in this sentence, and in the strip ('Since 2018 Chrome trusts a new certificate only if public logs hold it'). The strip also repeats p4's domain-owner monitoring. The strip item 'The log' explains the Merkle tree a third time (after ch14-hashing-p4 and p4's recall).
findings.fix: Change the parenthesis to "(RFC 6962, 2013)" and keep this last sentence. In the strip, end "Why it exists" at "...Gmail users in Iran." Reduce "The log" to "A proof for one certificate is its sibling at every level: log₂ N hashes."

findings.quote: Only the private key could have made a signature that verifies.
findings.problem: How a signature works is explained three times in a row: p3 ('a value only the holder of the private key could have produced'), the caption's first sentence, and the strip item 'Signing'.
findings.fix: Cut the strip item "Signing". The caption names the top half of the picture and p3 teaches it.

findings.quote: so NIST's 2024 standards replace them: ML-KEM for key exchange, ML-DSA for signatures
findings.problem: The caption repeats p7's list of replacements. The Fig 14.2 strip item 'After Shor' already gave the same list in Section 01.5, naming ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA four sections before they are explained.
findings.fix: Caption: "What survives Shor, and its price: an ML-KEM key share is 37 times larger than X25519's, an ML-DSA signature more than 50 times larger than Ed25519's. Browsers already pair X25519 with ML-KEM." Cut the Fig 14.2 strip item "After Shor".

findings.quote: an elliptic-curve key of 256 bits provides security roughly equivalent to an RSA key of 3072 bits
findings.problem: 256 bits against 3072 appears in the Fig 14.2 strip, here, in the Fig 14.9 strip, and in the Fig 14.10 caption. The Fig 14.10 strip 'Why RSA grows faster' repeats primer-p6's sub-exponential explanation.
findings.fix: p1: "The payoff is much smaller keys for the same security (Fig 14.10), so a TLS server using ...". Cut "a 256-bit elliptic-curve key matches 3072-bit RSA" from the Fig 14.2 strip and "a 256-bit key gives about 128 bits of security" from the Fig 14.9 strip. Shorten the Fig 14.10 strip's second item to a recall: "The attack on RSA is sub-exponential (the primer's callout); the best on a good curve is a generic square-root search, so twice the bits suffice."

findings.quote: The reason d undoes e is one line of algebra resting on one eighteenth-century theorem.
findings.problem: Two paragraphs in the same section open with the same shape: p2 'The reason the two parties land on the same secret is one line of algebra'. p7 also ends with 'The card below', the only place the book calls a figure a card.
findings.fix: "Why _d_ undoes _e_ rests on one eighteenth-century theorem, Euler's." End with "Fig 14.8 runs the whole protocol in honest small numbers."

findings.quote: Each step closes the gap the one before it left open.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer that sums up the caption's first sentence.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.quote: The hard problem underneath is the same discrete log; each was hardened against a different thing.
findings.problem: A summing-up closer. The two sentences before it already say what each curve was hardened against.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The paragraph ends on "...which keeps the key from leaking through timing."

findings.quote: Every cryptographic primitive in this chapter rests on a computational asymmetry
findings.problem: ch14-primer-p1 says every primitive except AES rests on a one-way function. Fig 14.13 keeps AES and SHA-256 after Shor, and the Fig 14.1 strip calls the one-time pad provably unbreakable. So 'every' and 'each generation's hard eventually becomes easy' overclaim against the chapter's own facts.
findings.fix: "Every public-key primitive in this chapter rests on a computational asymmetry that was, at the time of design, believed hard to reverse."

findings.quote: Password storage · plaintext to hash to salted hash to slow KDF
findings.problem: 'KDF' appears only in this figure title. It is never expanded anywhere in the book. The prose and caption say 'slow, memory-hard function'.
findings.fix: Title: "Fig 14.4 · Password storage · plaintext to hash to salted hash to slow hash" (or expand it once: "slow key-derivation function").

findings.quote: row by row, 64 MB of memory per guess
findings.problem: The drawn label says MB, while the figure's description and its strip say MiB ('64 MiB', 'OWASP's minimum is 19 MiB').
findings.fix: Label: "row by row, 64 MiB of memory per guess".

findings.quote: hashing would only lose half its bits of strength
findings.problem: 'Bits of strength' (here) and '128-bit security' (Fig 14.3 strip) are used in Sections 01.5 and 02. The chapter only says what they mean in Section 05, in the Fig 14.10 strip ('the bits of work an attacker must spend').
findings.fix: Caption: "...a quantum search would only halve the exponent of the work to invert a hash (2²⁵⁶ becomes 2¹²⁸)." In the Fig 14.3 strip: "...so a 256-bit hash costs about 2¹²⁸ work to collide, the level called 128-bit security."

findings.quote: or the group is an elliptic curve (X25519 in TLS 1.3)
findings.problem: 'Group' is used here as if known. The chapter defines it a section later (ch14-ecc-p2).
findings.fix: "Real sizes. p has 2048 bits or more, or the arithmetic runs on an elliptic curve instead (Section 05; X25519 in TLS 1.3)."

findings.quote: used for weeks to intercept (MITM) Gmail users in Iran
findings.problem: MITM is bolded as a term but never expanded in this chapter. 'Man-in-the-middle' is first explained in Chapter 15.
findings.fix: "...used for weeks to intercept Gmail users in Iran (a man-in-the-middle attack, **MITM**, Chapter 15)."

findings.quote: that ordinary people are entitled to strong cryptography (the cypherpunk movement)
findings.problem: The parenthesis hangs off the sentence. It names a movement the book never explains, and it is unclear whether it glosses the position or Zimmermann.
findings.fix: "...descend, ideologically, from the position Zimmermann and the 1990s cypherpunks argued for: that ordinary people are entitled to strong cryptography."

findings.quote: The 1976 Diffie–Hellman paper described a protocol for two parties who have never met to agree on a shared secret
findings.problem: This repeats ch14-history-p2 ('a way for two strangers to agree on a shared secret over a public channel that any eavesdropper could see') and the section title just above it.
findings.fix: "Diffie and Hellman's protocol rests on a single mathematical asymmetry: ..."

findings.quote: Ten rounds, for a 128-bit key, make every output bit depend on every input and key bit.
findings.problem: This restates p2's confusion and diffusion definitions and its round count. The strip item 'What each step adds' then assigns confusion and diffusion to the steps.
findings.fix: Delete the caption's second sentence.

findings.quote: each output bit depends complicatedly on the key
findings.problem: 'Complicatedly' is an awkward coinage that tells the reader nothing about what kind of dependence is meant.
findings.fix: "(each output bit depends on the key in a tangled, non-linear way)"

findings.quote: These are assumptions: nobody has proven that any one-way function exists; these are believed hard
findings.problem: Repeats p4 ('a contingent claim, not a mathematical one') and p8 ('nobody can prove it yet'). The repeated 'these are ... these are' makes the sentence clumsy. In the same strip, the RSA-896 record repeats the Fig 11.8 strip.
findings.fix: Cut the item "Not proven". In "The sizes", replace the record parenthesis with "(Fig 11.8)".

findings.quote: Hash functions are everywhere.
findings.problem: An opener that announces the list instead of starting it.
findings.fix: Delete it, so the paragraph opens with "*Password storage*: never store the password itself; ...".

findings.quote: Chapter 14 has unpacked the math under the rest of the book's security claims.
findings.problem: The closing paragraph repeats the chapter as a list (TLS, password storage, Bitcoin, Signal, CT). Signal's ratchet appears here for the first time, in the summary. The paragraph's real job is the threat-model hand-off to Chapter 15. If the owner wants a Ch14 consolidation coda (§4w finding 3), this is where it would go, so treat this as an owner call.
findings.fix: If no coda is wanted: "Every layer of cryptography in this chapter is a precise mathematical claim, and every claim has a precise **threat model**: the kind of adversary it withstands and the kind that breaks it." Then p11 follows.

findings.quote: FireEye discovered it after spotting unusual traffic on its own network in December 2020.
findings.problem: Unusual traffic is not how FireEye found the breach. Kevin Mandia (Aspen Institute, January 2021) and FireEye's CTO Charles Carmakal both said the first sign was an alert that a second phone had been enrolled in an employee's two-factor login. When staff called the employee, he said he had not registered it. The investigation that started there led to SUNBURST.
findings.fix: "FireEye found it in December 2020, after an alert that a new phone had been enrolled in one employee's two-factor login." Source: Dark Reading, "FireEye's Mandia: 'Severity-Zero Alert' Led to Discovery of SolarWinds Attack" (darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/fireeyes-mandia-severity-zero-alert-led-to-discovery-of-solarwinds-attack).

findings.quote: the BGP and DNS vulnerabilities they had in mind were real
findings.problem: No source puts DNS in the L0pht's 30-minute claim. The Washington Post (Timberg, 'A disaster foretold', 22 June 2015) says the takedown was 'by exploiting flaws in a key Internet routing protocol called BGP'. Space Rogue's own later account names only a BGP flaw that cascaded through routers. DNS seems to come from Mudge's much later remark that BGP was 'at least as big an issue as the DNS issue', which is a comparison with Kaminsky's 2008 bug.
findings.fix: "They were not joking: the BGP flaw they had in mind was real, and the testimony was carried verbatim into the Senate's published hearing record." Sources: Washington Post, Net of Insecurity part 3 (2015); Cris Thomas interview, lieu.house.gov/media-center/in-the-news/i-spoke-hacker-who-could-have-taken-down-internet-30-minutes.

findings.quote: It was the first time the American government heard, on the record,
findings.problem: Overclaims 'first'. On 26 September 1983 Neal Patrick of the 414s testified to a House committee on how easily he had broken into Los Alamos and Sloan-Kettering systems. That is a hacker telling Congress on the record how attackers see systems. The Washington Post calls the L0pht testimony 'among the most audacious of a rising chorus of warnings delivered in the 1990s', not the first.
findings.fix: "It was the starkest warning the American government had yet heard, on the record, that adversaries thought about computer systems differently ..." (the rest unchanged). Sources: Wikipedia 'The 414s' (House testimony, 26 Sept 1983); Washington Post 2015 (as above).

findings.quote: reroutes entire IP prefixes through a malicious autonomous system
findings.problem: The example given here contradicts the book's own Chapter 9. Fig 9.11 and its caption say Pakistan Telecom's /24 was 'meant to block YouTube at home but leaked worldwide by its upstream PCCW', and that the traffic was dropped, not relayed. Citing it as rerouting 'through a malicious autonomous system' makes it sound like a deliberate interception. The next sentence ('all your packets may now arrive at the attacker's machines') reinforces that.
findings.fix: "*BGP hijacking* (Chapter 9, Section 06; Pakistan/YouTube 2008, an accidental leak) sends entire IP prefixes to the wrong autonomous system, and a deliberate hijacker can receive the traffic. Same defence: ..."

findings.quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
findings.problem: The caption (ch15-network-p5) brings back the 'first answer wins' mechanism that §4g corrected. The ledger fixed fig 15.4 and ch15-network-p4 to 'keeps answering', because RFC 826 overwrites a cache entry with each later claim. The drawing now says 'the cache keeps the freshest claim', while its caption still says the attacker wins by answering faster.
findings.fix: Caption: "The attacker on the same LAN keeps answering ARP queries with its own MAC address, so the laptop's cache always holds the forged entry and every packet is redirected through the attacker's machine." Source: RFC 826 (merge flag updates existing entries); UNDER.md §4g Part IV fig 15.4 entry.

findings.quote: AWS now mandates IMDSv2
findings.problem: Overclaim, both in the caption and in the drawn line 'mandatory on new instances'. AWS's November 2023 announcement made only instance types released from mid-2024 IMDSv2-only by default, and IMDSv1 can still be turned back on. Older instance types still launch with v1 unless the account blocks it with the account-level setting. Amazon Linux 2023 disables v1 by default. 'Default' is accurate. 'Mandates' is not.
findings.fix: Caption: "at the cloud platform, AWS now defaults to IMDSv2, a session-token-based metadata service ...". Drawn line: "(the default on new instance types)". Source: AWS News Blog, 'Amazon EC2 Instance Metadata Service IMDSv2 by default' (Nov 2023); AWS EC2 User Guide, 'Transition to using IMDSv2'.

findings.quote: Stuxnet infected ~100K machines but did damage on perhaps a hundred.
findings.problem: No source supports 'perhaps a hundred', and it is probably off by an order of magnitude. The damage happened at one site, Natanz. ISIS (Albright, Brannan, Walrond, 22 Dec 2010) estimates that about 1,000 of roughly 9,000 IR-1 centrifuges were destroyed and replaced. A reader will take 'machines damaged' as about a hundred.
findings.fix: "Stuxnet infected ~100K computers but did damage at one site: about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz." Source: isis-online.org, 'Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant?' (2010).

findings.quote: intrusion detection system (IDS, early 2000s) answered that
findings.problem: Intrusion detection is older than this date suggests. Denning's model is from 1987, and commercial network IDS shipped in 1996–98 (ISS RealSecure, Snort in December 1998). By June 2003 Gartner was already calling IDS 'dead'. Zero trust's 'late 2010s' is also late: Kindervag coined the term at Forrester in 2010, and BeyondCorp was described in 2014, as the figure's own strip says. Fig 15.7 carries the same two labels.
findings.fix: Prose: "(IDS, late 1990s)" and "*Zero-trust architecture* (2010s)". Fig 15.7: "late 1990s: inspect what got in" and "2010s: trust no position". Sources: Denning, IEEE TSE 1987; Snort 1.0 release (1998); Kindervag, Forrester 'No More Chewy Centers' (2010).

findings.quote: for vulnerabilities reported through these channels
findings.problem: The sentence says Apple, Google and Microsoft pay through HackerOne, Bugcrowd and YesWeHack. All three run their own programs: Apple Security Bounty (security.apple.com), Google VRP (bughunters.google.com) and the Microsoft Bounty Program (MSRC). The platforms serve many other companies.
findings.fix: "*HackerOne*, *Bugcrowd*, *YesWeHack* are the major platforms, and Apple, Google and Microsoft run programs of their own; between them they pay independent researchers (from about $1K to $1M or more per finding, depending on severity)."

findings.quote: now the laptop sends every packet destined for the gateway to the attacker instead
findings.problem: Poisoning only the laptop's cache gives the attacker one direction. The gateway still sends its replies straight to the laptop. A full man in the middle (arpspoof, ettercap) also tells the gateway that the laptop's IP is at the attacker's MAC. As written, a reader will think one forged answer makes the attacker see both sides of the conversation.
findings.fix: After "...to the attacker instead." add: "It tells the gateway the same lie about the laptop, so the replies come through it too."

findings.quote: Properly configured, TLS authenticates endpoints and encrypts traffic
findings.problem: On the web, TLS normally authenticates only the server. Client certificates are rare, and the very next paragraph says only that the client checks the server's certificate. Read literally, the plural 'endpoints' says both sides are authenticated.
findings.fix: "Properly configured, TLS authenticates the server and encrypts traffic so that whatever the network does to a TLS-wrapped flow is detected, ..."

findings.quote: Stuxnet was deployed around 2009
findings.problem: In 2013 Symantec found an earlier version, Stuxnet 0.5, that was in the wild by November 2007. It attacked the UF6 feed valves through S7-417 PLCs. The 2009 date fits only the centrifuge-speed versions this paragraph describes, so as written it hides two years of operation.
findings.fix: "Stuxnet was deployed in 2009–2010 (an earlier version, closing gas valves instead, was in the wild by 2007), discovered in mid-2010 ..." Source: Symantec, 'Stuxnet 0.5: The Missing Link' (McDonald, O Murchu, Doherty, Chien, 2013); SecurityWeek coverage.

findings.quote: for that call site when it built the program for that call site
findings.problem: A phrase is duplicated: 'for that call site' appears twice in one clause. This is not a fact error, but it is a slip a reader will stop on.
findings.fix: "the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program."

findings.quote: private (235, 391)
findings.problem: The red elements never dim: their 'not yet' state has opacity 1. So at t=4 s the private box, the decrypt arrow '143²³⁵ mod 391' and 'anyone can lock with e / only d unlocks' are at full strength, while the public box, the 65 box, the encrypt arrow and the 143 box are still dim. The frame shows the unlock lit before the lock and before its own input, 143, exists.
findings.fix: Give the private box, the 143²³⁵ arrow and the two bottom labels a real dim state, like the green ones (or a neutral rgba(230,217,189,0.6) that still passes contrast). Then light them at their own times (0.37, 0.60, 0.67), so the reader sees keys, then lock, then unlock.

findings.quote: one run: 23 shares a day with 5
findings.problem: Several people land one to four days from someone already on the strip: persons 3 and 12 (x 337.0 and 338.0), 9, 13 and 20 (121.4, 120.4, 118.4), 17 and 22, 11 and 14, 8 and 21. At 375 px a day is under 1 CSS px and a mark is 2.7 px wide, so these pairs fuse into thick double marks. They look exactly like shared birthdays. When person 12 arrives, the reader sees an apparent match that the figure ignores, and the end frame shows five 'doubles' beside the one real match.
findings.fix: Hand-pick or re-seed the 22 non-matching days so no two are within 4 days (4 SVG units, about 3.5 CSS px). Keep person 23 on person 5's day (x 222.2), so the salmon mark is the only coincidence visible.

findings.quote: Every primitive in this chapter rests on a function that is quick one way and infeasible the other
findings.problem: Three paragraphs earlier, ch14-primer-p1 says 'Every primitive in this chapter except AES' is built on a one-way function. The caption drops the exception, and AES is the subject of Section 03, so a careful reader stops at the clash.
findings.fix: Open the caption with: 'Hashing and public-key cryptography rest on a function that is quick one way and infeasible the other: hashing (SHA-256), modular powers (Diffie–Hellman), multiplying primes, multiplying a point on an elliptic curve.'

findings.quote: Adding a point to itself k times is fast
findings.problem: Taken literally this is false: adding a point to itself k times, for a 256-bit k, takes about 2²⁵⁶ additions. The speed comes from doubling (P, 2P, 4P, …), and doubling needs the tangent line, which neither the figure nor the section ever gives. The caption's first sentence also restates ch14-ecc-p2 almost word for word, so the caption spends its words on a repeat and skips the step the reader lacks.
findings.fix: Replace the caption with: 'Adding a point to itself uses the tangent there, and doubling again and again (P, 2P, 4P, …) reaches k·P in about as many steps as k has bits, as repeated squaring does for powers. Recovering k from the result is the elliptic-curve discrete log, the trapdoor ECC rests on.'

findings.quote: server signs the transcript, encrypted
findings.problem: This red line never dims (its dim state has opacity 1). So at t=4 s it shows as done while the 'HKDF → handshake keys' box above it, whose keys encrypt the signature, is still dim. The chain reads out of order.
findings.fix: Give the line a dim state until 0.50 (after the handshake-keys box lights at 0.43), the same way the boxes have one.

findings.quote: AddRoundKey
findings.problem: The AddRoundKey pill's dim state has opacity 1, so it is lit through the whole round. During the SubBytes and MixColumns frames it looks as active or done as the current step, though AddRoundKey runs last (0.79). The other three pills light up in step order.
findings.fix: Dim the AddRoundKey pill until 0.79, like SubBytes, ShiftRows and MixColumns (use a neutral, contrast-safe dim tone if the red fails contrast at lower opacity).

findings.quote: Eve needs x: 5ˣ mod 23 = 8
findings.problem: Both red Eve lines have dim opacity 1, so 'Eve needs x' is at full strength from the first frame. It sits there before the shared key 2 is computed, which is the point it comments on, while every other row reveals in order.
findings.fix: Dim 'Eve sees 8 and 19' until 0.33 and 'Eve needs x: 5ˣ mod 23 = 8' until 0.63, the times they already light at.

findings.quote: ↑ to scale: 1976 to now is the last 3%
findings.problem: 1976 to 2026 is 50 of about 2,076 years, which is 2.4%, not 3%. Even the green band to 2030 is 2.6%. How it works says 'under its last 3%', which is right; the drawn note is not.
findings.fix: Draw '↑ to scale: 1976 to now is under the last 3%' (or 'the last 2.5%').

findings.quote: row by row, 64 MB of memory per guess
findings.problem: The picture says MB. The figure's description says 64 MiB, How it works gives OWASP's 19 MiB, and the argon2id setting really is 65,536 KiB = 64 MiB. A careful reader sees two different units for one setting.
findings.fix: Draw 'row by row, 64 MiB of memory per guess' (the generator scripts/figs/fig_14_4.py already says MiB).

findings.quote: plaintext to hash to salted hash to slow KDF
findings.problem: The figure label uses 'KDF', which is never expanded in the chapter, the figure or the glossary. The picture's own tab just says 'slow'.
findings.fix: Label: 'Fig 14.4 · Password storage · plaintext to hash to salted hash to slow hash'.

findings.quote: 256 bits against 3,072 at the 128-bit level the web uses today
findings.problem: 'today' is drawn only on the 128 row (RSA 3,072). Fig 14.8's How it works and caption give 2048 bits as RSA's real size, and that is the untagged 112 row here. So the reader cannot tell whether the RSA-2048 the chapter calls real is below today's level.
findings.fix: Tag the 112 row 'most RSA in use' and the 128 row 'the target'. In the caption write 'at the 128-bit level new systems aim for'.

findings.quote: makes the keys of Bitcoin and TLS
findings.problem: The hero draws y² = x³ + 7, which is secp256k1, Bitcoin's curve. ch14-ecc-p4 says TLS 1.3 uses Curve25519, a different curve. Pairing this equation with 'TLS' contradicts the chapter.
findings.fix: Tagline second line: 'makes Bitcoin's keys, and on a sister curve, TLS's'.

findings.quote: y² = x³ + 7
findings.problem: The curve path is sampled at even y steps. Across the near-flat stretch around x = 0 it jumps 59 units in one straight chord ('L202.1 183.6 L261.3 181.5', mirrored on the lower branch). At 1440 px this shows as a visible corner and a flat shelf at x ≈ −0.76 on both branches, on a curve the chapter calls smooth.
findings.fix: Regenerate the path sampled by x (or by arc length), for example every 2 SVG units in x across −1.9 to 3.2, so the bend near x = −0.8 is drawn as a curve.

findings.quote: The stricter term comes from Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper Wait-Free Synchronization, which proved a hierarchy of exactly which
findings.problem: The paragraph credits Herlihy's 1991 paper with the origin of the term 'wait-free'. The term was already in print before that paper. Herlihy's own references include R. Newman-Wolfe, 'A protocol for wait-free, atomic, multi-reader shared variables' (PODC 1987). The 1991 TOPLAS paper is the journal version of Herlihy's 1988 PODC paper, and its introduction (p. 125) speaks of 'most recent work on wait-free synchronization'. So Herlihy did not coin the term. He made the idea precise and built the consensus hierarchy on it. 'Exactly which' also claims too much: the paper proves that an object cannot be built wait-free from objects on lower levels, and that some objects are universal. It does not settle every pair of objects. The §4r ledger row (Pass 18) checked only that the paper uses 'wait-free' (75 times) and never 'lock-free'. It did not check where the term started, so this finding does not reopen anything the ledger settled.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper _Wait-Free Synchronization_ (first presented in 1988) made the stricter notion precise and proved a hierarchy of which atomic primitives can build which data structures wait-free, turning an engineering practice into a mathematical theory." Source: Herlihy, ACM TOPLAS 13(1), Jan 1991, pp. 124–126 (footnote on the PODC Aug 1988 preliminary version; reference [23], Newman-Wolfe, PODC 1987), cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf

findings.quote: A frame that must render in 16 ms, or one fixed compile, is Amdahl.
findings.problem: Both p7 and this figure define Gustafson as the case where the time is fixed, and p7 gives 'more pixels in a rendering' as its example. A frame with a fixed 16 ms budget is the textbook case of fixed time: real-time graphics spends extra cores on more pixels and effects inside the same 16 ms, which is Gustafson. A careful reader sees the fixed time limit filed under Amdahl, contradicting the definition in the line above, and stops.
findings.fix: "One fixed compile, or one query that must answer sooner, is Amdahl." (keep the Gustafson sentence that follows as it is)

findings.quote: Six patients received radiation overdoses of up to a hundred times the prescribed dose; three died.
findings.problem: 'Up to' makes a hundred times sound like the maximum, but the documented estimates go higher. At Tyler (first accident) the prescription was 180 rads and later simulations gave 16,500 to 25,000 rads, about 90 to 140 times. At Yakima the estimate was 8,000 to 10,000 rads against 86 prescribed, about 95 to 115 times. At Kennestone it was 15,000 to 20,000 rads against a typical 200. 'Roughly a hundred times' is the accurate summary.
findings.fix: "Six patients received radiation overdoses of roughly a hundred times the prescribed dose; three died." Source: Leveson and Turner, 'An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents', IEEE Computer 26(7), 1993, pp. 23, 27–28

findings.quote: // the race: counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run
findings.problem: This does not dispute the §4g range ('well short of two million'). It points out the condition the demo needs. With optimisation on, the compiler is allowed to assume no data race, so it folds each worker's loop into one add. I checked: clang -O1 and -O2 on x86-64 emit `addl $1000000, _counter(%rip)`, and on arm64 one ldr, add #1000000, str. Two threads then usually print exactly 2,000,000. On x86, even `++counter` on its own at -O1 compiles to one non-atomic `add [mem], 1`, not three instructions. A reader who builds the snippet with normal flags will not see the bug the comment promises.
findings.fix: Change the two comments to: "// the race (built without optimisation): counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run" and "++counter;   // three steps: LOAD; ADD; STORE"

findings.quote: browsers put each site in its own process for safety
findings.problem: Only Chrome (desktop; on Android only for some sites) and Firefox (Fission) put each site in its own process. Safari/WebKit site isolation was still being built through early 2026 and shares processes across sites in some modes. Saying 'browsers' in general is too broad.
findings.fix: "... and Chrome and Firefox put each site in its own process for safety." Source: WebKit Bugzilla site-isolation tracking bugs (e.g. bugs.webkit.org 296260, 307816, 2025–26); Chromium Site Isolation docs

findings.quote: Compare-and-swap · the atomic primitive everything else is built on
findings.problem: The figure's own strip contradicts the title. On ARM before v8.1 (and on POWER and RISC-V), CAS is itself built from a load-exclusive/store-exclusive pair, so it is not the bottom layer. Atomic increments on x86 use `lock xadd`, not CAS. CAS is universal in theory (Herlihy), but saying everything 'is built on' it in practice claims too much.
findings.fix: "Fig 16.4 · Compare-and-swap · the atomic primitive lock-free code is built on" (or "most other atomics are built on")

findings.quote: the bug surfaces only on ARM or POWER
findings.problem: RISC-V's memory model (RVWMO) also allows stores to be reordered with each other, so the same relaxed test can fail there. Naming only ARM and POWER leaves the reader thinking those are the only weakly ordered CPUs.
findings.fix: "... and the bug surfaces only on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM, POWER or RISC-V; ..." Source: RISC-V Unprivileged ISA spec, ch. 'RVWMO Memory Consistency Model'

findings.quote: valid for that call site when it built the program for that call site
findings.problem: The phrase "for that call site" appears twice in one clause, so the sentence reads as an editing slip and the reader has to parse it twice.
findings.fix: "...the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program."

findings.quote: Two defences protect modern machines against ROP and its relatives today.
findings.problem: Ch3 §06 (ch3-defenses-p9) already taught CFI, the shadow stack (CET) and ARM Pointer Authentication. ch15-memory-p1 says Ch3 only went "from stack canaries through DEP and ASLR to ROP", and p3 to p4 then teach all three again as if they were new: CFI gets first-use bold, the shadow stack is defined again in p4 and PAC is introduced from scratch. A reader who has read Ch3 sees the same explanation twice. The naming also differs (Ch3 "Control Flow Integrity", Ch15 "Control-Flow Integrity"), and the glossary puts CFI's first use at ch15-memory.
findings.fix: p1: "...traced the arms race from stack canaries through DEP and ASLR to ROP, and named the answers to ROP: CFI, shadow stacks and Pointer Authentication." p3: open with "Those answers now ship by default." and keep only what is new (Abadi 2005, which compilers ship it, indirect calls via function pointers and vtables, the cost). p4: keep PAC's new detail (per-process key, stack pointer as context, A12 2018) and cut the parenthetical that defines the shadow stack again. Spell the name one way in both chapters ("Control-Flow Integrity") and point the glossary's CFI first use at ch3-defenses.

findings.quote: reroutes entire IP prefixes through a malicious autonomous system
findings.problem: The example given is Pakistan/YouTube 2008, but Ch9 §06 (which this sentence cites) describes it as an announcement meant to block YouTube inside Pakistan that leaked worldwide, with the traffic dropped. That was neither malicious nor an attacker's machine trying a TLS handshake. A reader who remembers Ch9 meets a contradiction.
findings.fix: "*BGP hijacking* (Chapter 9, Section 06) reroutes entire IP prefixes to another autonomous system; Pakistan Telecom's 2008 leak of YouTube's prefix did it by accident, and a hijacker does it on purpose."

findings.quote: Parameterised queries are necessary but not sufficient
findings.problem: Ch13 §06 calls parameterised queries "clean and absolute" under the heading "The fix · parameterised queries · and only that", and this section's own strip says "Layer 2 is the real fix". Calling them "not sufficient" contradicts both, and the reader has to work out which is true. The intended point is that a single hand-built query reopens the hole.
findings.fix: "Parameterised queries are the cure wherever they are used, but one hand-built query reopens the hole, so the discipline is *defence in depth*: assume every other layer might be bypassed and design each layer as if it were the last one."

findings.quote: by reprogramming the PLCs that set the centrifuges' spin speed
findings.problem: PLC is used in p3, and again in Fig 15.8 and its caption, but is only defined two paragraphs later in p5. There the definition sits inside a nested parenthetical with stacked appositives ("built around PLCs, programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves"), a sentence the reader has to read twice. PLC is not in the glossary.
findings.fix: p3: "by reprogramming the PLCs (programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves) that set the centrifuges' spin speed". p5: "Industrial control systems (the computers that run factories, pipelines and power plants, built around PLCs) had been treated as low-priority..." Net zero.

findings.quote: the vendor gets 90 days to ship a fix; details follow 30 days after the fix, or at day 90
findings.problem: The 90+30 rule appears three times in a row: in p3 ("typically 90 days... 30 days after a fix, or at the deadline if there is none"), in this caption, and in the strip bullet "90+30". The strip's "Why it holds" repeats p3's last sentence (only reputation enforces it, and the alternative is worse for everyone). The caption's first sentence also restates p4 to p5 (learn on CTFs, work red, blue or bounty, meet at conferences).
findings.fix: Caption: "The field in three rings, held together by the disclosure clock: the bug fixed on day 75 is published on day 105, the one never fixed on day 90." p3: "...30 days after a fix, so users have time to update, or at the deadline if there is none." Strip: cut "Why it holds" and shorten the first bullet to "*Similar windows.* Other research teams use clocks of the same shape."

findings.quote: Security knowledge is not produced by individuals reading textbooks. It is produced by an ecosystem
findings.problem: This is the "Not X. Y." reveal the brief bans, and it reads oddly inside a textbook.
findings.fix: "Security knowledge comes from an ecosystem of people who break things, for sport and for pay, report what they break, and fix what others have broken."

findings.quote: Python's pickle attack surface, .NET's BinaryFormatter (deprecated 2020 but still in use)
findings.problem: "attack surface" carries the key-term mark here (the glossary's first-use site) but is never explained, and its glossary definition leans on Stuxnet and SolarWinds, which come later. The list is also uneven (a library, an "attack surface", a class), and its first item carries a relative clause plus a parenthetical, so the sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: "Every popular language has one: Java's Apache Commons Collections, whose ordinary classes can be chained into a payload that runs commands (the gadget idea of ROP); Python's pickle; .NET's BinaryFormatter, deprecated in 2020 but still in use." Move the key term to ch15-defense-p5: "Code-signing certificates are part of the *attack surface* (every place an attacker can reach into a system)...", then run npm run build:glossary.

findings.quote: the supply-chain equivalent of Certificate Transparency from Chapter 14
findings.problem: The comparison is asserted but never mapped. Nothing says what about SBOMs, reproducible builds or SLSA/sigstore resembles CT's public append-only log, and all four names arrive with no explanation.
findings.fix: "The 2020s response borrows Certificate Transparency's idea from Chapter 14, a public record anyone can check: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) list every component a product ships, reproducible builds let anyone rebuild the source and compare the bytes, and signed build provenance (SLSA, sigstore, which keeps a public log) records what went into each build."

findings.quote: Every network-layer attack on what you read or send ends in TLS and is neutralised there
findings.problem: This closing sentence says for the third time what p1 ("whatever the network does to a TLS-wrapped flow is detected") and p2 ("can deny service... but not impersonate") already said. "Only denial of service gets through" also sits uneasily beside Fig 15.3, where timing and who-talks-to-whom also get through.
findings.fix: End p6 at "...cannot complete a TLS handshake for the target's hostname." and cut the final sentence.

findings.quote: an attacker who finds a vulnerability tells the affected vendor
findings.problem: Wrong word. The person following responsible disclosure is a researcher, as the Fig 15.10 caption and the glossary ("whoever finds a vulnerability") put it. Calling them an "attacker" muddles the red/blue framing the section builds.
findings.fix: "the convention that a researcher who finds a vulnerability tells the affected vendor"

findings.quote: Spectre and Meltdown in Chapter 1. Buffer overflows in Chapter 3. Dirty COW in Chapter 4.
findings.problem: The chapter's opening lead runs five clipped dramatic fragments in a row. p8 at the end of the chapter repeats the same fragment shape.
findings.fix: "Attacks have run through this whole book: Spectre and Meltdown in Chapter 1, buffer overflows in Chapter 3, Dirty COW in Chapter 4, BGP hijacking in Chapter 9, SYN floods in Chapter 10, then DNS poisoning, XSS, CSRF, SQL injection and TLS misissuance."

findings.quote: Multi-core hardware (Chapter 16). The cloud and its distributed-systems mathematics (Chapter 17).
findings.problem: The seam into Part V is written as clipped fragments, the same shape as the chapter's opening lead.
findings.fix: "Part V, the last part of the book, is about where systems live _now_: multi-core hardware in Chapter 16, the cloud and its distributed-systems mathematics in Chapter 17, and, in the epilogue (Chapter 18), what you now see, after all this, when you press a key and the bytes flow."

findings.quote: the attack and defence landscape that gets in the way
findings.problem: Wrong phrase. It is unclear what the landscape gets in the way of, and defences do not get in the way of the data they protect.
findings.fix: "...and ended by surveying the attacks on all of it and the defences against them (Chapter 15)."

findings.quote: ROP (Chapter 3) and Stuxnet (Section 05) show a further habit
findings.problem: Chaining is introduced as something outside the patterns, yet Fig 15.9 has six patterns with no chaining and no ROP, and p7 says the six "name every specific exploit in this book". A careful reader asks where ROP fits.
findings.fix: "ROP (Chapter 3) is data-as-code too, the attacker's addresses taken for return addresses, and with Stuxnet (Section 05) it shows a technique any pattern can use: chaining pieces the attacker did not write..." (a one-clause change; the six-pattern device stays whole).

findings.quote: 05 · Defence systems · the layered organism
findings.problem: The section label promises an organism analogy that the section never uses or explains. The word appears nowhere else in the book.
findings.fix: "05 · Defence systems · five layers, all running"

findings.quote: web (the SQLi / XSS / SSRF of this chapter)
findings.problem: XSS was taught in Chapter 12 and only mentioned in this chapter, and SQLi belongs to Chapter 13. The reference points to the wrong place.
findings.fix: "_web_ (SQLi and XSS from Chapters 13 and 12, SSRF from this chapter)"

findings.quote: organised in five canonical categories
findings.problem: "canonical" appears twice in this paragraph ("the canonical first stop") and twice earlier in the chapter ("the canonical network attack", "the canonical modern example"), so it reads as a verbal tic.
findings.fix: "CTFs are organised in five standard categories" and "*PicoCTF* ... is the usual first stop"

findings.quote: Each layer is built as if the ones above it had failed.
findings.problem: The caption repeats p2's "design each layer as if it were the last one". Under the brief, the prose keeps the point and the caption names the picture.
findings.fix: Cut the caption's last sentence, so the caption is the single first sentence.

findings.quote: They stack rather than replace one another.
findings.problem: This repeats p1's last sentence ("none is sufficient alone, so a mature organisation runs all five at once").
findings.fix: Cut the caption's second sentence.

findings.quote: XSS another (the browser parses it as HTML/JavaScript), server-side template injection a third
findings.problem: Three examples where one does the job. ch15-culture-p1 and Fig 15.9 restate the same data-as-code list (SQLi, XSS, template injection) two sections later.
findings.fix: "SQL injection is one form (the database parses your input as SQL). *Deserialisation* attacks are the most direct:..." (also drops the hedge "perhaps").

findings.quote: That difference is what this chapter is about.
findings.problem: An announcing sentence that teaches nothing. p1 ends on the difference, and the next sentence states it.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence and open p2 with "Software engineering teaches you to think about correctness..."

findings.quote: On a data-flow diagram, processes face all six
findings.problem: "data-flow diagram" is never explained. "processes" here means a diagram element, not the OS process the reader learned in Ch4, so it is easy to misread.
findings.fix: "On a data-flow diagram (a sketch of a design's parts and the data moving between them), the parts that run code face all six, while stores of data and the flows between parts mainly face tampering, disclosure and denial."

findings.quote: gets only the statements it needs on its own tables, never ownership or the right to drop them
findings.problem: The strip's "Least privilege in practice" bullet repeats Ch13 §06's defence-in-depth strip ("only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on its own tables"), which p2 says Ch13 already covered.
findings.fix: Cut the "Least privilege in practice" bullet.

findings.quote: So the attacker tells it, and keeps telling it.
findings.problem: An aphorism-style closer. The mechanism it hints at (re-sending so the cache keeps the latest claim, Fig 15.4 step 3) is never stated plainly.
findings.fix: "ARP has no authentication and no signature, so the protocol believes whatever it is told: the attacker keeps re-sending its claim, and the laptop's cache keeps the latest one."

findings.quote: Java's readObject methods, Python's __reduce__ hook
findings.problem: `deserialize()` in the same paragraph is set in code, but readObject and __reduce__ are body text. The double underscores in the serif body look like leftover markup.
findings.fix: Wrap both in : readObject, __reduce__.

findings.quote: Prompt injection · 2022 → ?.
findings.problem: A question mark followed by a full stop reads as a typo.
findings.fix: "Prompt injection · 2022 → ?" (drop the full stop) or "Prompt injection · 2022 onward."

findings.quote: CCC (Chaos Communication Congress, the European centre, late December in Hamburg, run by a hacker club
findings.problem: Wrong expansion: CCC is the Chaos Computer Club, which runs the Chaos Communication Congress. "run by a hacker club with a more political tone" also leaves unclear whether the club or the congress has the tone.
findings.fix: "the *Chaos Communication Congress* (late December in Hamburg, run by the Chaos Computer Club, CCC, and more political in tone)"

findings.quote: internal red-team operations against your own employer
findings.problem: The person shifts mid-sentence: "takes it into companies, where the job is to attack their systems" becomes "your own employer".
findings.fix: "...adversary emulation (copying a real attacker's methods), and internal red teams that attack their own employer."

findings.quote: a small community of malware researchers (notably Symantec and Ralph Langner)
findings.problem: Symantec is a company, not a researcher.
findings.fix: "(notably Symantec's team and Ralph Langner)"

findings.quote: the company's own digitally-signed updates
findings.problem: An -ly adverb takes no hyphen. Related inconsistency: p1 and Fig 15.7 write "mid 2000s" / "mid 2010s", while p3 writes "mid-2010".
findings.fix: "digitally signed updates". Write "mid-2000s", "mid-2010s" in p1 (and the Fig 15.7 labels) to match p3.

findings.quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
findings.problem: The caption says the attacker wins by answering faster. The figure's own step 3 says the cache keeps the freshest claim, so the last answer wins and the attacker wins by re-sending constantly. In real ARP a later reply overwrites the cache (most OSes even accept unsolicited replies), so "faster" teaches the wrong mechanism. Owner's figure: report only.
findings.fix: For the owner: "The attacker keeps sending forged ARP replies, and the laptop's cache keeps the latest one, so every packet for the gateway goes through the attacker." (RFC 826 cache update; the prose fix in ch15-network-p4 carries the right mechanism either way).

findings.quote: CFI / Clang CFI | 2015 · indirect-call check
findings.problem: The timeline's dates disagree with the prose beside it. CFI sits at 2015 while ch15-memory-p3 says Abadi proposed it in 2005 (2015 is Clang's ship year), and "PAC · CET shadow stack 2017+" disagrees with p4's A12 2018 and CET 2020.
findings.fix: For the owner: "CFI 2005 (Abadi) · Clang CFI 2015"; "PAC 2018 (Apple A12) · CET 2020 (11th-gen Core)", matching ch15-memory-p3/p4.

findings.quote: AWS now mandates IMDSv2
findings.problem: Overstated. AWS made IMDSv2-only the default for newly released instance types (from mid-2024) and added an account-level default, but IMDSv1 can still be enabled on many instances. The drawn label "(mandatory on new instances)" is closer.
findings.fix: For the owner: "AWS now defaults new instances to IMDSv2" (AWS announcement, Nov 2023: newly released EC2 instance types IMDSv2-only from mid-2024).

findings.quote: Stuxnet infected ~100K machines but did damage on perhaps a hundred.
findings.problem: "machines" is ambiguous (the infected computers were not damaged), and the usual estimate of physical damage is about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz, not about a hundred.
findings.fix: For the owner: "infected ~100K computers but damaged only Natanz's centrifuges, about 1,000 of them" (Albright, Brannan, Walrond, ISIS report, Dec 2010).

findings.quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
findings.problem: Fig 15.4's caption still says the attacker wins by answering faster. That is the 'first wins' error UNDER.md §4g already corrected in the figure and in ch15-network-p4 (RFC 826: the cache takes the later claim, so persistence wins, not speed). Step ③ of the figure says exactly that ('the attacker re-sends constantly; the cache keeps the freshest claim'), and its headline says 'whoever keeps answering wins'. So the caption contradicts its own picture and brings back an error the ledger marked as fixed.
findings.fix: Corrected claim for the owner: 'The attacker on the same LAN answers the laptop's ARP query with its own MAC and keeps re-sending that claim, so the laptop's cache, which keeps the latest answer, holds the forged entry and every packet for the gateway goes through the attacker's machine.' (RFC 826; matches §4g row 'first wins → keeps-answering').

findings.quote: every request checked
findings.problem: Each spoke ends in a bar at the ring that stops it. Two of those stops contradict the chapter. (1) 'side channel / timing leaks' stops at the inner ring, 'every request checked' (zero trust), but checking who sends a request does nothing about a timing leak; Fig 15.9 gives the side-channel fix as 'constant-time code · isolation'. (2) 'supply chain / poisoned update' also stops at 'every request checked', but ch15-defense-p6 teaches that SolarWinds' backdoor came through the vendor's own signed updates, which pass every such check. The Gate 2 reader read the picture as 'each attack stopped by a layer', so readers will take these pairings as claims.
findings.fix: Keep the five attacks (the intended message names them). Rename the inner ring 'isolation' so the side-channel bar matches Fig 15.9's fix. Move the supply-chain bar out to the 'detection' ring (r = 140 instead of 100), since ch15-defense-p6 has FireEye finding SUNBURST by what it saw on its own network.

findings.quote: On a data-flow diagram, processes face all six, while data stores and the flows between them
findings.problem: The 'Per element' bullet in How it works is the Pass 29 handover item that is still open: 'data-flow diagram', 'processes' and 'data stores' are never taught (law 4). Its rule also clashes with the picture. Read as a process, the image CDN should face all six questions. Read as a store or flow, it should face tampering, disclosure and denial. The picture marks disclosure 'not here' and spoofing and elevation 'applies', which fits neither reading.
