A security reader will also object to 'nothing secret' in the desc: a CDN holds a TLS key and viewer logs (Cloudbleed, 2017, was a CDN leak).
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: '*Per part.* Which questions apply depends on what the part holds and lets people do: a part whose contents are all public and that records no one's actions can drop disclosure and repudiation, as the image CDN does.' In the desc, change 'since there is nothing to deny and nothing secret' to 'since nothing it serves is secret and no one's actions pass through it'.

findings.quote: details follow 30 days after the fix, or at day 90 if there is none
findings.problem: The 90+30 rule appears three times in a row: in ch15-culture-p3 ('30 days after a fix, or at the deadline if there is none'), in this caption, and again in strip bullet 1 ('if it does, details follow 30 days after the fix'). The caption's first sentence restates p4 and p5 (learn, work, meet). Strip bullet 2 ('Nothing enforces the norm but reputation... worse for everyone') paraphrases p3's last sentence. The caption only repeats the prose, and the strip repeats both (law 2).
findings.fix: Make the caption point at the picture's example: 'The norm that holds the field together, drawn as a clock: the bug fixed on day 75 is published on day 105, thirty days later so users can update, and the bug never fixed is published on day 90.' In the strip, cut bullet 2 and cut bullet 1's first sentence, keeping only 'Others use similar windows.' Or drop the strip entirely.

findings.quote: 2017+ · hardware-signed RA
findings.problem: The label sits under 'PAC · CET shadow stack', but only PAC signs return addresses. CET's shadow stack keeps a protected copy and compares it, as ch15-memory-p4 says. The date is also off: PAC first shipped in the Apple A12 (2018) and CET in 11th-generation Core (2020), the dates the prose gives, so neither shipped in 2017.
findings.fix: Corrected claim: '2018+ · hardware-checked return address' (PAC signs it, A12 2018; CET keeps a protected copy, Tiger Lake 2020; both as stated in ch15-memory-p4).

findings.quote: Combined with packet forwarding (any modern OS does this with one sysctl), the attacker is now MITM.
findings.problem: Fig 15.4 poisons only the laptop's cache ('all gateway-bound traffic'), so the attacker sees only outbound packets. The gateway still sends replies straight to the laptop. The full man-in-the-middle that Fig 15.3 shows (read and rewrite both ways) needs the gateway's cache poisoned too, which is what arpspoof and Ettercap do.
findings.fix: Corrected claim: 'Poisoning the laptop brings its outbound packets through the attacker; poisoning the gateway's cache the same way brings the replies too, and the attacker is a full man in the middle.'

findings.quote: 2003+ · randomisation
findings.problem: Fig 15.2 calls itself 'Fig 3.11 extended', yet it dates ASLR '2003+' where Fig 3.11 says '2001+'. PaX shipped ASLR in July 2001. Separately, 'Rust in kernel · 2022+' is drawn after 'ARM MTE · 2023', so the timeline runs backwards at its end. Pass 19 flagged the ASLR mismatch for the owner read and it is still unresolved.
findings.fix: Corrected claim: 'ASLR · 2001+ · randomisation' (PaX, 2001), matching Fig 3.11. Relabel the last dot 'Rust in kernel · 2022 → today' so its position at the 2026 end is explained.

findings.quote: Stuxnet infected ~100K machines but did damage on perhaps a hundred.
findings.problem: 'A hundred' of what? In this sentence 'machines' means infected computers, which Stuxnet did not damage. If it means centrifuges, the widely cited estimate is about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges taken out of service at Natanz. The figure has no source for the number.
findings.fix: Corrected claim: 'Stuxnet infected ~100K computers but damaged only Natanz's centrifuges: about 1,000 IR-1s were taken out of service in late 2009 to early 2010' (Institute for Science and International Security, Albright, Brannan and Walrond, December 2010).

findings.quote: fails validation: stopped at 1
findings.problem: The same event, a layer stopping the input, is coloured two ways. In run 1, layer 1 flashes salmon (the rect at y=53, #cf8d78) while its outcome line is green. In run 2, layer 4's refusal flashes green (#a9bf8e) along with its green line. Salmon marks the bad input and the gaps everywhere else in the figure, so the layer-1 flash reads as a failure.
findings.fix: Give the layer-1 flash rect (x=17 y=53) fill and stroke #a9bf8e, the same as layer 4's refusal flash.

findings.quote: publish
findings.problem: The sliding day marker (path M14,256 L20,266 L26,256) has its top edge on y=256, the baseline of the 'report' and 'publish' labels. As it sweeps, it runs over their descenders: in the t=8 s frame it touches the p and b of 'publish' at day ~96. Law 3 says nothing overlapping.
findings.fix: Lower the marker below the descenders, for example path 'M15,260 L20,268 L25,260 Z' (axis at y=270), or raise the two bottom-row labels to y=252.

findings.quote: The field as three rings
findings.problem: The desc (what a screen reader hears) says three rings, but the picture shows three boxes in a row joined by arrows (learn → work → meet).
findings.fix: Change the desc to 'The field as three steps joined by arrows: people learn on…'

findings.quote: the logs of everything
findings.problem: The prose brings in the SIEM because 'a single sensor saw only its own slice'. The caption says it gathers 'the logs of everything'. In the picture, the SIEM's dashed lines come only from the four machines. The IDS (the sensor) and the firewall feed nothing into it, so the cross-sensor step the prose describes is not drawn.
findings.fix: Either draw a dashed line from the IDS box to the SIEM, or match the words to the picture: caption 'every machine's logs in one place'.

findings.quote: output encoding for XSS
findings.problem: The How it works bullet uses 'output encoding', which the prose never teaches. It appears only in Fig 12.9's caption, which the Pass 29 handover already flagged as unexplained (law 4).
findings.fix: '…under the same supporting layers: for XSS, turning < and > into plain text before the page shows them; for SSRF, an allow-list of URLs the server may fetch.'

findings.quote: The trick: a speculative load used the secret to pick which memory location to touch
findings.problem: This insight strip teaches the whole Spectre/Meltdown cache-timing mechanism again. Chapter 1 already taught it in ch1-cpu-p11, its caption ch1-cpu-p10 and the strip under it. The strip never points back, so it reads as new material, which breaks 'never explain twice what the book has already explained'.
findings.fix: Replace the first two sentences with a back-reference: "*The cache as a side channel.* Chapter 1 showed how Spectre and Meltdown (January 2018) read a secret from the trace that thrown-away speculative work leaves in the cache." Keep the sentence about the fix and its cost (microcode, KPTI, ~5–30%).

findings.quote: read out the secret bit by bit
findings.problem: Chapter 1 (ch1-cpu-p11) says the attack loads one of 256 locations picked by the value of a secret byte, so each probe reveals a whole byte. 'Bit by bit' contradicts that.
findings.fix: If the mechanism stays, change it to "read out the secret byte by byte".

findings.quote: The classic example sounds harmless: two threads each increment a shared counter a million times.
findings.problem: Chapter 4 §05 (ch4-ipc-p12) already taught the lost update (two processes read a count of 5, both write back 6) and the semaphore set to 1 that acts as a mutex. ch16-races-p1 and p3 teach both as if they were new. The brief asks for one clause naming the earlier idea instead of a second explanation.
findings.fix: Open p1 with the link instead of its first sentence: "Chapter 4 showed two processes losing an addition on a shared count; threads share every variable, so the same race can strike any of them. The classic example: two threads each increment...". In p3: "The classic fix is the mutex (mutual exclusion lock), Chapter 4's one-at-a-time gate as a thread library object."

findings.quote: a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line
findings.problem: 'Cache line' is used here three sections before ch16-numa-p1 defines it ('the 64-byte block a cache stores and moves as one unit'). It appears nowhere earlier in the book, and the glossary dates its first use to ch16-numa. It also sits inside a parenthetical with an internal semicolon, while the subject 'Out-of-order execution ... and store buffers' waits a whole line for its verb 'let'. The sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: "Out-of-order execution (Chapter 1, Section 04) and store buffers (holding areas where a core parks its writes until the cache takes them, which can let a later write out before an earlier one) let writes appear reordered."

findings.quote: a CUDA warp is 32 threads running in lockstep
findings.problem: One unit of the GPU has three names. p1 calls it 'small cores', Fig 16.6 and its caption call it 'lanes', and p3 plus Fig 16.7's label call it 'threads' ('warp: 32 threads'). Fig 16.7's code then says 'if lane < 16' and 'lanes 0–15'. The prose never says that a lane is one of p1's small cores and runs one thread of a warp, so a newcomer cannot connect the figures to the text.
findings.fix: p1: "thousands of small cores (GPU makers call them lanes) running..."; p3: "a CUDA warp is 32 threads, one per lane, running in lockstep."

findings.quote: and MESI's cache-line ping-pong
findings.problem: The chapter close lists 'cache-line ping-pong' as one of three constraints, but the term only appears in Fig 16.11's How it works strip, which is closed by default. No prose paragraph explains it.
findings.fix: "...NUMA's penalty for non-local memory, and MESI's invalidations when several cores keep writing one cache line."

findings.quote: if A holds L1 and waits for L2 while B holds L2 and waits for L1, both wait for ever
findings.problem: The caption repeats p4's deadlock recipe and its lock-ordering remedy almost word for word. The strip's 'The wait-for graph' bullet repeats p4's definition of the graph and the cycle as well, so deadlock is explained three times in a row.
findings.fix: Caption, naming the picture: "Left: A and B take L1 and L2 in opposite orders, and their waits close a cycle. Right: both take L1 first, so B waits, A finishes, and no cycle forms." Cut the strip's 'The wait-for graph' bullet.

findings.quote: With relaxed ordering a weakly ordered CPU can show the flag first and the reader gets the old x
findings.problem: The caption retells p3's broken flag example and its release/acquire repair, which p3 has just told in full.
findings.fix: Name the rows: "Top, relaxed: the reader sees the flag before x and reads 0. Bottom, release and acquire: x is visible no later than the flag, so the reader reads 1."

findings.quote: Relaxed: the operation is atomic, nothing more. Release: earlier writes go out first.
findings.problem: The 'The four levels' strip bullet defines relaxed, release, acquire and sequentially consistent again, right after p3 defines all four. The C++ code comment also defines relaxed, so relaxed is defined three times in the chapter.
findings.fix: Cut the bullet, or replace it with something p3 lacks: "*Cost.* Each step up, from relaxed to release/acquire to sequentially consistent, restricts the CPU and compiler more and costs more."

findings.quote: S(N) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N): the serial share 1 − p costs the same on any machine
findings.problem: The 'The formula' bullet repeats the math callout (p2–p4) right above it, limit included. 'Other values' repeats p1's 90% → 10×, and 'Who' repeats p1's Gene Amdahl 1967. That makes four statements of the ceiling.
findings.fix: Cut 'The formula'. Trim 'Other values' to "50% parallel tops out at 2×, 99% at 100×: going from 95% to 99% parallel buys more than any number of extra cores." Cut the first half of 'Who'.

findings.quote: Amdahl keeps the job fixed and asks how much faster more cores make it
findings.problem: The caption repeats p7's framing almost verbatim ('Amdahl fixes the problem and asks how much faster more cores make it; Gustafson fixes the time...').
findings.fix: Name the rows: "Top, Amdahl: one fixed job, 15.4× faster on 64 cores and never past 20×. Bottom, Gustafson: a fixed time, about 61 times the work on 64 cores."

findings.quote: Two threads doing a million increments each typically end well short of two million
findings.problem: The 'At scale' strip bullet restates p1 ('nearly always well short of it and changes from run to run'). The code block's first comment says the same thing a third time.
findings.fix: Cut the 'At scale' bullet.

findings.quote: and all of them wait forever
findings.problem: p4 writes 'forever', but the caption (p5) and Fig 16.3's drawn label write 'for ever'.
findings.fix: Change p4 to "wait for ever" so it matches the caption and the figure without an SVG change.

findings.quote: typically 128 or 256 bits wide, which holds 4 or 8 32-bit numbers at once
findings.problem: In '4 or 8 32-bit' two numerals run together, so the reader has to parse it twice.
findings.fix: "which holds four or eight 32-bit numbers at once"

findings.quote: The increment that looks atomic (one indivisible step) in source code (counter++) is in fact three operations underneath
findings.problem: Two parentheticals in a row separate the subject from its verb, so the sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: "In source code the increment `counter++` looks **atomic** (one indivisible step), but underneath it is three operations: ..."

findings.quote: The first known software-caused medical fatalities were race conditions.
findings.problem: This is a category error: deaths are not race conditions. They were caused by one.
findings.fix: "The first known deaths caused by software came from a race condition."

findings.quote: Any concurrent state machine without explicit synchronisation will eventually be observed in every reachable state
findings.problem: The strip ends on a general moral, an aphorism closer of the kind the brief bans. The Therac story has already made the point.
findings.fix: End on the casualties ("...three died.") or tie it to the mechanism: "No test had hit the keystroke timing that exposed the overlap."

findings.quote: The cache is not just a performance mechanism; it is also the most expensive side channel in the machine.
findings.problem: A 'not just X; also Y' aphorism closer. 'Most expensive side channel' is an unsupported superlative.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence, or say it plainly: "Every cache is therefore also a side channel."

findings.quote: most of its scientific simulation, all of its real-time graphics
findings.problem: A reflexive triplet ('most of... most of... all of...'), and 'most of the world's scientific simulation' is an overclaim, since much supercomputing still runs on CPUs.
findings.fix: "Today GPUs run almost all machine-learning training and real-time graphics, and a growing share of scientific simulation."

findings.quote: Adding cores to a computation is not free, and it is not unbounded. Two laws govern what you can expect.
findings.problem: Nothing in the section explains 'not free'. 'Two laws govern what you can expect' only announces what follows.
findings.fix: Open on the law: "**Amdahl's law** (Gene Amdahl, 1967) says that if a fraction _p_ of a program is parallelisable, ..."

findings.quote: appears to contradict Amdahl's; it is actually the answer to a different question
findings.problem: An 'appears X; actually Y' reveal. The next sentence states the difference directly anyway.
findings.fix: "**Gustafson's law** (1988) answers a different question: what happens when the problem grows with the machine?"

findings.problem: The prose gives Gustafson's law in its harder form. The strip below then gives the transparent form (1 − p) + p·N and says the two are equal, so the reader meets two formulas for one idea, and the harder one comes first.
findings.fix: In p7 write "S(N) = (1 − p) + p·N" (the serial part plus N copies of the parallel part). Cut the equivalence from the strip's 'The two formulas' bullet.

findings.quote: memory orderings, the rules by which writes from one core become visible to others
findings.problem: Memory ordering is defined at the end of p1, then defined again in p3 ('a contract about what other cores are guaranteed to see'), in the same section.
findings.fix: End p1 at "...requires understanding _memory orderings_." and let p3 carry the definition.

findings.quote: If two threads' three-step sequences overlap, the writes can stomp on each other.
findings.problem: The section is titled 'Race conditions', and the glossary dates 'race condition' to this section, but the prose never names the bug. 'The race' first appears in p4 ('Locks solve the race') with no definition.
findings.fix: Append to p1: "...stomp on each other. This is a *race condition*: the result depends on the timing."

findings.quote: an atomic increment, Fig 16.4
findings.problem: Fig 16.4 shows a compare-and-swap retry, not the single-instruction atomic increment (`fetch_add`) from the code block. A reader who follows the pointer finds a different mechanism.
findings.fix: "(compare-and-swap, Fig 16.4, or an atomic increment)"

findings.quote: POSIX threads (1995) made the shared-memory model portable
findings.problem: The 'The standard' bullet repeats p1, which already names POSIX 1003.1c (1995) as the standard that codified threads.
findings.fix: Keep only what is new: "*Who uses which.* C, C++, Java and Rust default to threads; browsers put each site in its own process for safety."

findings.quote: x = 1; flag = true;
findings.problem: In one example the prose writes `flag = true`, while Fig 16.5 draws flag=1 and its description says 'a flag to 1'.
findings.fix: Change the prose to `x = 1; flag = 1;` (and 'observe `flag = 1`'), which avoids an SVG change.

findings.quote: thousands of small cores running in lockstep, each executing the same instruction on different data
findings.problem: This says thousands of cores run in lockstep. p3, Fig 16.6's strip and Fig 16.7 say lockstep holds only within a 32-thread warp.
findings.fix: "thousands of small cores, in groups that run in lockstep, each group executing one instruction on different data."

findings.quote: 8 × 5 = 40 CORES
findings.problem: The hero art is labelled 40 cores, while the chapter meta beside it reads 'Cluster: 1 machine · 8 cores · one shared memory'. Two core counts sit side by side on the opening screen.
findings.fix: Relabel the art without a count that clashes, e.g. "MANY CORES · ONE CHIP", or make the grid 8 cores. If the meta is the protected part micro-arc, leave the meta as it is.

findings.quote: Fast kernels keep data in shared memory
findings.problem: In this chapter 'shared memory' means the memory threads share (Section 01, Fig 16.1). Here it silently becomes CUDA's on-chip block memory, which the bullet above calls 'fast on-chip memory'.
findings.fix: "Fast kernels keep data in the block's on-chip memory (CUDA calls it shared memory)..."

findings.quote: A kernel launch is a grid of blocks, each block a set of warps, each warp 32 threads
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p3's hierarchy. The strip's 'The model' bullet repeats p3's last sentence ('writes code that looks like it runs on a single thread; the runtime replicates it').
findings.fix: Caption: keep only the divergence sentence, which the prose does not carry. Cut the strip's 'The model' bullet.

findings.quote: A bigger simulation, a larger model or more samples in the same hour is Gustafson
findings.problem: The 'Which applies' bullet repeats p7's closing sentence, the same examples and conclusion about supercomputers and GPU clusters.
findings.fix: Keep only the Amdahl half, which is new: "*Which applies.* A frame that must render in 16 ms, or one fixed compile, is Amdahl."

findings.quote: `counter++` looks like one step but is three: load, add, store.
findings.problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p1's three-step explanation, right above the picture.
findings.fix: Start the caption with the picture: "Thread 2 loads before thread 1 has stored, so both add one to the same 100 and both store 101: one increment is lost."

findings.quote: release store / acquire load
findings.problem: The legend says a bold outline marks a release store or an acquire load. But two reads that are neither carry the same 2-unit bold stroke: the relaxed run's 'x=0' read (rect x=268 y=89) and the release/acquire run's final 'x=1' read (rect x=334 y=209). By the figure's own key, the relaxed reader does an acquire load, and the plain read of x after the flag is an acquire too. Both contradict the caption and ch16-lockfree-p3, where only the flag load is acquire.
findings.fix: Set stroke-width="1.2" on the x=0 read box (x=268 y=89) and on the x=1 read box (x=334 y=209). Pink for wrong and teal for right already carry the result. Only the write flag=1 (x=136 y=153) and the read flag=1 (x=268 y=209) keep stroke-width 2, so the legend has exactly two matches.

findings.quote: Gustafson: same time, how much more?
findings.problem: Gustafson's fixed-time bar shows the serial 5% in pink and leaves the other 95% empty. The rect at x=20 y=158 has fill="none" plus a leftover fill-opacity="0.18", which looks like a fill that was lost. The Amdahl bar just above uses filled for time spent and empty for time no longer needed. Read with that key, Gustafson's N cores sit idle 95% of the fixed time, and the parallel work that fills it, the whole point of Gustafson, is never drawn.
findings.fix: Give the rect at x=20 y=158 fill="#4fd8c2" (keep fill-opacity 0.18, or use 0.85 to match the Amdahl bar). The fixed-time bar then reads serial 5% plus parallel 95% on N cores, all of it busy, above the growing 'work done' bar.

findings.quote: store 101 →
findings.problem: Steps that have not run yet are drawn ahead of time as ghosts. Thread 1's add and store and thread 2's add sit at group opacity 0.8, and thread 2's store at 0.63; the two load ghosts use 0.25. In the 3.7 s frame the pending boxes measure about 82% of the brightness of steps already run. So all six steps look done while the counter column shows only '100, 100', and the boxes no longer show the order of the interleaving, which is what the figure is about. Fig 16.4 has the same ghosts at 0.63 to 0.8 (the failed CAS, read 101 and the final CAS).
findings.fix: In both Fig 16.2 and Fig 16.4, draw every pending step the same faint way: a dashed outline with no text, so nothing faint has to pass the label-contrast floor. Alternatively, hide each box until its step runs. A step then looks executed only once its counter value appears.

findings.quote: cores, N
findings.problem: The x axis is logarithmic (1, 32 and 1024 evenly spaced, so each step doubles N), but nothing says so, and the y axis has no title. On this axis the curve starts nearly flat and climbs fastest between 8 and 64 cores, an S shape. The figure's description says the curve 'rises fast at first and then flattens', which contradicts the drawing. A newcomer who reads the axis as linear learns the wrong shape for Amdahl's curve.
findings.fix: Relabel the axis 'cores, N (doubling)' and put 'speedup' above the '20' tick on the y axis. Desc: 'Below, the speedup curve, drawn against doubling core counts, climbs to 5.9 at 8 cores, 15.4 at 64 and 19.6 at 1,024, and flattens against its ceiling of 20.'

findings.quote: link
findings.problem: The label 'link' is about 31 units wide at 13 px mono, centred at x=200 in a 28-unit gap between the sockets (socket 0 ends at x=186, socket 1 starts at about x=214). Its 'l' sits on socket 0's border and its 'k' crosses socket 1's border, which is visible at 375 px. Law 3 forbids overlap, and the font cannot shrink: 11 units would render at about 9.8 CSS px.
findings.fix: Widen the gap to at least 36 units: narrow each socket box by 4 units on its inner side and nudge that socket's cores and memory box inward. 'link' then sits clear of both borders at the same size.

findings.quote: read
findings.problem: Knockout clip-paths cut the timeline rules at every box slot, and the cuts are there whether or not the box is showing. Before a box appears, its slot is a gap. A 6-unit stub of rule is left floating between neighbouring slots: in the relaxed read row at x 262 to 268, the relaxed seen row at x 394 to 396, and the release/acquire seen row at x 196 to 202. Mid-run frames show broken rules with stray dashes that mean nothing.
findings.fix: Remove the clip-paths. Draw each rule whole, and give the boxes the card background as fill instead of fill="none", so a box covers the rule only while it is visible.

findings.quote: invalid
findings.problem: Invalid is drawn in two styles. Before 'A writes', C and D (and B before it reads) get a darker tile (fill 0.58 at 0.25 opacity) that has no legend entry. From 'A writes' on, they get the legend's lighter tile (0.4). So at 'A writes', C and D visibly change as if the invalidate reached their copies, though neither held the line ('D never held the line', per the description).
findings.fix: Draw every I with the legend's tile throughout (fill rgba(232,229,244,1) at fill-opacity 0.4). At 'A writes', B's tile is then the only one that changes to I.

findings.quote: if A holds L1 and waits for L2 while B holds L2 and waits for L1
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch16-races-p4 almost word for word (the deadlock recipe, then lock ordering preventing the cycle). It describes nothing that is drawn.
findings.fix: 'Left: each thread holds one lock and waits for the other's, and the waits close a cycle. Right: both ask for L1 first, so B waits until A has finished with both locks, and no cycle can form.'

findings.quote: 101 lost
findings.problem: The final counter mark reads as 'the value 101 was lost'. In fact the counter correctly holds 101; what was lost is thread 1's increment.
findings.fix: Change the mark to 'still 101' in pink. The bottom line already says 'expected 102, got 101'.

findings.quote: the two halves take turns while the other waits
findings.problem: Number mismatch: 'the two halves' cannot be followed by 'the other', so a careful reader stops on the sentence.
findings.fix: 'When a branch splits a warp, one half runs while the other waits, then they swap, so divergent code runs at a fraction of the speed.'

findings.quote: Make the read-modify-write one indivisible step (an atomic increment, Fig 16.4)
findings.problem: Fig 16.4 does not show a single atomic increment (that is the fetch_add in the code block). It shows a compare-and-swap retry: a read, a failed swap, a re-read and a second swap. A reader who turns to 16.4 for 'one indivisible step' finds a loop.
findings.fix: '*The fixes.* Make the read-modify-write one indivisible step (an atomic increment, or the compare-and-swap retry of Fig 16.4) or let only one thread in at a time (a mutex, Fig 16.3).'

findings.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.
findings.problem: This is not a factual error. The paragraph's last sentence repeats the one before it almost word for word (public/part-5.html lines 1690–1691). It looks like an old version of the sentence that was left in after the Terraform correction. Any reader will stop at it, and it breaks law 2.
findings.fix: Delete the final sentence "Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand." The sentence before it already says this.

findings.quote: These instruction-set extensions let a hypervisor run guest operating systems at near-native speed.
findings.problem: The sentence gives VT-x/AMD-V the credit for near-native speed, so the reader concludes x86 guests could not run that fast before 2005. That is false. VMware's binary translation and Xen's paravirtualization were already near native (Xen ran within a few percent, SOSP 2003). Adams and Agesen (ASPLOS 2006) found first-generation VT-x often slower than binary translation. What VT-x actually changed was that sensitive instructions now trap, which the Fig 17.1 strip already says. Pass 18 corrected this same misconception in the old caption (UNDER.md Pass 18 row 3: "the 10× belonged to naive emulation, not BT/PV").
findings.fix: "These instruction-set extensions made every sensitive instruction trap, so a hypervisor could run an unmodified guest without rewriting its code." Sources: Adams and Agesen, "A Comparison of Software and Hardware Techniques for x86 Virtualization", ASPLOS 2006; Barham et al., "Xen and the Art of Virtualization", SOSP 2003.

findings.quote: The technology dates to IBM's CP/CMS in 1968
findings.problem: This dates the origin of virtualization to 1968. The §4g Part V row corrected the same claim in ch18 ("IBM 'invented' virtualization in 1968") because CP-40, the first CP/CMS, was running in 1967; 1968 is the year CP-67/CMS shipped. ch18 now says "shipped in 1968", but ch17 still gives 1968 as the start.
findings.fix: "The technology dates to IBM's CP/CMS, running by 1967 and shipped in 1968: a hypervisor on the System/360 that ..." Sources: UNDER.md §4g Part V row (CP-40 ran in 1967, CP/CMS shipped 1968); Melinda Varian, "VM and the VM Community".

findings.quote: The field then waited until 2001 for Paxos Made Simple, which explained the same protocol in plain language.
findings.problem: This overstates the gap. Lamport's own notes on the paper say Butler Lampson "immediately understood the algorithm's significance" and explained it in lectures and in a paper ("How to Build a Highly Available System Using Consensus", 1996). De Prisco, Lampson and Lynch also published a specification and proof in 1997. Paxos Made Simple (2001) is Lamport's own plain retelling, not the first plain account.
findings.fix: "Butler Lampson explained it in plainer terms from 1996, and in 2001 Lamport retold it himself in Paxos Made Simple." Source: lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/pubs.html, notes on [123] The Part-Time Parliament and [140] Paxos Made Simple; Lampson, WDAG 1996.

findings.quote: downloads a layered image, creates the namespaces, configures cgroups, and starts the process; the whole thing takes a second.
findings.problem: The one second includes the download. On a first run, pulling nginx (tens of megabytes compressed, around 190 MB unpacked) takes several seconds on ordinary links before the container starts. The one-second figure only holds once the image is cached. The tenfold-to-hundredfold comparison is still right for a cached image.
findings.fix: "... and starts the process; once the image has been downloaded, starting it takes well under a second."

findings.quote: Before EC2, deploying a web service required buying or leasing physical servers, racking them in a colocation facility
findings.problem: "Required" overstates. Rented dedicated servers that you never racked yourself, and virtual private servers (Linode from 2003, on UML and later Xen), already existed. EC2's real change was minutes, an API and per-use billing. As written, the reader concludes no one could rent a server without colocation before 2006.
findings.fix: "Before EC2, deploying a web service at scale usually meant buying or leasing physical servers, racking them in a colocation facility, and waiting weeks for capacity."

findings.quote: serverless functions around 2018
findings.problem: AWS Lambda launched in November 2014, the same year as the figure's microservices point. Pass 18 added the sublabel "Lambda (2014) · FaaS" under serverless for exactly this reason (UNDER.md Pass 18 fact table, "fig 17.11 serverless sublabel"). The Pass 28 redraw dropped it, so the figure, its description and the caption now place serverless at about 2018 with no hint that it began four years earlier.
findings.fix: Bring back the Pass 18 note. Put "Lambda 2014" as a sublabel under serverless if it fits at 375 px; otherwise add a line to the strip: "AWS Lambda launched in 2014; the serverless wave peaked a few years later." Description: "serverless functions (AWS Lambda, 2014), widespread by about 2018". Source: AWS Lambda announcement, re:Invent, 13 November 2014.

findings.quote: AP stores settle diverged copies afterwards: last writer wins, vector clocks, or data types that merge by design (CRDTs).
findings.problem: Vector clocks do not settle a conflict. They detect that two versions are concurrent. In Dynamo, versions that cannot be merged automatically are returned to the client, which merges them in application code (the shopping cart union). The list makes vector clocks sound like a resolution rule alongside last-writer-wins and CRDTs.
findings.fix: "AP stores settle diverged copies afterwards: last writer wins, vector clocks that spot the conflict and hand both versions to the application to merge, or data types that merge by design (CRDTs)." Source: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store", SOSP 2007, §4.4.

findings.quote: a tight loop that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state
findings.problem: In programming, "tight loop" means a busy loop that spins without waiting. Kubernetes controllers do not poll like that. They sleep on a work queue and are woken by watch events from the API server, plus a periodic resync or requeue. The chapter's own code block shows this (RequeueAfter 30 s). A programmer reading "tight loop" will picture continuous polling.
findings.fix: "a loop, woken by every change it watches and by a periodic resync, that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state ..." Source: kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/ (controllers watch the API server); controller-runtime's Reconcile and RequeueAfter.

findings.quote: Type 2: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels, each an application plus a kernel driver, which is where its traps land.
findings.problem: This is dated for Parallels. On Apple silicon, and optionally on Intel Macs, Parallels Desktop (like VMware Fusion) runs on Apple's Hypervisor framework rather than a kernel extension of its own. Its traps land in macOS's built-in hypervisor support, not in a Parallels driver. The point still holds that traps land in the host kernel; "each ... plus a kernel driver" does not.
findings.fix: "Type 2: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels, applications whose traps land in the host kernel, through their own driver or the system's built-in hypervisor support (Apple's Hypervisor framework on Macs)." Sources: developer.apple.com/documentation/hypervisor; Parallels KB 128435 (Apple hypervisor avoids Parallels kernel extensions).

findings.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.
findings.problem: The paragraph's last sentence repeats, almost word for word, the clause just before it ('Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks...'). It looks like an editing slip. The Fig 17.4 strip ('Elsewhere') then says the same thing a third time.
findings.fix: Delete the final sentence 'Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.' Also delete the Fig 17.4 strip bullet 'Elsewhere', which repeats the prose.

findings.quote: takes whichever action will move current closer to desired. Run forever.
findings.problem: 'Run forever.' is a clipped dramatic fragment. 'A tight loop' also contradicts the code block just below, where a converged controller asks to run again after 30 seconds ('RequeueAfter: 30 * time.Second'). A controller does not spin.
findings.fix: '...is a reconcile loop: a loop that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state, takes whichever action will move current closer to desired, and then runs again, for as long as the object exists.'

findings.quote: Idempotent. A pass with nothing to fix changes nothing, so running the loop often is safe.
findings.problem: The strip's 'Level, not edge' and 'Idempotent' bullets repeat what ch17-k8s-p3 has just said (idempotent, robust, stateless). In p3 that sentence is also a reflexive triplet with the same opening three times ('The loop is idempotent... The loop is robust... The loop is stateless').
findings.fix: Make p3 one sentence: 'The loop is idempotent (a second run with nothing changed does nothing), robust (a failed command is simply retried on the next pass) and stateless (it compares what is with what should be and remembers nothing).' Cut the strip bullets 'Level, not edge' and 'Idempotent'. If the strip needs content, add the one new fact: 'Requeue. A controller with nothing to do asks to run again later (30 seconds in the code below), so drift is caught even when no event arrives.'

findings.quote: a container starts in milliseconds, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel
findings.problem: The start-time numbers disagree. The same paragraph says 'docker run nginx'... 'the whole thing takes a second' and calls it 'a tenfold to hundredfold improvement' over a VM's 'tens of seconds'. That ratio fits one second, not milliseconds. In ch17-containers-p3, microVMs boot 'in about a tenth of a second' while 'preserving most of containers' speed'. That claim fails if a container starts in milliseconds, and it reverses if a container takes a second.
findings.fix: '...a container starts in under a second, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel.' Then: 'Once the image is downloaded, `docker run nginx` creates the namespaces, configures cgroups, and starts the process in about a second.'

findings.quote: any two quorums must intersect in at least one node
findings.problem: The chapter explains majority overlap three times. ch17-consensus-p2 says 'any two of them share at least one acceptor', p6 says it again, and the Fig 17.5 strip says 'Any two majorities of the same cluster share a node... N nodes tolerate ⌊(N − 1)/2⌋ failures, which is why clusters run 3, 5 or 7'. The strip also repeats p4/p6's N = 2f + 1 and the point about cluster sizes. 'Quorum' is defined twice too: 'a quorum (a majority)' in p2 and again, in bold as if new, in p4.
findings.fix: In p2 write 'to a majority of acceptors', so 'quorum' is first defined in p4. In p6 replace 'The reason: any two quorums must intersect in at least one node, so' with 'The reason is the overlap Paxos relies on: any two quorums share a node, so'. Cut the strip's 'Majorities' bullet to 'In log replication an entry counts once a majority hold it, so any later leader's majority includes a node that has it.'

findings.quote: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout published Raft in 2014 as an understandable alternative to Paxos
findings.problem: The reader is told three times that Raft is the understandable alternative to Paxos: ch17-consensus-p1 ('Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout's Raft (2014), which was explicitly designed to be more understandable than Paxos'), p2 ('a complete design built to be understood') and this strip bullet.
findings.fix: Shorten the 'Where it runs' bullet to 'Where it runs. etcd, Consul and CockroachDB use Raft.'

findings.quote: in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash, no deterministic protocol is guaranteed both to agree and to finish
findings.problem: FLP is stated four times in one section: ch17-consensus-p8, the Fig 17.6 caption, this strip ('The theorem'), and the math callout p11. The strip's 'The escapes' bullet then gives the same three escapes, with the same examples (Paxos/Raft, Ben-Or, Dynamo), as p12.
findings.fix: Cut the strip bullets 'The theorem' and 'The escapes' and keep only 'In practice', which is new. The callout (p10–p12) then gives the formal statement and the escapes once.

findings.quote: Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony
findings.problem: Only the first of the three escapes listed rules out asynchrony. Randomisation (Ben-Or) works in a fully asynchronous system by giving up determinism. Eventual consistency weakens agreement. So the sentence contradicts its own list, and it contradicts p8's framing that each escape adds an assumption.
findings.fix: 'Real systems escape by dropping one of the theorem's conditions: partial synchrony (Paxos, Raft) assumes messages eventually arrive within some bound; randomisation (Ben-Or) gives up determinism and flips coins to break adversarial schedules; eventual consistency (Dynamo) weakens agreement, serving now and reconciling later.'

findings.quote: Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption.
findings.problem: This aphorism closer restates p8's own closer ('works around FLP by adding an assumption, and the assumption is the price'). The section ends on two versions of the same sentence.
findings.fix: Delete 'Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption.' In p8, end the sentence plainly: '...works around FLP by adding an assumption the theorem does not allow.'

findings.quote: Why? Because the moment you need multiple machines to agree on something
findings.problem: A rhetorical question stands in for a plain causal clause. It is followed by three clipped sentences in a row ('Messages can be delayed arbitrarily. Machines can crash. The network can partition...'), the clipped-fragment pattern the brief names.
findings.fix: 'Kubernetes' "source of truth", etcd, runs a distributed consensus protocol called Raft, because the moment you need multiple machines to agree on something (...), the network's unreliability becomes a mathematical problem: messages can be delayed arbitrarily, machines can crash, and the network can partition into halves that can't reach each other.'

findings.quote: Availability (every request gets a response)
findings.problem: By this definition the CP replica in Fig 17.7 is still available, because 'error: can't confirm' is a response. A careful reader stops when the figure calls an error-returning system 'unavailable'. Brewer's and Gilbert–Lynch's sense is a non-error answer.
findings.fix: '*Availability* (every request gets a real answer, not an error)'

findings.quote: Real networks do partition, so "consistent and available, without partition tolerance" is not an option
findings.problem: The caption and two of the three strip bullets repeat ch17-cap-p1. The 'The theorem' bullet repeats Brewer, Gilbert and Lynch and the C-or-A choice. 'Why not CA' repeats 'Network partitions happen whether you like it or not'. The caption restates p1's last two sentences (refuse and lose A, or serve stale and lose C).
findings.fix: Cut the strip bullets 'The theorem' and 'Why not CA' and keep PACELC. Shorten the caption so it names the picture: 'With the link cut, replica 2 can refuse the read (CP) or answer with the stale x = 1 (AP).'

findings.quote: Architecture is a series of trades, not of progressions
findings.problem: An aphorism closer in 'not X, Y' form. Its 'costume' image is used again in the Fig 17.11 caption ('only its costume changed') and in the figure title. It also clashes with the section title 'Architecture is fashion': fashion is arbitrary, trades are reasoned.
findings.fix: End p1 at '...and consolidated.' The pendulum figure carries the point. Use the freed space for the service-mesh sentence (see the finding on ch17-microservices-p3). Keep the image once, in the Fig 17.11 caption.

findings.quote: the same problems return every fifteen years in slightly different costume
findings.problem: Fig 17.11, two figures later, dates the swings at 1990s, ~2005, ~2014, ~2018 and 2020s, gaps of roughly 4 to 10 years. No interval in it is fifteen years. The section title makes the same claim ('the same problems return every fifteen years').
findings.fix: If the sentence stays, use 'every decade or so'. Change the title to 'Architecture swings · the same problems return every decade or so.'

findings.quote: In return each service deploys, scales and fails on its own.
findings.problem: Both the caption and the strip's 'What it buys' bullet repeat p1's motivation ('independent deployability, team autonomy, freedom for each team to choose its tools, fault isolation'). The caption's first sentence also repeats p1's 'every former function call became a network call'.
findings.fix: Caption: 'The same checkout, built two ways: two function calls inside one process, or two network calls between services, one of which times out and is retried.' Cut the strip bullet 'What it buys'.

findings.quote: A service mesh gives each service a proxy beside it, called a sidecar
findings.problem: No prose paragraph mentions service meshes. Fig 17.10 appears between the monolith figure and the Serverless heading, and its caption alone introduces 'service mesh', 'sidecar' and 'mutual TLS'. The reader is not told why a mesh exists, yet the chapter's opening lead lists 'service meshes' as one of the cloud's layered abstractions.
findings.fix: Add a sentence at the end of ch17-microservices-p1, paid for by cutting its closer: 'Much of that cost is now carried by a service mesh: a proxy beside every service that encrypts, retries and times out its calls (Fig 17.10).' The caption can then name the picture.

findings.quote: Containers abstract operating systems but preserve the cost of process isolation.
findings.problem: Four sentences in a row share one shape ('X abstracts Y but preserves the cost of Z'). The paragraph summarises the chapter and ends on an aphorism ('The skill of working in the cloud is, in part, knowing...'). 'Containers abstract operating systems' also contradicts Section 02, where a container shares the host's kernel. 'The cost of process isolation' names no cost the chapter taught.
findings.fix: 'Every layer hides the one beneath but not its costs: a VM still pays for each trap to the hypervisor, containers still share one kernel, Kubernetes still faces partial failure, and a serverless function still pays its cold start. When something breaks, the work is finding which layer it came from.'

findings.quote: SBOMs (software bills of materials, a list of every component inside a program), reproducible builds
findings.problem: Chapter 15 §05 (ch15-defense, 'SolarWinds 2020 · the supply-chain shape') already tells this story: the build compromise, the signed update, ~18,000 customers, and the same three responses (SBOMs, reproducible builds, signed build provenance). This strip tells it again. Its one new point is the cloud-era blast radius.
findings.fix: Cut to the new point: 'SolarWinds (Chapter 15) shows what the cloud era adds: one poisoned, vendor-signed update reached nearly eighteen thousand customers at once, across a trust boundary that sat in no customer's network.' Drop the re-listed responses and their definitions.

findings.quote: a software-update channel is architecturally identical to a worm
findings.problem: The analogy is never cashed out. The strip does not say which property an update channel shares with a worm (reaching every machine with code that runs there), or where the two differ (a worm spreads itself; an update channel is trusted and signed).
findings.fix: If the sentence survives the cut above: '...discovering that a software-update channel delivers code to every customer machine the way a worm would, except signed and trusted.'

findings.quote: doing the wrong thing at the right speed, is enough to end a company
findings.problem: An aphorism flourish. The same sentence repeats a word ('running different versions of the code are the distributed-systems version of a race condition'), so it has to be read twice. The race-condition comparison is only half cashed. The strip ends on 'is a response to...', the same shape p7 ends on ('are the industry's response to...').
findings.fix: 'A cluster whose machines run different versions of the code fails like a race condition: what happens depends on which machine a request reaches. Modern deployment systems check that every machine runs the declared version before traffic flows, and send a new build to a few machines first, watch it, then roll it out to the rest.'

findings.quote: The hypervisor underneath is invisible to the customer; the abstraction it provides is what they pay for.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer that restates p1 ('without knowing it isn't running on real hardware'). It teaches nothing new.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The paragraph ends on Instagram.

findings.quote: a set of cooperating control-plane components (the parts that decide what should run where)
findings.problem: Several glossary first-use marks land in the wrong place. 'control plane' is defined here but marked in Section 06's Fig 17.10 strip. 'container runtime' is marked in the Fig 17.3 strip, but Section 02 already uses it ('LXC, a userspace container runtime'). 'hypervisor' and 'virtual machine' are marked in ch17-virt-p1, but ch4-security-p6 defined both. Bold makes them read as new terms when they are not.
findings.fix: Here, write 'a control plane (the components that decide what should run where)' so the term is marked in Section 03, and drop the mark in the Fig 17.10 strip. Drop 'a userspace container runtime' from ch17-containers-p1 ('through LXC, which it soon replaced with its own'). Point the hypervisor and virtual-machine glossary entries at ch4-security.

findings.quote: AWS Firecracker (2018) and Kata Containers (2018) build "microVMs", lightweight VMs that boot in about a tenth of a second
findings.problem: Chapter 4 §06 already teaches microVMs: 'MicroVMs such as AWS Firecracker boot a minimal guest kernel in about 125 ms', plus why VMs isolate better (ch4-security-p11). The strip re-explains them as if new and does not link back. Its new content is Kata, gVisor and Lambda.
findings.fix: Open with the link and keep only what is new: 'Chapter 4's Firecracker microVMs (2018), and Kata Containers the same year, narrowed the trade between VM isolation and container speed; Google's gVisor (2018) attacks it from the other side...'

findings.quote: wrapping the container in a user-space kernel that intercepts every syscall
findings.problem: Spelling varies within the chapter: 'user-space' here, 'userspace' in ch17-containers-p1. The heading 'The MicroVM convergence' capitalises a term the text writes 'microVM'.
findings.fix: Use 'user-space' in both places, and 'The microVM convergence.'

findings.quote: downloads a layered image, creates the namespaces, configures cgroups, and starts the process
findings.problem: No prose explains 'layered image'. 'Layer' and 'Dockerfile' are explained only in the Fig 17.2 caption and strip, so the reader meets them first under the picture.
findings.fix: '...downloads a layered image (one read-only layer per build step, Fig 17.2), creates the namespaces...'

findings.quote: A proposer first sends a prepare message with a unique proposal number to a quorum (a majority) of acceptors
findings.problem: 'Proposer' and 'acceptor' are used as if known. The reader is not told that these are roles the nodes play.
findings.fix: 'Each node can act as a proposer, which suggests a value, or an acceptor, which votes on it. A proposer first sends a prepare message with a unique proposal number to a majority of acceptors;...'

findings.quote: Lamport proved it in 1989. The difficulty is cognitive.
findings.problem: Two clipped sentences in a row, the second a dramatic fragment.
findings.fix: 'Lamport proved it correct in 1989; the difficulty is understanding it.'

findings.quote: most students answered questions on Raft better than on Paxos. That is why etcd uses Raft.
findings.problem: Placed right after the classroom study, 'That is why' makes the study the reason etcd chose Raft. The real reason is understandability, which made Raft easier to implement correctly.
findings.fix: '...better than on Paxos. Easier to understand also meant easier to implement correctly, which is why etcd uses Raft.'

findings.quote: is (⌊ ⌋ means round down, so 5 / 2 becomes 2):
findings.problem: The parenthesis splits the copula 'is' from the formula on the next line, so the sentence has to be read twice.
findings.fix: 'A quorum, the smallest set of nodes whose agreement counts as the cluster's decision, is given below; ⌊ ⌋ means round down, so 5 / 2 becomes 2.'

findings.quote: 4 nodes need 3, giving the same fault tolerance as 3
findings.problem: The final '3' is ambiguous. Next to 'need 3' it reads as a quorum size, not a cluster of three nodes.
findings.fix: '(4 nodes need 3, so they survive one failure, no more than a cluster of 3)'

findings.quote: conjectured 2000, proven 2002 by Gilbert & Lynch
findings.problem: The Fig 17.7 strip says 'proved by Gilbert and Lynch (2002)'. The prose differs in both the verb form and the ampersand.

findings.problem: A compound that starts with an -ly adverb takes no hyphen.

findings.problem: 'Build time' is a noun here and takes no hyphen. The possessive also differs from Chapter 15, which writes 'SolarWinds' build environment'.

findings.problem: 'It' has no clear antecedent: Kubernetes, the containers, or 'what should run'.
findings.fix: 'and a fleet of worker nodes (the machines that run the containers)'

findings.quote: a small replicated key-value store that keeps agreement with Raft (Fig 17.5)

findings.quote: waiting for it risks waiting for ever
findings.problem: The caption and figure write 'for ever'. The prose around them writes 'forever' in the same sense ('spins forever' in p8, 'waits forever' in p12, and 'Run forever' in k8s-p3).
findings.fix: Choose one spelling for the chapter, e.g. 'waiting for it risks waiting forever' in the caption and 'in world 2, forever' in the figure.

findings.quote: then up again to many cores, many machines, many datacenters, many regions
findings.problem: The direction image is mixed: 'out from one transistor...', then 'up again', then 'no further "out" to go'. Nothing went 'up' before, so the reader stops on 'again'.
findings.fix: '...then outward again to many cores, many machines, many datacenters, many regions.'

findings.quote: so it needs a saga of steps and compensations instead of one transaction
findings.problem: 'Saga', 'compensations' and 'distributed tracing' are not explained here or elsewhere in the chapter. The strip relies on them for its point about what microservices cost.
findings.fix: '...so it needs a chain of steps, each with an undo step if a later one fails, instead of one transaction; following a request across services needs tracing that tags every call.'

findings.quote: no step of this path is written in either language: the code in the figure is C and JavaScript
findings.problem: This is false. V8, a station in this same figure, is written in C++: v8.dev/docs says "V8 is Google's open source high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, written in C++". Chrome/Chromium is C++, and so is much of Google's search serving. It also contradicts Chapter 6, which says C++ "now runs trading systems, game engines, browsers". The trace still has no C++ or Python station, but the reason the paragraph gives for that is wrong.
findings.fix: "Chapters 6 and 7 (C++ and Python) have none because they teach languages, not a layer the request crosses: C++ runs underneath several stations (the browser, V8, much of Google's serving code), but no station is a language."

findings.quote: what happens when you type google.com into your browser and press Enter?
findings.problem: The question in p1 and the path in the figure describe two different keystrokes. When you type google.com in the address bar, the browser's own navigation code (C++, not page JavaScript) asks www.google.com for GET /. No page JavaScript is running yet, and there is no /search, index lookup or ranking. The figure instead has JavaScript build GET /search, which can only happen on a Google page that has already loaded. That page's connection is normally still open, so DNS, TCP and TLS are skipped, as the figure's own strip says of later searches. So the strip's label "A first visit" contradicts the JS station, and the reader comes away thinking that typing google.com makes JavaScript send a search.
findings.fix: In p2, say which keystroke is traced: "The trace below follows the question's sibling, a search typed into Google's page, from the moment your finger closes a contact...". In the strip, replace the third bullet's opening with: "*A cold start.* The trace assumes the page's connection and DNS entry have expired; a search made while they are fresh skips DNS, TCP and TLS; and once a browser has learned Google speaks QUIC, ..."

findings.quote: V8's event loop picks it up (12)
findings.problem: V8 has no event loop; the program that embeds it supplies one. In Chrome, Blink runs the HTML event loop on the renderer's main thread (HTML Standard §8.1.7: "user agents must use event loops"). In Node it is libuv, as the book's own Fig 12.6 says: "libuv, a C library that holds the event loop". The drawn station "V8 · event loop" and the <desc> teach the opposite of Chapter 12.
findings.fix: Drawn station: "LOOP | browser event loop | Ch 12" and the next one "JS | V8 builds the request | Ch 12". In the <desc>: "the browser's event loop picks it up (12), and JavaScript, run by V8, builds the request (12)".

findings.quote: pods, orchestrated ... results ranked: cores, GPUs
findings.problem: The Google stations name open-source and generic stand-ins for Google's real machinery. Google Search runs on Borg, which Chapter 17 calls Kubernetes' ancestor. Borg's unit is the task or alloc, not the Kubernetes pod. Google serves its search ranking models on its own TPUs, not GPUs: "for the first time we're using the latest Cloud TPUs to serve search results" (Google blog, "Understanding searches better than ever before", Oct 2019). Likewise, p3's boundary "HTTP query → SQL parser" names a SQL parser, and a search-index lookup has none.
findings.fix: Drawn "pods, orchestrated" becomes "containers, orchestrated" (desc: "orchestrated containers (17)"). "results ranked: cores, GPUs" becomes "results ranked: cores, accelerators" (desc: "ranking on many cores and accelerators (16)"). In p3, "HTTP query → SQL parser" becomes "search query → index service".

findings.quote: RSA will retire when error-corrected quantum computers (the logical qubits of Chapter 14) can run Shor's algorithm at scale
findings.problem: RSA is being retired before such machines exist, because of harvest now, decrypt later. Chapter 14's Fig 14.13 strip teaches this, and this section's own Fig 18.3 strip says public keys "are moving to post-quantum algorithms now". NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 2024) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. As written, the sentence suggests RSA stays until the quantum machine arrives.
findings.fix: "RSA is already being retired, ahead of the error-corrected quantum computers (the logical qubits of Chapter 14) that could run Shor's algorithm at scale, and particular libraries will become archaic."

findings.quote: decide now: C's late vote may disagree, safety lost
findings.problem: Fig 17.5, one figure earlier, shows A committing x without D's copy ('D late'), and calls that safe because a majority holds it. Fig 17.6 then says that deciding without slow C's vote loses safety, and never says that A needs C's vote to reach a majority. Read together, the two figures seem to contradict each other: why was it safe to skip D but not C? Nothing in the picture, caption or description resolves this.
findings.fix: Say in the picture and the caption that C's vote is the deciding one. In both worlds, replace the drawn label 'A has waited…' under the bar with 'A needs C's vote…'. Change the caption's first sentence to: 'If messages can be delayed without limit, a node cannot tell a slow peer whose vote it needs from a crashed one.' Change the <desc> opening to 'Node A needs node C's vote to decide.'

findings.quote: CP: stay consistent ... replica 1 x = 2 ... write x = 2
findings.problem: In the CP row, replica 1 accepts 'write x = 2' and shows x = 2 even though the link is cut, so it cannot confirm the write with anyone. The next figure, Fig 17.8, says CP systems 'refuse rather than lie' and tags every CP row 'write refused'. Its caption adds that they 'refuse writes they cannot confirm', and the section before taught that a node needs a majority. A reader comparing the two figures sees a CP system accepting a write it cannot confirm, and then CP systems refusing such writes.
findings.fix: Show that the side taking the write still holds the majority, and make Fig 17.8 say that only the side without one refuses. In Fig 17.7's CP row, change the label under replica 1 from 'write x = 2' to 'majority: write x = 2' (22 characters; it still clears 'error: can't confirm'). In Fig 17.8, change each 'write refused' to 'minority refuses'. Change the Fig 17.8 caption's second sentence to start 'Coordination services and ledgers refuse writes on the side without a majority;'.

findings.quote: hypervisor answers the trap, guest resumes
findings.problem: The t = 0 frame is the still that reduced-motion readers see and the frame shown before the figure plays. It shows only the two stacks and this bottom line: no 'add' mark, no 'read CPU id' mark, and no trap. So the still talks about 'the trap' without ever drawing one, and the mechanism the figure exists for (ordinary instruction goes straight to the CPU, sensitive one traps) is missing. The house rule (UNDER.md: 't = 0 is the complete still') is broken. A related flaw: the white add dot vanishes as soon as it reaches the hardware, at 2.6 s, while 'add: runs straight on the CPU' stays on screen until 3.6 s. The 3.3 s frame therefore shows that line over an empty picture.
findings.fix: In scripts/figs/fig_17_1.py, move the shift so that t = 0 falls inside the hold where the pink dots rest in both hypervisor boxes (story time about 4.6 s, line 'read CPU id: traps'). Keep each white add dot visible on its hardware bar from TA1 until the trap returns (TB3), so the still shows both paths with their labels.

findings.quote: each an application plus a kernel driver, which is where its traps land
findings.problem: The How it works strip says a type 2 hypervisor's traps land in its kernel driver. The picture draws the type 2 hypervisor as an application box beside 'browser', sitting on top of 'host OS', and the pink 'read CPU id' dot stops in that application box. A reader who opens the strip is told the trap lands somewhere the picture does not show it landing.
findings.fix: Drop the clause that contradicts the drawing: 'Type 2: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels, each an application with a helper driver in the host's kernel.' Alternatively, keep the clause and draw a thin 'driver' strip at the top of 'host OS' under the type 2 hypervisor, with the pink dot stopping there.

findings.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.
findings.problem: The prose just before the figure (ch17-k8s-p3) says the Argo CD/Flux versus Terraform/Pulumi point twice in a row: 'Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks... applying them once.' is followed straight away by this sentence, which repeats it. The figure's How it works item 'Elsewhere' then says it a third time. That is a visible duplicate in frozen text and a law 2 breach, and the owner will stop on it.
findings.fix: Delete the last sentence of ch17-k8s-p3 ('Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.'). Replace How it works item 3 with one that adds something, for example: 'Requeue. With nothing to fix, the controller still re-runs on a timer (every 30 seconds in the code below), so drift nobody reported is caught too.' Then regenerate the glossary.

findings.quote: A service mesh gives each service a proxy beside it, called a sidecar, and all its traffic goes through
findings.problem: No prose in ch17 mentions a service mesh, a sidecar or mutual TLS. The figure appears straight after Fig 17.9 with no introduction, so the caption alone carries the explanation. Law 3 says the explanation lives in the prose, and a careful reader meets a new concept that the text never introduced.
findings.fix: Add one sentence to ch17-microservices-p1 after '...with one service down and the rest still running.', for example: 'To make all those network calls survivable, many teams put a small proxy, a sidecar, beside every service and let a central service mesh tell each one how to encrypt, time out and retry (Fig 17.10).' Then cut the caption to: 'Each service's traffic goes through its sidecar, so encryption, retries and timeouts happen there, configured centrally; a failed first attempt is retried before either app knows.'

findings.quote: databases / ledgers, orders ... database / sensor data, feeds
findings.problem: The label promises 'which database picked which side', but after product names were dropped in repair round 2, three of the six rows are just 'databases', 'database with a primary' and 'database'. The CP side has 'databases' tagged 'write refused' and the AP side has 'database' tagged 'keeps answering'. These read as the same thing on both sides, and the label's promise is not kept.
findings.fix: Name the rows by role without products, and fix the label. Label: 'Fig 17.8 · CAP in production · which kind of store picked which side'. Rows: 'ledger databases' (CP), 'primary-based databases' (CP), 'feed and sensor databases' (AP; 25 characters, still clears 'keeps answering').

findings.quote: copy-on-write filesystems for software distribution
findings.problem: The label's subtitle promises copy-on-write, but the picture shows only the layer cache, the rebuild and the push to a registry. Copy-on-write is a run-time mechanism, and only the How it works strip mentions it ('At run time'). It also has nothing to do with distribution, so the subtitle mixes two ideas and describes neither drawing.
findings.fix: Change the label to 'Fig 17.2 · Docker image layers · rebuild and ship only what changed' (and the SVG <title> to match).

findings.quote: next pass: 3 = 3, nothing to do
findings.problem: The label says 'observe, diff, act, repeat' and the prose says 'Run forever', but the white marker goes round the loop only once in each 12 s cycle (the crash pass). During 'idle' and 'next pass: 3 = 3, nothing to do' it sits still at observe for up to 4.6 s, so the 'next pass' the line announces is never drawn. The marker also travels along straight chords across the inside of the circle, not along the drawn loop.
findings.fix: In scripts/figs/fig_17_4.py, send the marker round observe → diff → act → observe once during the idle window (about 1.3 s, before the crash) and once again during 'next pass', with the diff line reading '3 = 3' and act doing nothing. Move it along the circle's arc between stations rather than in straight lines.

findings.quote: orders | login | payment ... payment call timed out: retry
findings.problem: In both rows the second call leaves 'login' and goes to 'payment', so the picture reads as the login service calling payment, an odd call graph for a checkout. Fig 17.10 has orders calling login, which suggests orders is meant to be the caller of both.
findings.fix: Order the boxes 'login | orders | payment' and draw the two calls from orders: orders → login (pointing left, 'check user') and orders → payment (pointing right, the call that times out). Change the <desc> to 'orders checks login, then calls payment'.

findings.quote: plain HTTP to its sidecar, which sends it on
findings.problem: The yellow request dot never leaves the orders sidecar. Both the first try and the retry appear out of nowhere at x = 180, in the middle of the dashed mTLS line below the orders pod. The retry stops at x = 290, short of the login sidecar, and the next dot pops up on top of the login sidecar. The step 'which sends it on' is skipped at both ends.
findings.fix: In scripts/figs/fig_17_10.py, start both flights at the orders sidecar (100,210), run them down and along the dashed path, and end the retry by climbing to the login sidecar (300,210), placing the first try's failure X on the path.

findings.quote: routes, certificates
findings.problem: The control plane's dashed lines and the falling route/certificate packets pass straight through each pod's 'app' box before reaching the sidecar. This suggests the app receives the routes and certificates, while the point of the figure (and its last line, 'neither app saw the failure') is that only the sidecar deals with them.
findings.fix: Run the control-plane lines down the outside of each app box (for example, along x = 184 and x = 384, beside the pods) into the side of each sidecar, so no line or packet crosses an app.

findings.quote: 5 2020s modular monolith
findings.problem: At the loop seam, the bob arrives at marker 5 (modular monolith) and then drifts 8 degrees back toward 'many' for 0.6 s. It parks next to marker 2 (SOA) and then jumps to marker 1. A sign slip on the generator's 'on its way back' overshoot (angs[-1] + 8) makes every loop end with a swing back out toward SOA, the opposite of the story, and then a teleport.
