search_points.quote: He called it an a-machine, for automatic machine
search_points.missing: In p4's last sentence, 'it' means the decider ("so it cannot exist"), so a reader first links 'a-machine' and the bold 'Turing machine' to the impossible decider. They have to re-read back to p4's second sentence to find that 'it' means the imagined device (tape, head, rules).
search_points.close_with: name the noun: 'He called his imagined device an a-machine'

search_points.quote: could only sit where none of their letters matched the scrambled letter beneath
search_points.missing: The text never says that nobody knew where the guessed words fell in the message, or that they were lined up letter by letter against the scrambled text. 'Sit where' and 'beneath' describe a layout the reader has never been shown, and how ruling out line-ups helped the Bombe search for the setting is left for the reader to work out.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the guess was slid along the scrambled text, every line-up where a letter landed on itself was struck out, and the Bombe tested the guess at the line-ups left

fact_doubts: ch1-context-p3: Hilbert and Ackermann's 1928 Entscheidungsproblem asks for a procedure that decides whether a statement of formal (first-order) logic is valid, meaning provable. It does not ask whether 'any mathematical statement' is true or false. This is the usual popular simplification and p4's link sentence depends on it, so this is minor and needs no change unless the fact ledger wants it recorded.

findings.quote: passes through sixteen chapters and the Bridge
findings.problem: The caption counts sixteen chapters. Two paragraphs earlier, p2 says the eighteen waypoints are "drawn from fourteen of the chapters and the Bridge", and the picture's Ch tags do give 14 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17). Ledger line 607 reaches sixteen by adding Ch 15 (the boundaries) and Ch 18 ("the figure itself"). But p3 says Ch 18 is not a station, and the same caption sentence names Chapter 15 again separately. So a reader sees fourteen in p2 and sixteen in the caption and stops.
findings.fix: Caption, sentence 1: "One search, followed from a key's contact to Google's ranking and back, passes through fourteen chapters and the Bridge, and crosses four trust boundaries that Chapter 15 defends." This matches p2 and the picture's Ch tags. It does not bring back the old error ("every chapter").

findings.quote: V8's event loop picks it up (12)
findings.problem: The row reads "V8 · event loop · Ch 12", which goes against what Chapter 12 teaches. Ch 12 says the browsers solved the problem with the event loop, and that Dahl "took V8, stripped away the browser, added a C library layer (… libuv today) that runs the event loop". Its Node figure draws V8 "beside libuv, a C library that holds the event loop". V8 runs the JavaScript. The event loop belongs to the browser.
findings.fix: Row: tag "LOOP", text "browser's event loop", Ch 12. Desc: "the browser's event loop picks it up (12), and JavaScript, run by V8, builds the request (12)". Rerun check:dashes and the Gate 1 sweep for the row.

findings.quote: type google.com into your browser and press Enter … GET /search
findings.problem: p1 asks what happens when you type google.com and press Enter, and p2 says the trace "follows that keystroke". That keystroke loads the home page (GET /). The picture traces a search instead: JS on a loaded page builds the request, then GET /search, an index lookup and ranking. The search also cannot open a new connection: a page that is already loaded has done DNS, TCP and TLS. The strip says "Later searches reuse the open connection", which suggests the first search does the handshakes; it does not.
findings.fix: p2, first clause: "The trace below answers it for the Enter that page exists for, a search typed into google.com: it follows the keystroke from the moment your finger closes a contact on a key (…)". Strip item 3: "*Drawn as a new connection.* DNS, TCP and TLS are drawn as if no connection were open; a search from a page already loaded reuses the page's connection and skips all three, and once a browser has learned Google speaks QUIC, the request rides UDP where TCP is drawn here (Fig 10.9)."

findings.quote: no step of this path is written in either language: the code in the figure is C and JavaScript
findings.problem: This contradicts the book itself. Ch 5 says "The browser rendering this page is C++, C's best-known descendant", and Ch 6 says C++ runs browsers. V8, which is a station in this figure, is a C++ program, and so is the browser that receives the keystroke. A reader who remembers Part II stops here.
findings.fix: "Chapter 7 (Python) has no station because no step of this path runs Python; Chapter 6 (C++) has none of its own, though the browser and V8 that carry the keystroke are written in C++." The count of four non-stations (6, 7, 15, 18) stays true.

findings.quote: the response returns the same way up
findings.problem: The green return bar runs the full height, and its animated dot climbs from RANK to the KEY row (translate -409 from y=466 to y=57). So the picture says the response passes back through "contact closes", "key's number decoded" and the keyboard interrupt. That is a wrong mechanism. p2 ends the trip "onto pixels on your screen", and the strip says "TLS decrypts, TCP reassembles, the browser parses, the GPU draws".
findings.fix: End the green bar and its dot at the JS row (y≈208), not at KEY. Relabel the line "the response climbs back to the screen" (38 characters, fits from x=40). Desc: "The response climbs back through the network and the browser onto the screen."

findings.quote: types, lambda calculus
findings.problem: The book never teaches the lambda calculus: the phrase appears nowhere else in the five parts. The figure says each layer shows the mathematics the book taught for it, so this is a slogan with no lesson behind it (law 4). Pass 29 handed this over ("Label 'types, lambda calculus': the lambda calculus is never taught", docs/pass-30-figures.md) to be fixed in the figure's turn. It was not fixed.
findings.fix: Label "types, pointer arithmetic" (24 characters, fits). Ch 5 teaches that "the compiler scales pointer arithmetic by the size of the type". Desc: "languages, types and pointer arithmetic".

findings.quote: graphs, request–response
findings.problem: Graph theory is paired with "the web" (Ch 11 and 12), but the same chapter's ch18-future-p3 credits "graph theory (Chapter 9)", which is routing and so the networks layer. The networks row ("information, control") covers Ch 8 and Ch 10 and leaves out Ch 9.
findings.fix: Rows: "networks · information, graphs, control" (28 characters, ends at x≈376 of 390) and "the web · request–response". Desc to match.

findings.quote: The full stack · sand to web service · math at every layer
findings.problem: The label promises sand at the bottom and a web service at the top. The picture runs from "transistor" to "distributed", and the caption agrees with the picture ("from the physics of a transistor to the consensus of a thousand machines"). Sand and web service belong to the chapter hero, not to this figure.
findings.fix: Label and <title>: "Fig 18.1 · The full stack · transistor to distributed system · math at every layer".

findings.quote: Bottom to top is the order of the book: Part I builds the machine
findings.problem: The strip names five parts, but the picture uses three colour bands with no key: teal for Part I, purple for II and III, gold for IV and V. A reader trying to match colours to parts fails. In the next figure (18.2) the colours mean something else: cryptography is purple and the web gold, the reverse of 18.1. In 18.5 Part III is gold and Part IV pink.
findings.fix: Add to strip item 1: "The three colours group Part I, Parts II and III, and Parts IV and V." Recolour Fig 18.2 by part to match: Boole, Turing and the transistor teal; ARPANET/UNIX, the web and Linux purple; public-key cryptography gold.

findings.quote: queueing, scheduling
findings.problem: In the build-up, rows not yet reached are dimmed to 0.52 to 0.6 opacity for teal and gold, but to 0.8 for purple. At 4 s, with the instruction set outlined, the kernel to the web rows (purple) look almost lit (measured text 189 against 225 when lit), while the gold rows are clearly dim (146 against 219). The frame reads as if the purple rows lit before the current one. Fig 18.1.5 shows the same thing: at 4.3 s the network rows look lit (189) while JS and the Google rows are dim (153, 146).
findings.fix: In both figures, dim the white description and Ch text of the purple rows to the 0.6 the gold rows use (white text keeps 4.5:1). Keep the purple label at 0.8 if it needs that for contrast.

findings.quote: Most have been the reference in their field for a decade or more.
findings.problem: The caption only repeats. Sentence 1 restates the label ("grouped by part of this book") and the drawn header ("one shelf per part"). Sentence 2 restates p1 ("nearly every entry has been the reference text of its field for a decade or more"). The picture shows shortened titles, and the caption never says where the full references are.
findings.fix: "Titles are shortened to fit the shelves; How it works gives each in full with its authors, and adds the companions, two of them free online."

findings.quote: HTTP query → SQL parser
findings.problem: The fourth boundary in the picture sits above "INDEX · index lookup", and the desc calls it "into the database". Google's search index is not queried through an SQL parser, so p3's example names a step the picture does not show.
findings.fix: In p3's list: "service → index database". This matches the desc's "into the database".

findings.quote: the pulse travelling along a single arc through eighteen distinct mathematical and engineering structures
findings.problem: The figure has no arc and no travelling pulse. It is a straight vertical list with a white ring that steps down it. The prose describes a drawing that is no longer there.
findings.fix: "the request stepping down a single line through eighteen distinct mathematical and engineering structures"

findings.quote: education tutoring by language models
findings.problem: The six boxes share colours in pairs with no key: biology and education teal, economics and physics gold, governance purple, art pink. A pairing suggests a grouping nobody can read. The strip's "Two directions" names a real split (a tool for asking questions, against markets, identity and media where the software is the thing itself), and the colours do not follow it.
findings.fix: Colour by the strip's split: biology, physics and education in one colour; economics, governance and art in another. Or draw all six in one colour.

findings.quote: no step of this path is written in either language: the code in the figure is C and JavaScript
findings.problem: This contradicts the book. Chapter 5 says "The browser rendering this page is C++", and Chapter 6 lists browsers among what C++ runs. V8, the engine at the two Ch 12 stations, is a C++ program, and so is most of Google's serving stack. The figure also shows no code, so "the code in the figure" points at nothing. The line was added as the §4g row-650 fix and brought in a new error.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Chapters 6 and 7 (C++ and Python) have no station of their own: no step's job is taught there, though C++ runs underneath several (the browser and V8 are C++ programs)."

findings.quote: passes through sixteen chapters and the Bridge

search_points.quote: recently used data, so most reads never make the trip to main memory
search_points.missing: Nothing says why a small store of recently used data would answer most reads: that needs the premise that programs keep reusing the same instructions and data. The only program this reader has traced (Fig 1.8) reads every cell once, so the 'so' does not follow for them.

fact_doubts: Section title 'Von Neumann's insight': Eckert and Mauchly, ENIAC's builders, had planned to store instructions in memory for EDVAC before the First Draft (Eckert's 1944 memo). The report carried only von Neumann's name, and who gets the credit is still disputed. p3 avoids this by saying 'The report's central idea'; only the title gives von Neumann sole credit. Low.

ch1-vonneumann-p6 'their clocks went from thousands of ticks a second to billions': early stored-program machines ran at roughly 0.5 to 2 MHz (EDSAC about 500 kHz, EDVAC 1 MHz, UNIVAC I 2.25 MHz). So 'hundreds of thousands' or 'about a million' would be closer than 'thousands'. Low, wording is loose.

search_points.quote: A positive voltage on the gate pulls electrons up under the oxide
search_points.missing: The p7 repair holds in the prose: the gate draws free electrons out of the n-type source and drain, and p-type silicon has holes, not free electrons. The figure undoes it. In the drawing (frames t0, t2.667, t5.333), about nine free electrons sit loose in the middle of the p-type body at 0 V and rise straight up into the channel when the gate turns on. The caption and picture description say 'pulls electrons up', and the junction barrier p7 describes is not drawn. So the reader meets two answers to 'where do the electrons come from?' and cannot tell which is right.
search_points.close_with: redraw Fig 1.5: p-type body nearly empty at 0 V, channel filling sideways from source and drain; caption 'draws electrons in from the source and drain under the oxide'

fact_doubts: ch1-transistor-p1 'It filled a room thirty metres long', Fig 1.7 picture 'a U of cabinets around a thirty-metre hall', caption ch1-transistor-p17 'ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall' and 'in life the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip': 30 m (100 ft) is the length of the machine, its 40 panels counted end to end (Wikipedia ENIAC: '100 ft (30 m) long'). The room was about 30 x 50 ft, roughly 9 x 15 m, with the panels in a U about 80 ft along the front (Penn Engineering history page, https://www.seas.upenn.edu/about/history-heritage/eniac/). With the 10 m scale bar, the drawing's U is 30 m across its top alone, so ENIAC is drawn about 1.5 to 2 times too large. The hall-to-chip ratio is about 1,200x if the room is meant; about 2,000x holds only for the 30 m machine length. Not in §4g. Smallest fix: 'It was thirty metres long' (p1), with the figure text following.

ch1-transistor-p9 'Within months, Robert Noyce ... independently did the same on silicon': Noyce had the monolithic planar idea in January 1959 (patent filed July 1959). Fairchild's first working planar IC came in 1960. 'Within months' is true of the idea, not of a working device. Low.

Fig 1.6: the 2017 Epyc point is a package of four dies plotted as 'transistors per chip'. It is the only point that keeps 'follow the dashed two-year line for more than forty years' true: the last single-die point near the line is the 2008 Core i7. The strip discloses the four dies, and the point is already queued (docs/pass-30-figures.md, row fig-1-6). Listed only so it is not lost. Low.

ch1-transistor-p7 'the oxide is the same compound' (silicon dioxide): true of the classic MOSFET. Since 2007, leading-edge chips (including the 3 nm M4 the section features) use a hafnium-based high-k gate insulator over a thin SiO2 layer. Defensible at the book's depth. Low; report only if the owner wants precision here.

Chapter 1 says "program counter" in lower case, Fig 3.3's strip and the table call RIP the "instruction pointer", and here it gets a capitalised "Program Counter". The link between them comes after the strip and table have already used the new name.
findings.fix: "`RIP`, the instruction pointer, is x86's name for Chapter 1's program counter, and it is itself a register, so changing what it points to changes what the CPU does next."

findings.quote: Traps, interrupts, exceptions: the same mechanism, three names
findings.problem: The heading presents three synonyms. The paragraph under it (p4, with p1) instead makes "trap" the family and exceptions, interrupts and system calls kinds of trap.
findings.fix: Heading: "Traps: system calls, exceptions, interrupts".

findings.quote: The one door between the two worlds
findings.problem: The section title says one door. Its own Fig BR.3 (kept original) is titled "256 doors into the kernel", and p4 says SYSCALL has a separate entry point of its own.
findings.fix: Section title: "The only way into the kernel".

findings.quote: The path of one syscall
findings.problem: Chapter 1 and the section's own prose say "system call". The short form "syscall" appears here unannounced, right after the SYSCALL instruction is named, so it reads as the instruction.
findings.fix: Heading: "The path of one system call"; the strip's "syscall table" can stay once p2 adds "(syscall for short)" after its first "system call".

findings.quote: the kernel programs the local APIC timer
findings.problem: "Local APIC" appears here in Section 04 with no gloss. chBridge-timer-p2 calls the same thing "each core's interrupt controller", and the two names are joined only in Section 05's Fig BR.7 caption.
findings.fix: chBridge-timer-p2: "a counter in each core's interrupt controller (on x86 the local APIC, the circuit that delivers interrupts to the core)".

findings.quote: blocks of 4 KiB on x86-64
findings.problem: ch1-memory-p9 gives the same 4,096-byte page as "4 KB". The Bridge switches to KiB/GiB/MiB without comment. Also, the **pages** key-term mark sits here on the second explanation, while the first (ch1-memory-p9) is plain.
findings.fix: ch1-memory-p9: "fixed-size blocks called pages, typically 4 KiB (4,096 bytes)". chBridge-mmu-p2: "It translates whole pages (Chapter 1), 4 KiB on x86-64: ...".

findings.quote: a last-in-first-out buffer that grows as functions are called and shrinks
findings.problem: Part I uses "buffer" for a fixed-size block for incoming data (ch1-memory-p11, ch2-twos-p10), and the overflow sections put buffers inside the stack. Calling the growing stack itself a buffer blurs the term the next three sections depend on.
findings.fix: "...the _stack_: a last-in-first-out region that grows as functions are called and shrinks as they return."

findings.quote: ARM Pointer Authentication, in Apple Silicon, tags each return address
findings.problem: The prose never gives the abbreviation, but Fig 3.10's caption and Fig 3.11 (both kept original) say only "PAC".
findings.fix: "ARM Pointer Authentication (PAC), in Apple Silicon, tags each return address..."

findings.quote: There is one more negative than positive because 0 takes a "positive" slot.
findings.problem: Repeats ch2-twos-p8 almost word for word, a few lines above it.
findings.fix: Cut that sentence from the strip's "The slots" bullet.

findings.quote: A **logic gate** is a small circuit of a few transistors that takes one or two input bits
findings.problem: The previous section already defined it (ch2-boole-p7: "A switch circuit computing one of the three operations is now called a gate"). Section 03 then defines it again as a new key term.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence from ch2-boole-p7 and move its naming note to ch2-gates-p1: "A **logic gate** (no relation to the transistor's gate terminal) is a small circuit...".

findings.quote: Two switches in a row let current through only when both are on, a rule called AND
findings.problem: "Series means AND" is taught three times: here, in ch2-boole-p6 (Shannon's relays), and again in ch2-gates-p2. Chapter 2 is where it belongs.
findings.fix: ch1-transistor-p5: "Off and on can stand for 0 and 1, and switches wired together can follow rules on them that add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's (Chapter 2 builds them)."

findings.quote: a cache called the *translation lookaside buffer*, the TLB, which remembers recent virtual-to-physical translations
findings.problem: The TLB is glossed four times in one section: Fig BR.4's caption, its strip, p5, and Fig BR.5's caption ("the TLB, a small cache of recent translations").
findings.fix: Fig BR.5 caption: "Programs touch the same few pages again and again, so the TLB can answer most accesses at once. ..." (drop the gloss); p5: "So the MMU includes the TLB (translation lookaside buffer)...".

findings.quote: ASLR debuted in PaX (a Linux patch) in 2001
findings.problem: The text numbers ASLR "Defence three" after the NX bit (2003), and p1 frames each defence as following the one before. Fig 3.11 (kept original) also draws 2003 before 2001. Yet ASLR is the older of the two.
findings.fix: ch3-defenses-p6: "ASLR debuted in PaX (a Linux patch) in 2001, two years before the NX bit reached x86 hardware, and became default on most operating systems by the late 2000s."

findings.quote: 0x4011e7 → attacker's code
findings.problem: The attack panel fills the buffer with 'A's and aims the return address at a low code-segment address. ch3-overflow-p5 describes shellcode placed in the buffer and the return address aimed at it, which would be a stack address. The picture shows a jump into existing code, not the injection the text teaches.
findings.fix: For the owner: label the buffer bytes as shellcode and the address as one inside the buffer (e.g. "0x7ffd…e0 → shellcode in buffer"); or leave the figure and accept the mismatch.

findings.quote: SAME OVERFLOW · CANARY DETECTS IT BEFORE RIP IS HIJACKED
findings.problem: "Same overflow" suggests Fig 3.7's greet() with its 16-byte buffer. Fig 3.8 instead draws char buf[64] overrun by 200 bytes.
findings.fix: For the owner: "AN OVERFLOW · CANARY DETECTS IT BEFORE RIP IS HIJACKED", or redraw with buffer[16].

findings.quote: a mathematician who died before seeing what he built
findings.problem: ch1-context-p8 has Turing designing the Bombe, which he saw at work at Bletchley. The same hero's "Era covered 1936 → 1974" also stops short of a chapter that runs to the Apple M4 (2024) and Spectre (2018).
findings.fix: Hero lead: "...there was a mathematician who did not live to see the world his idea built." Era covered: "1936 → present".

search_points.quote: or leave a file's pages unread until needed
search_points.missing: Nothing so far says that a file (for example the program's own instructions on disk) can sit in a program's virtual memory as pages, so the reader cannot tell which file is meant or why it would have pages in memory.
search_points.close_with: say which file, and that its pages join the program's memory but are read from disk only when first touched

search_points.quote: pass the MMU's checks, because they write only into the program's own writable memory
search_points.missing: p10 has just said the MMU enforces execute permission, yet the attack runs instructions placed in a data buffer, and the reader cannot see why that execute step gets past the MMU (DEP is only named).
search_points.close_with: one clause: the stack used to be marked executable, and DEP is the defence that marks it not

fact_doubts: Table row 'L3 Cache | On the CPU package' (with L1/L2 'On the CPU die') suggests L3 sits off the die. In nearly all current desktop and laptop CPUs, L3 is on the same die as the cores (on AMD, the core chiplet). Older systems had off-chip L3.

ch1-memory-p9 says 'Between the CPU and the RAM sits the MMU', the same place p2 gives the caches. In modern CPUs the MMU and its TLB are part of each core and translate before or alongside the L1 lookup, not after the caches on the way to RAM.

ch1-memory-p1 says 'Each level holds a copy of part of the level below it', and the table lists HDD as the level below SSD. In most machines an SSD and an HDD are alternatives, not one caching the other (hybrid setups aside).

search_points.quote: Each stage takes one clock tick, or cycle.
search_points.missing: The reader learned 'cycle' as the instruction cycle, one round of the loop per instruction (p2; Fig 1.9 says one instruction goes round per cycle), so 'Each still takes five cycles' (p8) reads as five rounds of the loop, and nothing says that one round now spans several clock ticks.
search_points.close_with: say a clock cycle is not the instruction cycle: one round, fetch to writeback, takes several ticks, one per stage

search_points.quote: Fig 1.11 adds a fifth stage, MEM, for reading or writing data in memory
search_points.missing: Section 03 said code and data share one bus that carries one transfer at a time, an instruction fetch included ('the bottleneck the next sections return to'), yet in Fig 1.11 one instruction's IF and another's MEM touch memory in the same cycle (column 4: i1 MEM, i4 IF), and the reader cannot see how both reach memory at once.
search_points.close_with: a clause: fetch and MEM each read their own small cache (one for instructions, one for data), so they do not queue for the bus

search_points.quote: then loads one of 256 memory locations, picked by the byte's value
search_points.missing: The reader was told only that a byte is eight bits, never that eight bits make 256 different patterns, so 256 is an unexplained number and the attack's one-location-per-possible-value logic (on locations the attacker is allowed to read) has to be guessed.
search_points.close_with: ', one for each value a byte can hold (eight bits give 256 patterns), all in the attacker's own memory'; p2's hex sentence could carry the same count (four bits give 16 patterns, one per digit)

fact_doubts: ch1-cpu-p2 and the Fig 1.9 strip put the program-counter update at writeback ('the program counter moves to the next instruction'; 'move the counter on by the instruction's length'). That is the simple non-pipelined model. In a pipeline (p7, Fig 1.11) the counter moves on at fetch, or instruction 2 could not be fetched in cycle 2 while instruction 1 is only being decoded. Fine as a first model, but it conflicts with p7 for an attentive reader. Owner call: one clause at p7, or leave it.

ch1-cpu code block: '; This is roughly what C's "int x = 5 + 3;" compiles to' is not right. C compilers fold a constant expression even with no optimisation (gcc -O0 emits a single store of 8), so no compiler produces mov 5 / mov 3 / add for it. 'roughly' does not cover a different instruction sequence. Something like 'what C's "x = a + b;" compiles to, with a = 5 and b = 3 in registers' would be accurate. Low severity.

search_points.quote: without it, every program could read every other program's memory
search_points.missing: The boundary as taught separates Ring 3 programs from the kernel and the hardware, and the Fig 1.14 strip says Ring 3 is refused only the kernel's memory. Two programs both sit in Ring 3, so this reader cannot say how the rings keep one out of the other's memory. The figure also files RAM under hardware that Ring 3 'cannot touch', yet Fig 1.8 showed a program reading and writing memory with plain load and store instructions.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the kernel tells the CPU which memory each program may use and the CPU refuses the rest (Section 06 shows how)

fact_doubts: Fig 1.13 How it works, 'The cost': the idle gaps between jobs while decks were loaded were tackled by batch monitors and resident supervisors (GM-NAA I/O, 1956; IBSYS). Time-sharing (McCarthy 1959) went after the programmer's turnaround wait and interactive use. Calling the inter-job idle time 'the waste time-sharing set out to remove' gives it the wrong remedy. The bug-and-another-hour's-wait half of the same bullet is the part time-sharing really answered.

ch1-kernel-p8: 'In 1969 ... designed an operating system called UNIX around a four-word creed: everything is a file.' The name (Unics, then UNIX) dates from 1970. 'Everything is a file' is a later summary of the design, not a creed Thompson and Ritchie stated in 1969: their 1974 paper speaks of special files for devices. The point is low severity, but 'designed around a creed' reads as a historical claim.

findings.quote: Add one bit to the key and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.
findings.problem: This sentence comes straight after 'Factoring is kinder... each extra bit costs less than a doubling', so it reads as a rule for RSA keys and contradicts the sentence before it. It is also wrong for curve keys: Section 05 (fig-14-9 strip, fig-14-10 strip) says a 256-bit curve key gives about 128 bits of work, because a square-root search means twice the bits only square the work. The paragraph's closing 'At 256 bits of key' then suggests 2^256 work for a 256-bit key, which goes against the 256-to-128 table in Fig 14.10. The rule holds only for a brute-force search through keys.
findings.fix: Move the sentence to just after 'roughly O(2^n).' and scope it: 'For a search through every possible key, add one bit and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.' Then 'Factoring is kinder...' follows as written. Change 'At 256 bits of key' to 'At 2^256 steps'.

findings.quote: Chapter 15 returns to them.
findings.problem: Chapter 15 never returns to Spectre and Meltdown in prose. They appear only as labels in kept-original Figs 15.2 and 15.9 and in a list inside the fig-15-9 caption. The return that actually explains them is Chapter 16, Section 06 (ch16-numa-p4, 'The cache as a side channel'). A reader who reaches Ch15 looking for the promised return will not find it.
findings.fix: ch1-cpu-p11: 'Chapter 16 returns to them.'

findings.quote: from the silicon (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III)
findings.problem: Part II is The Software (kernel, C, C++, Python), not silicon. The Part IV opener says it correctly: 'Parts I, II, and III built the machine that moves bytes (silicon, kernel, network)'.
findings.fix: 'from the silicon and the kernel (Parts I and II) through the network (Part III)'

findings.quote: BGP hijacking (Chapter 9, Section 06; Pakistan/YouTube 2008) reroutes entire IP prefixes through a malicious autonomous system.
findings.problem: The example cited does not match what Chapter 9 taught. Fig 9.11 and its caption describe Pakistan Telecom's /24 as a domestic block, leaked worldwide by its upstream PCCW, with the traffic dropped (the Ch9 hero calls it a 'misconfigured router'). Nothing was malicious and nothing was routed onward. A reader who remembers Fig 9.11 will stop here.
findings.fix: '*BGP hijacking* (Chapter 9, Section 06; the Pakistan/YouTube leak of 2008) sends entire IP prefixes to the wrong autonomous system, by mistake or by design.'

findings.quote: in ECDSA and Ed25519 (the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses)
findings.problem: This says TLS 1.3 uses only the curve signatures. The same section's figure strip lists 'Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS for the server's signature', and Section 04 says the same (ch14-publickey-p6: 'the long-term RSA or ECDSA key only for signing'; fig-14-8 strip: 'where it appears it only signs'). Ch11's example chain (R11, ISRG Root X1) is RSA.
findings.fix: Replace the parenthesis with '(which TLS 1.3 uses alongside RSA-PSS)'.

findings.quote: The defence is clean and absolute: never build queries by string concatenation.
findings.problem: Chapter 13 calls parameterised queries a clean and absolute defence, under the heading 'The fix · parameterised queries · and only that'. Chapter 15 then opens its account of the same defence with 'Parameterised queries are necessary but not sufficient'. Fig 15.5's own strip resolves it ('Layer 2 is the real fix; the others exist for the day it is missing'), but the prose sentence contradicts Ch13 head-on.
findings.fix: ch15-web-p2: replace 'Parameterised queries are necessary but not sufficient, so the discipline is' with 'Parameterised queries are the cure wherever they are used; the danger is the one endpoint that skips them, so the discipline is'.

findings.quote: The attacks here are about confused deputies.
findings.problem: The sentence before lists three attacks, the third being 'a backend rebuilding objects from data a visitor sent' (deserialisation), and then calls them all confused deputies. ch15-web-p6 and Fig 15.9 file deserialisation under data-as-code, not confused deputy. The same paragraph later says the attacks reduce to two shapes.
findings.fix: Replace 'The attacks here are about _confused deputies_. A confused deputy is code that has authority...' with 'The first two are _confused deputies_: code that has authority to do something, tricked into using that authority on the attacker's behalf. The third is data the backend ends up running as code.'

findings.quote: Six structural attack patterns now name every specific exploit in this book.
findings.problem: ch15-culture-p1 adds a habit that is not one of the six: 'ROP (Chapter 3) and Stuxnet (Section 05) show a further habit: chaining pieces the attacker did not write'. Neither ROP nor Stuxnet appears in the six-pattern map (Fig 15.9). Nor does denial of service (SYN floods, Chapter 10, which the Ch15 hero lists among the book's attacks). The 'every' in p7 (and 'Every attack' in p1) is therefore false by the chapter's own account. p1 also lists 'SSRF (this chapter), and the Capital One breach' as if they were two examples, but Capital One is the SSRF example (ch15-web-p4).
findings.fix: p7: 'Six structural attack patterns now name most of the exploits in this book.' p1: 'Almost every attack in this book is...' and 'CSRF (Chapter 12) and SSRF (this chapter, the Capital One breach) are confused-deputy attacks'. Fig 15.9 is kept-original and stays.

findings.quote: 2003+ · randomisation
findings.problem: Fig 15.2 is titled 'Fig 3.11 extended through 2026', but it moves ASLR from Fig 3.11's '2001+' to '2003+'. ch3-defenses-p6 says 'ASLR debuted in PaX (a Linux patch) in 2001'. A reader comparing the two timelines sees the date change for no reason.
findings.fix: Owner call (both figures are kept-original): change Fig 15.2's ASLR label to '2001+ · randomisation' to match Fig 3.11 and ch3-defenses-p6.

findings.quote: Chapter 3, Section 06, traced the arms race from stack canaries through DEP and ASLR to ROP.
findings.problem: Chapter 3, Section 06 also explained CFI, the shadow stack (Intel CET) and ARM Pointer Authentication (ch3-defenses-p9). ch15-memory-p3/p4 then present all three as new, under the heading 'the contemporary defences'. The two accounts also disagree on scope. Ch3 introduces CFI right after 'A ret is an indirect jump', which implies CFI covers returns. Ch15 says CFI checks indirect calls and 'Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication'. The name is also spelled 'Control Flow Integrity' in Ch3 and 'Control-Flow Integrity' in Ch15.
findings.fix: ch15-memory-p1: end with '...to ROP, and named the answers: CFI, shadow stacks and Pointer Authentication.' Cut p3/p4 to what Ch3 did not give: Abadi 2005 and the call-site allow-list; PAC in Apple A12 (2018); CET since 2020. In ch3-defenses-p9 write 'Control-Flow Integrity (CFI), the compiler records where each indirect call may legally land', so both chapters leave returns to the shadow stack and PAC.

findings.quote: O(|R| × |S|), yet the right choice when one side is tiny
findings.problem: Section 03 uses big-O notation (O(|R| × |S|), O(|R| + |S|)) and 'a hash table' (ch13-sql-p4) as if the reader already knew them. Big-O is first explained in Section 05 (ch13-indexes-p1: 'Engineers write this cost O(N)...'), and putting a key's hash at a position in an array only in ch13-indexes-p4. Chapter 4 (ch4-scheduling table and strip) also uses O(log N) without explaining it, so ch13-indexes-p1 is the book's first gloss of the notation.
findings.fix: Move the gloss to its first use. In ch13-sql-p4, after 'costs N×M row-comparisons', add '(engineers write such a cost O(N×M): the work grows with the product of the two row counts)'. Keep ch13-indexes-p1's O(log N) and O(1) parenthesis, starting 'In the same notation, ...'.

findings.quote: Chapter 13, Section 06, covered the mechanism and the layers.
findings.problem: Defence in depth for SQL injection is explained twice in full: ch13-injection-p6 (ORM, least privilege, WAF, input validation) and Fig 15.5 with its strip (validation, parameterised queries, ORM, least privilege, monitoring). The two layer lists also differ (WAF in Ch13, monitoring in Ch15), so 'covered... the layers' points at a different set.
findings.fix: Keep Fig 15.5, the stronger mechanism. Cut ch13-injection-p6 to one forward pointer: 'Parameterised queries close the hole; Chapter 15 stacks the layers that catch the one endpoint that forgot them (Fig 15.5).' If the insight strip stays, make its layers match Fig 15.5's five.

findings.quote: Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962, 2013; mandatory in Chrome since 2018) closes that hole
findings.problem: The DigiNotar 2011 case and 'Chrome requires public logging since 2018' appear three times: in the fig-11-12 strip (Part III), in ch14-tls-pqc-p4, and again in the fig-14-12 strip ('Why it exists'). p4 also says twice what browsers demand ('mandatory in Chrome since 2018'; 'refuse to trust certificates that are not in at least two CT logs'). The fig-14-12 'Signing' bullet repeats p3. ch14-tls-pqc-p3 also explains the certificate chain again, which Ch11 already did (ch11-tls-p4, Fig 11.12).
findings.fix: In p4, replace the abstract 'a misbehaving CA could issue a fraudulent certificate...' with the concrete case: 'as when the breached Dutch CA DigiNotar issued a false certificate for *.google.com in 2011 (Chapter 11)'. Delete the fig-14-12 strip bullets 'Why it exists' and 'Signing'. Cut 'mandatory in Chrome since 2018' from p4's opening parenthesis.

findings.quote: typically 90 days, the standard of Google's Project Zero research team
findings.problem: The 90+30 disclosure clock is given three times: in p3, in the fig-15-10 caption, and in the '90+30' strip bullet. The strip's 'Why it holds' bullet restates p3's 'sustained by reputation... worse for everyone' almost word for word.
findings.fix: p3: '...tells the affected vendor, gives them a fixed window to fix it, and only then publishes (Fig 15.10 runs the clock).' Delete both strip bullets. The caption already gives the 90 and 30 days.

findings.quote: At GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson found public-key cryptography between 1969 and 1974
findings.problem: The strip bullet 'First, in secret' tells the GCHQ story (names, 1969 to 1974, declassified 1997). Three paragraphs later the insight strip 'The hidden Cocks' (ch14-history-p6) tells it again in full.
findings.fix: Delete the fig-14-1 strip bullet 'First, in secret'.

findings.quote: RSA is roughly 1000× slower than AES per byte processed.
findings.problem: Every point in the insight strip has already been made. Public key only agrees the key and AES carries the data: ch14-symmetric-p1 and ch11-crypto-p7 (which also gives the 1000×). Forward secrecy: fig-14-7 strip ('Fresh secrets... which is forward secrecy') and ch11-tls-p6. TLS 1.3 using RSA or ECDSA only to sign: fig-14-7 strip and fig-14-8 strip. The strip also says 'only for signing' twice within itself.
findings.fix: Delete ch14-publickey-p6. If one line is wanted, keep only: 'RSA is roughly 1000× slower than AES per byte, which is why it never touches bulk data.'

findings.quote: the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection
findings.problem: 'A join is a product plus a selection' is said four times in one section: p1 ('the last of them derived from the others'), the fig-13-2 strip ('a join is a product followed by a selection'), and p3 twice ('bolt a selection onto it and you have rebuilt the join from parts'; then this closing clause). The six fundamental operators are also listed twice (the strip, and p3's '(σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ)').
findings.fix: Keep p3's 'bolt a selection onto it and you have rebuilt the join from parts'. Cut 'the last of them derived from the others' from p1. Delete the fig-13-2 strip bullet 'The rest of the algebra'. Delete p3's closing clause '; the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection'.

findings.quote: Relational algebra works on sets: no duplicate rows.
findings.problem: The fig-13-2 strip bullet 'Sets and bags' (π drops duplicates, SQL keeps them unless DISTINCT) is the same explanation p4 gives two paragraphs later, at greater depth.
findings.fix: Delete the fig-13-2 strip bullet 'Sets and bags'.

findings.quote: Filtering first gives the same answer with fewer rows to join
findings.problem: Selection pushdown, σ(R ⨝ S) = σ(R) ⨝ S when the test uses only R's columns, is stated with its formula in ch13-algebra-p6 (which already points to Fig 13.3). The fig-13-3 strip 'The rewrite' repeats it in the same words.
findings.fix: Delete the fig-13-3 strip bullet 'The rewrite'.

findings.quote: A relation is a set of tuples that all share the same structure
findings.problem: Relation is defined three times in two sections: ch13-codd-p1 ('a table of rows in no fixed order (to a mathematician, a set of tuples)'), ch13-codd-p4 ('a row (tuple) in a table (relation)'), and again as if new in ch13-algebra-p1.
findings.fix: ch13-algebra-p1: 'In a relation (Section 01's table of rows in no fixed order), each row is a tuple and each column an attribute.'

findings.quote: Every insert and update must keep each index in step, so too many indexes slow every write.
findings.problem: The write cost of indexes is already in p1 ('each insert or update has to keep the index in sync'). 'PostgreSQL has hash indexes but B-trees dominate' is in p4, and the strip's 'Hash' bullet says it again.
findings.fix: Delete the strip bullet 'The cost of any index' and the clause 'yet almost every index people create is a B-tree'.

findings.quote: here nearly everyone is an adult, so scanning wins
findings.problem: Figs 13.2 and 13.3 run the same query on the same users and orders tables, but the details disagree. In Fig 13.2 only 2 of 4 users pass age > 18, and the Ch13 hero has 3 of 5. The orders column is 'item' in Fig 13.2 and 'product' in Fig 13.3's SQL. Dan is 17 in Fig 13.2 and 9 in the hero, which also adds Eli 27.
findings.fix: Fig 13.3: 'SELECT name, item'. Strip: '(here half the users pass, so scanning wins)'. Hero: make Dan 17 to match Fig 13.2.

findings.quote: lets a query optimiser parse a complex SQL statement into a tree of relational operators
findings.problem: Which part does what: ch13-sql-p1 and Fig 13.3 say the compiler parses the SQL into the tree and the optimiser then rewrites it ('parsed: the algebra tree | optimiser: push σ down'). Here the optimiser does the parsing.
findings.fix: 'That is what lets the database parse a complex SQL statement into a tree of relational operators, and lets the optimiser rewrite that tree algebraically into an equivalent but faster one.'

findings.quote: Read Committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement
findings.problem: The isolation levels are lower-case in p6, Fig 13.7, its caption and its strip (read committed, repeatable read, serializable), then capitalised in p8 (Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable), as if they were different names.
findings.fix: p8: 'read committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement, repeatable read one per transaction, and serializable also tracks...'

findings.quote: the optimisation tooling (Selinger's planner, the WAL, the B-tree)
findings.problem: Section 04 taught the WAL as the mechanism behind durability and atomicity, not as optimisation. Grouping it under 'optimisation tooling' mislabels what it does.
findings.fix: 'the machinery underneath (Selinger's planner, the WAL, the B-tree)'

findings.quote: The same experiment on Tux, the Linux penguin, has illustrated this since 2004.
findings.problem: p4 already describes the Tux experiment ('Encrypt the Linux mascot Tux with ECB...') and GCM ('counter mode plus a tag that detects tampering'). The strip bullets 'The famous one' and 'What to use' say both again.
findings.fix: Delete the strip bullet 'The famous one'. In p4, cut 'Modern systems use GCM, counter mode plus a tag that detects tampering, as TLS 1.3 does.' to 'TLS 1.3 uses GCM (below).' so the strip's GCM bullet carries the detail once.

findings.quote: Cryptography uses the same rules over a finite field instead of the real numbers
findings.problem: The group properties are in p2 and again in the strip's 'A real group'. 'Over a finite field, not the reals' is in the strip and opens p4. Curve25519, secp256k1 and 256-bit prime fields are in the strip's 'In use' and again in p4. p4's protocol list (TLS 1.3, SSH, Signal, WireGuard) repeats p1's.
findings.fix: Delete the fig-14-9 strip bullets 'A real group' and 'In use' (keep 'The numbers'). In p4, drop 'used by TLS 1.3, SSH, Signal, and WireGuard'.

findings.quote: SLH-DSA rests only on the hash functions of Section 02
findings.problem: One paragraph says three times that SLH-DSA is built only on hashes: 'a signature alternative built only on hash functions', then 'SLH-DSA rests only on the hash functions of Section 02', then 'a signature that needs nothing but a hash function'. The same paragraph also switches from ML-KEM to 'Kyber public keys are ~1.2 KB' just after renaming it.
findings.fix: '*SLH-DSA* (formerly "SPHINCS+") is a signature built only on the hash functions of Section 02. The first two rest on lattice problems: [lattice definition as is]. Neither basis is factoring or discrete log, and no polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for either. SLH-DSA is the hedge: if lattices hide a weakness, it still stands. The cost is real: ML-KEM public keys are about 1.2 KB against a curve's 32 bytes...'

findings.quote: NIST's 2024 standards replace the last three with lattice problems (ML-KEM, ML-DSA)
findings.problem: The primer's strip bullet 'After Shor' gives away the content of Section 06 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) four sections early. ch14-primer-p4 already points forward to Section 06, and p7 and Fig 14.13 then say it again in full.
findings.fix: Delete the fig-14-2 strip bullet 'After Shor'.

findings.quote: It must satisfy three security properties.
findings.problem: Chapter 11 told the reader 'Three properties matter: determinism, preimage resistance, avalanche effect' and called a hash a fingerprint 'uniquely identifying' the data. Chapter 14 gives a different three (preimage, second preimage, collision) and shows that collisions exist at 2^128 work, so 'uniquely' was not true. The two lists of 'three properties' do not line up.
findings.fix: ch14-hashing-p1: 'It must satisfy three security properties, of which Chapter 11 met only the first.' ch11-crypto-p4: replace 'uniquely identifying it' with 'identifying it for every practical purpose'.

findings.quote: the log is immutable in practice
findings.problem: Chapter 11 said Git still uses SHA-1. ch14-hashing-p1 calls SHA-1 'now-broken', and the fig-14-3 strip says collisions were produced in 2017. The reader is then told Git's log is immutable in practice with no word on why a broken hash is still safe here.
findings.fix: 'the log is immutable in practice, even on SHA-1, since forging a commit needs a second preimage, not a collision'

findings.quote: used for weeks to intercept (MITM) Gmail users in Iran
findings.problem: MITM is set in bold as a glossary term in Chapter 14. Part III never names man-in-the-middle, and the term is explained only in ch15-network-p2.
findings.fix: 'used for weeks to intercept Gmail users in Iran from the middle of the connection (a man-in-the-middle attack, Chapter 15)'

findings.quote: HKDF, built on HMAC (SHA-256 or SHA-384, by cipher suite), for every key
findings.problem: HMAC appears only here in the book and is never explained. A newcomer gets a second unexplained acronym inside the gloss of the first.
findings.fix: 'HKDF, built on SHA-256 or SHA-384 (by cipher suite), for every key'

findings.quote: the OWASP Top 10, the standard list of the worst web risks
findings.problem: Part III uses 'the OWASP Top 10' as known (ch12-security-p5: 'XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10'). The gloss arrives only in Chapter 13.
findings.fix: Move the gloss to ch12-security-p5: 'on the OWASP Top 10, the standard list of the worst web risks', and drop it from ch13-injection-p1.

findings.quote: the OWASP Top 10, the curated list of the most consequential web vulnerabilities
findings.problem: Chapter 15 introduces terms again that Chapter 13 already glossed, in different words, as if new. The OWASP Top 10 (ch13: 'the standard list of the worst web risks') and the web application firewall (ch13-injection-p6 named WAFs and said what they do; ch15-web-p4 explains it again: 'software that screens incoming web requests').
findings.fix: ch15-web-p1: 'Many of the best-known entries on the OWASP Top 10 reduce to...'. ch15-web-p4: 'Capital One's web application firewall (Chapter 13)'.

findings.quote: the SQLi / XSS / SSRF of this chapter
findings.problem: Three paragraphs earlier the same section places XSS in Chapter 12 and SQL injection in Chapter 13. Only SSRF is from this chapter.
findings.fix: '(the SQLi, XSS and SSRF of Chapters 13, 12 and this one)'

findings.quote: by reprogramming the PLCs that set the centrifuges' spin speed
findings.problem: PLC is used in p3 and in the fig-15-8 caption, but the gloss ('PLCs, programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves') comes only in p5.
findings.fix: p3: 'by reprogramming the PLCs (programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves) that set the centrifuges' spin speed'. p5: 'built around PLCs', with the gloss dropped.

findings.quote: Zero-trust architecture (late 2010s) makes that conclusion structural
findings.problem: Zero trust is dated to the late 2010s in p1 and on the Fig 15.7 label, but the strip says Google's BeyondCorp was 'described from 2014', the mid 2010s, the same era p1 gives EDR.
findings.fix: Strip: 'Google's BeyondCorp (described from 2014, widely copied by the late 2010s)'.

findings.quote: the attacker's server cannot present a valid TLS certificate for the legitimate hostname
findings.problem: 'TLS certificate verification defeats an on-path attacker' is said in p1, p2, the fig-15-3 caption, and twice more in p6 ('cannot present a valid TLS certificate'; 'cannot complete a TLS handshake for the target's hostname').
findings.fix: p6: '*DNS poisoning* (Chapter 11, Section 03; Kaminsky 2008) sends a victim to the attacker's server; *BGP hijacking* (Chapter 9, Section 06) sends whole prefixes there. Both end as in Fig 15.3: no valid certificate for the real hostname, so only denial of service gets through.'

findings.quote: one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program for that call site
findings.problem: 'For that call site' appears twice in one clause, a leftover from an edit. A reader will stop on it.
findings.fix: 'the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program.'

findings.quote: and weak passwords in rsh
findings.problem: Ch9 uses rsh as already known and says the Morris worm exploited 'weak passwords in rsh'. Ch10 is where rsh is first explained, as a command that logs listed hosts in 'without a password'. So rsh appears before it is explained, and the two chapters disagree about whether rsh uses passwords at all. Historically the worm abused rsh's passwordless trust between hosts and guessed weak passwords for rexec.
findings.fix: ch9-security-p2: replace 'and weak passwords in `rsh`' with 'and the trust between machines that let `rsh` (remote login) skip the password for listed hosts, helped along by guessing weak passwords'. Optionally, in ch10-attacks-p7, write 'trusted `rsh`, the passwordless login the Morris worm abused (Chapter 9): on the assumption…'

findings.quote: the same-origin policy, CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were retrofitted over thirty years
findings.problem: The chapter closer counts the same-origin policy among the defences 'retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked'. But ch12-security-p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say the policy shipped in Netscape 2.0, 'the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'. It came with the language, not after attacks.
findings.fix: ch12-security-p10: 'The security mechanisms around it began with the same-origin policy, which shipped with the language itself; CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and the rest were retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked.'

findings.quote: needs three of its primitives: hashing, symmetric encryption, and public-key cryptography
findings.problem: The crypto briefing promises 'enough to read the TLS handshake'. But it only explains public-key encryption (the public key locks, the private key unlocks) and Diffie–Hellman. Section 05 then depends on digital signatures: 'The signature, made with the certificate's private key, proves the server…', and Fig 12's chain 'checks each signature with the public key of the certificate above it'. That is the reverse direction, and Part III never explains it. Chapter 14 is the first place that does.
findings.fix: ch11-crypto-p7, after 'Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key.', insert: 'Run the other way, the pair gives a *signature*: the owner of the private key can sign a message, anyone holding the public key can check the signature, and nobody without the private key could have made it. That is how a server proves who it is (Section 05).'

findings.quote: Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows.
findings.problem: The only 'MAC' Part III has taught is the 48-bit MAC address of Chapter 8. Here MAC means a message authentication code, which is never expanded. The prose in ch11-tls-p2 calls the same thing 'a hash of the entire transcript'. So one term has two meanings, and one object has two names.
findings.fix: Fig 11.11 strip: 'Each Finished carries a keyed hash of the whole transcript, so tampering shows.'

findings.quote: Wi-Fi 6 at about 20 dB is allowed about 6.7 bits per hertz
findings.problem: Fig 8.4 labels Shannon's limit for 'Wi-Fi 6' as 6.7 bits per hertz. Three figures later, Fig 8.7 says Wi-Fi 6 packs '10 [bits] in each symbol' (1024-QAM). A newcomer compares the two numbers and concludes that Wi-Fi 6 beats Shannon's limit. The missing fact is that 1024-QAM is used only above about 30 dB.
findings.fix: Fig 8.4: relabel the point 'Wi-Fi at 20 dB · 6.7' and say 'a Wi-Fi link at about 20 dB' in the desc and strip. Fig 8.7 strip: 'Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024, 10 bits, only when the signal stands above about 30 dB (Fig 8.4); Wi-Fi 7 4096, 12 bits; both drop to fewer as it degrades.'

findings.quote: a misconfigured router in Pakistan to take YouTube off the air for the whole world
findings.problem: The Ch9 opener blames a router in Pakistan and says the outage hit the whole world. The section's own figure says the announcement was 'leaked worldwide by its upstream PCCW', that it won 'almost everywhere', and, in the strip, 'No malice… the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream, where PCCW passed its customer's announcement on without filtering it.'
findings.fix: ch9-hero-lead: 'It also let one bad route announcement from Pakistan, passed on unfiltered by its upstream provider, take YouTube off the air across most of the world for two hours.'

findings.quote: A forger never sees the reply, so it cannot hold a TCP conversation
findings.problem: The Fig 9.10 strip says a forger cannot hold a TCP conversation. Chapter 10 then tells how Mitnick did exactly that: with a spoofed source, he predicted the ISN and blind-sent the ACK and a command. The Ch9 rule is stated as absolute and the Ch10 story breaks it. The same strip says the SYN flood 'relies on' spoofing, while ch10-attacks-p2 says 'often spoofed'.
findings.fix: Fig 9.10 strip: 'One way only. A forger never sees the reply, so it can hold a TCP conversation only by guessing what the replies said (Chapter 10's Mitnick attack); spoofing suits single packets, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood uses it.'

findings.quote: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections, RFC 9000, 2021) replaces TCP entirely for HTTP traffic.
findings.problem: QUIC is introduced in full twice, and the second time it is presented as new. Both passages say it runs over UDP, rebuilds reliability, streams and congestion control, carries TLS 1.3 inside, and began at Google in 2012 before the 2021 IETF standard. Head-of-line blocking is also defined twice: in Ch10 as the TCP lost-packet stall, then in ch11-modern-p2 as the HTTP/1.1 slow-response queue. Neither passage refers to the other.
findings.fix: ch10-modern-p6: replace the head-of-line parenthesis with 'Loss in one stream no longer stalls the others, a gain Chapter 11 shows in full (Fig 11.15).' ch11-modern-p5: open with 'QUIC, met in Chapter 10 (Section 05), was built for exactly this: each stream is ordered independently, so a lost packet on stream A no longer holds back stream B.' Then cut the repeated list of what it rebuilds and the 2012–2017 rollout history.

findings.quote: Receivers periodically advertise a window (how many more bytes they have buffer space to accept)
findings.problem: The receive window is explained in Section 02 and again in Section 04, almost word for word ('senders never have more than that many in flight' and 'The sender never has more than that many bytes in flight'). The two passages also disagree: Section 02 says receivers advertise it 'periodically', while ch10-aimd-p2 and the Fig 10.4 caption say 'In every ACK'.
findings.fix: ch10-why-p2: replace the sentence with 'The receiver's advertised *window* (Section 04) caps how many bytes may be in flight.'

findings.quote: Part I closed inside a CPU. Part III leaves the CPU.
findings.problem: The reader has just finished Part II, and the Part III tagline right above says 'Parts I and II built one machine… Part III steps off the motherboard.' The first line of the part then skips Part II entirely, which reads as if the reader had missed something.
findings.fix: ch8-bridge-p1: 'Parts I and II stayed inside one machine. Part III leaves it.' The rest of the paragraph, which ties back to Chapter 1's transistor, can stay.

findings.quote: Every layer of the network stack, from here onward, exhibits the same arc
findings.problem: Two consecutive chapter-closing insight strips make the same point. Ch10 says 'protocol invented for a reason; protocol exploited; protocol patched'. Ch11 says 'Every protocol in this chapter follows the same arc… none of these protocols was correctly designed at first issue.' The same lesson also closes ch8-ethernet-p11 and ch9-security-p2.
findings.fix: Cut the last sentence of ch10-attacks-p9 ('Every layer of the network stack, from here onward, exhibits the same arc: …'), leaving it on 'State is the attack surface'. ch11-modern-p7 then makes the arc point once, with its examples.

findings.quote: By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests
findings.problem: QUIC/HTTP/3 usage is given twice, with different years and measures: 'well over a quarter of web requests' in 2024 (Ch10) and 'roughly a third of web traffic by volume' in 2026 (Ch11). The reader is left comparing two numbers for the same thing.
findings.fix: Keep one figure. Cut 'By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests, and the share is growing.' from ch10-modern-p6 and leave the 2026 figure in ch11-modern-p5.

findings.quote: Promises (standardised in ES6, the 2015 edition of the language's ECMAScript standard)
findings.problem: Fig 12.2 has just taught the editions as ES3, ES5 and ES2015, and Fig 12.4 labels the same edition 'promises, ES2015'. This paragraph adds a third name, ES6, and explains ECMAScript again as if it were new.
findings.fix: 'Promises (standardised in ES2015, Fig 12.2)'.

findings.quote: is just IEEE 754 (Chapter 2.6)
findings.problem: In the HTML only 'Chapter 2' is linked and '.6' trails after it. The link goes to #ch2, not to the floating-point section. 'Chapter 2.6' is a numbering style the book uses nowhere else; elsewhere it writes 'Chapter 11, Section 03'.
findings.fix: '(Chapter 2, Section 06)', linked to part-1#ch2-float.

findings.quote: became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986
findings.problem: The Morris worm is told again from scratch: Cornell student, aged 23, fingerd overflow, about ten percent of the internet, first conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Chapter 3 opened its buffer-overflow section with the same story, and Ch9 gives no back-reference. The machine count also differs: 'about six thousand' in Ch3, 'between five thousand and ten thousand' here.
findings.fix: In ch9-security-p2, introduce him as 'Robert Tappan Morris, the Cornell graduate student of Chapter 3, whose father…' and cut 'became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986' (Chapter 3 already says it). Keep the network-side material (re-infection, CERT).

findings.quote: described by Robert T. Morris (later of the worm) in a 1985 Bell Labs technical report
findings.problem: Ch9 names him 'Robert Tappan Morris'. Ch10 says 'Robert T. Morris (later of the worm)'. A reader may wonder whether this is the same person or his father, who is also mentioned in Ch9.
findings.fix: 'described by Robert Tappan Morris, three years before his worm (Chapter 9), in a 1985 Bell Labs technical report'.

findings.quote: At twenty-one, in his 1937 master's thesis at MIT, he showed that George Boole's nineteenth-century algebra
findings.problem: Chapter 2 already told the 1937 thesis in full: age 21, MIT, Boole's algebra in relay circuits. It also gave a different accolade (Goldstine's). Ch8 retells it as news and adds Gardner's, while only gesturing at 'Chapter 2 of this book'.
findings.fix: ch8-shannon-p2: 'Shannon is one of the strangest figures in twentieth-century science. Chapter 2 met him at twenty-one, putting Boole's algebra into relay circuits in his 1937 master's thesis; Howard Gardner later called it "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century." It was the moment Boolean logic stopped being philosophy and started being engineering.'

findings.quote: HTTP is the simplest protocol in this book
findings.problem: Chapter 10 has just presented UDP, three pages long with an eight-byte header, as 'the simplest thing you can do with IP' under the title 'The simplest thing that could possibly work'.
findings.fix: 'HTTP is simple enough to speak by hand.'

findings.quote: every protocol we have built (IP, TCP, HTTP, DNS) operates in cleartext
findings.problem: Chapter 10 has already built QUIC, which 'builds reliability, encryption… into one protocol', and Ch8 covered WPA. 'Every protocol we have built' is therefore not true as stated.
findings.fix: 'Up to here, almost every protocol we have built (IP, TCP, HTTP, DNS; QUIC is the exception) operates in cleartext.'

findings.quote: about twenty separate operations across four layers
findings.problem: The 'four' are the four exchanges of Fig 11.3: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. Under Chapter 8's model, DNS and HTTP (and arguably TLS) all sit in the single Application layer, so 'four layers' misuses a term the book defined.
findings.fix: 'it performs about twenty separate operations in four exchanges, one after another, and the page appears only at the end.'

findings.quote: Sixty parallel requests now share one connection
findings.problem: Earlier in the same paragraph the page needs 'HTML, then 10 stylesheets, then 30 JavaScript files, then 50 images', which is 91 resources. The 'sixty' matches nothing.
findings.fix: 'Every one of those requests now shares one connection, with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.'

findings.quote: Wi-Fi runs around 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz; cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
findings.problem: In the same section, Fig 8.2 and its strip give Wi-Fi '2.4, 5 and 6 GHz' and cellular 'from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz'. Fig 8.7's strip then says '2.4 or 5 GHz'. That is three versions of the same bands.
findings.fix: ch8-substrates-p4: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.' Fig 8.7 strip: 'such as 2.4, 5 or 6 GHz for Wi-Fi'.

findings.quote: so light travels tens of kilometres between amplifiers
findings.problem: The spacing on fibre is given three ways: 'tens to hundreds of kilometres between repeaters' (p3), 'repeaters every 50 to 100 km' (Fig 8.1) and 'tens of kilometres between amplifiers' (Fig 8.2). One device is also called both a repeater and an amplifier.
findings.fix: Fig 8.2 strip: 'At 1550 nm fibre loses about 0.2 dB per km, so light travels 50 to 100 km between repeaters (Fig 8.1).'

findings.quote: Every diagram so far has assumed two devices on one wire
findings.problem: Fig 8.1 crossed the Atlantic through repeaters, and Fig 8.2 traced a request from laptop to router to provider to data centre. Both are multi-hop paths, so the seam misdescribes the chapter's own pictures.
findings.fix: 'Every diagram so far has followed a bit across a single hop: one wire, one Ethernet segment.'

findings.quote: The first standard Ethernet, 10BASE5 (10 Mbps over coaxial cable), used Manchester encoding
findings.problem: Section 04 introduces Ethernet and 10BASE5 before Section 05 introduces Ethernet itself. Section 05 then introduces 10BASE5 again ('the standardised 10BASE5… over a single thick coaxial cable').
findings.fix: ch8-encoding-p3: 'The first standard Ethernet (Section 05) used Manchester encoding because it could not afford to lose synchronisation on a long run of zeros.'

findings.quote: In switched Ethernet each link joins just two devices, so collisions no longer happen
findings.problem: 'Switches ended collisions' is said three times in one section: p4 ('collisions stopped happening'), the Fig 8.8 strip 'Today', and the Fig 8.10 strip 'No more collisions'.
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 8.10 strip bullet 'No more collisions'.

findings.quote: The first 24 bits are an OUI, bought by a manufacturer from the IEEE
findings.problem: The OUI split is explained three times: in p7 (with the B8:27:EB example), in the Fig 8.9 caption (with the same example) and in the strip bullet 'The halves'.
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 8.9 strip bullet 'The halves'.

findings.quote: the asker caches the answer for a few minutes
findings.problem: The Fig 8.9 strip says entries 'age out after seconds to minutes, depending on the system'.
findings.fix: ch8-ethernet-p8: 'the asker caches the answer;' and leave the expiry to the strip.

findings.quote: In practice the top three blur into the application
findings.problem: Why TCP/IP folds OSI's layers is explained four times in one section: in p3, the Fig 8.11 caption, the Fig 8.12 caption and the Fig 8.12 strip bullet 'HTTP as an example'.
findings.fix: Cut 'In practice the top three blur into the application, which is why the internet runs on the four layers of TCP/IP.' from the Fig 8.11 caption, and cut the Fig 8.12 strip bullet 'HTTP as an example'.

findings.quote: IANA handed out its last blocks of IPv4 addresses on 3 February 2011
findings.problem: The strip bullet 'The dates' repeats ch9-v6-p1 word for word ('at IANA's central pool on 3 February 2011, and at the regional registries over the years that followed'). The caption gives 2011 a third time.
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 9.8 strip bullet 'The dates'.

findings.quote: Twelve organisations run it as thirteen named servers
findings.problem: The strip bullet 'The root' repeats ch11-dns-p3 almost verbatim: twelve organisations, thirteen servers a. to m.root-servers.net, anycast, over a thousand sites.
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 11.5 strip bullet 'The root'.

findings.quote: TLS 1.3 uses Diffie–Hellman key agreement: each side sends a public half and combines the other's
findings.problem: The Fig 11.10 strip repeats AES's key sizes and CPU speed from p6 ('Symmetric'). It then repeats the Diffie–Hellman mechanics from p7 ('In TLS'), which Section 05 explains a third time in ch11-tls-p2.
findings.fix: Cut the 'Symmetric' bullet. Replace 'In TLS' with: 'In TLS. Section 05 shows the exchange inside the handshake (Fig 11.11).'

findings.quote: The resolver caches the answer for the time to live (TTL) the authoritative server sets
findings.problem: Chapter 9 taught TTL as the IP header's hop counter, which drops by one per router. Here the same acronym is a time in seconds, with no note that the meaning has changed.
findings.fix: 'The resolver caches the answer for its time to live (TTL), a span of time set by the authoritative server, not the hop count of the IP header's TTL (Fig 9.4): typically 5 minutes to 24 hours.'

findings.quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
findings.problem: The SYN cookie is built on a 'keyed hash' that is 'hard to forge without the server's secret key'. Cryptographic hashes are explained only in Chapter 11, Section 04.
findings.fix: 'a keyed hash (a fingerprint of those values mixed with the server's secret key; Chapter 11, Section 04 explains hashes) of the (source IP, …)'.

findings.quote: Classic Reno halves on a loss signalled by repeated ACKs
findings.problem: The Fig 10.5 strip in Section 04 uses 'Reno' as a known name. Classic TCP's variants (Tahoe, Reno, NewReno) are introduced only in Section 05.
findings.fix: 'Additive increase, multiplicative decrease: AIMD. Classic TCP (Reno, Section 05) halves on a loss signalled by repeated ACKs…'

findings.quote: browsers send it as the CORS preflight
findings.problem: CORS is used as a known term in Chapter 11. It is explained only in the Fig 12.8 strip in Chapter 12.
findings.fix: 'OPTIONS asks what the server allows, and browsers send it before some cross-site requests to ask permission (CORS, Chapter 12).'

findings.quote: read every byte of an HTTPS request from voltage to JSON
findings.problem: JSON is used as known in the Ch11 opener and in the Fig 11.4 strip ('a JSON Merge Patch… a JSON Patch'). It is introduced only in the Ch12 opener and Fig 12.2. The opener also makes for Chapter 11 alone the promise that the Part III tagline makes for the whole part, and ch12-security-p11 fulfils it at the end of Chapter 12.
findings.fix: ch11-hero-lead: 'By the end of this chapter you will be able to follow an HTTPS request from voltage to the page it returns.' Fig 11.4 strip: 'It is idempotent only when its format is: a patch that sets fields to values gives the same result applied twice; one that appends to a list does not.'

findings.quote: a handful of cryptographic primitives invented in the 1970s by mathematicians
findings.problem: The chapter's own briefing dates AES to 'NIST 2001' and leans on SHA-256, which is also from 2001. Only Diffie–Hellman (1976) fits 'the 1970s'.
findings.fix: 'plus a handful of cryptographic primitives, the deepest of them invented in the 1970s,'

findings.quote: (voltage on copper, IP datagrams, reliable TCP streams)
findings.problem: Chapter 9 calls them packets throughout. 'Datagram' has so far been used only for UDP (Fig 10.1).
findings.fix: '(voltage on copper, IP packets, reliable TCP streams)'.

findings.quote: its engineering is forty years of careful refinement
findings.problem: The same opener shows 'Era covered 1974 → present', and the section title below says 'written 1974, still in force'. That is fifty-two years.
findings.fix: 'its engineering is half a century of careful refinement'.

findings.quote: copper, fiber, radio
findings.problem: The Ch8 opener and the Part III contents entry for Chapter 8 spell it 'fiber'. Every other use in Part III, fourteen in all, is 'fibre', and the book's British spelling and 'centre' agree.
findings.fix: 'copper, fibre, radio' in ch8-hero-lead and in the Part III contents entry ('Physics of the substrate: copper, fibre, radio').

findings.quote: reroutes entire IP prefixes through a malicious autonomous system
findings.problem: This back-reference cites 'Chapter 9, Section 06; Pakistan/YouTube 2008' as a malicious reroute. Chapter 9's own strip says 'No malice. The block was a domestic order; the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream.'
findings.fix: 'reroutes entire IP prefixes to the wrong autonomous system, by mistake or by design.'

findings.quote: Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership)
findings.problem: In April or May 1995 the partnership already exists. Two paragraphs later, 'In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun' and renamed the language. Which came first?
findings.fix: ch12-eich-p1: 'Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, already in talks with Netscape over Java)'.

findings.quote: everything else in the next five chapters is what we build on top of it
findings.problem: Part III has five chapters, and this sentence is in the first of them. From here 'the next five' would run to Chapter 13, which is in Part IV.
findings.fix: 'everything else in Part III is what we build on top of it.'

findings.quote: The same methods, headers and status codes, but sent as binary frames with compressed headers
findings.problem: The Fig 11.2 strip makes Section 06's opening point ahead of time: 'the headers, methods, and status codes you saw in Section 02 are unchanged.'
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 11.2 strip bullet 'HTTP/2 and HTTP/3', or shorten it to a pointer: 'HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep all of this and change the packing (Section 06).'

findings.quote: generalising the linked-notes program he had already built for himself at CERN
findings.problem: p2 introduces the same program a second time ('a little hypertext program Berners-Lee had written years earlier for himself, called ENQUIRE'). Similarly, p5's httpd, WorldWideWeb and first-page details reappear in the Fig 11.1 strip.
findings.fix: p1: 'generalising ENQUIRE, the linked-notes program he had built for himself at CERN'. p2: replace the clause with 'design notes in Berners-Lee's own ENQUIRE'.

findings.quote: The first V8, in 2008, had no interpreter and compiled everything straight to machine code.
findings.problem: This repeats ch12-node-p1 ('V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code'). Likewise, the Fig 12.6 strip 'History' repeats ch12-node-p3's JSConf EU, November 2009.
findings.fix: Cut that first sentence of the Fig 12.5 strip 'Then and now'. In Fig 12.6 'History', keep only 'libuv was written for Node in 2011, to bring it to Windows.'

findings.quote: The policy arrived with JavaScript itself, in Netscape Navigator 2.0.
findings.problem: ch12-security-p2 has just said the same thing: 'introduced in Netscape 2.0, the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'.
findings.fix: Fig 12.8 strip 'History': keep only 'Cookies follow older, looser rules: they ignore the port, for one.'

findings.quote: passes through sixteen chapters and the Bridge
findings.problem: The caption says the trace passes through sixteen chapters. Two paragraphs earlier, ch18-trace-p2 says 'drawn from fourteen of the chapters and the Bridge', and ch18-trace-p3 names the four chapters that are not stations (6, 7, 15, 18): 18 minus 4 is 14. The figure's own labels agree with fourteen: Ch 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16 and 17, plus the Bridge.
findings.fix: One search, followed from a key's contact to Google's ranking and back, passes through fourteen chapters and the Bridge, and crosses four trust boundaries that Chapter 15 defends.

findings.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.
findings.problem: The paragraph's last sentence repeats the clause right before it ('Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks...'). This is an editing leftover and is in the published HTML. Fig 17.4's strip ('Elsewhere.') says the same thing a third time.
findings.fix: Delete the final sentence of ch17-k8s-p3, so the paragraph ends '...working out the changes needed (the plan) and applying them once.' Then either cut the Fig 17.4 strip bullet 'Elsewhere.' or reduce it to 'Argo CD and Flux watch a Git repository as the desired state.'

findings.quote: types, lambda calculus
findings.problem: Fig 18.1 says each layer is the mathematics the book built, but the lambda calculus appears nowhere else in the book. Part II (Chapters 4 to 7) never names or teaches it, so the reader meets an unexplained term in the book's summary figure. The figure's desc repeats it ('languages, types and the lambda calculus').
findings.fix: Give the languages layer mathematics the chapters actually taught, for example 'types, pointer arithmetic' (Chapter 5's 'Pointers as math', Chapter 7's dynamic typing). Change the desc to match: 'languages, types and pointer arithmetic'.

findings.quote: a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line
findings.problem: Section 03 uses 'cache line' as a known term. It is defined only three sections later, in ch16-numa-p1 ('the 64-byte block a cache stores and moves as one unit'). Part I never uses the term, so the gloss inside the store-buffer parenthesis depends on a word the reader does not have yet.
findings.fix: Define it at first use in ch16-lockfree-p3: 'a write whose cache line (the 64-byte block a cache moves as one unit) is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line'. In ch16-numa-p1, shorten the gloss to 'every cache line (Section 03)'.

findings.quote: Consistency (every read returns the most recent write)
findings.problem: One word now names two different properties. ch13-acid-p2 defined Consistency as ACID's C: 'a transaction that begins in a valid database state ends in one, with its rules intact'. CAP's C is a different property (every read sees the latest write), and the text never says so. A reader coming from Chapter 13 will try to reconcile the two definitions.
findings.fix: *Consistency* (not the C of Chapter 13's ACID, which keeps a database's rules intact, but: every read returns the most recent write)

findings.quote: The price of shared memory shows up the first time two threads modify the same variable concurrently.
findings.problem: The lost update is presented as new here, but the book has explained it twice already. ch4-ipc-p12: 'The price of sharing is coordination: if two processes each read a shared count of 5, add 1 and write back 6, one addition is lost.' ch7-gil-p2: two threads decrementing a reference count, 'one decrement is simply lost'. ch4-ipc-p12 also introduced the mutex ('Initialised to 1, a semaphore admits one process at a time, a mutex'), yet ch16-races-p3 introduces it as new ('The classic fix is a mutex'). Neither paragraph refers back, although ch18-final-p2 promises 'Every reference back is explicit'.
findings.fix: Open ch16-races-p1 with the back reference and keep only the new part (the instruction-level cause): 'Chapter 4 lost an addition between two processes, and Chapter 7 a reference count between two threads. Here is why, one level down: two threads each increment a shared counter a million times...'. In ch16-races-p3: 'The classic fix is the mutex of Chapter 4, a lock only one thread can hold...'

findings.quote: a speculative load used the secret to pick which memory location to touch
findings.problem: ch1-cpu-p11 (with Fig 1.12) already gives the full Spectre and Meltdown mechanism: speculative work, a secret-picked load, a timed cache read. This strip explains it again with no back reference. The two versions also disagree: Ch1 says each timed read 'reveals the byte' (one of 256 locations), while this strip says the secret is read 'bit by bit'. And Ch1 says 'Chapter 15 returns to them', but Chapter 15 only lists them; this strip in Chapter 16 is the real return.
