findings.fix: Replace the mechanism with a back reference and keep the new material (the cost of the fix, the side-channel lesson): 'In January 2018, Spectre and Meltdown (Chapter 1, Fig 1.12) turned the cache that thrown-away speculative work leaves warm into a way to read memory across security boundaries, byte by byte. The fix needed...'. If the mechanism stays, change 'bit by bit' to 'byte by byte'.

findings.quote: nearly eighteen thousand customers of a network-management vendor installed a routine update of Orion
findings.problem: ch15-defense-p6 already tells this attack: about 18,000 customers, a signed Orion update, a compromised build environment, and the response (SBOMs, reproducible builds, signed build provenance). This strip retells all of it and says 'Chapter 15 has the attack in detail'. Its new point is the cloud-era blast radius. It also glosses SBOMs and reproducible builds, which Chapter 15 used without explanation, so the explanations arrive two chapters after the terms.
findings.fix: Cut the strip to its new point: '*SolarWinds, 2020* (Chapter 15). The cloud era amplifies supply-chain compromise: one poisoned vendor update reaches every customer at once, across a trust boundary that sat in no customer's network.' Move the glosses for SBOMs and reproducible builds into ch15-defense-p6, where the terms first appear.

findings.quote: Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption.
findings.problem: The FLP result is stated three times: ch17-consensus-p8, the Fig 17.6 strip 'The theorem.', and p11. The escapes are listed twice: the Fig 17.6 strip 'The escapes.' (partial synchrony with Paxos and Raft, Ben-Or's coins, Dynamo) and p12, in the same order with the same examples. The closing line repeats p8's 'works around FLP by adding an assumption, and the assumption is the price'.
findings.fix: Cut the Fig 17.6 strip bullets 'The theorem.' and 'The escapes.' (the callout carries both), and delete p12's last sentence, since p8 already makes the point.

findings.quote: resolve into layers, follow the math underneath, locate the security boundary, name the historical decision
findings.problem: The four moves are listed almost word for word in ch18-intersect-p3 ('resolve into layers, follow the math, locate the security boundary, name the historical decision. Those four moves work in any computational domain'). ch18-final-p1 gives them again as prose, and ch18-final-p3 lists them a third time. That is three statements in the last three sections.
findings.fix: Keep them in the final note only. In ch18-intersect-p3, end at '...has, on top of that vocabulary, the discipline that produced it.' and drop the list and the 'Those four moves' sentence. In ch18-final-p3, write 'The reasoning skills the book asked for are not specific to any year of computing.' without listing them again (final-p1 already has them).

findings.quote: New chips and new paradigms (quantum, neuromorphic, who knows what else) will sit alongside the stack this book described.
findings.problem: This restates ch18-future-p1 ('None of these will replace the stack this book described; all of them will sit alongside it as additional substrates'). The next sentence, 'Some of the specific content will go out of date; most of the structural content won't', restates ch18-future-p3's whole argument about what survives and what fades. Both points were made three sections earlier.
findings.fix: Delete the first three sentences of ch18-final-p3 ('The substrate is changing. ... most of the structural content won't.') and start the paragraph at 'The reasoning skills the book asked for...'.

findings.quote: thousands of small cores running in lockstep, each executing the same instruction on different data
findings.problem: The GPU's basic unit has three names, and the text never says how they relate. It is 'cores' here and in Fig 16.6's title, 'lanes' in Fig 16.6's picture, caption and strip ('about 17,000 lanes') and in Fig 16.7 ('if lane < 16'), and 'threads' in ch16-gpu-p3 and Fig 16.7 ('warp: 32 threads'). A newcomer cannot tell whether a lane, a core and a thread are the same thing.
findings.fix: Introduce 'lane' once and tie the three together. In p1: 'thousands of small cores (lanes, in GPU terms) running in lockstep'. In p3: 'a CUDA warp is 32 threads, one per lane, running in lockstep.'

findings.quote: no step of this path is written in either language: the code in the figure is C and JavaScript
findings.problem: One station of the trace is V8, the Chapter 12 engine that runs the event loop, and V8 is written in C++. ch12-node's strip already places C++ next to V8 ('partly in C++ on top of V8'), so the claim that no step is written in C++ is wrong and contradicts the book's own Chapter 12.
findings.fix: Chapters 6 and 7 (C++ and Python) have no station of their own: the code drawn in the figure is C and JavaScript, although the engine that runs that JavaScript, V8, is itself written in C++.

findings.quote: invented by a Lincolnshire schoolteacher who died in 1864
findings.problem: The figure directly below (Fig 18.2) places Boole's algebra at '1854 · Cork, Ireland', but nothing in the book ever mentions Cork. Chapter 2 presents him only as a schoolteacher from Lincoln (ch2-boole title and p1). Prose and picture appear to disagree about who and where.
findings.fix: The Boolean algebra in your CPU was invented by a self-taught schoolteacher from Lincoln, by then a professor in Cork, who died in 1864.

findings.quote: The kernel is a state machine over processes.
findings.problem: Fig 18.1 directly below gives the kernel 'queueing, scheduling', which is what Chapter 4 taught (ch4-scheduling-p8, queueing theory and Little's Law), and puts 'state machines' on the instruction set. Prose and figure disagree about which layer is which mathematics.
findings.fix: The kernel's scheduler is queueing theory over processes.

findings.quote: graphs, request–response
findings.problem: Fig 18.1 puts graph theory on the web layer and gives networks only 'information, control'. ch18-future-p3 says 'graph theory (Chapter 9)', and Chapter 9 is the network layer ('BGP & routing: The graph that nobody owns').
findings.fix: Networks: 'information, graphs, control'. The web: 'request–response'. Change the desc to match.

findings.quote: The transistor came out of three physicists at Bell Labs in 1947.
findings.problem: ch1-transistor-p2 says the transistor was 'invented in 1947 at Bell Labs in New Jersey by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, physicists in William Shockley's group'. That is two inventors, with Shockley as their group leader. 'Three physicists' reads as a different count.
findings.fix: The transistor came out of William Shockley's group at Bell Labs in 1947.

findings.quote: CPU | interrupt taken | Ch 3
findings.problem: Interrupts are taught in the Bridge (chBridge-trap-p4 'Traps, interrupts, exceptions', and Fig BR.6, the timer interrupt). Chapter 3 mentions interrupts only in passing, as one of the things that change RIP. The station sends the reader to a chapter that does not explain what the station shows.
findings.fix: Label the station with what Chapter 3 taught, which keeps the count at fourteen chapters: 'CPU | RIP jumps to the handler | Ch 3'. Change the desc to 'the CPU's instruction pointer jumps to the kernel's handler (3)'.

findings.quote: Make the read-modify-write one indivisible step (an atomic increment, Fig 16.4)
findings.problem: Fig 16.4 shows a compare-and-swap retry loop, not an atomic increment. The code block in the same section calls its atomic increment (fetch_add) 'no lock at all, single CPU instruction'. The pointer mixes the two, and the reader cannot tell whether an atomic increment is one instruction or a retry loop.
findings.fix: Make the read-modify-write one indivisible step (an atomic instruction: fetch_add in the code below, or the compare-and-swap retry of Fig 16.4)

findings.quote: Two threads doing a million increments each typically end well short of two million
findings.problem: The strip's 'At scale.' bullet repeats ch16-races-p1 ('two threads each increment a shared counter a million times... well short of it and changes from run to run'), and the code comment in the same section says it a third time ('counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run').
findings.fix: Delete the 'At scale.' bullet from the Fig 16.2 strip.

findings.quote: An arrow from each waiting thread to the holder of the lock it wants; deadlock is exactly a cycle
findings.problem: The strip's 'The wait-for graph.' bullet repeats ch16-races-p4 almost word for word ('a cycle in the "wait-for" graph: an arrow from each waiting thread to the thread whose lock it wants').
findings.fix: Delete the 'The wait-for graph.' bullet; the strip keeps 'Lock ordering.' and 'Livelock.', which add something new.

findings.quote: the serial share 1 − p costs the same on any machine
findings.problem: The 'The formula.' bullet restates the math callout (ch16-amdahl-p3 and p4: the formula, the p/N term shrinking, S → 1/(1 − p)). The 'Who.' bullet repeats p1 and the pull-quote attribution (Amdahl, AFIPS, 1967). The formula appears a fourth time in Fig 16.9's strip.
findings.fix: Delete the 'The formula.' and 'Who.' bullets from the Fig 16.8 strip and keep 'Other values.'

findings.quote: codified the alternative, the thread: a separate stream of execution
findings.problem: The thread is introduced as a new term, but ch7-gil-p1 already defined it ('threads, streams of instructions that share its memory and can run on separate cores at once'), and Chapter 12 relied on it.
findings.fix: Tie it back: '...codified the alternative, the thread (the shared-memory stream Chapter 7's GIL rationed): a separate stream of execution...'

findings.quote: out-of-order execution, branch prediction, caches, all the machinery of Chapter 1
findings.problem: Chapter 1 never uses the term 'branch prediction'. It says the CPU 'guesses which way it will go' (ch1-cpu-p9, Fig 1.12, 'Speculative execution'). Here and in Fig 16.6's strip the term is used as if the reader already had it.
findings.fix: out-of-order execution, branch guessing and speculation, caches, all the machinery of Chapter 1

findings.quote: a hypervisor on the System/360 that let many isolated CMS sessions
findings.problem: 'Hypervisor' is bolded as a new term, but ch4-security-p6 defined it and Fig 4.19 drew it. Fig 17.1's strip repeats Fig 4.19's strip (VT-x and AMD-V; KVM, Xen, ESXi, Hyper-V). ch17-containers-p3 explains Firecracker microVMs again after Fig 4.19's strip ('The middle ground') and ch4-security-p11 already did. None of these refers back to Chapter 4.
findings.fix: Refer back once and keep only what is new: '...a hypervisor (the layer Chapter 4 drew beneath virtual machines in Fig 4.19) on the System/360...'. In ch17-containers-p3: 'The microVMs Chapter 4 mentioned, AWS Firecracker (2018) and Kata Containers (2018), ...'

findings.quote: a container starts in milliseconds
findings.problem: The same paragraph later says 'the whole thing takes a second', and calls that a 'tenfold to hundredfold' gain over a VM's 'tens of seconds'. Milliseconds would be a thousandfold gain. Fig 4.19 also says VMs 'boot in seconds', against 'tens of seconds' here.
findings.fix: Where a VM takes seconds to tens of seconds to boot, ... a container starts as fast as a process, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel. Later in the paragraph: 'the whole thing, download included, takes about a second.'

findings.quote: the same problems return every fifteen years in slightly different costume
findings.problem: Fig 17.11 dates the swings at 1990s, about 2005, about 2014, about 2018 and the 2020s, which are steps of four to nine years, with one full out-and-back taking about thirty years. Neither matches 'every fifteen years', and the section title repeats the claim.
findings.fix: Architecture is a series of trades, not of progressions, and the same problems keep returning in slightly different costume. Change the section title to match: 'Architecture is fashion · the same problems keep returning.'

findings.quote: IV data and secrets, V the machines working as one
findings.problem: The parts' own titles, which Fig 18.5 uses, are 'Part IV · Data and Security' and 'Part V · The Modern Machine'. This strip names the same parts differently.
findings.fix: Bottom to top is the order of the book: Part I builds the machine, II the software on it, III the network, IV data and security, V the modern machine, many machines working as one.

findings.quote: Most have been the reference in their field for a decade or more.
findings.problem: The caption repeats ch18-reading-p1 ('nearly every entry has been the reference text of its field for a decade or more') with a different quantifier ('most' against 'nearly every').
findings.fix: End the caption after its first sentence: 'One shelf for each part of the book, each holding the books that go deeper than its chapters did.'

findings.quote: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout published Raft in 2014 as an understandable alternative to Paxos
findings.problem: ch17-consensus-p1 already gives the authors, the year and the design aim ('Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout's Raft (2014), which was explicitly designed to be more understandable than Paxos'), and p2 says it a third time ('a complete design built to be understood').
findings.fix: *Where it runs.* etcd, Consul and CockroachDB use Raft.

findings.quote: the control plane issues and rotates the certificates
findings.problem: 'Control plane' is bolded here, the bold that marks a glossary term, but in the mesh sense. ch17-k8s-p1 defined it first for Kubernetes ('the parts that decide what should run where'). The same bolded term now names two different things, and the glossary will carry only the mesh sense.
findings.fix: Unbold it here and write 'the mesh's control plane issues and rotates the certificates'. If the term needs a glossary entry, bold it at its definition in ch17-k8s-p1.

findings.quote: any two quorums must intersect in at least one node
findings.problem: The majority-intersection argument appears three times: ch17-consensus-p2 for Paxos ('any two of them share at least one acceptor... a witness'), here, and in Fig 17.5's strip ('Any two majorities of the same cluster share a node'). 'Quorum' is defined in p2 ('a quorum (a majority)') and then introduced again in p4 as a new italic term.
findings.fix: Refer back in p6: 'The reason is Paxos's trick again: any two quorums share a node, so two leaders...'. In p4, drop the italics and the redefinition: 'A quorum (the majority of Section 04's Paxos) is:'. In the Fig 17.5 strip, cut the sentence 'Any two majorities of the same cluster share a node...'.

findings.id: ch4-vm-p2 / ch4-vm-p7 / ch4-vm-p8 / fig-4-8 vs chBridge-mmu-p2 / chBridge-mmu-p5 / fig-br-4
findings.quote: Walking all four levels on every access would turn each memory access into five
findings.problem: ch4-vm-p1 says the Bridge already showed the MMU and TLB, and that this section covers the kernel's side. Then p2 defines the MMU again in bold. p4 and p5 redo the Bridge's 512 GB flat-table arithmetic and the split into four levels of 512 entries. p7 and p8 retell chBridge-mmu-p5 almost sentence for sentence: the 5x cost, the >99% hit rate, the translations dropped on a switch unless tagged. Fig 4.8 redraws Fig BR.4's walk down from CR3. Two details also disagree: p2 says the MMU is 'built into the CPU' where the Bridge says it sits 'between the CPU and the RAM', and the units change from KiB/GiB to KB/GB.
findings.fix: Keep p1 and turn p2 to p8 into a recall. p2: "Every load and store uses a virtual address, which the MMU of Fig BR.4 translates through the page table the kernel builds and keeps current." Keep Fig 4.8 as the one new picture (a real address split into its four indices) and cut p4 and p5 to the 2^36-pages count that Fig 4.8 needs. Replace p7 and p8 with: "A TLB hit (Fig BR.5) skips the walk. What the kernel has to manage is the switch: changing CR3 drops the old process's translations unless each entry carries an address-space tag (PCID on x86)."

findings.quote: so a NULL access always traps
findings.problem: The section opens by saying that dereferencing a null pointer is undefined, so the standard requires nothing, 'not even a crash'. Fig 5.8's strip adds that Linux builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks. The NULL subsection then presents a guaranteed crash, and Fig 5.9's strip says it 'always traps'. A careful reader will ask how undefined behaviour can always crash. The missing link: the trap happens only if the compiled code still contains the access. ch5-ub-p5 also says 'the very first page' where the strip says 'the lowest pages'.
findings.fix: Strip: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's mmap_min_addr), so a NULL access that reaches the processor traps." Add to the end of ch5-ub-p5: "That crash is the lucky case: because the dereference is undefined, the optimiser may assume the pointer was never NULL and delete a check that follows it, which is why Linux builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks." In p5, say "the lowest pages".

findings.quote: a lock on every object slowed single-threaded code, which is most code, by 30–50%
findings.problem: p2 says a lock on every object was what made earlier GIL removals too slow (30–50%). Fig 7.4's strip then says the successful PEP 703 build 'uses per-object locks'. The reader is not told why the same mechanism now costs 5–10%.
findings.fix: p2: "Removing it has been tried many times, but earlier attempts made every reference-count update atomic and slowed single-threaded code, which is most code, by 30–50%. PEP 703, accepted in 2023, lets the thread that owns an object update its count without atomics (biased reference counting), which cuts the slowdown to about 5–10%." The strip can then keep "per-object locks and biased reference counting".

findings.quote: a moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state, and reading it is allowed but tells you nothing
findings.problem: Two paragraphs earlier, p4 and Fig 6.8 show v1's pointers set to null, and the caption says 'v1 is left empty but still valid'. The glossary entry for move semantics also says 'valid but empty'. The closing strip then says a moved-from object is unspecified and reading it 'tells you nothing'. The reader cannot tell which applies to v1.
findings.fix: "Use-after-move: apart from a few types such as the vector of Fig 6.8, which is left empty, a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, so reading it is allowed but tells you nothing you can rely on."

findings.id: ch4-scheduling-p4 (CFS row) / fig-4-4 (strip) / ch4 closer ¶1 vs ch13-indexes-p1
findings.quote: O(log N) per scheduling decision via a red-black tree.
findings.problem: Big-O notation appears three times in Chapter 4 (the table, Fig 4.4's strip and the closer) with no gloss and no glossary entry. The book first explains O(N) and O(log N) in ch13-indexes-p1, in Part IV.
findings.fix: Table: "Each decision costs one step more each time the number of processes doubles (written O(log N)), thanks to a red-black tree." Fig 4.4 strip: "removing it and inserting a process each take one step more each time the tree doubles, so it stays quick with thousands runnable." Closer: "does this in a handful of steps even with thousands of processes".

findings.quote: converts it into a signal called SIGSEGV ("segmentation violation"), which by default kills the process
findings.problem: ch4-vm-p12 and Fig 4.9 already teach this path: an unmapped address such as NULL, a page fault, SIGSEGV, the program killed with 'segmentation fault'. ch4-ipc teaches signals. ch5-ub-p5 introduces SIGSEGV as if it were new ('a signal called') and retells the whole path. Fig 5.9's own strip admits it is Fig 4.9's invalid exit.
findings.fix: Rewrite p5 as a recall: "NULL, the pointer value 0, points nowhere by convention, and the kernel leaves the lowest pages of every address space unmapped, so a NULL access takes the invalid exit of Fig 4.9: SIGSEGV, and the 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)' that has greeted C programmers for fifty years." Then add the undefined-behaviour point from the finding above.

findings.id: fig-5-3 (caption ch5-bell-labs-p8) / fig-5-2 (strip) / ch5-bell-labs-p5 vs ch5-portability-p7
findings.quote: which is why C, unlike B, gave its pointers types
findings.problem: The same story (B saw only words, the PDP-11 addressed bytes, so Ritchie added types) is told in ch5-portability-p7, again in Fig 5.2's 'Why C' strip bullet, again in ch5-bell-labs-p5, and again in Fig 5.3's caption and strip. The PDP-11 is also introduced twice (ch5-portability-p2 'shipped in 1970', ch5-bell-labs-p5 'sold from 1970 onwards').
findings.fix: Tell it once, in ch5-portability-p7, and make Fig 5.3 its picture (add "(Fig 5.3)" after "had no direct way to reach one"). Cut Fig 5.2's "Why C" bullet. Shorten ch5-bell-labs-p5 to the machine itself: "The PDP-11 was a 16-bit minicomputer the size of a refrigerator, with eight registers, byte-addressable memory and a clean, regular instruction set. To a first approximation, C is a portable PDP-11 assembler." End Fig 5.3's caption at "by 1 and a pointer to an integer by 2".

findings.quote: A class compiles to a struct plus ordinary functions, its methods, at no extra cost.
findings.problem: p5 gives Section 03's content in advance: a class is a struct plus functions at no cost, and a virtual method costs one hidden pointer and one call through a table. ch6-classes-p2 and p3 then explain both again in full. The zero-cost principle is also already stated in ch6-stroustrup-p2 and the chapter hero, and it has its own section (05).
findings.fix: Cut ch6-stroustrup-p5 to: "What Stroustrup built was a deal: you may add abstraction without losing speed. Section 03 shows the deal in memory." Or delete it, since ch6-stroustrup-p2 already states the principle.

findings.quote: CPython's pipeline has four stages.
findings.problem: ch7-interpret-p3 and Fig 7.1's strip already give the pipeline: source becomes tokens, then an AST, then bytecode, then a C loop runs each opcode. ch7-cpython-p2 presents the same four stages as new and only refers back for the loop. An earlier pass flagged this and it is still unchanged.
findings.fix: Start ch7-cpython-p2 with "Section 01's pipeline, stage by stage:" and keep only what is new (indentation changes as tokens, the stack machine, ceval.c). Shorten ch7-interpret-p3's second sentence to: "Python source is compiled, at runtime, into bytecode: small, simple opcodes for an imaginary processor (Section 05 follows each stage)."

findings.id: ch4 closer ¶1 (no id; 'What you now understand' after ch4-security) vs ch4-scheduling-p3 / chBridge-timer-p2
findings.quote: decides which process gets the CPU at each microsecond
findings.problem: Chapter 4 and the Bridge say the scheduler runs on timer ticks, 'typically 100–1000 times per second', so every 1 to 10 ms. The closer says 'each microsecond', which is 1,000 to 10,000 times too often.
findings.fix: "decides which process gets the CPU next, hundreds of times a second."

findings.quote: so work that must respond quickly runs on time rather than merely fairly
findings.problem: EEVDF is said to make urgent work 'run on time' (the strip says 'latency-sensitive work runs on time'). A few paragraphs later, general-purpose schedulers 'guarantee nothing about the worst case', and deadlines need a real-time kernel. A reader may conclude that Linux's default scheduler now meets deadlines.
findings.fix: p5: "so work that must respond quickly gets the CPU sooner, rather than merely in turn." Strip: "so latency-sensitive work is picked sooner, though without the guarantee a real-time kernel gives."

findings.quote: you give up an order of magnitude of performance
findings.problem: The hero promises a 10x cost. The chapter's own numbers are much larger: 'hundreds of CPU instructions' per statement (ch7-interpret-p3), nine multi-instruction steps against one add (Fig 7.7), and about 10,000x for pure-Python matrix multiply (Fig 7.9). An earlier pass flagged this and left it because heroes were treated as untouchable. Heroes are not on the current owner-text list, but this may still be an owner call.
findings.fix: "you give up much of the machine's speed, a hundredfold or more in a pure-Python loop, and you get back code that reads like the pseudocode in your head."

findings.id: ch6-classes h3 'Inheritance is layout' (no id) vs fig-6-4
findings.quote: Inheritance is layout
findings.problem: The subheading promises the layout of inheritance (ch6-classes-p1: 'a Circle object begins with a complete Shape'), but only Fig 6.4 sits under it, and Fig 6.4 shows dispatch through a vtable slot. There is no prose under the heading. An earlier pass flagged this and it is unchanged.
findings.fix: Rename the heading "One call, many classes", or add one sentence under it: "A Circle object begins with a complete Shape, its vptr first, so code compiled for a Shape finds every field where it expects; Fig 6.4 shows what that buys."

findings.quote: one misbehaving program that never yields freezes the entire machine

fact_doubts: ch2-boole-p5: the dates are right (Boole died in 1864, the electron was found in 1897, so 33 years). The reasoning is not. The colon presents the electron as the reason Boole never saw electricity used in computing, but electricity was used in computing before 1897: Hollerith's electric tabulator ran the 1890 US census, and relays and the telegraph already existed in Boole's lifetime. The clause after the colon does not support the claim before it.

ch2-boole-p1: both ages are true only as upper limits and read like milestones. Boole opened his own school in Lincoln at 19, in 1834 (MacTutor; Wikipedia 'George Boole'), not 'by twenty-six'. His first paper appeared in the Cambridge Mathematical Journal in 1840-41, at about 24-25, and he won the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1844, at 28, so 'by thirty-two was publishing original mathematics' undersells him. MacTutor also says he learned Latin from a tutor (William Brooke), not on his own. Wikipedia says he may have.

fig-2-2 (picture label 'BOOLE · 1847' above two overlapping circles, caption 'Boole's A · B'): overlapping-circle diagrams are Venn's, from 1880, after Euler's circles. Boole worked only in symbols and wrote xy, not A · B. The drawing presents a later picture and notation as Boole's own from 1847. Low severity: the caption describes the circles as a picture of the idea, not as Boole's drawing.

fact_doubts: ch2-twos-p10: 'an Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch'. The Lions inquiry report puts the complete loss of guidance at 37 s after main-engine ignition (H0), which is 30 s after lift-off, and the break-up from about H0 + 39 s. So '37 seconds after launch' mixes up the two clocks. Also, the strip sets the case right after the silent wrap, so a reader will assume the value wrapped. It did not: the 64-bit float to 16-bit signed conversion raised an Operand Error that nothing handled, and that shut down both inertial reference units. (Source: Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report, 1996, https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~arnold/disasters/ariane5rep.html.)

fact_doubts: Fig 2.11 desc ('a double keeps only the first 52 bits and rounds') and the words drawn ('a double keeps 52 bits'): a double keeps the 52 bits after the implied leading 1, which is 53 significant bits counted from the first 1. It does not keep the first 52 bits after the binary point, because the exponent absorbs the leading zeros of 0.0001... Low severity, but read literally it contradicts p6, which this reader has just learned.

Code-block comment after ch2-float-p7 ('cutting off the infinite repeating binary fraction'): IEEE 754 rounds 0.1 to the nearest double, which here is upward (0.1000000000000000055511...). It does not truncate. Truncating would give the double below, 0.0999999999999999916733..., the opposite sign of error. The comment just above it, 'In binary, 0.1 is actually approximately:', is followed by a decimal string. It means the stored binary value written out in decimal.

ch2-float-p1 lists C among languages whose answer is 0.30000000000000004. The computed value is the same double in C, but C prints that string only with %.17g. Its default %f prints 0.300000 and %g prints 0.3. 'The answer' holds for the value, so this is a note only.

Fig 2.12 / ch2-float-p11 Patriot numbers: 0.000000095 s per tick, 3.6 million ticks, 0.34 s, 28 killed, 25 February 1991 and the fix arriving the next day all check out against Skeel (SIAM News 1992) and GAO/IMTEC-92-26. The ~570 m figure is the popular estimate, 0.34 s x 1,676 m/s. The GAO table gives a 687 m range-gate shift at 100 hours. In the real fault, the improved time conversion was used in some code paths and not others, so two times carrying different errors were subtracted; a uniform clock lag on its own would have cancelled out. The book's simplification is fine at its depth. Note only.

fact_doubts: Fig 3.6 draws main's frame with "main's variables" above "main's rbp", which in this grows-down drawing puts the variables at a higher address than the saved rbp. In a real x86-64 frame the saved rbp sits at the top, just under the return address, and the local variables go below it at rbp minus an offset. Fig 3.2's [rbp-4] and Fig 3.7's buffer / saved rbp / return address order both show it that way, so Fig 3.6 reverses the order inside main's frame.

ch3-call-p6 says "The CPU has no way to verify" the return address. That holds for plain call/ret. Unless a later section qualifies it, the sentence is too absolute.

fact_doubts: chBridge-mode-p6: 'one instruction (SYSRET on x86-64 ...) switches the CPU to Ring 3 and jumps to the start of the first user program'. Linux x86-64 enters its first user process through the IRET path: ret_from_fork_asm ends in swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode, which runs IRETQ. SYSRET is the fast return from a system call. Also, ARM's ERET goes to EL0, and ARM has exception levels, not rings, so 'Ring 3' is loose for ARM. Suggest 'SYSRET or IRET'.

chBridge-mode-p4: IN and OUT are not strictly reserved for Ring 0. They run in Ring 3 when CPL <= IOPL or when the TSS I/O permission bitmap allows the port (Linux ioperm/iopl). 'Reserved for Ring 0' describes the default, not a fixed rule. Low.

fig-br-1 How it works, #GP: 'no error code comes back'. #GP does push an error code (often 0) for the kernel's handler. The phrase means the program gets nothing back, as the old caption made clear, but it can read as a claim about the hardware. Low.

The reader cannot tell which way addresses run in this drawing, and cannot square it with 'the stack grows downward'.

search_points.quote: an entry for every page a process could address would take 512 GiB
search_points.missing: The reader cannot rebuild 512 GiB. The book never says how much a process can address (48 bits, so 2^36 pages) or how big an entry is (8 bytes). Chapter 1's 'seemingly gigabytes long' (ch1-memory-p8) works out to a table of a few megabytes, so the number reads as a contradiction, and 4 × 9 + 12 = 48 bits on a 64-bit machine is left unexplained too.

search_points.quote: so a trap lands in kernel code whichever process was running
search_points.missing: The reader is never told that a trap leaves CR3 unchanged, so the kernel's entry address is still translated through the running process's own tables. Without that step, nothing explains why every process's tables must map the kernel.

fact_doubts: Fig BR.4 picture description: 'a store to the next page up, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010'. With 4 KiB pages the offset is the last three hex digits, so 0x7fff_a3c4_0010 is on page 0x7_fffa_3c40, and 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 is 0x10000 bytes (64 KiB, 16 pages) higher. The next page up would be 0x7fff_a3c4_1010. Fig BR.5's labels 'a3c4 -> a200' and 'a3c5 -> b731' reuse BR.4's four-digit underscore groups as if they were page numbers, but those digits are address bits 16 to 31, not the page number. A reader who checks against 'last twelve bits = offset' finds the two figures disagree.

p4 'The kernel never runs the walk itself': true on x86-64 and ARM64, which walk the tables in hardware. Some architectures (MIPS, older SPARC) refill the TLB in kernel software on every miss. The section is set on x86-64, so this is minor, but the sentence reads as universal.

p1 and Fig BR.4 title 'between the CPU and the RAM': the MMU and TLB sit inside each core, ahead of even the L1 cache. p7's 'Each core has its own TLB' implies this, which sits a little oddly next to 'between the CPU and the RAM'. Logically right as a simplification, so minor.

search_points.quote: using details no real fault produced

A reader who remembers Fig 3.4 (RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9) sees what looks like a collision. More exact: 'in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, R9' or 'in registers, much as for a function call'.

chBridge-trap-p3 (caption), 'typically in under a microsecond': true of the bare crossing (tens to a few hundred ns, even with mitigations). But the sentence also covers 'the kernel does the work', and a write to a terminal often takes a few microseconds. Low; 'typically' partly covers it.

search_points.quote: to stop nearly all of them on a core with a single task
search_points.missing: p1 says a stuck program can only be taken back by the tick, and p5 says even killing a misbehaving program depends on it. The sentence that follows only answers the sharing question.

fact_doubts: chBridge-timer-p2 calls the hardware timer 'a counter in each core's interrupt controller'. That holds for x86 (the local APIC timer). On ARM, which the How it works strip names, the generic timer belongs to the core itself, and the interrupt controller (GIC) only delivers its interrupt. Low severity: the sentence states the x86 arrangement as if it were universal.

chBridge-timer-p2 lists the steps as 'restores that program's registers, points CR3 at its page tables and returns into it', which reads as an order. In Linux the CR3 write (switch_mm) comes before the new program's user registers are restored on the return to user mode. Low severity: correct if read as a set of actions, slightly off if read as a sequence.

search_points.quote: the C library's `system()` called with `"/bin/sh"`
search_points.missing: Fig 3.4 taught that system()'s argument must be in RDI, but the overflow only writes stack memory, so this reader cannot say how the attacker makes system() run with "/bin/sh".

The Pass 29 owner-call fix left out the half that answers this ('on 64-bit cannot load the argument registers').

search_points.missing: The heading above p8 reads as if ROP beat defence four. p9 and Fig 3.11 then show defence four (CFI, shadow stack, Pointer Authentication, 2017+) arriving after ROP (2007) as the answer to it, so this reader re-reads to work out what 'it' refers to and which item is defence four.

search_points.missing: Severity low to medium: DEP marks data pages (the stack) non-executable, as p5 says. Code has to stay executable, so 'mark code non-executable' contradicts p5 and makes this reader stop. Already listed in docs/pass-30-owner-calls.md §B.

fact_doubts: Fig 3.9 (kept original): in Runs 1 and 2 the heap's address (0x55A8…, 0x55C4…) is lower than .text's (0x562B…, 0x55F1…), yet it is drawn above .text. search_points.quote: Then it makes one MMIO write, to a register called the doorbell
search_points.missing: The abbreviation MMIO appears here (and again in 'MMIO loads') but is never introduced: p2 names memory-mapped I/O with no '(MMIO)', so the reader has to stop and work out what MMIO stands for. fact_doubts: Fig BR.7 (low): the GPU frame buffer starts at 0xC000_0000 and the network card's registers at 0xC010_0000. That leaves the frame buffer only 1 MiB. A 1920x1080 screen at 4 bytes a pixel needs about 8 MB, and GPU frame-buffer windows are usually 256 MiB or more. So for this pair, the strip's claim 'the addresses shown are typical' does not hold. A gap such as the network card at 0xD000_0000 would be realistic.

Fig BR.7 How it works, 'Not cached' (low, defensible simplification): 'a frame buffer is write-combining, which batches stores but still sends them all'. Write-combining can merge repeated stores to the same bytes before they go out, so only the last value written to each byte is sure to reach the device. This does no harm for a frame buffer, but 'sends them all' overstates it.

fig-br-9 (drawn label and <desc>, severity low): 'no MMIO or DMA: no disk, no network' overstates the case. chBridge-io-p2, two sections earlier, names a third channel on x86: the IN and OUT port instructions. Port I/O alone can drive a disk (legacy ATA PIO through ports 0x1F0-0x1F7) and a network card (the NE2000). A reader who remembers io-p2 may stop at 'no disk'. Possible fix: 'no MMIO or DMA: no fast disk, no network', or leave it and let the closed strip's 'Not strictly one to one' cover it.

chBridge-synthesis-p6 (severity low): 'under every forced switch from one process to another, a timer tick that took the CPU back' is too strong. In Linux an involuntary switch also happens on return from a device interrupt that woke a higher-priority task, or from a reschedule inter-processor interrupt, with no tick involved. Fig BR.8 in this Part already shows an IRQ waking process A. The timer guarantees the kernel a turn; it is not under every forced switch. Possible fix: 'under the guarantee that a stuck process can be switched out, a timer tick that takes the CPU back', or 'under every time-slice switch'. §4g line 643 fixed only the 'took the CPU back' wording, so this change would not undo a ledger correction.

Checked, no doubt: 'Linux is more than thirty million lines of code, most of it drivers' holds (the tree is about 36 to 40 million lines in 2024-25, and drivers/ is roughly 60 percent of it). Note for the record: the Pass 29 P1 repair holds. p4 now names all five features (page tables, trap handlers, timer, devices, Ring 3). The cut strip bullet 'One level down' is gone from the live page. p5 now reads 'Part II, which reads the kernel as a real program', so the 'It' with no clear antecedent is fixed. Considered and not logged as search points: 'drivers, filesystems, network stacks' in p4 are passing example labels that 'and other services' glosses. A novice does not yet know that a filesystem is what turns disk blocks into files, so the gap between p1's 'files and networking' and p4's 'built on top of that minimum' would not register with them. 'hardware tables' in p5 is a roadmap phrase the argument does not depend on.

search_points.missing: The book has drilled that a Ring 3 program cannot touch hardware or reach a device's registers (ch1-kernel-p5, Fig BR.7's strip: only the kernel maps device ranges). So this reader cannot explain how a driver running in Ring 3 operates its device. p12 hits the same gap again ('a few kinds of driver run as ordinary programs in Ring 3').
search_points.close_with: one clause: the kernel maps just that device's registers into the driver's address space and passes its interrupts on to it as messages

search_points.quote: a Mach microkernel core and a BSD UNIX layer sharing Ring 0
search_points.missing: The two designs were set up as a speed-against-safety trade decided by what runs in Ring 0. XNU puts both parts in Ring 0, so the reader cannot say what 'sits in the middle' buys: does a driver bug take down one process or the whole machine?
search_points.close_with: say that with everything in Ring 0 it keeps monolithic speed and risk, and only the microkernel's message style survives inside

search_points.missing: Nothing says why a module needs this lookup or what it returns: a separately built module cannot know where in memory the kernel's functions sit, and the table gives the address each call should jump to. Without that, 'looked up by name' (and 'linked against', 'resolves' in the description and strip) cannot be explained back.
search_points.close_with: a clause: the table pairs each kernel function's name with its address, which a separately built module cannot know in advance

search_points.quote: He also predicted Linux, tied to the 386, would not last.

search_points.close_with: 'tied to one Intel chip, the 386, then in every PC'

fact_doubts: ch4-anatomy-p1 says 'The Linux kernel, as of 2025, is roughly 30 million lines'. Public counts put the mainline tree above 40 million total lines in early 2025 (Phoronix, around 6.14-rc1). About 30 million holds only for code lines without comments and blank lines, or for the 2021 to 2022 tree. Check against §4g. chBridge-synthesis-p4's 'more than thirty million' is safe either way.

ch4-anatomy-p10, 'lsmod on a running system lists hundreds of them': true for a typical desktop distribution (often 100 to 250). A minimal server or embedded build may list only dozens. Minor; 'often over a hundred' would be safe.

search_points.missing: Three paragraphs earlier (p12), writing to a read-only page was the standard example of an invalid fault that ends in SIGSEGV. Nothing says how the kernel tells this copy-on-write write apart from an illegal one, so the reader cannot see why this fault leads to a copy and not a kill.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the kernel keeps its own note that these pages are really writable, so a fault on one means copy, not kill

search_points.quote: A discard that fell between the copy and the write sent the write
search_points.missing: By the rule p15 just taught, a write that comes after the copy is discarded should fault again and get a fresh copy. The reader cannot see why it reached the file instead. The missing step is that the kernel carried out the write after its own check, and its retry treated the write as a plain read; only Fig 4.11's closed strip hints at this.
search_points.close_with: say the kernel did the write itself after checking, so after the discard the page it found was the file's own

search_points.quote: The kernel asks two questions, and three accesses take the three exits
search_points.missing: The first cause p3 gives for a fault, a page that has never been used, matches none of the three categories. It is legal but in neither RAM nor on disk, so the tree's 'page in RAM? no' would send it to 'read disk' when there is nothing on disk to read. Only the closed strip mentions a fresh zero-filled page.
search_points.close_with: half a sentence in p10: a page touched for the first time gets a fresh zeroed page, which is a minor fault

fact_doubts: ch4-vm-p11 and Fig 4.9 (ch4-vm-p13): 'Cost: milliseconds' for a major fault fits a spinning disk only. The book's own memory table (ch1-memory-p2) gives an SSD read as about 50,000 ns (0.05 ms). On a machine with an SSD a major fault costs tens of microseconds to about 0.1 ms, roughly 100 times a minor fault rather than 1000. The fix at UNDER.md line 1111 settled the ratio but not the SSD case.

ch4-vm-p2 says the MMU is 'built into the CPU', but ch1-memory-p9 and chBridge-mmu-p1 say it 'sits between the CPU and the RAM'. Both are true (it sits on the CPU die, between the cores and RAM), but a reader who has just read those two passages may stop at the apparent contradiction.

search_points.quote: O(log N) per scheduling decision via a red-black tree.
search_points.missing: The O( ) notation is never explained before this point (the book only teaches it later, in ch6-complexity), and the red-black tree is named before p5 introduces any tree. p5 later gives only 'stays quick even with thousands', so the reader cannot say what this trade-off cell claims.

search_points.quote: which rebalances itself as processes come and go, so it stays quick
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say why a tree finds and re-files a process faster than a sorted list, or what 'balance' protects, so a slogan stands where the mechanism should be. Fig 4.4's last frame then reshapes the whole tree (13.0 lands at the top, 12.4 drops to the bottom, 10.0 moves up) and nothing tells the reader why, although the description says 13.0 'goes back into the tree on the right'.
search_points.close_with: one clause: each step down the tree skips half the remaining processes, so thousands take about a dozen steps; rebalancing stops the tree growing into one long lopsided chain

search_points.quote: round robin and MLFQ give up average wait to start every job almost at once
search_points.missing: 'Wait' is never defined. The reader cannot see how round robin starts every job sooner than FCFS yet has a higher average wait (12.75 against 8.75), or why 'avg wait' and 'first run after' are the same number for FCFS and SJF but far apart for round robin.
search_points.close_with: define wait once: all the time a job sits ready but not running until it finishes, including the gaps between its turns

search_points.quote: Approximates SJF without knowing job length.
search_points.missing: The table (p4) says MLFQ approximates SJF, but Fig 4.5 gives MLFQ the worst average wait of the four (13 against SJF's 7.75) and the caption groups it with round robin. The reader cannot reconcile the two or say in what sense MLFQ resembles SJF.
search_points.close_with: say that SJF's gain is short jobs running first, which MLFQ gets when short or interactive jobs mix with long ones; here all four jobs are long and CPU-only, so it behaves like round robin

fact_doubts: Table, SJF row (p4): 'Pick the process with the shortest remaining time' is the preemptive rule (shortest remaining time first). Fig 4.5's SJF never preempts: A keeps the CPU after B arrives at t=1 needing 4 units, while A still has 7 left. Under the remaining-time rule B would take over and the average wait would be 6.5, not 7.75. The figure's numbers are correct for non-preemptive SJF, so the row should say 'shortest job among those waiting' or the figure should preempt.

Fig 4.4, last frame: after 13.0 goes back in, the tree is redrawn with 13.0 at the root, 10.0 moved up and the old root 12.4 dropped to a leaf. A red-black tree insert puts 13.0 in as a leaf (left child of 15.5), with at most a local recolouring or rotation, and 12.4 stays the root. What the frame shows is a full rebuild into a perfect tree, which a red-black tree never does. It also contradicts the figure's own description ('goes back into the tree on the right').

Fig 4.4, first frame: the CPU box says 'idle for an instant' while the next process is being chosen. At that instant the CPU is running the kernel's scheduler, not idling; the Bridge's Fig BR.6 labels the same gap 'kernel: tick, scheduler picks next'.

p10 (and Fig 4.6 strip): 'one server with random arrivals, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ)'. That formula (M/M/1) also needs random (exponentially distributed) service times. With fixed service times at 95% load the time in the system is about 10.5 service times, not 20. Something like 'random arrivals and random service times' would make it exact.

search_points.quote: the kernel looks up the inode for `/`
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say where inodes are kept or how a number like 4827 leads the kernel to one. That includes the first inode, for /, which no directory lists. Fig 4.12 also draws the inode outside the row of disk blocks, although p1 says the filesystem builds everything out of those blocks.
search_points.close_with: one clause: inodes sit in a numbered table on the disk itself, and / always has a fixed, known number

search_points.quote: UNIX took the inode concept beyond regular files.
search_points.missing: The reader has just learned that a file is an inode plus its data blocks, read through the block list (p3). A keyboard or /dev/urandom has no data blocks, so the reader cannot say what such a file's inode holds, or what a read does instead of reading blocks.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a device file's inode names a driver instead of blocks, so read and write run that driver's kernel code

search_points.quote: a socket arrives through a different door
search_points.missing: The book has never said what a socket is. The reader can only guess that it means p6's network connection, and nothing turns 'a different door' into its literal meaning: the connection is created by its own system call, not by open.
search_points.close_with: say a socket is a network connection, created by its own system call instead of open

search_points.quote: By default ext4 and NTFS journal metadata only (inodes, bitmaps, directories)
search_points.missing: p9 says every intended modification goes to the journal first and lands whole or not at all. The strip then says that by default file contents bypass the journal. The reader cannot square the two, or say what protects the data in p8's crash between writing data and writing metadata. 'bitmaps' also appears where the figure says 'free list'.
search_points.close_with: p9: by default only the bookkeeping is journaled, and the data goes to its place before the commit

search_points.quote: A change goes to new blocks, and one final pointer switch makes it current
search_points.missing: The reader has not been told that the filesystem hangs as a tree of blocks from one root, each block holding the addresses of the blocks below it. So 'which pointer' and why a new block forces a new parent and a new root have nothing to rest on. Fig 4.14 shows the tree later but calls it 'a file's tree' (p11 promises snapshots of the whole filesystem), never ties root and node to p2's inode block list, and never says why each parent is rewritten.

fact_doubts: ch4-fs-p9: 'every intended modification is written first' overstates what ext4 and NTFS do by default. The inode diagram's '12 direct' entries for a 24,873-byte file make the same assumption.

ch4-fs-p6: 'Your keyboard is /dev/input/event0' is too definite. The event number depends on the order devices are found, and event0 is often the power button or lid switch. 'a keyboard appears as /dev/input/eventN' would be safe.

The section's own figure shows this: its strip says 64-bit RISC-V's `addw` "adds 32-bit `int`s", the ARM line uses the 32-bit `w` registers, and ch3-call-p3 says the 32-bit `int` arrives in EDI/ESI, the lower halves of the 64-bit registers. Fig 5.1 is slightly inconsistent with itself. The drawing says "a in rdi, b in rsi", but its How it works strip (and ch3-call-p3) says the arguments arrive in `edi`/`esi`. fact_doubts: ch5-bell-labs-p1, 'In a windowless room' (low): this has been in the text since the initial commit (ecdaf33) and has no §4g row. Ritchie's own account (The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System) says Thompson found 'a little-used PDP-7 computer'. The pre-Pass-27 caption said 'in a corner of Bell Labs'. 'Windowless room' looks like added colour with no source, and 'discarded' (p1) and 'unused' (p3) also go further than Ritchie's 'little-used'.

ch5-bell-labs-p3, 'He started writing a small operating system for it, partly to play a space-travel game he had ported from Multics' (low): Ritchie's account gives a different order. Space Travel went from Multics to a GECOS Fortran version, and then Thompson and Ritchie rewrote it to run on the bare PDP-7, cross-assembled on GECOS, before any operating system existed. Only after that did Thompson start the file system and the OS, to get a better place to work. The game did not need the OS. The 'written to play the game' version is the popular retelling.

ch5-bell-labs-p4 (Fig 5.2 caption), 'carried over largely by recompiling' (low): Johnson and Ritchie, 'Portability of C Programs and the UNIX System' (BSTJ 1978), describe the 1977 Interdata 8/32 move as needing a retargeted compiler (the portable C compiler) and real changes to the kernel's machine-dependent parts. 'Largely by recompiling' may make the move sound easier than it was. It is defensible as a simplification under law 4. Check it against the source before keeping it.

What C really lacked was hiding per type, and functions bound to the data they operate on.

In C++ classes an object counts as a Logger only if its class derives from a declared Logger base class. The 'anything with log()' form came with templates (1990s) and concepts (C++20). fact_doubts: ch7-types-p3: 'a network socket' is given as an object with a read() method, but Python's plain socket.socket has recv()/send() and no read(). Checked locally: hasattr(socket.socket(), 'read') is False. Only ssl.SSLSocket, or the file object returned by sock.makefile(), has read(). The example does not hold for an ordinary Python socket.

ch7-types-p2: the claim that dynamically typed languages '(Python, JavaScript, Ruby)' run until the mistake 'and dies there with a TypeError' is true of Python and Ruby but not of JavaScript in general. JavaScript usually converts a string passed where a number is wanted instead of raising an error (1 + "a" gives "1a", "5" * 2 gives 10).

search_points.id: fig-6-6 How it works, bullet 'A trap in C' (under caption ch6-zerocost-p3)
search_points.quote: The usual comparator `return *(int*)a - *(int*)b;` overflows for large values
search_points.missing: The reader has never been told that a comparator answers with a negative, zero or positive number, so they cannot see why subtracting compares. The book never taught cast notation like `*(int*)a`. `x` and `y` appear without introduction, and nothing says a C comparison such as `(x > y)` gives 1 or 0, so they cannot tell why the replacement is safe.
search_points.close_with: cut the bullet (it is off the section's point), or say plainly that a comparator returns the sign of a minus b and that subtracting can overflow

fact_doubts: Fig 6.6 title ('same algorithm, different cost') and caption ch6-zerocost-p3 ('Same algorithm'): the C standard does not fix the algorithm qsort uses. glibc's qsort is a merge sort with a heapsort fallback; glibc swapped it for introsort in October 2023 and put the merge sort back on 2024-01-15, before the 2.39 release. musl's qsort is a smoothsort and the BSD/macOS one is a quicksort, while std::sort is an introsort. The cost per comparison still holds. The old caption's 'the same comparison-based sort', or 'the same job', would be exact.

Fig 6.6 How it works, 'A trap in C': 'overflows for large values' is loose. `a - b` overflows only when the two values are far apart with opposite signs, for example INT_MAX - (-1). Two large values with the same sign never overflow. The §4g row's own wording, 'when the operands are far apart', is the accurate one.

Fig 6.6 drawing (low): the qsort path counts a 'load the two values' step, but the std::sort path (compare, branch) leaves out loading the element it compares, which the inlined loop also has to do. The figure is schematic, but counting the load on one side only slightly overstates the 5-to-2 gap.

search_points.quote: Imported modules keep their bytecode in a cache until their source changes
search_points.missing: The book has never said what a Python module is or what importing one means. The word "import" appears nowhere earlier, and the only modules so far were kernel modules. So the reader cannot tell which of a program's code gets cached and which does not, yet the figure's lane title ("Python · an imported module") and the caption depend on that difference. Only the closed strip says that a script run directly is recompiled every time.
search_points.close_with: a module is a code file another file loads with `import`; the file you run is recompiled each run

search_points.quote: the interpretation is paid for on every run
search_points.missing: p1 ended by framing the choice as translating into machine instructions "once, in advance, or every time it runs". Here, though, Python's translation (to bytecode, not to machine instructions) is cached, and what happens on every run is "interpretation". The strip then describes turning bytecode into machine code at run time as something only a JIT does. So the reader cannot tell whether an interpreter turns their program into machine instructions at all.
search_points.close_with: say plainly that the eval loop never writes machine code for your program and only runs its own prebuilt C code for each opcode; make p1's "every time" match that

fact_doubts: ch7-interpret-p1 says Russell's Lisp eval was "the first interpreter that mattered". Earlier interpreters were in real use before it: Mauchly's Short Code (UNIVAC, 1949–50) and Backus's Speedcoding (IBM 701, 1953), which led to FORTRAN. The claim is arguable at best; "the first Lisp interpreter" is safe.

ch7-interpret-p3 says "Every Python statement becomes hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop". The count has no source and "every" makes it a universal claim. Since 3.11, CPython's specialising interpreter runs a simple statement such as `x = a + b` on small ints in roughly a hundred instructions or fewer, and `pass` compiles to almost nothing. UNDER.md §4g already removed an unsourced "~150 instructions" count from Fig 7.7 for this reason (line 551). "Dozens to hundreds" or "many times the work" would be safer.

search_points.quote: C++11 is the pivot, adding move semantics, lambdas, `auto` and smart pointers
search_points.missing: The caption calls C++11 the pivot, and the figure draws a 'classic | modern' style band, but the only reason given is a list of four feature names. Nothing in this section or earlier explains any of them, so this reader cannot say what changed in 2011 (the glossary places 'move semantics' here, but the prose never teaches it).
search_points.close_with: one plain clause on what C++11 changed for the programmer (or fewer, glossed names), so the pivot and the classic/modern band have a reason

search_points.quote: costs one hidden pointer in each object
search_points.missing: 'Object' has appeared only in passing (ch5-survives 'adding objects', ch6-complexity-p5, p2's 'the current object'). The book never says how an object relates to a class (one thing made from it, with its own copy of the struct in memory), so after 'a class compiles to a struct' this reader cannot tell what there is one of per object.
search_points.close_with: a half-clause: an object is one thing made from a class, its own copy of the class's struct in memory

search_points.quote: A virtual method, whose version is chosen while the program runs
search_points.missing: This reader does not know why one method would have several versions: each kind (a Circle that is a Shape, ch6-complexity-p5) can bring its own, and code holding 'a Shape' learns which only when the program runs. Without that, the hidden pointer (pointing to what?) and the table (holding what?) cannot be followed, and the link back to ch5-pointers-p7's vtables of function addresses is never made.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a Circle and a Square each supply their own version of a Shape's method; each object points to its kind's table of those functions' addresses (Chapter 5's vtables), and the call goes through it

fact_doubts: ch6-stroustrup-p2: 'Simula 67 ... expressly for writing simulations.' Simula I (1962-65) was the simulation language. Dahl and Nygaard designed Simula 67 as a general-purpose language, with simulation supplied as a library class (SIMULATION). Source: Nygaard and Dahl, 'The Development of the SIMULA Languages', HOPL 1978.

ch6-stroustrup-p2: 'the words class, object, virtual ... all originate there.' The word 'class' (as 'record class') came from C. A. R. Hoare's 1965-66 record-handling proposal, which Dahl and Nygaard adopted for Simula 67. Simula 67 introduced the object-oriented sense, but the word itself was Hoare's. Low severity.

ch6-stroustrup-p3: 'The first version, in 1979, was C with Classes.' Stroustrup began the work in 1979, but the first C with Classes translator (Cpre) was in use from about 1980 (Stroustrup, 'A History of C++: 1979-1991', 1993). Low severity.

ch6-stroustrup-p5: 'one hidden pointer in each object.' This holds under single inheritance. Under multiple inheritance an object carries one such pointer per base class that has virtual methods. It is a fair simplification at the book's depth. Low severity.

search_points.quote: 3.13: optional build, no GIL
search_points.missing: The drawing never expands or explains GIL (only the hidden desc spells out 'global interpreter lock'), so this reader cannot say what the 2024 build took out or why it ends the timeline. It is explained later at ch7-gil, section 04 of this chapter.
search_points.close_with: expand it and point ahead in a few words, e.g. 'no GIL (the one-thread-at-a-time lock of §04)'

search_points.quote: Text became Unicode
search_points.missing: Unicode has not been taught anywhere up to here (no earlier section and no KNOWN TERM), so this reader cannot say what Python 2's text was or why changing it broke old code.
search_points.close_with: a short gloss, e.g. 'text became characters from any alphabet (Unicode), not raw bytes'

search_points.quote: 1/2 became 0.5, and print became a function: each one broke old code
search_points.missing: The old behaviour is never given (1/2 used to give 0 because whole-number division dropped the remainder; print was a statement written without brackets), so this reader cannot see what changed or why old code broke.
search_points.close_with: put the old form beside each: '1/2 (was 0)', 'print "x" became print("x")'

fact_doubts: p1 'He had spent three years on a research language called ABC': van Rossum's own account (python-history.blogspot.com, 'Personal History - part 1, CWI', 2009) gives 'After 4 or 5 years the ABC project was terminated' and calls ABC the language 'on which I'd spent four years of my life'. By late 1989 he had also moved to CWI's Amoeba group. The sentence's 'had spent' allows that, but 'three' contradicts him. Suggested fix: 'four years'. This wording has been in the text since before Pass 27 and has no §4g entry.
p1 'most of the world's introductory programming courses': an unsourced overclaim. The usual evidence (Guo 2014) covers only top US computer science departments. 'many' or 'a large share' would hold.

p2 tags '1 + "a" is an error rather than a guess' with 'Explicit is better than implicit'. The Zen line it echoes is 'In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess.' The tag is defensible (no hidden conversion), but an owner who knows the Zen may stop here. Low.

Consistency within the section (not a fact error): ABC is 'a research language' in p1 and 'a teaching language' in Fig 7.2, and the spelling is 'USENET' in p1 but 'Usenet' in the figure. Each pair is true, but the reader meets two labels for one thing.

Glossary defect (not section prose): public/glossary.json entry 'inheritance' carries the object-oriented definition taught at ch6-classes-p1 ('one struct embedded inside another') but links to section ch7-vanrossum. There the word appears only as the strip label 'The inheritance.' in its everyday sense (what Python took from ABC), so the glossary link lands the reader in the wrong section. The same mis-attribution makes pass-29-known-terms.json list 'inheritance' as taught here. Fix with a DEFINITION_OVERRIDES / section override pointing at ch6-classes, or by rewording the strip label (e.g. 'From ABC.').

search_points.quote: The attenuation is a function of frequency, distance, and material.
search_points.missing: So far the reader knows the signal only as a voltage step (p1, ch2-binary), so they cannot say what its 'frequency' is or why it changes how much the signal weakens. 'Attenuated' is not glossed either until Fig 8.1 says 'fades'.
search_points.close_with: 'attenuation (weakening) grows the faster the voltage switches'

search_points.quote: a signal guided along a line, in copper or in glass
search_points.missing: The title, p1 ('the same voltage transition ... across an ocean', 'the physics is unchanged') and p3 ('a voltage signal ... a hundred kilometres of fibre') all say the voltage itself makes the trip. But Fig 8.1 shows a pulse of light in glass, and ch1-transistor-p7 taught that glass is an insulator. The reader cannot explain how a voltage becomes light and back again: the strip's 'without turning it back into electricity' takes for granted a conversion that nothing ever states.
search_points.close_with: one line: at the cable end the voltage steps switch a light on and off, and a sensor turns them back (section 02 shows how)

search_points.quote: fades, is restored, arrives noisy but readable
search_points.missing: The prose never mentions repeaters. The figure says each one 'restores' the signal, yet it arrives 'weakened and noisy', so the reader cannot tell what a repeater restores (strength) and what it leaves in (the noise picked up along the way, which gets amplified too).
search_points.close_with: 'repeaters boost its strength, noise and all; the threshold still reads it'

search_points.quote: are the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart
search_points.missing: The caption's main claim depends on 'orders of magnitude', a phrase the book has not used before (powers of ten), and it sits in a sentence that does not parse ('the same thing over ... apart'), so the reader has to re-read it to find the claim.
search_points.close_with: 'are the same thing, though one trip is a million million times longer'

fact_doubts: Fig 8.1 desc and strip: 5,600 km is roughly the great-circle distance from New York to London (about 5,570 km). Real cable routes are longer (often 6,000+ km), and measured one-way latency is about 30 to 37 ms, so 'about 28 ms' is the physical floor, not the typical figure.

Fig 8.1 strip: 'the older 3.3 V and 5 V levels survive only at the edges of boards and chips' overstates it. 3.3 V is still the standard I/O and supply rail for many chips across a board, and USB supplies 5 V.

search_points.quote: or running C code, can let go of the lock
search_points.missing: Two sections back (ch7-interpret-p3) the reader learned that CPython is a C loop that runs C code for every opcode, so every Python thread is already running C code. They cannot tell which C code this means (a C library the program calls) or why that code may drop the lock when the interpreter's own C code may not.
search_points.close_with: name it as a C library the program calls, which works on its own data and touches no Python object's count

search_points.quote: For thousands of network waits, Python's `asyncio` shares one thread among many tasks
search_points.missing: p1 has just said that a thread waiting on the network lets go of the lock, so threads already handle waits, and the reader cannot say what asyncio gains over one thread per wait. The p4 caption's 'no locks' benefit does not settle it, because p2 told them the GIL already runs one thread at a time.
search_points.close_with: one clause: each thread costs memory and kernel switches and can be switched at any point; tasks are cheap and switch only at await

search_points.quote: PEP 703's free-threaded build uses per-object locks and biased reference counting
search_points.missing: This is in Fig 7.4's How it works strip. The prose said that a lock on every object slowed code by 30–50%, and now the cheap new design is said to use per-object locks too. 'Biased reference counting', the only thing offered as the difference, is never explained, so a reader who opens the strip ends up more confused than before.
search_points.close_with: a plain clause: the thread that owns an object updates its count without a lock, and only other threads pay for one

fact_doubts: Fig 7.4 How it works strip: 'in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs somewhat slower in it'. My recollection, not checked against the docs: Python 3.13's free-threading guide gives that build's single-threaded overhead as about 40% on pyperformance, because the specializing interpreter is switched off there. The 'about 5–10%' figure in p2 is the 3.14 result. 'Somewhat' understates the 3.13 cost, and a reader may take 5–10% to be 3.13's number.

ch7-gil-p2: 'a lock on every object slowed single-threaded code ... by 30–50%'. From memory, unchecked: the Python FAQ describes Greg Stein's free-threading patch, the first removal attempt, as running ordinary code 'about twice as slow' as the GIL interpreter, and worse on Linux. Check whether 30–50% fits every attempt, or whether the range needs a source.

ch7-gil-p2: 'a count of how many names point to it'. CPython counts every reference (list slots, attributes, arguments), not only names. This is likely acceptable at this depth, but strictly it is narrower than the truth.

search_points.quote: read the digits out of both
search_points.missing: From Chapter 2 the reader thinks of an int as a fixed-width binary number. Nothing says what 'digits' an int object holds or why they have to be read out, so step 5 cannot be explained back. (CPython stores an int as a row of base-2^30 'digits' so it can grow without limit, and the book never says so.)
search_points.close_with: 'read the numbers out of both', or one strip line: a Python int has no size limit, so its value is stored as a row of chunks

search_points.quote: the interpreter specialises hot instructions once it has seen their types
search_points.missing: Neither 'hot' (run often) nor 'specialises' (swaps in a faster instruction for the types it has seen) has been defined. Specialising is explained later in the fig-7-7 strip. 'Hot' is never explained; the ch7-interpret strip also used it without a definition.
search_points.close_with: 'once an instruction has run often, the interpreter swaps in a faster version for the types it keeps seeing'

search_points.quote: using computed gotos where the compiler supports them
search_points.missing: 'Computed gotos' is never explained. 'The compiler' here means the C compiler that builds CPython, but this section has just used 'the compiler' for CPython's bytecode stage (p2), so the reader cannot tell what supports what.
search_points.close_with: drop the expert term, or 'jumps straight from one handler to the next where the C compiler that builds CPython allows it'

fact_doubts: Fig 7.6 strip: dis.dis("a + b * c") prints this bytecode with RESUME 0 before it and RETURN_VALUE after it (checked on 3.14.0). A reader who runs it will see two lines the figure does not show.

Fig 7.7 caption and picture: 'every + ... packs a new object' / 'make an int object for the result'. CPython takes results from -5 to 256 from its small-int cache, so 2 + 12 returns the existing 14 object. This is probably an acceptable simplification of the generic path. Not raised: ceval.c 'ten thousand lines' and 'one million lines of C', which the UNDER.md ledger already considered and declined.

search_points.quote: the entire stream is corrupted from there onward
search_points.missing: The reader cannot see why one miscounted flat stretch spoils every bit after it instead of adding one wrong bit. Fig 8.6 then shows the bits after the run (1 1) read correctly, which looks like a contradiction and sends the reader back to p2.
search_points.close_with: one clause: an extra or missing bit pushes every later bit one place out, so everything after it is misread

search_points.quote: Between two equal bits the line also changes at the boundary to get ready.
search_points.missing: The receiver is said to read only the mid-bit edges, but nothing says how it tells them apart from the boundary edges it has to ignore. In Fig 8.6's run of zeros an edge comes every half bit, and p2 has just said the receiver's sense of time drifts.
search_points.close_with: say it expects an edge about one bit period after the last mid-bit edge and ignores any that come halfway

search_points.quote: Radio, DSL and cable modems cannot send bare on-and-off levels
search_points.missing: The reader is told these media cannot carry plain high and low levels but not why, so 'a wave the medium carries well' reads as a claim with nothing behind it. The step that an on-off signal is itself made of frequencies these media do not carry (an antenna sends out only oscillations) is missing.
search_points.close_with: one clause on why: an antenna radiates only oscillations, and these lines pass only certain frequency bands, so the bits go onto a wave in that band

search_points.quote: packing many bits into each symbol: 10 in Wi-Fi 6
search_points.missing: The prose and Fig 8.7 show only two sizes and two phases (one bit each), so changing both gives two bits at most. Nothing outside the closed strip says each property can take many distinguishable values, or that 1024 combinations make 10 bits.
search_points.close_with: in p6: QAM uses many sizes and phases, each combination is one symbol, and 2^k combinations carry k bits (16 give 4)

fact_doubts: ch8-encoding-p2: 'the entire stream is corrupted from there onward' overstates it. A real NRZ receiver re-times itself on the next edge, so the damage is one slipped bit. Everything after goes wrong only because it is shifted one place, not because the receiver stays lost (Fig 8.6 itself shows the bits after the run read correctly).

ch8-encoding-p6 and Fig 8.7: for digital data the matching names are ASK and FSK, alongside PSK. AM and FM are the usual names for the analogue schemes, so 'AM, FM, PSK' mixes the two naming families. This is minor and defensible as a teaching choice.

search_points.quote: Different chunks may take different paths, arrive out of order, get duplicated, or get lost
search_points.missing: The reader was just told the network's only job is to pass each chunk closer, so they cannot see how a chunk could arrive twice. Paths explain the reordering and failures explain the losses, but nothing explains a copy, and the receiver's job as described (reassemble, ask for retransmissions) never deals with an extra one.
search_points.close_with: either drop 'get duplicated' or add a clause: a late chunk that gets resent can arrive twice, and the receiver keeps one copy

fact_doubts: ch9-circuits-p1 says 'for almost exactly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice'. The first commercial telephone exchange opened in 1878 (New Haven). The packet alternative came with Baran (1960–64), Davies (1965) and the ARPANET (1969), about 82–91 years later. 'Almost exactly' claims more precision than those dates give. The chapter opener's 'a century' is fine, and 'about a century' would be safe here too.

search_points.quote: That is the trick behind the twist.
search_points.missing: No earlier sentence says the two copper wires are twisted around each other, so 'the twist' points at nothing. The reader has to work it out backwards from 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer' two sentences later. The figure's drawn words never say 'twisted pair' either (only its <desc> does, and the figure comes after).
search_points.close_with: say it first: the two wires are twisted around each other (a twisted pair)

fact_doubts: UNDER.md §4g REGRESSION, Fig 8.2. The drawn label on the router-to-provider hop reads 'copper / Ethernet, up to 100 m', and the <desc> says 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run)'. §4g already corrected exactly this ('Fig 8.2: the router-to-provider hop labelled "Ethernet runs up to 100 m" ... the hop to the provider is DSL (a few km), coax or fibre', 2026-10-11). Commit 93184ba (Pass 30 Gate 2, repair round 1) brought it back: it removed the untaught 'DSL' and swapped 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km' for 'Ethernet, up to 100 m', and the desc's 'Ethernet to 100 m, DSL for a few kilometres' for 'Ethernet, up to 100 m per run'. Inside the book this clashes with p2, which says copper runs stop at about 100 m. The drawing also leaves out the 'or fibre' that the caption gives for this hop. A label without the abbreviation would fix it, e.g. 'copper phone line or fibre, a few km'.

Inconsistent frequency ranges. In p4 cellular runs '700 MHz to several GHz', but the figure's strip says 'below 1 GHz to tens of GHz'. §4g corrected the figure to tens of GHz (5G mmWave is 24 to 47 GHz), and low bands start below 700 MHz (600 MHz). p4 also gives Wi-Fi as '2.4 GHz and 5 GHz', while the figure says 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.

p5: 'WPA3 (2018, still standing)'. The Dragonblood attacks on WPA3's SAE handshake (Vanhoef and Ronen, 2019: downgrade and side-channel) were patched, but so was KRACK. The text counts WPA as 'broken 2008' (Beck-Tews, a partial attack on TKIP) and WPA2 as 'broken 2017' (KRACK). By that measure WPA3 also fell in 2019, so 'still standing' needs a qualifier.

p5: TEMPEST is called 'a US classification programme'. It is an NSA codename and a set of standards for limiting compromising emanations. 'Classification programme' misdescribes it, and the concern goes back to 1943 (the Bell 131-B2 mixer), even if the name dates from the 1960s. Low severity.
p5: 'an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed'. What Van Eck reconstructed was the picture on the monitor, not the monitor. A wording slip.

Repeater spacing is given three ways. p3 says 'tens to hundreds of kilometres between repeaters', the Fig 8.2 strip says 'tens of kilometres between amplifiers', and Fig 8.1 says 'repeaters every 50 to 100 km'. At 0.2 dB per km, 100 km is the same 20 dB budget the copper paragraph treats as the limit. Hundreds of km holds only for unrepeatered links. Low severity.

search_points.quote: Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz and signal-to-noise ratio SNR
search_points.missing: Bandwidth is never explained anywhere in the book. The reader's everyday meaning (internet speed in Mbps) clashes with the unit hertz and makes 'bit rate given bandwidth' sound circular. It is relied on again in p12 ('at most 2B independent pulses per second', 'Bandwidth buys pulses per second'), on Fig 8.4's axis and in the caption's '3.4 kHz band'.
search_points.close_with: bandwidth = the width of the range of frequencies the channel passes, in hertz; the faster the signal can wiggle, the more pulses per second

search_points.quote: the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N
search_points.missing: The reader cannot see why a range of levels is the square root of a power. The derivation's first step therefore has to be taken on trust, in a paragraph whose whole job is to read the formula off the physics.
search_points.close_with: levels are voltages, and power grows with voltage squared, so a voltage spread is the square root of a power

search_points.quote: A phone line at 30 dB allows about 10 bits per hertz
search_points.missing: A reader who puts 30 into B · log₂(1 + SNR) gets about 5, not 10. Nothing says that the formula's SNR is a plain power ratio and that 30 dB means the signal is 1,000 times the noise. ch8-substrates-p2 defined decibels only as cable loss.
search_points.close_with: (30 dB: the signal is 1,000 times the noise, and log₂ 1,001 ≈ 10)

search_points.quote: there exists a coding scheme that achieves arbitrarily low error rate
search_points.missing: Error-correcting coding is never explained in the section or earlier. The reader does not know that a code adds redundant bits so the receiver can find and fix flipped ones, so cannot see how any 'coding' beats noise. Worse, p6 just used 'coding' for compression, which removes redundancy, the opposite job.
search_points.close_with: one clause: an error-correcting code adds extra check bits so the receiver can repair errors, spending some rate to buy reliability

search_points.quote: H = −Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)
search_points.missing: p4 defines entropy as the average number of yes-or-no questions, then gives a formula with a minus sign and log₂ of probabilities. Nothing links the two, so the reader cannot explain why this formula counts questions.
