search_points.close_with: a symbol with chance 1/8 is pinned down by 3 halving questions (log₂ 8 = −log₂ ⅛); entropy averages that over symbols, weighted by how often each comes

search_points.quote: a long run of them can be stored in about 0.81 bits per flip
search_points.missing: From ch2-binary the reader knows that n bits name only 2^n outcomes, so 100 flips seem to need 100 bits. How grouping flips gets below one bit per flip is never shown.
search_points.close_with: give the likely runs short codes and the rare ones longer codes, so the average falls below one bit per flip

fact_doubts: ch8-shannon-p1: 'Before this paper, "amount of information" was a metaphor' overstates it. Hartley (1928, 'Transmission of Information', Bell System Technical Journal) had already defined a quantitative measure of information, the log of the number of possible messages, and Nyquist (1924) worked along the same line. The callout's own title, Shannon–Hartley, names him.

ch8-shannon-p6: 'Every modern lossless compressor, from ZIP to PNG, sits somewhere on Shannon's curve' is imprecise. Real compressors sit above the entropy floor, not on it, and the curve the reader sees next (Fig 8.3) is only the two-symbol coin case, which ZIP and PNG do not code.

search_points.quote: Transport moves byte streams reliably or messages unreliably end to end.
search_points.missing: The book never says that Network's packets can be lost or arrive out of order. So 'reliably' has nothing to contrast with, offering 'unreliably' as a service makes no sense, and the reader cannot say what Transport ('end to end') adds over Network, which already gets packets across many networks. The same gap leaves Fig 8.11's TCP header without a job. Never explained in this section.
search_points.close_with: one clause in p2: Network may lose or reorder packets; Transport, run only by the two end machines, repairs that (stream) or leaves it (messages)

search_points.quote: since real applications usually handle their own session semantics
search_points.missing: Nothing says what OSI's Session layer (or Presentation) does: p2 gives all three top layers one phrase ('about what the bytes mean'), Fig 8.11 says Session 'adds nothing', and its strip's '5: session handling' is circular. So the reason given for folding them into Application cannot be followed. Explained only in part later, in Fig 8.12's caption ('sessions and formats') and strip ('connections, content negotiation and compression').
search_points.close_with: name each job once in p2: Session opens, keeps and closes a conversation; Presentation sets the data's form (encoding, compression, encryption)

search_points.quote: packets that need to find their way across that graph
search_points.missing: 'That graph' points at nothing: the book never uses 'graph' for a network of nodes and links, and the only graphs in Chapter 8 are plotted curves (Figs 8.3, 8.4). The antecedent, p2's 'global graph of nodes', was cut in the law-4 rewrite (f01c84e) and replaced with 'many networks joined together', so this reference no longer points at anything.
search_points.close_with: 'across that web of networks' (or 'across them'), with no graph word

fact_doubts: ch8-layers-p2: 'Data Link moves frames between machines joined directly by one cable or radio link' says less than the previous section just taught. In switched Ethernet (ch8-ethernet-p4, Fig 8.10) each host has its own cable to the switch, and frames cross the switch between two cables. Wi-Fi frames likewise pass through the access point. The link layer reaches the whole local network, not one cable. A reader fresh from Fig 8.10 may notice the clash. Suggested wording: 'between machines on the same local network'.

search_points.quote: multiplying two 1000 × 1000 matrices (grids of numbers) takes a billion multiply-adds
search_points.missing: The section says a matrix is a 'grid of numbers' but never says what multiplying two of them involves. A reader who multiplies cell by cell gets a million operations, so they cannot see where a billion comes from. Fig 7.9's caption and its 'three nested loops' strip both lean on that billion.
search_points.close_with: a clause: each of the million answer cells is one row times one column, 1000 products added up

search_points.quote: pickle.loads(data) looks like a parser and is an interpreter
search_points.missing: Pickle is never explained, before this point or after it. The reader does not know it is Python's built-in way to save any object as bytes and load it back, so they cannot see why loading one looks like parsing, or why the bytes might come from an attacker.
search_points.close_with: a short gloss: pickle, Python's built-in format for saving objects as bytes and loading them back

search_points.quote: the only real fix is to never deserialise pickled data you didn't sign
search_points.missing: The coda's fix depends on two words the book has not taught yet. 'Deserialise' is never defined. 'Signing data' (a check, made with a secret key, that proves the bytes are your own and unchanged) does not arrive until Part IV. The reader also isn't told that a session cookie lives in the visitor's browser and comes back from there, so cannot see why the cookie example is attacker-controlled or why signing it is the fix.
search_points.close_with: say deserialise means unpickle, and add a clause: a cookie comes back from the visitor's browser, and a signature proves the bytes are the ones you sent out

fact_doubts: ch7-datasci-p7: 'Every web framework that accepted pickled session cookies has been bitten by this' is a universal claim nobody can check. Examples: Django's PickleSerializer and Werkzeug's old SecureCookie both signed their pickled cookies, and were exploitable mainly when the signing key leaked. So 'every ... bitten' sits awkwardly next to the next clause, which offers signing as the fix. Suggest 'Many web frameworks ...', or saying the attacks came through leaked keys.

Reader-facing glossary attribution (not prose): in public/glossary.json the 'Baran' and 'Cerf' entries point to part-2 ch7-datasci ('Chapter 7 · 06 · Why Python won data science'). The cause is that the names first appear in Part II's end-of-part tagline. The glossary page and the Part III tooltips will send the reader to the Python section, which says nothing about either man. They are taught in Part III (Paul Baran in Ch9, Fig 9.3). The section packet's 'TERMS THIS SECTION TEACHES: Baran; Cerf' shows the same misattribution.

Checked and found correct, no action: BLAS began in 1979 and Level 3 dgemm came in 1990. NumPy ships OpenBLAS on Linux and Windows and can use Accelerate on Apple Silicon. AVX2 handles 4 doubles, AVX-512 8 and NEON 2. 1000^3 = 10^9 multiply-adds. Fig 7.9's bars sit at 0.012 s and 120 s on the 48 px-per-decade axis, four decades apart, which matches the caption. The `request` typosquat of `requests` really happened (the Tencent report in 2020, and the counterfeit dependency pulled in by 'keep' in 2022). But UNDER.md's ledger credits it to the Sonatype 2022 ransomware incident, which actually named requesys, requesrs and Requesr. The book text is unaffected; only the internal ledger note is wrong.

search_points.quote: every Ethernet frame still carries the header structure invented for that shared cable
search_points.missing: Nothing in the section or earlier says what an Ethernet frame is or what its header holds, yet frames carry the rest of the section (Fig 8.9, Fig 8.10, p10, p11). The reader also can't see why a shared cable needed addresses at all. MAC addresses only arrive at p7.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a frame is one chunk of data on the wire, and its header names the destination and source MAC, so on a shared cable each card keeps only frames addressed to it (MAC explained later at p7)

search_points.quote: their signals collide, both notice, jam and stop
search_points.missing: The reader can't say what a jam is or why a station that has already noticed the collision sends one before stopping. The figure shows it as a step ('send a jam'), but neither it nor the prose explains it.
search_points.close_with: a few words: a short burst that makes sure every station, including the other sender, notices the collision

search_points.quote: Each then waits a random number of slots, so one goes first
search_points.missing: 'Slot' is never defined, so the reader doesn't know how long one is. They just watched B start because A's signal hadn't reached it yet, so they can't see why waiting one slot means B will now find the line busy instead of colliding again.
search_points.close_with: define the slot as a fixed wait long enough for a signal to cross the whole cable and back, so a station waiting one slot hears one that went at zero

search_points.quote: rapidly send frames with a million different fabricated source MACs
search_points.missing: p7 said the MAC is burned into the card at manufacture, so the reader can't see how one machine on one port can send a million different source addresses. Nothing says that the source field of a frame is just bits the sender writes and that nobody checks them.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the burned-in address is only a default; software writes each frame's source field, and the switch takes it on trust

search_points.quote: fills the table to capacity, and falls back to what it does
search_points.missing: The reader learned from Fig 8.10 that the switch already knows where A and B sit, so 'table full' doesn't explain why it would stop knowing where real destinations are and start flooding.
search_points.close_with: one step: the fake entries crowd out the real ones (or outlast them when they expire and cannot be relearned), so real destinations become unknown and are flooded

fact_doubts: ch8-ethernet-p2: Possibly dramatised. The usual account (Metcalfe's own oral history) has him first reading Abramson's ALOHA paper during a stay in Washington, then visiting Hawaii. So 'the rejection sent him ... onto a flight to Hawaii' and 'analysed the math on the plane home' need a source. UNDER.md records only that the ALOHA math was added at PARC to the revised thesis.

ch8-ethernet-p3: The widely reproduced hand-drawn Ethernet diagram is usually dated 1976 (drawn for Metcalfe's National Computer Conference talk). May 22, 1973 is the date of the 'Alto Ethernet' memo. Check whether a sketch on yellow paper dated May 22, 1973 really exists and that the Computer History Museum holds it.

ch8-ethernet-p7: 'Raspberry Pi devices begin B8:27:EB' is true only for older boards (up to the Pi 3 series and Zero W). Pi 4, 400 and 5 use other Raspberry Pi Ltd prefixes such as DC:A6:32, E4:5F:01, 2C:CF:67 and D8:3A:DD.

fig-8-10 How it works (minor): 'both directions on separate wire pairs (full duplex)' holds for 10/100BASE-T. Gigabit copper Ethernet sends both directions over all four pairs at once, using echo cancellation. Full duplex does not in general mean separate pairs.

search_points.quote: recomputes the checksum; the rest travels untouched
search_points.missing: The book has never said what a checksum is (Fig 8.11 only labels FCS as 'checksum'), so this reader cannot explain why a router has to recompute it after changing the TTL. The drawn 'TTL changed, so recompute the checksum', with 12849 becoming 13105, and the strip's 'covers only the header' have nothing to rest on.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a number worked out from the header's bytes so the next router can spot damage; change a byte and it changes

search_points.quote: lowers the time to live by one
search_points.missing: Nothing says why a packet should have a lifetime at all. The strip only says a router drops it at 0 and that traceroute uses this, so this reader may conclude TTL exists for traceroute. p1's 'when to drop it' is never tied to it.
search_points.close_with: so a packet sent round in circles by a routing mistake dies instead of looping forever

search_points.quote: since IP cannot ask for a single fragment again
search_points.missing: ch9-circuits-p3 taught that in packet switching 'the receiving end reassembles them and asks for retransmissions'. Here IP cannot ask, and the section never says that IP only forwards or drops, that resending belongs to TCP in the layer above, or that the whole packet is then sent again.
search_points.close_with: IP never asks for anything again; resending is TCP's job (Chapter 10), and it resends the whole packet

search_points.quote: IPv6 forbids router-side fragmentation entirely.
search_points.missing: The paragraph has just made splitting the only way a too-big packet can cross a smaller link, then forbids it. It never says what an IPv6 router does with a packet that does not fit, and the strip's 'Path MTU discovery finds the smallest link' does not say how a sender can learn the size of links on a route it cannot see.
search_points.close_with: the router drops it and tells the sender 'too big, the limit is N'; the sender resends smaller packets (path MTU discovery)

fact_doubts: ch9-ip-p1 'The first twenty bytes of a packet on the wire are the IP header': on an Ethernet wire the Ethernet header comes first, as Fig 8.11 draws it. The IP header opens the packet, not what is on the wire. It is also at least 20 bytes rather than exactly 20: options can take it to 60, which the strip's 'IHL ... almost always 5' admits while p1 says 'fixed-format'.

ch9-ip-p1 'every router on the path reads to figure out ... what the higher-layer protocol is': routers that only forward never use the Protocol field. The receiving host reads it to pass the payload to TCP or UDP. Routers look at it only when they filter traffic.

ch9-ip-p1 'designed in 1981' (low): the same header layout already appeared in RFC 760 (January 1980) and in earlier drafts. 1981 is the date of RFC 791, which the caption cites correctly. Checked and correct: Fig 9.4's checksums (12849 at TTL 64, 13105 at TTL 63) and Fig 9.5's fragment arithmetic (1480 + 1480 + 1040 = 4000; offsets 0, 185, 370).

search_points.quote: His case for the third ... became the design argument of the ARPANET.
search_points.missing: p3 has just said the ARPANET was built so universities could share computers, "not to survive a war". Baran's case was survival, so a caption saying that case "became the design argument of the ARPANET" reads as if the war purpose came back, and the reader re-reads to work out which is true.
search_points.close_with: separate shape from purpose, e.g. "his third shape became the ARPANET's shape, though not its purpose"

fact_doubts: ch9-arpanet-p1 "560 kilometres up the coast": the straight line from UCLA (Westwood) to SRI (Menlo Park) is about 505 km. 560 km matches the often-quoted "350 miles", which is closer to the road distance. It is defensible as "up the coast", but the fact gate may want "about 500 kilometres" or a check against §4g. Low priority.

ch9-arpanet-p2 "The Cuban Missile Crisis had just shown the world...": the crisis was October 1962, two years into the Baran work the sentence dates 1960 to 1964 (he started at RAND in 1959/60). So it made the problem more urgent but did not come before it, and "had just shown" reads as if the crisis prompted the work. Chronology quibble, low priority.

search_points.quote: Google is AS 15169, your ISP has its own
search_points.missing: ISP is never expanded anywhere in the book. Up to here the text says only 'internet provider' (ch8-substrates-p6 and Fig 8 caption), yet Fig 9.7 hangs every label on the acronym ('your ISP', 'regional ISP'), so the reader has to guess what it stands for.
search_points.close_with: expand it once at first use: 'your internet provider (ISP)'

search_points.quote: eight bytes of header with two ports, a length and a checksum
search_points.missing: Nothing up to here says what a transport port is. Part III has only shown switch ports (ch8-ethernet) and NAT port numbers (ch9-v6), never what a port is for. So this reader cannot say why 'destination port 53' means DNS, what 'source port 51234' is, or what UDP adds to IP at all, since p1 called it 'just send packets'. The old caption's gloss ('which service to deliver to') was dropped in the redraw, and neither the drawing nor the strip nor the prose puts it back.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a port is a number that says which program on the machine gets the bytes (53 is the DNS server's; the sender picks its own so the reply can find it)

search_points.quote: TCP's three-message setup (Section 03) would double the time the lookup takes
search_points.missing: If you count messages, three setup messages plus a request and a response come to five, not double the two. The reader is never told that the time is counted in round trips, or that the third setup message goes out together with the request. So the setup adds one round trip to a lookup that takes one round trip.
search_points.close_with: 'adds a full round trip before the question can even go out, doubling a one-round-trip lookup'

fact_doubts: ch10-udp-p1: 'every game' overstates the case. Many online games run over TCP (World of Warcraft is the well-known example, and so are many turn-based and mobile games). 'Every video call' overstates it too: WebRTC calls fall back to TCP/TLS relays when UDP is blocked. 'Most real-time games and video calls' would be accurate.

search_points.quote: so a forged source gets through and any reply goes to the address it names
search_points.missing: The section never says what a forger gains from a packet whose reply it never sees (hiding who sent it, or aiming the replies at a victim). The figure even shows the reply going elsewhere, so the danger promised by "at your peril" stays abstract and the reason ISPs bother to filter (p1) is left unstated.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the forger hides itself and the replies land on whoever owns the address it wrote

search_points.quote: meant to block YouTube at home but leaked worldwide by its upstream PCCW
search_points.missing: p4 introduces hijacking as "a more dramatic attack", but its canonical example turns out to be a domestic block that escaped by mistake ("leaked"). Fig 9.12 then defines a route leak as a mistake where nobody attacked, so the reader cannot say what made 2008 a hijack and not a leak.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a hijack is announcing addresses you do not hold, whether on purpose or by error; PCCW failed to filter it

search_points.quote: P1 prefers them, since routes from a paying customer usually win
search_points.missing: p4 says forwarding "always" prefers the most specific route, and here a business preference decides instead. The reader is never told that the leaked routes cover the same blocks, so specificity ties and policy decides. Without that, the two rules seem to contradict each other.
search_points.close_with: one clause: specificity decides between blocks of different sizes; for the same block, the network's policy (customers first) decides

fact_doubts: ch9-security-p2: "somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (... about ten percent of the internet of the time)". The usual figure is about 6,000, itself a guess of ten percent of roughly 60,000 hosts (Paul Graham's account). An upper bound of ten thousand would be well over ten percent of that internet, so the range and the percentage do not agree. (Morris's age of 23 is a ledger-documented owner choice and is not reported.)

ch9-security-p2: "weak passwords in rsh". The worm's rsh attack used trusted-host relationships (.rhosts/hosts.equiv), where no password was asked at all. Its password guessing went through rexec and user accounts. Sources usually say "rsh/rexec and weak passwords", so tying weak passwords to rsh alone is slightly off.

search_points.quote: each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table
search_points.missing: The reader knows a port only as a physical socket on a switch (ch8-ethernet); here it is a number written as 100.64.0.11:5000 or 'port 40001', and without knowing that every packet carries such a number for its conversation, the reader cannot see how one shared address gets each reply back to the right home (the NAT rewrites the sender to 203.0.113.5 port 40001, the server replies to that, and the table maps it back to home A).
search_points.close_with: one clause: a port is a number in each packet naming its conversation, so a reply to port 40001 can be looked up and passed back to home A

search_points.quote: thousands of homes share one public address
search_points.missing: Each home in the figure still has an IPv4 address (100.64.0.11 and so on), so the reader cannot explain why those addresses do not use up the same scarce supply, or why the server could not just reply to them; the step left out is that the 'shared' 100.64 range is used again inside every ISP and never appears on the public internet.
search_points.close_with: a phrase: the 100.64 addresses are reused inside every ISP and cannot be reached from outside, so only the one public address counts

search_points.quote: a v6-only machine and a v4-only machine cannot talk to each other directly
search_points.missing: The whole 'structurally so' argument rests on this incompatibility, but the text never says why it holds (IPv6 is a different header whose 128-bit address fields a v4-only machine cannot read, and the 32-bit fields of Fig 9.4 have no room for a v6 address), so to the reader it reads as an assertion instead of a mechanism.
search_points.close_with: a clause: the v4 header has room for 32-bit addresses only, so v6 needs a new header that old machines cannot read

search_points.quote: so it never collides with home networks' own 192.168 addresses
search_points.missing: In the How it works strip (The shared range), the figure shows each home as one 100.64 address, and this line suddenly gives homes their own 192.168 addresses as well, with 'this layer' as a second layer; the reader was never told that every home router numbers its devices from the same 192.168 range, so they cannot see what would collide or why it matters.
search_points.close_with: a phrase: every home router already numbers its own devices 192.168.x.x behind it, so the ISP's layer needed a different range

fact_doubts: ch9-v6-p2 'thousands of homes share one public address': one address has only about 65,000 ports to share out, and fixed-line CGNAT setups usually put tens to a few hundred customers on each address (some mobile networks go higher). 'Many homes' or 'hundreds of homes' may be safer.

Fig 9.8 strip 'the regional registries ran dry over the following years': AFRINIC was still handing out small blocks from its final pool (exhaustion phase 2) in the mid-2020s, so not every registry has strictly run dry. Worth checking, or soften to 'most regional registries'.

ch9-v6-p1 'between 35% and 45% of internet traffic is IPv6 in 2025' vs the Fig 9.8 strip 'close to half of Google's users': these are two different measures. Google's figure was around 45 to 49% in 2025, which is above the prose's top figure, and traffic counted by volume at exchange points is lower than either. 'Depending on how you count' covers this, but a reader sees two numbers that do not quite agree.

search_points.quote: acknowledges the client's plus one
search_points.missing: The reader has not yet been told that an acknowledgement names the next byte the receiver expects; the book first says so in Fig 10.4 in ch10-aimd. So 'plus one', and the strip's 'SYN counts as one byte', still leave them expecting ack 4170, since 4170 is the number they received.
search_points.close_with: one clause in the caption or the 'Plus one' strip: an ACK names the next byte it expects, and SYN used up 4170, so the ACK says 4171

search_points.quote: Most connections take one well-trodden path
search_points.missing: Fig 10.2 has just shown the server going LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED in an ordinary handshake. The prose then gives a single path through SYN_SENT and says the off-path states handle simultaneous opens, closes and lost FINs, which contradicts that figure. The reader cannot tell whether SYN_RCVD is normal or a failure state until the Fig 10.3 caption says which side is which.
search_points.close_with: say this is the path of the side that opens and closes first; add the server's path (LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK); keep 'off-path' for CLOSING and the rare moves

fact_doubts: ch10-handshake-p3: 'The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs' is not accurate. Five states are off the listed path: LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK and CLOSING. The first four are the passive (server) side's ordinary path, as Fig 10.3 itself shows. Only CLOSING is used just for simultaneous close, and a simultaneous open reuses SYN_RCVD. A lost FIN is handled by resending it on a timer, plus TIME_WAIT (which is on the path) answering a resent FIN, not by an off-path state.

ch10-handshake-p3: 'Most connections take one well-trodden path' describes one end only. Each connection has two ends, each with its own path. Also, the side that closes first is not always the client (HTTP servers often close first), though the Fig 10.3 caption frames this correctly as the figure's own scenario.

search_points.quote: the congestion-control state, and a few dozen other values
search_points.missing: The reader has never met congestion control. p1 has just said every piece of TCP's machinery serves one of four goals, and this item fits none of them, so the reader stops to ask whether it is flow control under another name or a fifth goal. It is never explained in this section; Section 04's title (Flow and congestion control) is the first sign that it is a separate thing.
search_points.close_with: a short clause such as 'congestion control (slowing down when the network itself is overloaded, Section 04)', and a softer p1 claim, or drop the item from the list

fact_doubts: ch10-why-p1 vs p3: 'Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals' clashes with the TCB's 'congestion-control state'. Congestion control (Jacobson, 1988) protects the network, not the receiver. It was not among the 1974 goals, and Section 04 treats it as separate from flow control.
ch10-why-p2: 'Receivers periodically advertise a window' is loose. TCP carries the window field in every segment the receiver sends (each acknowledgement), not on a separate schedule.

ch10-why-p1: 'which they called simply TCP'. The 1974 paper calls it a 'transmission control program (TCP)', and 'Protocol' came later. Its abstract also lists more than four functions (end-to-end error checking, creating and destroying connections), so 'designed to do four things' simplifies the paper. Low severity.

search_points.quote: Each retransmit produced more retransmits, while neither side was, locally, doing anything wrong.
search_points.missing: The reader cannot explain why the useful rate fell 800-fold instead of the link staying busy at about 32 kbps. The missing step is that the link's capacity went on copies: resent packets, many of them dropped again further along or merely delayed past their timer, so almost no new data got through.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the wires stayed full, but nearly everything on them was a repeat or a packet that would be dropped later

search_points.quote: begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment
search_points.missing: The section's central variable is used as if already known. The prose never says that the congestion window is a second limit on bytes in flight, that the sender keeps it for itself (nobody advertises it), or that the sender sends no more than the smaller of this window and the receive window. Only Fig 10.4's closed strip says so.
search_points.close_with: name it at first use: the sender's own cap on bytes in flight, its guess at what the network can take; the smaller of the two windows wins

fact_doubts: ch10-aimd-p8: calling efficiency 'the network is fully utilised' overstates what AIMD gives. AIMD converges to an oscillation around the full-link line, not to sitting on it: in the book's own Fig 10.5 the window drops to 12 on a path that carries 24 after every loss. The link is fully used only at the peaks, unless router buffers cover the gap. §4g row 561 already corrected the same overclaim in Fig 10.6's caption ('peaks on the capacity line'). A phrase such as 'the link is filled at each peak' would match it.

ch10-aimd-p5/p6: p5 says the 1988 paper's fix was slow start and AIMD, then p6 says 'The algorithm has two phases' and describes halving on three duplicate ACKs, with a full reset only on a timeout. That is Reno's fast recovery, from 4.3BSD-Reno in 1990. The 1988 algorithm (Tahoe) reset cwnd to one segment on every loss and used slow start to climb back to half the old window. Fig 10.5's strip does say 'Classic Reno', but the prose reads as if the halving were the 1988 fix. Low severity.

ch10-aimd-p5: Jacobson and Karels (1988) say the throughput 'dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps'. They do not call 32 kbps the path's 'design capacity', and the IMP trunks of the time ran at 56 kbps. 'Its normal throughput of 32 kilobits per second' would match the source. Low severity, and unverified beyond the paper's wording.

search_points.quote: includes _links to other documents_ as inline elements rather than appendices
search_points.missing: The HTML entry says what HTML is for but never what it is: "markup" and "inline elements" are never explained, so the reader cannot picture how a link sits inside a document that p8 then calls "just text".
search_points.close_with: one tiny example: a few words wrapped in a tag that carries a URL

search_points.quote: the long empty stretch is the quiet, the cluster at the bottom is the take-off
search_points.missing: In the drawing the long empty stretch runs from Dec 1991 to Apr 1993, but the label "2½ quiet years, one machine" sits on the Mar 1989 to Aug 1991 band. The reader cannot tell which stretch is the quiet one, or what happened between the announcement and the giveaway.
search_points.close_with: point the strip at the labelled band, or name the 1992 gap

search_points.quote: There was no Web Consortium yet, no licence, no fee.
search_points.missing: If joining was free from the start, the reader cannot see why the caption has the web taking off only after CERN gave the software away in April 1993. Nothing says what the software's status was before that.
search_points.close_with: a clause: until April 1993 CERN owned the code and could still have charged for it

search_points.quote: the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it
search_points.missing: As written, Xanadu's links break too, so the reader cannot see what Xanadu demanded that the web does not, or why that demand means "a central authority".
search_points.close_with: say the link system was one shared register that every link and target had to join, run by someone, and that this is what kept links working

fact_doubts: p1 "in Building 31 at CERN": the UNDER.md §4g row for Fig 11.1 (line 565) removed "CERN Building 31" from the figure as unsourced, but the prose still states it. Either source it or remove it from p1 as well (fact-ledger law).

p9 Xanadu: Nelson's design kept every document permanently at a fixed address, with two-way links held by the system, so its links were not supposed to break at all. "If the target moved or disappeared, the link broke and the publisher was supposed to update it" does not describe Xanadu.

p9 "if the URL no longer resolves, the click gets back a 404": a 404 comes from a server that answers but has no document at that path. A URL that no longer resolves (its host name is gone) gets no 404, only a failure to connect. The next section teaches resolving, so readers will notice the mix-up.

p11 "every later attempt to build a 'private web' (AOL, MSN, Compuserve...)": CompuServe (1979) and AOL (1989, from Quantum Link in 1985) ran their walled gardens before the 1993 release. Only MSN (1995) came later.
p8 "None of the three protocols": only HTTP is a protocol. p4 itself calls HTML a format, a URL is an address scheme, and p3 calls all three conventions.
p5 "The original page was reconstructed in 2013": the 2013 CERN restoration put up the earliest surviving copy, which dates from 1992. No copy of the 1990–91 original is known to survive.

ch12-browser-p2 'removed from browsers entirely by 2017', and the fig-12-1 How it works strip 'browsers had dropped the plugin interface they needed by 2017': this is not accurate. Chrome 45 dropped NPAPI in September 2015 and Firefox 52 in March 2017, but Firefox 52 ESR ran the Java plugin until 2018, Safari dropped NPAPI only in Safari 12 (September 2018), and Internet Explorer 11 ran applets through the ActiveX Java plugin until IE was retired in June 2022. Oracle deprecated the Applet API in JDK 9 (2017) and removed the browser plugin in JDK 11 (2018). A wording that holds: 'dropped by the major browsers between 2015 and 2018' or 'deprecated by Oracle in 2017'.

ch12-browser-p3 'small, untyped snippets', read against p2 'a real language that checked its types': this contradicts what the book taught earlier. ch7-types-p2 classes JavaScript as dynamically typed: it does check types, at runtime, and dies with a TypeError. The word that sits closest to 'untyped' is ch5-portability-p7's 'typeless', which means BCPL and B, where every value is a bare machine word. A careful reader may take JavaScript to be typeless like BCPL. What it actually lacked was declared types and a compile-time check. A wording that holds: 'small snippets with no type declarations', or 'dynamically typed snippets'.

ch10-modern-p2 "It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs": Mishra et al.'s TCP congestion-control census (ACM SIGMETRICS 2019, Gordon tool; IETF 2020 slides) estimated BBR variants already carried more than 40% of downstream internet traffic in 2019, while only about 22% of the top 20,000 sites used it. CUBIC is the most common default by host count, but "great majority of traffic" looks overstated. No §4g row sources it. Possible safer wording: "what most internet hosts run" or "the most widely deployed".

ch10-modern-p4 "BBR can be two to ten times faster than CUBIC": no §4g row sources the range. Cardwell et al. (ACM Queue 2016) report 2 to 25 times higher throughput on Google's B4 WAN and large gains under random loss. For "home routers with oversized queues" the gain is shorter queueing delay, not a higher rate, and the book's own Fig 10.8 shows loss-based TCP at the same 1 Gbit/s delivery rate past the knee. An attentive reader comparing the two may notice the mismatch. Pin the source, or say what "faster" means there (less waiting).

ch10-modern-p6 "By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests": no §4g row. Cloudflare's own May 2022 to May 2023 analysis put HTTP/3 at about 28% of requests (blog.cloudflare.com/http3-usage-one-year-on). A third-party summary of Cloudflare Radar's 2024 Year in Review gives about 20.5% (I did not confirm this on Cloudflare's own page). W3Techs' roughly 30% counts websites, not requests. On the 2024 figure, "well over a quarter" looks too high. Pin the source and date (for example, "by 2023, more than a quarter of requests Cloudflare sees"), or soften to "about a fifth to a quarter".

ch10-modern-p1 "Classic TCP (Tahoe, Reno, NewReno) was designed for the late-1980s internet": Tahoe is from 1988 and Reno from 1990, but NewReno dates from 1999 (RFC 2582). This is minor: it was a fix inside the same classic design, so the sentence is only loosely true. Low.

search_points.quote: The signature, made with the certificate's private key, proves the server is who
search_points.missing: Section 04 (ch11-crypto-p7, Fig 11.10) taught only that the public key locks and the private key unlocks. The book never explains what a digital signature is, or how something made with a private key gets checked with the public key and so proves identity. Neither this section nor any earlier one does, yet the chain check at ch11-tls-p4 and the Fig 11.12 caption ('checks each signature with the public key of the certificate above it') rests on it.
search_points.close_with: one sentence on first use: a signature is computed with the private key over the data's hash; anyone can check it with the public key, and only the key's holder could have made it

search_points.quote: its very first reply: certificate, signature and all
search_points.missing: p2 leans on the certificate (what it 'says', and 'the certificate's private key') before the reader knows a certificate is a signed file that binds the server's name to its public key. That is explained later at ch11-tls-p4. Earlier pages only name certificates in passing (ch10-attacks-p8, ch11-crypto-p4).
search_points.close_with: a half-clause at first use: the certificate, a signed file binding the server's name to its public key (more below)

search_points.quote: Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows.
search_points.missing: This reader knows MAC only as the Ethernet MAC address (ch8-ethernet), a hardware identifier. The book never introduces a message authentication code (a hash keyed with the shared secret), and p2 called the same thing plain 'a hash of the entire transcript', so the strip reads as a contradiction.
search_points.close_with: 'a hash keyed with the shared secret (a MAC, message authentication code)', or just 'a keyed hash'

fact_doubts: ch11-tls-p1 'It is what the lock icon in your browser refers to': Chrome 117 (September 2023) replaced the padlock with a neutral 'tune' icon. Safari and Firefox still show a lock, so the claim holds only for some browsers. Low severity.

ch11-tls-p4 'roughly 150 such roots in the major stores': fits Mozilla's and Chrome's root stores (about 130 to 150). I believe Microsoft's root program trusts noticeably more (a few hundred), but have not checked the count. Writing 'in Mozilla's store, for example' would make the line exact. Low severity.

search_points.quote: is the lever all of public-key cryptography pulls on
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say what an 'RSA key' is or how a hard-to-factor product of primes protects anything. Public-key cryptography is explained only later, at p7, and p7 never ties the key pair back to factoring. Only the closed strips of Fig 11.8 ('The product goes into the public key') and Fig 11.10 make that link, so the 617-digit 'key' in the caption stays unclear too.
search_points.close_with: one prose clause at p7: the public key carries the product, and opening without the private key means factoring it

search_points.quote: each side combines its own private half with the other's public half
search_points.missing: 'Combines' names no operation, so the reader cannot see why two different combinations reach the same number, or why an eavesdropper holding both public halves cannot do the same. This is the mechanism the next section's TLS 1.3 handshake relies on, and the Fig 11.10 strip repeats the same slogan.
search_points.close_with: a one-line toy example showing why both results match and why the eavesdropper's step runs backward

fact_doubts: p4 'uniquely identifying it': inputs of any size go into a fixed 256-bit output, so the hash cannot be unique (endlessly many inputs share each hash). What makes it work as a fingerprint in practice is collision resistance: no one can find two inputs with the same hash. The three listed properties leave that out, and preimage resistance does not imply it.

p4 'and so does every TLS handshake': TLS 1.3 handshakes can run on SHA-384 (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, the first suite in OpenSSL's default list), and some certificate chains are signed with SHA-384. 'Nearly every' would be safe.

Fig 11.10 strip: 'linked by mathematics (Fig 11.8) ... solving the hard problem' sits right before 'TLS 1.3 uses Diffie–Hellman key agreement'. That leads the reader to think factoring guards TLS 1.3's key agreement. Factoring is RSA's hard problem; (elliptic-curve) Diffie–Hellman rests on the discrete logarithm. This is a misleading implication rather than a false sentence.

Checked and correct: 61 × 53 = 3233, and 53 is the 16th prime. A 2048-bit product has 617 digits and its prime factors about 308 each. Both SHA-256 hashes are right, and they differ in 124 bits. g = 01100111 and e = 01100101. RSA-250 (829 bits, February 2020, about 2,700 core-years) is right. AES (NIST 2001, 128-bit blocks, 128/192/256-bit keys, 10 to 14 rounds) is right. The RSA-896 September 2026 record is already verified in UNDER.md ledger row 579.

search_points.quote: it performs about twenty separate operations across four layers
search_points.missing: Fig 11.3 shows four exchanges (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP), nothing that adds up to twenty, and they are not the four TCP/IP layers of Fig 8.12, which puts DNS and HTTP in the same Application layer, so the reader can't line the claim up with the picture.
search_points.close_with: say 'four exchanges in a row', matching the caption, or name the twenty

search_points.quote: One curl, fully traced
search_points.missing: The figure title, its picture and its strip all rely on 'curl', which the book has not introduced, and the prose just before is about a browser, so the reader can't tell what a curl is or why the client changed.
search_points.close_with: a gloss: curl, a command-line program that fetches one URL and prints the reply

search_points.quote: Caches assume safety; retry logic assumes idempotency.
search_points.missing: The reader knows CPU caches but has never been told what a cache on the network path does (keeps a reply and answers a repeat request itself, so the server never sees it), so they can't explain why a cache needs safe requests; the retry half is shown in Fig 11.4, the cache half never is.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a cache answers a repeat GET from its stored copy, so only a request that changes nothing can be answered that way

search_points.quote: on a flaky network, occasionally charge a credit card twice
search_points.missing: Chapter 10 taught that TCP retransmits until nothing is lost, so the reader can't see how a reply gets 'lost' or why the client would resend the whole request; the missing step is that TCP only helps while the connection survives, and after a break or time-out the client can't know whether the request ran (partly given later at ch11-http-p10: server crash, client time-out).
search_points.close_with: a sentence: if the connection breaks or times out, TCP can't say whether the request ran, so the client sends it again on a new connection

search_points.quote: because HTTP itself does not guarantee what its method properties promise
search_points.missing: The double charge happened with a POST, which the section says promises no idempotency at all, so the reader re-reads looking for a promise that was broken and finds none; the 'because' doesn't follow from the example.
search_points.close_with: say POST promises nothing about a resend, and the key adds that promise; or that method properties are promises the server's code has to keep, which nothing in HTTP enforces

fact_doubts: ch11-http-p1: 'Open a TCP connection on port 80 to any web server ... the server will reply with ... the document' overstates for 2026. Most public servers answer plain HTTP on port 80 with a 301/308 redirect to HTTPS, not the document. A bare HTTP/1.0 request with no Host header gets the default virtual host or a 400 on name-based shared hosting.

ch11-http-p1: 'HTTP is the simplest protocol in this book' sits uneasily with ch10-udp, which calls UDP 'the simplest thing you can do with IP' (title: 'The simplest thing that could possibly work'). The qualifier 'simple enough to speak by hand' saves it only if read as the measure.

search_points.quote: at a high enough SYN rate the table fills and legitimate clients cannot connect
search_points.missing: ch10-why-p3 told the reader that a Linux server holds a million TCBs, and the caption's own numbers (a few thousand SYNs a second, each held about 30 s) come to roughly 100,000 entries, so the reader cannot see why the table fills. Nothing says this table is the 'SYN backlog' that Fig 10.11 later names.
search_points.close_with: one clause: half-open connections wait in a separate, much smaller queue, the SYN backlog

search_points.quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
search_points.missing: No earlier section uses the word 'hash', so the reader cannot say what the server computes or why recomputing it later gives the same number. The closest earlier idea is ch3-defenses-p9's pointer-authentication code, 'computed from it and a key'. Never explained in this section.
search_points.close_with: a plain gloss: a fixed-size scrambled number computed from those values plus a server secret; same inputs, same number

search_points.quote: earns a reconstructed connection and a TCB
search_points.missing: A TCB holds 'a few dozen' values (ch10-why-p3) and the cookie is a 32-bit hash, so the reader cannot see how it 'encodes the necessary state' or what the server rebuilds the TCB from. Nothing says the ACK itself brings back the addresses, ports and both sequence numbers.
search_points.close_with: one sentence: the ACK repeats addresses, ports and sequence numbers; the cookie only proves they answer a real SYN-ACK

search_points.quote: a few bits encoding the MSS hint the server would normally have remembered
search_points.missing: MSS (also drawn in Fig 10.11 as 'MSS hint') has never been expanded or explained, so the reader cannot say what setting the cookie has to carry or why the server would normally have remembered it. This caption is kept original, so the fix belongs in prose.
search_points.close_with: in p4's prose: MSS, the largest segment the client will accept, the one setting squeezed into a few cookie bits

search_points.quote: injects a TCP RST (reset) segment with a sequence number in the receiver's window
search_points.missing: The reader is never told that a receiver ignores segments numbered outside its window, or that an attacker on the path can read the current numbers off the passing traffic. Without that, they cannot say why this attack 'turns on sequence numbers' or how it differs from hijacking, which has to predict the numbers.
search_points.close_with: a clause: out-of-window segments are ignored, and an on-path attacker reads the live numbers off the traffic

search_points.quote: SYN-flooded a trusted host on Shimomura's network to take it out of the conversation
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say why the trusted host had to be silenced. p2 said a SYN-ACK sent to an uninvolved host simply goes unanswered, and nothing says that the real host, getting a SYN-ACK it never asked for, would answer with a RST and kill the forged connection.
search_points.close_with: a clause: otherwise it would answer the unexpected SYN-ACK with a RST, tearing the forged connection down

search_points.quote: the network can never authenticate who you are, only what you say
search_points.missing: Taken literally, it says the network does authenticate what you say, but the section has just shown that forged addresses and forged segments are accepted at face value. The reader re-reads to work out what the slogan means.
search_points.close_with: plain words: the network checks nothing; it carries whatever address and bytes a sender writes

search_points.quote: random ISNs (state in the unguessable), TLS (state cryptographically authenticated)
search_points.missing: The strip presents all three defences as 'making the protocol stateless under attack', but random ISNs and TLS keep their state. The reader cannot see how they make anything stateless, and the closing 'pushes state into harder places' says something different.
search_points.close_with: say SYN cookies remove state, while random ISNs and TLS make the state that remains unguessable or unforgeable

fact_doubts: p6–p7: 'TCP hijacking' is defined as injecting data into an existing connection. But Morris's 1985 Bell Labs report and the Christmas 1994 attack as p7 tells it were blind spoofing of a new connection by predicting the server's ISN. In Shimomura's own 25 Jan 1995 account, taking over an existing connection was a later, separate step (a loadable kernel STREAMS module), not the one described. The label does not match the example.

p2: a SYN-ACK that reaches a live, uninvolved host normally draws a RST, which frees the server's slot at once. Floods work because the spoofed sources do not answer. 'goes nowhere or to an uninvolved third party ... waits for the third ACK that never arrives' blurs this, and p7's need to silence the trusted host depends on it.

p7: 'cellular networks Shimomura himself had earlier helped secure' is weakly supported. His documented work was cellular-phone security research (Mitnick stole his OKI phone software), and he found Mitnick by cellular direction-finding with Sprint engineers in Raleigh. I found no source saying he had helped secure the networks Mitnick used.

p8: RFC 1948 (1996) was Informational, so 'requirement' overstates it, and it already proposed a keyed-hash (MD5) ISN. 'Modern stacks generate ISNs cryptographically (RFC 6528, 2012)' implies the cryptographic step came only in 2012, when RFC 6528 mainly moved the same scheme onto the standards track.

search_points.quote: discovered a practical, fast variant that worked against essentially every DNS resolver
search_points.missing: The paragraph names Kaminsky's variant but never says what it was. Guessing one 16-bit ID (65,536 tries) already sounds easy, so this reader cannot tell why the 1990s attack was only theoretical. The text never says that a lost race leaves the real answer cached for the TTL, which gives the attacker one try per name per TTL.
search_points.close_with: one sentence: a failed guess caches the real answer, so Kaminsky asked for fresh made-up names (1.bank.com, 2.bank.com, ...), turning every one into a new race whose forged reply names the attacker as bank.com's server

search_points.quote: added source port randomisation, multiplying the attacker's guessing space from 2¹⁶ to 2³²
search_points.missing: The book has never explained what a transport port is; it has only shown ports as header numbers (53, 80, 51234). This paragraph also said only the ID has to match. So the reader cannot see why a forged reply must reach the port the query left from, that resolvers used to keep that port fixed, or why randomising it adds 16 bits. The fig 11.7 label gives the 16 bits only after the paragraph.
search_points.close_with: a clause: a port is a 16-bit number that picks the receiving program; a reply is accepted only at the port the query came from, which resolvers used to keep fixed

search_points.quote: (duplicate response, wrong source)
search_points.missing: Low severity. This label sits under '→ ignores real answer' and says the real reply comes from the wrong source. The real reply comes from the real server's address, the same address the attacker spoofed. The resolver drops it only because the query has already been answered.
search_points.close_with: owner's call (kept-original); the accurate reading is 'duplicate response: query already answered'

fact_doubts: ch11-dns-p1 pairs example.com with 93.184.216.34 ('translate the second into the first'). The §4g fact ledger (Fig 11.3 row, Pass 28) records that example.com has moved to other addresses and stopped drawing it, but the prose still implies the old mapping.

ch11-dns-p2 'By the early 1980s the file had grown to thousands of entries': the internet host count was about 213 in 1981 and 562 in August 1983. It passed 1,000 only in late 1984 and about 2,000 in 1985. 'Hundreds' fits the early 1980s; 'thousands' fits only the mid-1980s.

ch11-dns-p1 'billions of times per second across the planet': no source is given. The largest public resolvers report on the order of a trillion queries a day, which is tens of millions per second. A global rate in the billions per second may be an order of magnitude or more too high.

ch11-dns-p5 'usually under 50 milliseconds the first time': a truly cold walk is three round trips from the resolver (root, com, then the domain's own servers) and often takes 50 to a few hundred ms. Under 50 ms holds mainly when the root and com referrals are already cached, as the Fig 11.6 strip says, so 'the first time' overstates it.
ch11-dns-p7 '(UDP queries are still spoofable in principle)': the weakness being described is that replies can be forged. 'Queries' names the wrong message.

search_points.quote: Neither is a new HTTP: the headers, methods, and status codes
search_points.missing: The section title says these upgrades 'broke compatibility on purpose', but the body only says the HTTP layer is unchanged. It never says what broke: an HTTP/1.1-only server cannot read binary frames, and QUIC needs UDP to get through. Nor does it say how a browser and server agree on a version, which matters because ch11-http-p1 promised that HTTP/1.0 still works against modern servers.
search_points.close_with: one sentence: old software cannot read the new packing, so browser and server first agree on a version (inside the TLS handshake; HTTP/3 is advertised by the server and then tried), and the speed was worth that break

fact_doubts: ch11-modern-p2: 'Sixty parallel requests now share one connection' does not match the example a few lines earlier (HTML + 10 stylesheets + 30 JavaScript files + 50 images = 91 resources). A careful reader will look back for where sixty came from.

ch11-modern-p5: 'nearly all of Google's own' traffic on HTTP/3 looks overstated and has no source. Google's own published figure (SIGCOMM 2017) was about 30% of its egress, and clients whose networks block UDP fall back to TCP. 'Roughly a third of web traffic by volume' also has no source. Public measurements such as Cloudflare Radar count requests, not volume, and show about 20 to 30%. The ledger already dropped a similar unsourced 'Google's whole edge runs HTTP/3' claim from Fig 10.9 (UNDER.md line 564).
ch11-modern-p5: 'QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections, RFC 9000, 2021)': that expansion belongs to Google's original protocol. RFC 9000 uses QUIC as a plain name, not an acronym. Minor.

search_points.quote: Objects inherited straight from other objects
search_points.missing: This reader knows inheritance only as Ch6's class layout (ch6-classes: a Circle object begins with a complete Shape), so cannot say what it means for an object to inherit from another object when there is no class, or what classes later became 'a shorthand' for.
search_points.close_with: one clause: an object that lacks a property looks it up on the object it is linked to; classes later became shorthand for making that link

search_points.quote: meant JavaScript could never expose the difference
search_points.missing: The text never says which difference it means (integer versus floating-point arithmetic, or exact versus rounded), so the reader cannot follow why having no integer type matters, and after Ch2.6 may even wonder whether whole-number counting in JavaScript is inexact.
search_points.close_with: name the difference: no separate exact whole-number type the programmer can choose, apart from rounded fractions

search_points.quote: `[] + {} === "[object Object]"`
search_points.missing: The reader has not been told that `[]` is an empty array and `{}` an empty object in JavaScript, or that `+` turns both into text ('' and '[object Object]') and joins them, so the example shows an odd result without the coercion that produces it.
search_points.close_with: a short gloss: + turns both sides into text, '' and '[object Object]', and joins them

search_points.quote: In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems
search_points.missing: p1 has already put Bill Joy inside 'the Netscape-Sun partnership' in spring 1995, so a partnership announced in December looks like a contradiction, and the reader re-reads p1 to work out whether there were two deals.
search_points.close_with: call it the joint Netscape-Sun announcement of JavaScript under the existing deal, with Sun licensing the name

fact_doubts: ch12-eich-p3: 'In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems'. Netscape had agreed to license Java from Sun in May 1995 (announced at SunWorld on 23 May 1995). The event of 4 December 1995 was the joint Netscape and Sun announcement of JavaScript, made under a trademark licence from Sun. It was not a new partnership, and p1 already treats the partnership as existing in spring 1995.

ch12-eich-p6: 'no integer type at all ... could never expose the difference'. ES2020 added BigInt, an arbitrary-precision integer type, as one of the 'careful additions' the paragraph itself describes. 'Could never' therefore overstates the case. Doubles also hold whole numbers exactly up to 2^53.

ch12-eich-p1: 'What he got in his first week was a different brief'. The timing is not verified. Eich's own accounts give the 'must look like Java' order from management in spring 1995 without naming a week. The HOPL history (Wirfs-Brock and Eich, 2020) may say he was first put on server work. Check it against the source.

search_points.quote: Every operation that might take time (fetching a URL, reading a file, waiting for a timer) returns immediately
search_points.missing: With only one thread, the reader cannot say who fetches the URL or counts the timer once the call has returned. The section never says the browser and operating system do the waiting off the JavaScript thread and put the callback in the queue when the work finishes. p2 only says passively 'from completed I/O, expired timers'. Ch7 Fig 7.5 and the Bridge's DMA give the pieces, but this section never joins them.
search_points.close_with: one clause in p1: the browser and the operating system do the waiting outside the JavaScript thread, then queue the callback

search_points.quote: its promise callback in the microtask queue
search_points.missing: Fig 12.3's example rests on `promise.then(log3); // done:`. The reader is told 'Promises (below)' at p2 and does not yet know what a promise is, what `.then` hands over, or what 'done' or 'settled' means. So they cannot say why log3 enters the microtask queue at once. p4 explains Promise later; 'settled' is never explained, and Fig 12.4's strip also relies on it.
search_points.close_with: a half-sentence at p2: a Promise is an object for a value that arrives later, `.then(f)` runs f once it has arrived ('settled')

search_points.quote: with `.then()` and `.catch()` chained horizontally
search_points.missing: 'Horizontally' is the direction the pyramid of doom grows ('indentation marching across the screen'), and Fig 12.4 draws the promise chain as a flat vertical column. So the reader cannot see how Promises fix the nesting, and goes back over the sentence.
search_points.close_with: 'chained one after another at the same depth' (a flat column, as Fig 12.4 shows)

fact_doubts: ch12-loop-p4 'microtasks arrived with Promises': in browsers the microtask queue came first with MutationObserver (shipped in 2012). Native Promises followed (2014, standardised in ES2015) and used the queue that already existed. 'Promises made microtasks central' would be safer.

search_points.quote: watched the progress bar on a file upload in a browser and realised
search_points.missing: The sentence gives a progress bar as the cause of Dahl's insight, but it never says what the bar showed him about the server. The reader cannot get from watching an upload bar to the idea that thread-per-connection servers are the wrong shape.
search_points.close_with: one clause saying what the progress bar revealed about the server while the upload was arriving

search_points.quote: were exactly the wrong shape for systems with many slow connections
search_points.missing: The reader knows what threads and processes are (ch7-gil-p1, ch4) but was never told what one waiting thread or process costs. So they cannot explain why one per connection is the wrong shape, what problem 'Browsers had already solved this' refers to, or why p4 says thread-per-request 'would have collapsed'.
search_points.close_with: one sentence on what each idle waiting thread costs (memory for its own stack, scheduler switching) once there are thousands of them

search_points.quote: A file read takes a pool thread and goes to the disk
search_points.missing: p3 has just condemned threads that sit waiting on the disk, and the open figure now shows Node sending one of only four threads to wait on the disk. The reader cannot see how this differs from Apache, or how four threads serve the thousands of slow connections in p4. The answer (sockets take no thread because the OS reports which are ready, and only file work borrows a shared thread) appears only in the closed How it works strip.
search_points.close_with: one open clause in caption or prose: network waits take no thread because the OS reports ready sockets, and only file work borrows one of a few shared threads

fact_doubts: ch12-node-p1: 'interpreted a statement at a time' may be wrong. Mocha (and SpiderMonkey after it) compiled each script to bytecode and interpreted the bytecode. It did not interpret statement by statement.

ch12-node-p1: 'By 2008 ... JavaScript engines had become aggressive optimising compilers' looks too early. V8 in 2008 had only a fast non-optimising compiler (full-codegen, with inline caches). Its first optimising compiler, Crankshaft, shipped in December 2010, and TraceMonkey arrived in 2008-09.

ch12-node-p3: 'which then sat waiting on the disk'. When connections are slow, a thread-per-connection server's threads mostly wait on the client's network, not the disk. Naming the disk fits awkwardly with 'many slow connections'.

Fig 12.6 How it works: 'libuv asks the OS which ones are ready (epoll ..., kqueue ..., IOCP on Windows)'. That describes epoll and kqueue, but IOCP is completion-based: it reports finished operations, not ready sockets.
ch12-node-p4: 'Within five years Node had become the default backend for Silicon Valley startups' is probably an overstatement for 2014, when Rails, Python and Java were still at least as common.

search_points.quote: copies the part of the URL after the `?` into the page unsafely
search_points.missing: Reflected XSS has just shown that the part after `?` goes to the server, yet Fig 12.9's DOM-based row puts the payload after `#` and says it 'never touches the server'. Nothing says the part after `#` stays in the browser, so the reader cannot square the prose with the figure.
search_points.close_with: say the part after `#`, which the browser never sends to the server

search_points.quote: flows into HTML, JavaScript, or attribute contexts without proper output encoding
search_points.missing: The defence against reflected and stored XSS ('output encoding', 'escape by default', 'HTML-escape' in Fig 12.9) is never explained. The reader cannot say how escaping stops the browser from treating injected text as code.
search_points.close_with: one clause: escaping turns < and > into codes the browser shows as text, not tags

search_points.quote: The XSS attack from Fig 12.9 is neutralised even though the injection succeeded.
search_points.missing: p8 shows CSP blocking only a script loaded from an unlisted origin. Every Fig 12.9 injection is an inline `<script>steal()</script>` sitting inside a same-origin page, which looks like 'self'. 'Inline scripts' (first used in p5) is only explained afterwards, at Fig 12.11/p9, so at this point the conclusion does not follow.
search_points.close_with: say in p8 that inline code is refused unless the policy names it, so Fig 12.9's inline scripts fail too

search_points.quote: do not attach this cookie to cross-site POST requests; only to top-level navigations
search_points.missing: 'Top-level navigation' is never explained, and the reader needs it to tell Lax from Strict: what kind of cross-site request still carries the cookie under Lax, and why that is safe.
search_points.close_with: gloss: clicking a link that moves the whole tab to the site (a GET)

fact_doubts: p10 says the same-origin policy was 'retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked', but p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say it shipped in Netscape 2.0 together with JavaScript. A reader notices the contradiction (p1's 'invented over thirty years' is fine).

p5 caption: 'XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10'. The list comes out every few years (2017, 2021, 2025), not yearly, and since 2021 XSS has been folded into the Injection category instead of standing on its own.

kept-original (Fig 12.9), low severity: step 3 of the reflected row says 'same-origin with example.com', but the URL is search.example.com. Fig 12.8 has just taught that a different subdomain is a different origin. The prose can avoid echoing the slip.

kept-original (Fig 12.9), low severity: modern browsers percent-encode < and > in location.hash (the URL Standard's fragment percent-encode set), so the literal `innerHTML = location.hash` payload only fires after a decode step. It is a classic illustration, not current behaviour verbatim.
kept-original (Fig 12.10), pedantic: the form action "bank.com/transfer" has no scheme, so it is a relative URL and would resolve under evil.com. A real attack needs https://bank.com/transfer.

p7: SameSite=Lax also withholds the cookie on cross-site image, frame and fetch requests, not only on POSTs, and it attaches the cookie only on top-level GET navigations. 'Only to top-level navigations' can be read as including a top-level cross-site POST form submission, which Lax blocks.

p10, low severity: 'exported from the browser to the server fourteen years after birth'. Netscape's LiveWire already ran server-side JavaScript in 1996. Node.js (2009) is when it went mainstream, so 'went mainstream on the server' would be safer.

search_points.quote: The HTML is parsed into a tree
search_points.missing: Parsing into a tree is known from ch7-interpret-p2 and ch7-cpython-p2, but the book has shown HTML only as 'a simple format for documents' with links (ch11-bernerslee-p4), never its elements or tags. So the reader cannot say what the DOM tree's nodes are or why HTML forms a tree, and 'each box' (p1), 'an element's width' (fig-12-7) and 'a DOM node' (p3) all depend on that.

fact_doubts: ch12-dom-p3: 'the framework computes the minimum set of DOM mutations' overstates. React's reconciliation is a heuristic diff (linear, keyed) and makes no promise of a minimum. Svelte does not diff at all: it compiles direct, targeted updates. 'a small set' or 'only the changes needed' would be safe.

search_points.quote: the schema, the queries, and the storage layout were entangled
search_points.missing: The reader has never met 'schema' (it appears nowhere in Parts I to III and is not explained here), so they cannot name the first of the three tangled things, and Codd's whole complaint of brittleness rests on how those three depend on each other.
