search_points.quote: there is no other structure (no pointers, no hierarchies, no embedded references)
search_points.missing: The reader has just followed pointers from a customer to their orders twice (IMS and CODASYL in p2), so they cannot say how a relational database finds that customer's orders once pointers are banned, and 'join' sits in the next sentence's list with no explanation.
search_points.close_with: one line saying each order row carries the customer's number and a join matches rows on that shared value

search_points.quote: System R at IBM San Jose or Ingres at Berkeley (DB2, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server)
search_points.missing: p5 says Ellison built Oracle from Codd's paper and shipped it before IBM, which matches this paragraph's own definition of 'written fresh to speak the SQL that System R introduced', so the reader cannot tell which prototype Oracle descends from or how; explained later at ch13-codd-p7 (the caption's 'through IBM's published SQL'), but that describes the same thing as written fresh.
search_points.close_with: say what Oracle took from System R (its published SQL design, no code), or move Oracle into the written-fresh group

fact_doubts: ch13-codd-p4: the 1970 paper defined permutation, projection, join, composition and restriction ('restriction' is Codd's 1970 word for what is now called selection), and it noted only that the usual set operations also apply. The data sublanguage it proposed rested on applied predicate calculus. The algebra as a query basis (selection, projection, join, union, difference) comes from Codd's 1971 and 1972 papers, so the list reads as slightly anachronistic for 'the paper proposed'.

ch13-codd-p4: 'independence principle' is not Codd's term. The paper's term is data independence: application programs stay unaffected by changes in how data is represented and stored (ordering, indexing, access paths). Describing the result rather than the procedure is how that is achieved, not what the term means.

ch13-codd-p6: Postgres (1986) was a new system Stonebraker started as the successor to Ingres. It was not built on Ingres's code, so 'became the basis for' overstates; the figure's 'led to' is accurate. Calling it 'open-source' in 1986 is also anachronistic: the code was released under a BSD-style licence from 1989.

ch13-codd-p6 / p7: Oracle shares no code with System R. It is an independent implementation of the SQL that IBM published from System R, which is what p6 itself calls 'written fresh to speak the SQL'.

ch13-codd-p8: 'He spent his last decade increasingly frustrated': Codd died in 2003, but the evidence given (the 1985 rules) and his RM/V2 book (1990) both come well before his last decade (1993 to 2003). 'His later years' would fit the evidence.

search_points.quote: and join (⨝), the last of them derived from the others
search_points.missing: Read plainly, 'the others' means selection and projection. Both work on one table, so this reader cannot see how a pairing of two tables could be built from them. The real recipe (a cross product, then a selection) only comes later, at ch13-algebra-p3 and in the fig-13-2 How it works strip.
search_points.close_with: name the parts here, e.g. 'built from a cross product and a selection (below)'

search_points.quote: the same rows with far fewer of them to join (Fig 13.3 shows it)
search_points.missing: Fig 13.3 is not in this section. It is in Section 03 (ch13-sql) and the text is not a link, so the reader stops to hunt for a figure they have not reached yet. The prose already carries the rule without it (the figure comes later, at fig-13-3 in ch13-sql).
search_points.close_with: '(Fig 13.3, in Section 03, shows it)' or make it a link

fact_doubts: ch13-algebra-p3: 'queries that follow a chain of any length, a manager's manager's manager ... sit outside it'. A chain of fixed length three can be written with two self-joins, which is exactly what the rename sentence just before shows. What falls outside the algebra is a chain of unknown length (every manager up to the top, however many levels). The example as written reads as if three levels were already impossible. Suggest 'every manager above someone, however many levels up'.

ch13-algebra-p4: 'duplicates are allowed unless you write SELECT DISTINCT'. SQL's UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT also remove duplicates by default; only the ALL forms keep them. DISTINCT is not the only exception. Low severity.

fig-13-2: the join's result table shows only name and item. A join (⨝) in the algebra keeps every column of both inputs (id, name, user_id, item), so the drawn result is really a join followed by a projection. This is a teaching simplification; low severity, and only worth fixing if the figure is touched for another reason.

search_points.quote: PostgreSQL's log is redo-only: an aborted transaction's row versions simply stay invisible.
search_points.missing: This is in Fig 13.6's How it works strip. The reader has just been told that recovery undoes every uncommitted change that reached the pages. Now one engine does no undo at all, and the reason given rests on 'row versions' that stay 'invisible', which only MVCC explains, at p8 (and p8 never says that an aborted transaction's versions are skipped), so the reader re-reads to see how PostgreSQL ever gets Bob back to 50.
search_points.close_with: cut the PostgreSQL clause from this strip, or move it to sit after p8

search_points.quote: snapshot isolation still allows write skew, which only serializable prevents.
search_points.missing: This is in Fig 13.7's How it works strip. It says PostgreSQL's repeatable read already blocks all three anomalies in the table, so the only thing left for serializable is 'write skew', which the book never explains. 'Snapshot isolation' only becomes readable at p8. The reader can no longer say what serializable adds, and p8's Serializable abort rule then has no example of the overlap it catches.
search_points.close_with: drop the write-skew clause, or give one plain two-transaction example at p8

fact_doubts: ch13-acid-p4: 'appends a record of the intended change ... and forces it onto physical storage (the fsync() system call). Only then does the engine modify the data pages' reads as one fsync per change, with the page changed only afterwards. Real engines change the page in memory at once and buffer the log records. The write-ahead rule is that a log record reaches disk before its changed page does, and that the commit record is forced before the commit is acknowledged. As written it also sits badly with Fig 13.6's strip, 'A commit costs one log flush'.

ch13-acid-p1: 'ACID ... is the contract every relational database makes with its users'. p2 defines Isolation as serializable, but the defaults of PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server (read committed) and InnoDB (repeatable read) are weaker, and some relational engines (MySQL's old MyISAM) have no transactions at all. 'Every' overclaims. Low priority.

search_points.quote: A lookup descends from the root, one page per level, to the leaf
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say how a lookup picks which child to read at each level, or why 15, 30 and 45 appear both in an upper node and again in a leaf. The old caption carried this step (internal nodes route lookups by comparing the sought key against theirs; the leaves hold the real key and row-pointer pairs), and now only the numbers in the drawing do, so a newcomer has to work it out from the picture (20 < 30 goes left, 20 ≥ 15 goes right).
search_points.close_with: one clause: an upper node's keys are signposts (smaller goes left, equal or larger right), copies of keys whose rows sit in the leaves, which is also why hundreds of keys mean hundreds of children

search_points.quote: a quick check of whatever else landed in the same slot
search_points.missing: Chapter 11 (ch11-crypto-p4) taught a hash as a 256-bit fingerprint that 'uniquely' identifies its input, so the reader cannot see how that result becomes a position in an array of ordinary size, or why another key would ever land in the same slot. Only Fig 13.9's toy remainder explains it, after this point: 27 and 43 share bucket 7.
search_points.close_with: say the hash is cut down to the array's size (the remainder), so different keys can share a slot

search_points.quote: range queries (`WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200`) cannot use the index
search_points.missing: The reader has just learned that one key is found by hashing it, so they cannot see why a range of whole numbers (100 to 200 here, 40 to 45 in Fig 13.9) is not found by hashing each value in turn. 'Cannot use the index' and the caption's 'the only way to find them is to look in every one' therefore do not follow from what was said.
search_points.close_with: a clause: most ranges hold values that cannot be listed one by one (any name from Al to Am, any price from 10 to 20), so only an ordered index can walk them

fact_doubts: Fig 13.9 How it works, 'it also serves ORDER BY and prefix matches such as LIKE 'Al%'': in PostgreSQL a default B-tree index can serve a LIKE prefix only under the C collation or with a text_pattern_ops / varchar_pattern_ops operator class. The claim holds in principle and holds for MySQL InnoDB, so this is low priority. Checked and correct: the bucket arithmetic (37 × id mod 8 sends 40, 41, 43 and 45 to buckets 0, 5, 7 and 1, and 27 and 43 share bucket 7), Fig 13.8's five page reads, PostgreSQL hash indexes WAL-logged since version 10, and Bayer and McCreight at Boeing in 1970.

search_points.quote: an index on age only if few rows pass
search_points.missing: The reader has not been told what a database index is, so cannot see why it is only worth using when few rows pass and why a full scan wins otherwise. (Indexes are not explained anywhere in this section; 'CREATE INDEX' in p2 is only a name.)
search_points.close_with: one plain clause: an index jumps straight to the matching rows, but each jump is a separate read, so when most rows match, one straight pass is cheaper

search_points.quote: one with a hash table and one with a sort
search_points.missing: 'Hash table' is never defined. The only hash this reader knows is the SHA-256 fingerprint from ch11-crypto. Fig 13.4 later shows buckets chosen by remainder, but nothing says those buckets are the hash table or that the remainder does the hash's job.
search_points.close_with: name the link once, in the prose or the caption: a hash table sorts keys into buckets by a quick function of the key (here the remainder), so finding a key means checking one bucket

search_points.quote: a million a side: a trillion against a few million
search_points.missing: The figure fixes four buckets. With a million keys, each bucket would hold about 250,000, so the reader cannot see why a probe still costs about one step. The missing fact is that the real table gets roughly as many buckets as rows.
search_points.close_with: a few words: the table gets about as many buckets as rows, so each bucket holds one or two keys

search_points.id: fig-13-4 (How it works, 'Nested loop' and 'Merge join')
search_points.quote: the inner side has an index on the join key
search_points.missing: Indexes are still unexplained, so the reader cannot see why one 'index lookup' replaces a scan of the whole inner table, or why an index hands the merge join its rows already sorted.
search_points.close_with: the same short gloss of an index (a sorted lookup structure that finds a key without scanning), given once at its first use

search_points.quote: finds the cheapest order in which to join them
search_points.missing: Every join in this section has two tables. The reader has not been told that a query can join several tables, or that the pair joined first sets how many rows the next join must handle. So 'cheapest order' and 'building up from each small group' cannot be explained back.
search_points.close_with: one clause: with three or more tables, the pair joined first sets the size of what every later join faces

fact_doubts: ch13-sql-p2: 'DML changes the data' lists SELECT, but SELECT only reads. Some texts file it separately as DQL. The sentence is wrong as written for one of its four examples.

ch13-sql-p5 (caption): 'a million a side: a trillion against a few million' (and 'about ten' for five a side) is true for the hash join, and for the merge join only when the inputs are already sorted. Sorting two million-row inputs first takes roughly 2 x 20 million comparisons (n log2 n), so a merge join from unsorted input costs tens of millions, not a few million. The picture's 'once sorted' qualifies this; the caption does not.

ch13-sql-p6: 'invented for IBM's System R by Patricia Selinger'. The 1979 SIGMOD paper has five authors (Selinger, Astrahan, Chamberlin, Lorie, Price). Selinger led the work, but naming her alone simplifies it. 'Patricia Selinger and colleagues' would be exact.

search_points.quote: a key-shifted Caesar, where different positions used different shifts
search_points.missing: The text never says the shifts come from a short keyword that repeats. Without that, the reader cannot see what 'regularity' Babbage and Kasiski found, since p1 has just said the weakness was each letter always getting the same substitute, and different shifts at different positions removes it.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the shifts came from a short keyword that repeated, so the pattern recurs every keyword-length letters

search_points.quote: The one-time pad is provably unbreakable
search_points.missing: This is the term the section teaches (the 'exception' in the How it works strip), but the strip gives only what it costs, never what it does. The reader cannot say how a one-time pad differs from the broken Vigenère, which also 'used different shifts' at different positions, or why it leaves no regularity to find.
search_points.close_with: say each letter gets its own truly random shift and the key is never reused, so nothing repeats

search_points.quote: Each leader runs to the event's year on a line from 50 BCE to 2030
search_points.missing: 'Leader' is a typesetting word for the thin line from a label to its point. A novice reads it as a person or as the event itself, and 'on a line' (the timeline bar) makes it harder, so the first How it works step sends the reader back to re-read.
search_points.close_with: 'each label's thin line points to its year on the bar'

fact_doubts: p4: 'settled soon after in the Bernstein and Junger appeals' overstates the case. The Ninth Circuit's 1999 Bernstein panel opinion was withdrawn when rehearing en banc was granted, and the case ended without a final ruling on that point. Only Junger v. Daley (6th Cir., 2000) holds that code is speech, and there is no Supreme Court ruling. 'Established in' or 'affirmed by the Junger appeal' would be safer.

Fig 14.1 drawn note '1976 to now is the last 3%': 1976 to 2026 is 50 of about 2,076 years, roughly 2.4%. Even the drawn line out to 2030 gives 54 of 2,080, about 2.6%. 'Under 3%' (the wording the How it works strip uses) would be exact.

search_points.quote: an apostrophe in the input terminates the developer's quoted string
search_points.missing: The book never says that SQL puts a text value between apostrophes and ends it at the next apostrophe. It showed status='paid' and LIKE 'Al%' without stating that rule. Fig 13.10's code also mixes the program's double quotes with SQL's single quotes. So this reader cannot explain why an apostrophe the user types ends a string the developer wrote, and may take 'the developer's quoted string' to mean the double-quoted pieces.
search_points.close_with: one sentence in p2, since the figure is kept original: SQL writes a text value between apostrophes (name='alice') and reads it up to the next apostrophe. Once the pieces are glued together, the database gets one line and cannot tell which apostrophes the user typed

search_points.quote: Parameterised queries close the primary vulnerability, but a serious application stacks more layers
search_points.missing: p4 called this defence 'clean and absolute', so this reader cannot see why more layers are needed or how that layer could 'fail' (the strip's last line says 'even when one layer fails'). The missing step: the fix only protects the queries written with it, and one query built by hand anywhere in the code reopens the hole.
search_points.close_with: half a sentence: because one query still built by hand anywhere in the program reopens the hole

search_points.quote: a driver that only emulates this must escape every value correctly instead
search_points.missing: This reader knows 'driver' only as the kernel code that runs a piece of hardware (ch4-anatomy), and 'escape' was never explained in plain words (it appears only as 'HTML-escape' in the kept-original Fig 12.9). So this caveat to an 'absolute' defence cannot be followed: some libraries only pretend to send values separately and fall back on marking apostrophes in the text.
search_points.close_with: gloss driver as 'the library a program uses to talk to the database' and escape as 'mark each apostrophe so the parser reads it as a letter'

search_points.quote: the SQL text, a placeholder where each value goes, is parsed once
search_points.missing: Read as written, the phrase in commas says the SQL text is a placeholder. The reader has to re-read and check the picture to see that the text contains a placeholder for each value.
search_points.close_with: 'the SQL text, with a placeholder where each value goes,'

fact_doubts: fig-13-10 caption (kept original): Sony never confirmed that its 2011 PlayStation Network breach (77 million) was SQL injection. The LulzSec breach of Sony Pictures the same year was. Already logged as an owner call in docs/pass-30-figures.md and UNDER.md §4g, so it is noted here only so the list is complete.

fig-13-10 (kept original): the vulnerable login query compares pw directly with the typed password, which means passwords are stored as plain text. Yet the UNION payload line says it 'exfiltrates every password hash'. If pw held hashes, the query as drawn would never match a real login. The figure contradicts itself here. Minor.

ch13-injection-p7: the WAL is listed under 'optimisation tooling' with 'fifty years of battle-testing'. The book taught the WAL as the durability and atomicity mechanism (ch13-acid-p4) and dates its redo/undo form (ARIES) to 1992. 'Fifty years' fits Codd's model and the B-tree (1970) better than it fits the WAL.

search_points.quote: while preserving the algebraic structure that makes hard problems possible
search_points.missing: The reader cannot say why wrapping around makes undoing hard: p3 says ordinary powers have an easy inverse (school logarithms), and nothing says what the wrap takes away, so Fig 14.2's '5ˣ mod 23 = 8 → x = ?' being hard has to be taken on trust.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the wrap scrambles size, so the result gives no clue to the exponent; no logarithm works, only trying

search_points.quote: multiplication has division, squaring has square root, and each takes about as long backward
search_points.missing: Here multiplication is listed as easy to undo, yet in Fig 14.2 just below (and in Fig 11.8 before it) multiplying primes is one of the four one-way functions; nothing says that division needs one factor already known, while factoring gets only the product.
search_points.close_with: 'division undoes a product only if you hold one factor; given the product alone, you must search'

search_points.quote: hashing would only lose half its bits of strength
search_points.missing: 'Bits of strength' is never defined, so the reader cannot tell whether losing half of them leaves SHA-256 safe (2²⁵⁶ tries down to 2¹²⁸) or broken; the 2²⁵⁶ figure sits in the closed strip, and the 'one more bit doubles the work' rule only arrives later, in the callout (p6).
search_points.close_with: 'n bits of strength means about 2ⁿ tries; half the bits is 2¹²⁸, still out of reach'

search_points.quote: multiplying a point on an elliptic curve
search_points.missing: The other three panels give real numbers, but panel 4 gives none, and the book has never said what a point on an elliptic curve is or what multiplying one by k means, so the reader cannot see what is easy forwards and hard backwards. The term has appeared only as a name (ch11-crypto-p7). Section 05 (ch14-ecc) presumably explains it, and nothing here points there.
search_points.close_with: a clause: 'points on a curve can be added by a fixed rule; k × G is G added to itself k times (Section 05)'

search_points.quote: Add one bit to the key and the work doubles
search_points.missing: This sentence comes straight after 'Factoring is kinder... each extra bit costs less than a doubling', so it reads as though factoring's work doubles per bit after all; the reader has to work out that it belongs to the exponential O(2^n) case two sentences earlier.
search_points.close_with: move it to follow 'roughly O(2^n)', or open it with 'For exponential work,'

fact_doubts: ch14-primer-p6: 'At 256 bits of key, "hard" is several orders of magnitude beyond the entire computational capacity of Earth running until the heat death of the universe.' Heat death is usually put at about 10^100 years (about 3×10^107 s). Even at today's roughly 10^21 operations per second, Earth's total over that time comes to about 10^128 operations, far more than 2^256 ≈ 10^77. The claim holds against the age of the universe (about 4×10^17 s, which gives about 10^38 ≈ 2^128), not against heat death. Also, the callout's own example, a 256-bit elliptic-curve key, falls to about 2^128 work (the generic square-root attack), not 2^256.

ch14-primer-p6: 'Factoring is kinder, called sub-exponential... which is why an RSA key needs thousands of bits where an elliptic-curve key needs 256.' Discrete logarithms modulo a prime fall to the same number field sieve and are just as sub-exponential. That is why classic Diffie–Hellman needs the 2048-bit prime of p2 (and the strip's 3072-bit discrete logs). As written, the callout suggests only factoring is kinder and modular powers are fully exponential.

ch14-primer-p2: 'with a 2048-bit prime as the modulus instead of 12'. This is true for classic Diffie–Hellman. RSA's 2048-bit modulus, though, is the product of two primes (the 3233 of Fig 14.2, the 2048-bit key of Fig 11.8), and elliptic curves work modulo primes of about 256 bits. Stated as cryptography's general case, it is loose, and a reader carrying Fig 11.8 may mix the two up.

search_points.quote: public image CDN
search_points.missing: Nothing in the book says what a CDN is, though it was used three times before (ch11-dns, ch11-modern, ch12-security). The prose never mentions this example either. The sighted reader sees 'not here' for repudiation and disclosure and has to work out why (nothing secret, no action anyone could later deny). That reason is only in the hidden <desc>, not in the drawn words, the caption or the strip.
search_points.close_with: plain label or one clause: a server that hands anyone the site's public pictures, so nothing is secret and nobody acts there

search_points.quote: On a data-flow diagram, processes face all six
search_points.missing: This is in the How it works strip ('Per element'). The book never teaches 'data-flow diagram', 'data stores' or 'flows'. 'Processes' here means something other than the known OS term, so a reader who opens the strip cannot follow why some elements face six threats and others three (Pass 30 flagged this and it is still there).
search_points.close_with: cut the bullet, or say: in a sketch of the design, the programs, the places data rests and the arrows it travels along

fact_doubts: ch15-mindset-p1 says 'the first time the American government heard, on the record' how attackers think. Neal Patrick of the 414s testified on hacking before a House subcommittee in September 1983, so 'first time' looks overstated.

ch15-mindset-p1 says 'the BGP and DNS vulnerabilities they had in mind were real'. The 1998 testimony did not name the flaws. Later accounts (Mudge, e.g. Washington Post 2015) point to BGP. I could not find a source for DNS.

ch15-mindset-p3 says STRIDE was 'published by Praerit Garg and Loren Kohnfelder at Microsoft in 1999'. It was an internal Microsoft paper ('The threats to our products', April 1999), not a public publication at the time.

search_points.quote: and the round key is XORed in
search_points.missing: The reader has one key of 128, 192 or 256 bits. Each round XORs in 'the round key', the figure starts 'after the first key XOR', and the strip mentions 'round keys taken backwards', yet nothing says what a round key is or how it comes from the one key (a 256-bit key cannot be XORed straight into a 128-bit grid). It is never explained.
