search_points.quote: SubBytes is the only non-linear step, the source of confusion
search_points.missing: (How it works strip, Fig 14.5) Confusion was defined in p2 as the output depending in a tangled way on the key, but SubBytes is a fixed table with no key in it, and 'non-linear' is never explained. The reader cannot see why this key-free step is what makes the key relation tangled.
search_points.close_with: say the other steps are plain XORs and sums an attacker could unwind like simultaneous equations, and the irregular table placed between key XORs stops that

search_points.quote: or a running counter. Modern systems use GCM, counter mode plus a tag
search_points.missing: The reader cannot see how a counter gets into a block's encryption. The Fig 14.6 strip (ch14-symmetric-p5) then says counter mode is 'AES encrypting a running counter', which leaves no place for the message, because nothing says the encrypted counter is XORed onto the message block. So the mode the section recommends cannot be followed.
search_points.close_with: AES encrypts counter values 1, 2, 3…, and each result is XORed onto one message block, a one-time pad made by AES

search_points.quote: the ciphertext of the block before it (CBC)
search_points.missing: The first block has no block before it, so the reader cannot say what it is mixed with. The mixing itself is only ever called 'mixes'/'mixed' and is never named as XOR.
search_points.close_with: a random starting block (the IV), sent in the clear, is XORed into block one, and each later block is XORed with the ciphertext before it

fact_doubts: ch14-symmetric-p1 'your VPN tunnel ... are AES too': WireGuard, the protocol behind many current VPNs, uses ChaCha20-Poly1305, not AES. Some TLS connections also run ChaCha20-Poly1305 (the Fig 11.11 strip names it), so 'usually AES' would be exact.

ch14-symmetric-p2 'Each round applies the same four steps': in AES the last round leaves out MixColumns, and one extra AddRoundKey comes before round 1 (Fig 14.5 shows it as 'after the first key XOR'), so the sentence is slightly off.

ch14-symmetric-p2 'no shortcut is known that recovers the key from plaintext and ciphertext': biclique cryptanalysis (2011) finds the key about four times faster than brute force (about 2^126.1 for AES-128). 'No practical shortcut' would be exact. Minor.

search_points.quote: Adding a point to itself k times is fast
search_points.missing: The only rule given needs a line through two different points, so the reader cannot add P to itself (the tangent at P is never mentioned), and cannot see why adding k times is fast when k must be huge, since Section 04 showed a small secret falls to trying every value.
search_points.close_with: one clause: to add a point to itself, use the line that just touches the curve at P; doubling again and again (P, 2P, 4P, 8P…) reaches kP in about as many steps as k has bits, like repeated squaring

search_points.quote: Cryptography uses the same rules over a finite field instead of the real numbers
search_points.missing: A reader who opens the strip meets 'finite field' (and 'prime fields' two lines later) before the prose has said what one is. Explained later at ch14-ecc-p4 ('the integers modulo some large prime').
search_points.close_with: gloss it where it first appears: 'over a finite field (the integers modulo a large prime, Section 01.5's clock)'

search_points.quote: In real cryptography the curve is defined not over the real numbers but over a finite field
search_points.missing: The reader learned point addition only as a drawing (a line, its third crossing, a reflection) and cannot say how that works on a finite scatter of points modulo p, where there is no line to draw. Fig 14.9's own strip stresses 'a scatter of points, not a line'.
search_points.close_with: one sentence: the drawing is really a formula on the coordinates (slope, then the third point's x and y), and the same formula is worked out in arithmetic mod p

fact_doubts: ch14-ecc-p4: 'Bitcoin's curve was picked for constants chosen by a simple public rule' states Satoshi's motive as fact. Satoshi never said why secp256k1 was chosen; the 'nothing up my sleeve' reason is a later reading by commentators. SEC 2 itself says Koblitz-curve constants were picked to allow a fast endomorphism, which only makes them predictable as a side effect. Safer wording would be 'Bitcoin's curve has constants fixed by a simple public rule'.

ch14-ecc-p2: the definition of a group ('grouping does not matter, and one point acts as zero') leaves out inverses. Every element also needs an opposite; on the curve, that is a point's reflection. The section teaches 'group' as a term, so a reader takes away an incomplete definition. Minor.

Title and ch14-ecc-p3 call the elliptic-curve discrete log 'the trapdoor'. Strictly, a trapdoor function is a one-way function with a secret that makes inverting it easy, as in RSA. The discrete log is a one-way function with no trapdoor, which is the book's own term in Section 01.5. Minor terminology looseness, not a reader stop.

search_points.quote: discrete exponentiation is easy to compute, discrete logarithm is hard
search_points.missing: This reader knows an ordinary logarithm is one calculator button, and the primer (ch14-primer-p3) gave squaring and square root as an easy pair. Nothing here says why undoing g^a mod p is hard: the wrap-around scatters the powers (5, 2, 10, 4, 20, 8, … mod 23), so there is no getting warmer and the only way back is to try.
search_points.close_with: a line or figure strip showing 5^x mod 23 jumping with no order, so the only way back is search

search_points.quote: repeated squaring (g, g², g⁴, g⁸, …) reaches a huge exponent
search_points.missing: The squares only give the exponents 1, 2, 4, 8, …. The figure just below uses 5⁶ and 5¹⁵, and this reader cannot see how those exponents are built from the list, so they cannot explain why any exponent takes only about as many steps as it has bits.
search_points.close_with: one clause: multiply together the squares the exponent's binary digits pick (5⁶ = 5⁴ × 5²), wrapping mod p as you go

search_points.quote: an RSA or elliptic-curve (ECDSA) signature to prove the server's identity
search_points.missing: The section teaches RSA only as anyone locking with e and the holder unlocking with d. Then the Fig 14.8 strip and this strip say RSA's only remaining job in TLS 1.3 is signing, and this reader cannot say how the same key pair produces a signature that anyone can check (Part III treated a signature as a black box, and ch11-crypto-p1 promised Chapter 14 would open it).
search_points.close_with: one sentence: the holder raises a hash of the message to d; anyone raises the result to e and compares

fact_doubts: p1: 'computing g^a mod p takes microseconds'. At the 2048-bit size the strip gives, one full modular exponentiation takes about a millisecond on one core, and p6 says 'a few milliseconds per handshake', so the two sentences read as inconsistent. Consider 'about a millisecond' or 'well under a second' in p1.

p6: 'Diffie–Hellman is in the same performance class as RSA (a few milliseconds per handshake)'. This is true of finite-field DH. The elliptic-curve DH that the same strip says TLS uses (X25519) takes tens of microseconds, far faster than an RSA-2048 signature.

p6: 'TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral key exchange'. TLS 1.3 also allows PSK-only resumption (psk_ke), which has no (EC)DHE and so no forward secrecy. Fig 11.13's strip states it precisely: 'every full handshake has forward secrecy'.

search_points.quote: valid for that call site when it built the program for that call site
search_points.missing: The sentence that states CFI's rule says 'for that call site' twice, so the reader stops to work out whether two different things are meant. The duplicate came in with the Pass 29 law-4 rewrite (commit 9aea00a).
search_points.close_with: delete the second 'for that call site'

search_points.quote: Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below.
search_points.missing: ch3-defenses-p9 taught that a ret is an indirect jump and that CFI checks indirect jumps, so it is the defence against ROP. Here CFI checks only indirect calls and leaves returns to other defences. The reader cannot square the two chapters, and cannot see how a check that skips returns guards against ROP, which is built from returns. The 'relatives' it actually blocks (gadgets reached through an overwritten function pointer, JOP in Fig 15.2) are never named.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the CFI that compilers ship checks only calls through pointers (ROP's relatives); the returns from Chapter 3 go to the shadow stack and PAC

search_points.quote: ASLR | 2003+ · randomisation
search_points.missing: Fig 15.2 calls itself 'Fig 3.11 extended', yet it dates ASLR 2003+ and draws it after DEP/NX. ch3-defenses-p6 says PaX shipped ASLR in 2001, and Fig 3.11 says 2001+. Low severity; flagged before as a register flag but never ruled.
search_points.close_with: owner call: 2001+ to match Fig 3.11 and the prose

search_points.quote: PAC · CET shadow stack | 2017+ · hardware-signed RA
search_points.missing: The CET shadow stack signs nothing. It compares a protected copy of the return address, as ch15-memory-p4 and ch3-defenses-p9 both say, so the shared label 'hardware-signed' is wrong for CET. Low severity.
search_points.close_with: owner call: 'hardware-guarded return address'

fact_doubts: ch15-memory-p3: 'valid for that call site' / 'the call site's allow-list' fits Clang's type-based CFI. MSVC's Control Flow Guard, also named here, keeps one program-wide set of valid targets (any address-taken function start), not a list per call site. The gadget example still holds, because a mid-function gadget is not a function start.

ch15-memory-p4: 'a mismatch causes an exception' is right in effect. On ARMv8.3 cores without FEAT_FPAC, a failed check does not trap straight away: it corrupts the pointer, and the return then faults on an invalid address.

ch15-memory-p4: 'cryptographically signed ... verifies the signature' is common usage (Apple says it too), but PAC is a keyed MAC, not a public-key signature: one secret key both computes and checks the code, like HMAC in Ch14. ch3-defenses-p9 put it more precisely ('a code computed from it and a key'). Low.

search_points.quote: So a 256-bit hash holds out against collisions only to about 2^128 work
search_points.missing: The caption never says that a match becomes likely once the number of pairs gets close to the number of possible values (253 pairs against 365 days). Without that, the reader cannot get from 'the pairs grow as the square' to 2^128 (2^128 tries make about 2^256 pairs, roughly one for every possible hash).
search_points.close_with: one clause: the odds turn even once the pairs come close to the number of possible values (253 against 365), and 2^128 tries give about 2^256 pairs

search_points.quote: mixes the running 256-bit state with bits of the current block
search_points.missing: 'The running 256-bit state' and 'compression function' are used as if the reader already knows them. Nothing says the state starts at fixed values, takes in each 512-bit block in turn and is the hash at the end, so the reader cannot picture how the input bits reach the output.
search_points.close_with: half a sentence: a 256-bit value starts fixed, each block is stirred into it, and its final value is the hash (or drop the two terms)

search_points.quote: breaks every descendant: the log is immutable in practice
search_points.missing: The book never says what a Git commit is (a saved version of a project that names the version before it). 'Immutable' also does not follow from 'a different hash': a forger could recompute every later hash in milliseconds, and the text never says that other people already hold the newest hash and would see it change.
search_points.close_with: a few words on what a commit is, and that anyone holding the latest ID would notice a rewritten history

search_points.quote: which allows compact proofs that a specific leaf belongs to the tree
search_points.missing: The reader knows root, node and leaf from the B-tree but cannot see how the proof works. Nothing says the leaves are the hashes of the items, that the root hash stands for the whole set, or that a proof is just the few sibling hashes on the path up to the root, so the reader cannot explain 'audited without downloading every certificate'.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the root hash stands for everything; to prove one leaf, hand over the sibling hashes up to the root and let the checker rehash them

search_points.quote: makes every guess expensive
search_points.missing: Fig 14.3 has just said that finding an input for a given hash takes about 2^256 work, so the reader cannot see how a stolen hash can be 'guessed' at all. The missing step: people choose passwords from a small pool of likely ones, so the attacker hashes each likely password and compares, and preimage resistance does not help against that.
search_points.close_with: one sentence in p4: the attacker hashes common passwords and compares them with the stolen hashes; hashing hides the password but does not stop guessing

search_points.quote: a per-user salt makes equal passwords look different
search_points.missing: 'Salt' is never defined. The reader is not told that it is a random value for each user, stored openly next to the hash and hashed together with the password, so they cannot say why it makes equal passwords look different or why it forces the attacker to guess row by row.
search_points.close_with: a few words: a random value per user, stored next to the hash and hashed in with the password

search_points.quote: a slow, memory-hard function
search_points.missing: The text never says why needing 64 MiB per guess makes guessing expensive. A reader whose laptop has gigabytes of memory sees 64 MiB as small, and nobody tells them that the memory each guess needs limits how many guesses the attacker's hardware can run at once. The figure title's 'KDF' is also never spelled out or explained.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the memory each guess needs limits how many guesses an attacker's hardware runs at once; spell out 'KDF' or drop it from the title

fact_doubts: ch14-hashing-p4: 'a certificate authority's (CA's) log of issued certificates'. Certificate Transparency logs are public, append-only logs run by independent operators (RFC 6962), and each one records certificates from many CAs. They are not the issuing CA's own log, so the wording suggests each CA audits itself.
Fig 14.4: the drawn label reads '64 MB of memory per guess', while the picture description says '64 MiB' and the How it works strip uses MiB ('19 MiB'). The units disagree (64 MiB is about 67 MB).

Checked and consistent, no action: SHA-256('p4ssw0rd') = 48d2a5bbcf42..., and the salted values match SHA-256('7f3a:p4ssw0rd') = 24a8b7da... and SHA-256('c2e9:p4ssw0rd') = 57bea797...; OWASP's argon2id minimum of 19 MiB with 2 passes; SHAttered at about 2^63; LinkedIn 2012 used unsalted SHA-1; bcrypt 1999, scrypt 2009, Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015.

search_points.quote: HKDF stretches it, mixed with a hash of the conversation, into separate AES-GCM keys
search_points.missing: The section never says what HKDF is or how it turns one shared point into several separate keys that reveal nothing about it. Chapter 11 (Fig 11.11 strip) only named it, and this strip's "built on HMAC" adds a second term that is never explained, yet the promised "which keys derive from which" depends on it.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a key-derivation function that hashes the shared secret with a label and the transcript (through HMAC, a hash that takes a key), once per key, so each key is new and none leads back to the secret

search_points.quote: easy in two dimensions and believed infeasible in hundreds, even for a quantum computer
search_points.missing: On the regular grid described, the reader would just round each coordinate, in any number of dimensions. The text never says why the problem gets hard, what the easy forward direction of this one-way function is (the primer promised one), or how the key holder can still solve it.
search_points.close_with: a slanted grid given by long, skewed directions; pushing a grid point slightly off it is easy, finding the grid point again is hard, and the private key is a short, nearly square set of directions that makes rounding work

search_points.quote: provides a signature alternative built only on hash functions
search_points.missing: p3 has just taught that a signature needs a private key whose work the public key can check, and Chapter 11 said a hash has no key, so the reader cannot see how a hash function alone can make a signature.
search_points.close_with: one sentence: the private key is a set of random secrets and the public key is their hashes; signing reveals the secrets that the message's hash picks out, and anyone hashes them again to check

fact_doubts: ch14-tls-pqc-p3: "(the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses)" makes it sound as if TLS 1.3 never signs with RSA. RSA-PSS is allowed in TLS 1.3 and common, because most server certificates are RSA. The book itself says so in Fig 14.11's strip ("Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS"), in ch14-publickey-p6 and in Fig 14.8's strip ("where it appears it only signs"), so a reader meets a contradiction.

ch14-tls-pqc-p7: on a regular square grid the nearest point is found by rounding each coordinate, in any number of dimensions. The hardness comes from a grid described by a skewed basis. ML-KEM and ML-DSA formally rest on module-LWE and module-SIS (noisy linear equations), which are related to the nearest-point problem but are not literally it.

ch14-tls-pqc-p6: "Diffie–Hellman, RSA, and their elliptic-curve forms ECDH and ECDSA" pairs ECDSA with RSA. ECDSA is the elliptic-curve form of DSA, a discrete-log signature, and no elliptic-curve RSA is in use. docs/audit/outside.json has already logged this.
ch14-tls-pqc-p11: "from the silicon (Parts I and II)". Part II is the software layer (kernel, C, C++, Python), not silicon. docs/audit/outside.json has already logged this.

search_points.quote: now the laptop sends every packet destined for the gateway to the attacker instead
search_points.missing: 'Gateway' first appears here (earlier the word only occurs inside 'Border Gateway Protocol'), and ch8-ethernet's ARP only covered sending to an address on the local network. So the reader cannot see why poisoning one cache entry captures all their internet traffic and not just the packets meant for the router itself; the missing step is that every packet leaving the LAN is sent to the router's MAC address.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the gateway is the LAN's router, the next hop for every packet bound off the LAN, so its MAC is where all outside traffic goes

search_points.quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
search_points.missing: The caption says speed wins the laptop's cache. Fig 15.4's step 3 ('the cache keeps the freshest claim'), its title ('whoever keeps answering wins') and p4's 'keeps telling it' all say the latest answer wins, so the reader cannot tell what makes the laptop believe the attacker over the real gateway's reply.
search_points.close_with: make the caption match step 3: the cache keeps the latest answer, so the attacker wins by repeating, not by being fast

search_points.quote: any modern OS does this with one sysctl
search_points.missing: 'sysctl' is never defined, so the reader cannot tell what the single step is that turns the attacker's machine into a forwarder, and stops on the unfamiliar word.
search_points.close_with: 'with one setting', or a gloss: a single operating-system setting

fact_doubts: ch15-network-p5 (caption): 'answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway'. Most ARP implementations overwrite the cache with the latest reply, and many also accept replies nobody asked for. Spoofing works by sending forged replies again and again, not by winning a race. The kept-original Fig 15.4 (step 3) already says so, and the caption contradicts it.

ch15-network-p4/p5: poisoning only the laptop's cache sends just laptop-to-gateway traffic through the attacker. The gateway's replies still go straight to the laptop's real MAC. A real two-way man-in-the-middle also poisons the gateway's cache for the laptop's IP. The text calls the one-way case a 'transparent intermediary' and says 'the attacker is now MITM' (p2 defines MITM as relaying each side's traffic to the other).

ch15-network-p6: 'reroutes entire IP prefixes through a malicious autonomous system', with Pakistan/YouTube 2008 as the example. ch9-security itself says that announcement was meant to block YouTube inside Pakistan, leaked worldwide by accident, and the traffic was dropped. It was not malicious and did not route traffic through to an interceptor.

ch15-network-p1: 'TLS authenticates endpoints'. Ordinary web TLS authenticates only the server; client certificates are rare. The kept-original Fig 15.3 itself says 'server cert verified by Alice'. Its 'cannot impersonate either side' holds only because the client's login happens inside the encrypted channel.

ch15-network-p5: 'any modern OS does this with one sysctl'. sysctl is a Unix-family tool (Linux, BSD, macOS). Windows turns on IP forwarding through the registry or netsh, so 'any modern OS' is Unix-centric.

ch16-threads-p1: 'By 1990 ... The child process ran in parallel with the parent'. Most UNIX machines in 1990 had one CPU, so a forked child ran interleaved with its parent by time slicing (the illusion ch4-scheduling-p1 describes), not literally in parallel. The same goes for 'scheduled onto a different core' in the 1995 POSIX framing: multi-core chips arrived in 2001 (POWER4) and reached consumers in 2005, so in 1995 that meant a different processor in a multiprocessor machine. Low severity, a simplification; 'ran alongside' or 'concurrently' would make it exact.

Fig 16.1 How it works, 'The standard': 'C, C++, Java and Rust default to threads'. C had no standard thread API until C11 (pthreads is POSIX, not part of the C language), and neither C nor C++ defaults to any concurrency model. The accurate claim is that threads are these languages' standard or native concurrency primitive. Low severity, in the closed strip.

search_points.quote: match it against signatures of known attacks
search_points.missing: Until now every 'signature' in the book meant a private-key proof (Ch 11, Ch 14), and this section uses that meaning again at p4 to p6. Here the word means a recognisable pattern left by a known attack, and the text never says so, so the reader cannot explain how an IDS matches traffic or what 'no signature yet' means.
search_points.close_with: a short gloss: a signature here is a byte pattern known from an earlier attack, not a cryptographic signature

search_points.quote: evidence lived on the endpoint, not in network logs: in which process spawned which
search_points.missing: The reader knows what a process is and that fork creates one, but nothing says why one process starting another proves an attack. Every other generation in this paragraph gets a concrete case (port 80, Helsinki and Tokyo); this step gets none.
search_points.close_with: one example, e.g. a web server or a document reader starting a command shell (as Ch 3's shellcode does), which normal use never does

search_points.quote: by reprogramming the PLCs that set the centrifuges' spin speed
search_points.missing: The abbreviation PLC is used here and throughout Fig 15.8 with no expansion and no word on what kind of thing it is. It is explained only at p5 ('PLCs, programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves'), two blocks later.
search_points.close_with: move p5's gloss to this first use

search_points.quote: supply-chain equivalent of Certificate Transparency from Chapter 14: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), reproducible builds
search_points.missing: The reader knows how Certificate Transparency works, but nothing says how SBOMs, reproducible builds or signed build provenance work, or how any of them would have caught an altered build like SUNBURST. The analogy and the three remedies are never connected.
search_points.close_with: one clause, e.g. that a reproducible build lets anyone rebuild the published source and compare the bytes, so a build altered in secret no longer matches

fact_doubts: ch15-defense-p1 dates the IDS generation to the 'early 2000s', but the same figure's How it works strip names Snort, which was released in 1998. Commercial IDS products (e.g. ISS RealSecure, 1997) and the research behind them (Denning's IDES, 1980s) are older. 'Late 1990s' would be safer.

ch15-defense-p6: FireEye found its own breach in December 2020 through a security alert about an extra device registered for an employee's two-factor login. It did not come from spotting 'unusual traffic on its own network'. Tracing that breach led to the Orion backdoor.

Fig 15.8 (kept original): 'did damage on perhaps a hundred' machines has no clear unit or source. The figure most often cited is about 1,000 centrifuges taken out of service at Natanz. This is not clearly wrong, so it is listed here and not as a kept-original error.

Code block comment '++counter; // three instructions: LOAD; ADD; STORE' (and p1 'nearly always well short'): on x86-64 the compiler usually emits one memory-destination add/inc. That is still a non-atomic read-modify-write, so three steps but not three instructions. At -O2, GCC and Clang may legally fold the whole non-atomic loop into one 'add 1000000' (a data race is undefined behaviour), so the demo often prints exactly 2,000,000. 'Well short, different every run' holds for unoptimised builds. 'Three steps' (the word Fig 16.2 uses) would be safe.

Code block comment 'single CPU instruction' for counter.fetch_add: true on x86 (lock xadd/add), ARMv8.1+ with LSE (ldadd) and RISC-V A (amoadd). On ARMv8.0 without LSE it compiles to a load-exclusive/store-exclusive retry loop. Minor.

Insight strip ch16-races-p6, 'The first known software-caused medical fatalities were race conditions' plus 'A specific keystroke sequence': the two Tyler, Texas deaths (1986) came from the keystroke-edit race. The Yakima death (Jan 1987) came from a different bug: a one-byte flag counter (Class3) wrapped round to zero and skipped the turntable check. That bug was also timing-dependent, but the strip implies all three deaths came from the keystroke race. Low severity.

search_points.quote: show a further habit: chaining pieces the attacker did not write
search_points.missing: The prose groups the book's attacks as data-as-code, confused deputy and a 'chaining' habit (ROP, Stuxnet). Fig 15.9 then gives six patterns: chaining is not one of them, and four of them never appear in the prose. So the reader cannot place ROP and Stuxnet, or square this with p7's claim that 'six structural attack patterns now name every specific exploit in this book'.
search_points.close_with: p1 names the six patterns and says where chaining (ROP, Stuxnet) sits among them, or that it is a way of combining them

search_points.quote: only then publishes: 30 days after a fix, or at the deadline
search_points.missing: The section never says why publishing a bug that is still unfixed on day 90 helps anyone (Fig 15.10 circles it, and the strip only says 'silence' is worse). To this reader it looks like handing attackers a weapon, so the convention's logic cannot be explained back.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the deadline is what makes vendors fix, attackers may find the bug anyway, and once told, users can protect themselves

fact_doubts: ch15-culture-p4: 'PicoCTF (Carnegie Mellon's teaching CTF, free, runs continuously)'. The picoCTF competition is held once a year (in spring). What runs all year is its practice site, picoGym. Low priority.

search_points.quote: a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write
search_points.missing: No earlier page defines 'cache line'. Chapter 1 only says a cache keeps a copy of the data and its neighbours (ch1-memory strip). So this reader cannot say what a write is waiting for, or why one write's line is at hand and another's is not, and that is the step this gloss uses to explain why writes leave out of order.
search_points.close_with: name the line in the gloss: the block of neighbouring bytes a cache copies whole, which the core must fetch before a write to it can land

search_points.quote: the matching demand: everything the releaser promised is visible before any later load runs
search_points.missing: The paragraph explains only how writes get reordered, and release already guarantees that x is visible by the time the flag is. So this reader cannot say what would go wrong on the reading side without acquire. Nothing says the reading core can also run its load of x early, before its load of the flag (out-of-order execution from Chapter 1 applied to loads). 'Before any later load runs' hints at this but never says it.
search_points.close_with: one clause: the reading core can also run its load of x ahead of its flag load, and acquire forbids that

fact_doubts: ch16-lockfree-p1, 'The stricter term comes from Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper': Herlihy already used 'wait-free' and gave the hierarchy in his PODC 1988 paper 'Impossibility and universality results for wait-free synchronization', and the idea goes back to Lamport's 1977 work on concurrent reading and writing. The ledger check (UNDER.md, 'wait-free' appears 75 times in the TOPLAS paper) shows the paper uses the term, not that the term started there. 'Made precise in' or 'formalised in' would be safer than 'comes from'.

ch16-lockfree-p3, 'Out-of-order execution ... and store buffers ... let writes appear reordered': out-of-order cores still retire stores in program order into the store buffer. x86 executes out of order yet keeps stores in order, as the fig-16-5 strip itself says. Writes overtaking each other comes from the store buffer and cache side. What out-of-order execution mainly reorders is loads, and that is the reading-side hazard acquire exists for (see the p3 B search point).

search_points.quote: requires a separate PUT request before GET, breaking the simplest SSRF pattern
search_points.missing: The reader knows GET and PUT (ch11-http) and how SSRF works, but cannot say why a PUT-first rule stops it. The missing step: a simple SSRF only chooses the URL of a plain GET the server sends, so it cannot make the server send the PUT that gets the token first.
search_points.close_with: a simple SSRF picks only the address of a GET, so it cannot send the PUT that fetches the token

fact_doubts: ch15-web-p5 'AWS now mandates IMDSv2': overstated. Since mid-2024, only newly released EC2 instance types run IMDSv2-only by default, and accounts can set IMDSv2 as their default. IMDSv1 is still available on most instance types and launches. Kept-original fig-15-6 says the same ('mandatory on new instances'), so report it as kind kept-original, low severity.

ch15-web-p4 'SSRF became one of the most common high-impact vulnerabilities': OWASP 2021 added SSRF (A10) on the strength of its community survey, and its incidence rate in the OWASP data was low (about 2.7%). 'High-impact' holds. 'One of the most common' is doubtful.

ch15-web-p6 '.NET's BinaryFormatter (deprecated 2020 but still in use)': marked obsolete in .NET 5 (2020) and its implementation removed in .NET 9 (2024), where calls now throw. 'Still in use' is true only of .NET Framework and older apps.

ch15-web-p6 'Python's __reduce__ hook' as code that runs while the object is rebuilt: __reduce__ runs when the object is pickled. On unpickling, what runs is the callable that __reduce__ named. Minor imprecision. The earlier gate wording was 'pickle runs __reduce__'.

search_points.missing: The step from the two shares to the formula is never given: count the one-core running time as 1, so the N-core time is (1 − p) + p/N, and speedup is the old time divided by the new one. Without it the reader cannot see why the formula starts with "1 /". p1's "90% parallel code" also points them at a share of the code, when p is a share of the running time (only Fig 16.8's drawn label says "time").
search_points.close_with: one sentence before the formula: one-core time = 1, N-core time = (1 − p) + p/N, speedup = 1 divided by that time

search_points.quote: the parallel portion scales, and effective speedup
search_points.missing: The paragraph has just said Gustafson fixes the time, but "speedup" has so far meant the same job finishing sooner. The reader cannot say what is sped up when the time does not change until they learn the number counts how many times more work N cores do in that time than one core would. That is explained later, at Fig 16.9 ("work done", ch16-amdahl-p8).
search_points.close_with: name it here: work done in the same time, compared with one core

search_points.missing: From "the sequential portion stays constant while the parallel portion scales" the reader cannot reach N − (1 − p)(N − 1). The form that follows directly, (1 − p) + p·N (serial share done once, parallel share done on each of N cores), appears only in Fig 16.9's closed How it works strip.
search_points.close_with: give (1 − p) + p·N in the prose with its one-line reading; keep the other form as "the same as"

search_points.quote: the speedup is 5.9× on 8 cores, 15.4× on 64 and 19.6× on 1,024
search_points.missing: The drawn axis spaces 1, 32 and 1,024 evenly, so each step is a doubling, and neither the picture nor the caption says so. As drawn, the curve starts slow and is steepest in the middle, the opposite of the "rises fast at first" in the figure's description. A reader matching the caption's numbers to the curve has to stop and re-read the axis.
search_points.close_with: label the axis as doubling (e.g. "cores, N (doubling)") or say so in the How it works strip

fact_doubts: ch16-amdahl-p1: "a fraction p of a program is parallelisable" and "a program with 90% parallel code" are loose. In Amdahl's law p is the share of the one-core running time, not of the code. Figs 16.8 and 16.9 get this right ("time for one job: 5% serial", "5% of the time serial"), so the prose and the figures disagree on what p counts.

Fig 16.8 How it works, "Other values": "going from 95% to 99% parallel buys more than any number of extra cores" holds for the ceilings (20× vs 100×), but not at small core counts. On 16 cores, 99% parallel gives 13.9×, below the 20× that 95% approaches with unlimited cores. It is true only once the machine has roughly 25 or more cores.

Fig 16.8 picture vs its description: the <desc> says the curve "rises fast at first and then flattens", but on the drawn doubling axis it is S-shaped. A screen reader and a sighted reader get different shapes (see search point at ch16-amdahl-p6).

All drawn numbers checked against the formulas and correct: Fig 16.8 S(N) for p = 0.95 at N = 2…1,024 (1.9, 3.5, 5.9, 9.1, 12.5, 15.4, 17.4, 18.6, 19.3, 19.6); Fig 16.9 Amdahl times (0.53, 0.29, 0.17, 0.11, 0.08, 0.06) and Gustafson work (2.0, 3.9, 7.7, 15.3, 30.5, 60.9). Gustafson's two forms are algebraically equal. The dates (AFIPS 1967; Gustafson 1988, Sandia, 1,024 processors) check out.

search_points.quote: and MESI's cache-line ping-pong
search_points.missing: The prose only ever presents MESI as the thing that keeps caches correct (p1, caption p3) and never says it costs time. The idea that two cores writing one line keep invalidating each other, so every write waits for the line to move, appears only in Fig 16.11's closed How it works strip. A reader who never opened that strip cannot explain why MESI belongs in a list of limits on parallel speed next to Amdahl and NUMA.
search_points.close_with: one clause in the prose (p1 or p5) saying that two cores writing the same line take turns invalidating it, so each write waits for the line to cross

fact_doubts: ch16-numa-p4: 'a lasting ~5–30% slowdown' overstates the KPTI cost for today's machines. KPTI is switched on only for CPUs that are vulnerable to Meltdown. AMD processors never needed it, and Intel CPUs from about 2019 on (Cascade Lake and Ice Lake onward) fix Meltdown in hardware, so they run without it. The 5–30% range is the worst case on syscall-heavy loads on affected older Intel parts, and PCID made it smaller.

ch16-numa-p4: 'The fix needed updates to ... microcode and kernel page-table isolation' merges two different attacks. KPTI answers Meltdown. Microcode updates (IBRS/IBPB) and retpolines mitigate Spectre variant 2. Spectre variant 1 has no general fix, only barriers placed in the code one site at a time, and the Spectre class is still not fully closed. Read as written, 'the fix' suggests both attacks were simply fixed.

ch16-numa-p4: 'read out the secret bit by bit' does not match ch1-cpu-p11, which tells the same reader that each probe of 256 locations reveals a whole byte ('the fast one reveals the byte'). A reader who remembers Chapter 1 will notice. 'byte by byte' would agree with it.

ch16-numa-p1: 'the 64-byte block' is stated as if every machine used it. It holds for x86 and most ARM cores, but Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and later, which the book names in ch1-cpu-p4) report 128-byte cache lines (sysctl hw.cachelinesize = 128). Not verified here. 'typically 64 bytes' would cover both.

ch16-gpu-p1: 'most of its scientific simulation' and 'most of the world's machine learning ... inference' are arguable as stated. Many simulation codes still run on CPU-only systems, even though the largest supercomputers use GPUs. A lot of inference runs on CPUs, phone neural chips and Google TPUs. 'Much of' would be safer, or the claim could be limited to the largest systems.

Fig 16.6 How it works: 'A desktop CPU has 8 to 24 cores' leaves out common mainstream desktop parts with 4 to 6 cores (for example 6-core Ryzen 5 and 4-core Core i3). '6 to 24' or 'typically 6 to 24' would be accurate. A minor point.

search_points.quote: Against a VM, that is a tenfold to hundredfold improvement in start time
search_points.missing: The paragraph first says a container starts in milliseconds, then says `docker run` takes a second, and the tenfold-to-hundredfold figure only works with the second number, so the reader can't tell which start time is meant or what fills that second (fetching the image, setting up namespaces and cgroups).
search_points.close_with: say the process itself starts in milliseconds and the second goes mostly to fetching and setup, then work out the ratio from one stated figure

search_points.quote: and a tenfold one in density
search_points.missing: 'Density' is never defined (how many containers fit on one machine compared with VMs), and p3 relies on it again in 'containers' speed and density'.
search_points.close_with: a gloss: density, how many fit on one server

search_points.quote: Each Dockerfile step produces one read-only layer
search_points.missing: Neither the prose nor the figure says that an image is built by running a recipe file (the Dockerfile) one step at a time, or that a layer is the set of files one step added or changed, so 'layer' has nothing concrete to attach to.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a Dockerfile is the image's build recipe, and each step's layer holds the files that step added or changed

search_points.quote: FROM a Linux base
search_points.missing: p1 has just said a container shares the host's kernel while a VM carries a whole operating system, so the reader can't tell what a 'Linux base' layer holds if not an operating system with its kernel (it holds a Linux system's files and libraries, no kernel).
search_points.close_with: say the base layer is a Linux system's files and libraries, without a kernel

search_points.quote: Change app.py and only its layer is rebuilt and pushed
search_points.missing: 'Registry' (in the drawing) and 'pushed' are never explained: the reader doesn't know images are uploaded to a shared online store that `docker run nginx` downloads from (p1 never says where the download comes from), so it's unclear why sending only one layer matters.
search_points.close_with: one clause: a registry is the online store images are pushed to and pulled from, as `docker run nginx` did in p1

search_points.quote: wrapping the container in a user-space kernel that intercepts every syscall
search_points.missing: To this reader a kernel is the Ring 0 program that system calls trap into, so 'a user-space kernel that intercepts every syscall' reads as a contradiction. Nothing says how it catches the calls, what 'from the other side' means, or why this protects the host (the container's calls are answered by an ordinary program that passes only a few on to the real kernel, so a kernel bug is harder to reach).
search_points.close_with: one sentence: gVisor is an ordinary process that answers the container's system calls itself and passes only a few to the host kernel, shrinking what a container can reach

search_points.quote: As hardware virtualization gets cheaper and faster, VMs lose their speed penalty
search_points.missing: Nothing in the strip says hardware virtualization got cheaper or faster. It shows microVMs that are light for a reason it never gives (a minimal guest kernel and few emulated devices) and gVisor, which is not a VM at all, so the closing cause doesn't follow from what came before.
search_points.close_with: say what a microVM strips out and draw the closing sentence from that

fact_doubts: ch17-containers-p1 'downloads a layered image ... the whole thing takes a second': this holds only when the image is already on the machine. A first pull of nginx (tens of MB) usually takes several seconds.

ch17-containers-p3 Lambda microVMs 'never shared between functions or customers': AWS's Lambda security overview (as I recall it) says execution environments are never shared across functions, but a microVM is dedicated to one account and may be reused by environments of different functions in that account. The fact ledger (UNDER.md §4g) cites Firecracker NSDI'20, so check the current AWS wording before changing anything.

ch17-containers-p3 Kata Containers 'boot in about a tenth of a second, weigh a few megabytes': these are Firecracker's figures (under 125 ms, under 5 MiB). Kata's VMs usually carry tens of MB of overhead and boot more slowly.
ch17-containers-p3 closing cause: microVM speed comes mainly from software (a minimal device model and guest kernel), not from hardware virtualization getting cheaper.

ch17-containers-p2 'Each Dockerfile step produces one read-only layer': only steps that change files (RUN, COPY, ADD) produce file layers. Steps such as ENV and CMD change only the image's settings. Minor, since all five steps drawn do produce layers.

search_points.quote: only sensitive ones, such as asking what processor this is or touching a device
search_points.missing: The reader learned in the Bridge (chBridge-mode-p4) that only instructions that control the whole machine are guarded. Reading the CPU id controls nothing, and the guest really is running on that processor, so the reader cannot say what makes an instruction 'sensitive' or why the hypervisor must step in with its own answer here. Fig 17.1 animates this as its one example, and the strip's 'every sensitive instruction traps cleanly' depends on knowing it.
search_points.close_with: one clause: sensitive means it reads or changes the real machine, which the hypervisor must guard or fake, so each guest sees only the machine it was promised (e.g. the processor the VM claims to be)

fact_doubts: ch17-virt-p1: 'These instruction-set extensions let a hypervisor run guest operating systems at near-native speed' says the speed came from VT-x/AMD-V. Read after 'VMware founded 1998', that implies x86 virtualization before 2005 was slow, which is the direction of the error §4g row 3 corrected. Xen (SOSP 2003) was already within a few percent of native, and Adams–Agesen 2006 found first-generation VT-x often slower than VMware's binary translation. The Pass-18 caption gave BT/PV credit as near-native; that credit went when the caption was cut, and neither the current caption nor the strip carries it. VT-x's real gain was clean trapping for unmodified guests (simpler hypervisors such as KVM); near-native memory performance came later, with nested paging (AMD NPT 2007, Intel EPT 2008).

ch17-virt-p3: 'After EC2, a single API call got you a fresh VM ... in any of dozens of regions worldwide'. The sentence splits speed ('today, in under one') and billing ('by the hour at launch, by the second today') into then and now, but not regions. EC2 launched in 2006 in one region (US East), and the second (EU, Ireland) came in December 2008. 'Dozens' is true only today.

ch17-virt-p2 strip ('Examples'): 'VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels, each an application plus a kernel driver, which is where its traps land.' Parallels Desktop since version 16 (macOS Big Sur, 2020, and every Apple-silicon Mac) ships no kernel extension of its own. It uses Apple's Hypervisor.framework, so traps land in macOS's own kernel and are passed up to the app. VMware Fusion 12 did the same. VMware Workstation on Windows can also run on top of Hyper-V. 'Each ... plus a kernel driver' is dated for Parallels at least (low severity).

search_points.quote: every piece of logic that maintains some kind of object
search_points.missing: This reader knows 'object' only from the object-oriented code in Part II, so they cannot say what a controller maintains. The missing idea: Kubernetes stores each thing it is asked for (a pod, 'three copies of this pod') as a record of desired state in etcd. The Fig 17.3 strip ('watch one kind of object') leans on the same word, and so does the caption's 'a new pod is stored there'.
search_points.close_with: one clause: an object is a stored record of what should exist, such as 'three copies of this pod'

search_points.quote: Chapter 10's TCP congestion control is the same shape
search_points.missing: Chapter 10 (ch10-aimd-p1, p7) taught that nobody tells TCP the right speed and that it finds the limit by overshooting. So this reader cannot find TCP's 'declared desired state', and cannot say which part of the shape matches.
search_points.close_with: name the part that is shared (observe, compare, correct, repeat) and say TCP has to find its target because none is declared; or drop the parenthesis

search_points.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan
search_points.missing: The paragraph's last sentence repeats the sentence before it in shorter form. The reader re-reads both, looking for a difference that is not there. This breaks law 2. The Fig 17.4 strip ('Elsewhere') says the same thing a third time.
search_points.close_with: delete the last sentence of the paragraph

search_points.quote: the next pass sees two of three and starts one
search_points.missing: Fig 17.3 has just shown that a pod is started only by a node's kubelet, after the scheduler picks the node, and that every component talks only to the API server. So this reader cannot explain how a controller 'starts one pod' (in the code, cluster.Create). The missing step: the controller writes a new pod record through the API server, and the scheduler and a kubelet then start it.
search_points.close_with: say the controller asks the API server for one more pod, and the Fig 17.3 path (scheduler, kubelet) starts it

search_points.quote: // the reconcile loop, simplified
search_points.missing: p3 says the loop is 'a tight loop' and should 'Run forever', so this reader looks for a loop in the code and finds none. Reconcile runs once and returns, and after Create or Update it asks for no re-run. They cannot tell who calls it again or when, or what a 'Request' is, or which queue 'Requeue' puts it back into.
search_points.close_with: one comment line: Kubernetes calls this whenever the object or its pods change, and again after RequeueAfter; req names the object to check

fact_doubts: ch17-k8s-p3, 'Chapter 10's TCP congestion control is the same shape': TCP congestion control is a feedback loop with no declared target. ch10-aimd-p1 says no central authority tells TCP the answer. So the 'declared desired state' half of the pattern does not apply to TCP; only the feedback loop is shared.

ch17-k8s code block and Fig 17.4: the code reads actual state and creates pods through a separate cluster handle (cluster.Get, cluster.Create), and the figure says the controller 'starts one pod'. In Kubernetes, a controller such as the ReplicaSet controller reads and creates Pod objects through the API server, and the kubelet starts the containers. That is what the Fig 17.3 caption itself says ('every component talks only to the API server'), so the code and Fig 17.4 contradict the caption one figure earlier.
ch17-k8s-p3, 'a tight loop': Kubernetes controllers are not tight (busy) loops. They wake on watch events and on requeues, with a periodic resync. The code's own RequeueAfter is 30 seconds.

search_points.quote: types, lambda calculus
search_points.missing: The book never explained lambda calculus (nothing before this section mentions it), so this reader cannot say what mathematics the languages layer realises, in a figure whose whole claim is "math at every layer". Types is known from ch7-types.
search_points.close_with: a few plain words on what lambda calculus is, or a label for mathematics the book did teach

search_points.quote: The kernel is a state machine over processes.
search_points.missing: The book never named the states a process moves between. Then Fig 18.1, directly below, labels the kernel "queueing, scheduling" and gives "state machines" to the instruction set. The old caption's "over registers", which said what the instruction set's states are, is gone. So the reader re-reads, unsure which layer is the state machine or what its states are.
search_points.close_with: make the prose and the figure agree, and name the states in passing (registers, or running/ready/waiting)

fact_doubts: ch18-math-p1 "Distributed consensus is quorum arithmetic over asynchronous nodes": the book's own FLP passage (ch17-consensus) says that in a fully asynchronous system with one crash, no protocol can be guaranteed to both agree and finish. Quorums keep consensus safe under asynchrony, but Paxos and Raft need partial synchrony to make progress. A reader who remembers FLP may read this as a contradiction.

ch18-math-p1 "TLS is number theory over network packets" and Fig 18.1 "cryptography: number theory, curves": only TLS's key exchange and signatures are number theory. Its bulk cipher (AES) is not, and ch14-tls-pqc says key exchange is moving to ML-KEM, which is lattice-based. Fine as a simplification, but the book itself has shown the reader this is incomplete.
Fig 18.1 "graphs, request–response": request–response is a protocol pattern, not mathematics, so it sits oddly under the title "math at every layer". Minor.

search_points.quote: Consistency (every read returns the most recent write)
search_points.missing: The reader already knows Consistency from ACID (ch13-acid-p2: a transaction leaves the database with its rules intact). Here the same capitalised word means something else, and nothing says the two differ, so the reader goes back to square them.
search_points.close_with: a clause saying this is not ACID's consistency: here it means every copy gives the latest value

search_points.quote: the cut-off replica can refuse, staying consistent but unavailable
search_points.missing: p1 defines Availability as 'every request gets a response', and the drawing has replica 2 reply 'error: can't confirm'. By the book's own definition that error is a response, so the reader can't see why refusing counts as losing availability.
search_points.close_with: define A as every request getting a real answer, not an error

search_points.quote: the first group refuses writes it cannot confirm
search_points.missing: In Fig 17.7 the consistent side accepts the write on replica 1 and refuses only the read on replica 2. Fig 17.8 then shows every CP store refusing writes. p1's 'wrong side of the split' never says which side keeps serving (the side with a majority, or the primary), so the reader can't tell whether a CP store refuses reads, writes or both, or on which side.
search_points.close_with: one plain statement: the side holding a majority keeps serving, and the other side refuses both reads and writes

search_points.quote: a database with a primary, which steps down without a majority
search_points.missing: 'Primary' is used as a familiar noun but never introduced. The reader has met Raft's leader, not a primary, so they can't say what steps down or what the majority is counted over.
search_points.close_with: a gloss: a primary (the one copy that takes every write, like Raft's leader)

search_points.quote: TrueTime (GPS and atomic clocks bounding clock error) makes consistent transactions cheap
search_points.missing: This is in the How it works strip. No earlier page links accurate clocks to consistency, and Spanner is never introduced, so the reader can't see why better clocks would make consistent transactions cheap.
search_points.close_with: cut the clock clause and keep 'Google's private network makes partitions rare; Spanner still chooses consistency'

fact_doubts: Fig 17.7, CP panel: during the partition replica 1 shows x = 2, so it accepted a write it cannot pass on. It is only one of two replicas. Under the majority rule from ch17-consensus (Q = 2 for N = 2), and under Fig 17.8's own 'primary steps down without a majority', a CP store would refuse this write too. The drawing holds only if replica 1 is a fixed primary, which nothing says, so the two figures contradict each other as drawn.

ch17-cap-p1 defines Availability as 'every request gets a response'. Gilbert and Lynch require a response from every non-failing node that receives a request, and the usual short form says 'a (non-error) response'. Without that qualifier, Fig 17.7's 'error: can't confirm' would technically count as available. Defensible as shorthand, but the figure exposes the gap.

search_points.quote: two leaders elected in different terms cannot both have a majority without sharing a witness who would force one to step down
search_points.missing: Terms are sequential election periods (p2), so the reader cannot see how two leaders could be in charge at the same time, or how a shared node could 'force' a leader to step down. The missing facts: an old leader cut off by a partition does not know a newer term has begun, and a node that has seen the newer term turns the old leader away, so it learns of that term and stops leading.
search_points.close_with: one clause: messages carry their term number; a node that has seen a higher term refuses the old leader, which steps down when it hears of it

search_points.quote: Any two majorities of the same cluster share a node, so a committed entry can never be lost
search_points.missing: The 'so' rests on the overlap alone. The reader cannot see why the shared node stops a later leader that lacks the entry from overwriting it. The step they need is the vote rule in the next bullet: the shared node holds the entry and will not vote for a candidate whose log lacks it, so whoever wins already has it.
search_points.close_with: join the two bullets: the shared node refuses any candidate missing the entry

search_points.quote: so real systems assume delays end and use timeouts
search_points.missing: The figure offers two branches: 'decide now: safety lost' and 'keep waiting: liveness lost'. 'Time out' then reads as stopping the wait and deciding, which is the first branch. The reader cannot see what a node does when its timeout fires that avoids a wrong decision (it starts a new election or round, and a decision still needs a majority). So they also cannot see that a false assumption costs only liveness, which is how p2's 'correct under any pattern of message loss' stands up against FLP. Only the closed strip's last bullet hints at this.
search_points.close_with: a clause: a timeout starts a new election, never a decision, so a wrong guess costs time, not agreement

search_points.quote: Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony: partial synchrony
search_points.missing: The stated link fits only partial synchrony. The reader cannot see how flipping coins, or giving up immediate agreement, 'rules out pure asynchrony', or how coin flips 'break adversarial schedules'. The link the list needs: each escape drops one condition of the FLP statement in p11 (the bound on delays, 'deterministic', or full agreement itself).
search_points.close_with: map each escape to the FLP condition it drops: timing / determinism / agreement

fact_doubts: ch17-consensus-p12: 'Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony' is true only of partial synchrony. Ben-Or's randomised protocol runs in a fully asynchronous system and escapes FLP by not being deterministic. Eventual consistency (Dynamo) gives up agreement, not asynchrony. The Fig 17.6 strip frames the three escapes correctly ('Partial synchrony ... randomness ... or weaker agreement'). 'Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption' is also a stretch for eventual consistency, which does not solve consensus at all.

ch17-consensus-p6: in Raft, overlapping majorities plus one vote per term are what guarantee at most one leader in a given term. Leaders of different terms can exist at the same time for a while (a stale leader cut off by a partition), and the overlap only stops the stale one from getting new entries committed. As written, 'two leaders elected in different terms cannot both have a majority' is imprecise: the stale leader did have a majority when it was elected.

search_points.quote: Fig 18.2 · The civilization timeline · seven moments that made the rest possible
search_points.missing: The seven moments come in three colours (teal for 1854 to 1947, violet for 1969 to 1976, gold for 1989 and 1991), and no key anywhere says what they mean. p1 has just sent the reader to Fig 18.1, which uses the same three colours for bands of the stack, but the colours don't match up: cryptography is gold there and public keys are violet here, while the web and the kernel are violet there and the web and Linux are gold here. fact_doubts: ch18-civilization-p1 "The Boolean algebra in your CPU was invented by a Lincolnshire schoolteacher": the book's own ch2-boole-p5 says later logicians "reshaped it into the Boolean algebra used today", so "invented by" claims more than the book itself grants (wording such as "began with" would agree with ch2-boole-p5).

verdicts.reason: 'Using details no real fault produced' is vague, and the reader is never told that a real fault hands the handler anything. Fact check: a real page fault loads the faulting address into CR2 and pushes an error code. `int 14` does neither, because software interrupts push no error code and leave CR2 at the last real fault. The handler would therefore act on a stale address. That is the actual harm, and the reason DPL exists rests on it.
verdicts.fix: Replace 'using details no real fault produced' with: "acting on the address of some earlier fault, because a real page fault records the address that failed and `int 14` records nothing". verdicts.reason: p6 defines a VM as a whole computer imitated on a hypervisor. Fig 4.19 draws the hypervisor beneath each guest kernel. p11 itself says 'unless the hypervisor has a flaw too', which tells the reader the hypervisor is the wall. How hardware virtualisation keeps guest Ring 0 from the real machine is deeper than this chapter's baseline reader needs. The finding is a deeper question than the section sets out to answer.

ch1-context-p4 proves that no machine can read any program and decide whether it ever stops. p15 says the verifier proves every program terminates, which contradicts the earlier proof until one step is stated: it accepts only programs simple enough to prove and refuses the rest, even some that would have ended. The caption and strip hint at this ('a loop it cannot bound is refused'). It is also a nice payoff for Chapter 1.
verdicts.fix: ch4-security-p15, after 'and never crash': '(Turing showed in Chapter 1 that no checker can decide this for every program, so the verifier settles for less: it accepts only programs simple enough to prove, such as loops with a known bound, and refuses everything else, even some programs that would have ended.)'

verdicts.reason: The bullet is in the closed strip, but it is jargon-dense and the figure does not use it. eth0, Ethernet pair, bridge and routing are unknown until Part III, so a reader who opens the strip cannot explain any of it back. The figure shows only the container's network address.

verdicts.reason: Checked: BoringSSL commit 5813c2c 'crypto: switch to C++' moves nearly all of BoringSSL to C++ (C ABI kept), and ssl/ was converted piecemeal from 2017. verdicts.reason: Ritchie 1979 ('The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System'), checked: 'Thompson [found] a little-used PDP-7 computer with an excellent display processor'. Nothing about a windowless room (unsourced colour) and nothing about it being discarded. The book also calls the same machine 'discarded' (title, p1) and 'salvaged ... unused' (p3). Those imply a cast-off; Ritchie's machine belonged to another group. Folds in #10.
verdicts.fix: p1: "At Bell Labs in 1969, Ken Thompson found a little-used PDP-7 and started writing a programming environment for himself." Title: "Two men, a spare minicomputer, four years." p3: replace "Thompson salvaged an unused PDP-7" with "Thompson took over a little-used PDP-7". Source: pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.828/2005/readings/ritchie79evolution.html

verdicts.reason: Ritchie's 'The Development of the C Language', checked: 'In 1971 I began to extend the B language by adding a character type' (NB, which already had int, char, arrays, pointers). He renamed it C only after building the fuller type system; the most creative period was 1972. So 'In 1972 Ritchie added types' misdates the first types. 'By 1972' is true and keeps Fig 5.2's 1972: C.
verdicts.fix: "By 1972 Ritchie had added types, so the compiler knew a `char` (one byte) from an `int` (a word), and he called the result *C*: the language that comes after B." Source: plan9.io/cm/cs/who/dmr/chist.html

verdicts.reason: Real contradiction inside the figure: the drawn label says RISC-V is 'always 4', while its own strip says the compressed extension shrinks both instructions to 2 bytes. RISC-V with the C extension (the default in RV64GC Linux) has 2-byte forms. ARM64 is always 4. Fig 5.1 is not in kept_original.
verdicts.fix: Label: "x86: 1 to 15 bytes each · ARM64: always 4 · RISC-V: 4, or 2 compressed" (check it still fits at 375 px; if not, "x86: 1 to 15 bytes · ARM64: 4 · RISC-V: 4 or 2"). Caption: "x86's variable-length bytes against the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V" (drop 'fixed'). Also the <desc> phrase 'fixed 4 bytes of ARM and RISC-V' becomes 'the 4-byte words of ARM and RISC-V'.

verdicts.reason: 'Always traps' contradicts the chapter's own account: p1 says UB can be 'not even a crash', and Fig 5.8's strip names -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks because the optimiser can delete null accesses. Also root can lower mmap_min_addr, and NULL plus a large offset lands past the unmapped page. What holds is the hardware fact about address 0 and the lowest pages. Cheap fix. Folds in #15.
verdicts.fix: Fig 5.9 strip: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so an access at or near address 0 traps instead of reading data."

verdicts.reason: 'Kills it for exhausting memory' describes the typical outcome on Linux (OOM killer), Android and iOS, and is a simplification the baseline reader needs no more precisely. malloc returning NULL is a separate failure the chapter does not teach here, and an unchecked NULL ends in a crash anyway. The three places agree with each other. Over-strict.

verdicts.reason: 'By 1969 Bell Labs had pulled out' is true as read ('by' a point within 1969): the withdrawal happened in 1969 (Ritchie: 'slow ... withdrawal' across 1968-69), and the next sentences place the PDP-7 find in 1969. Nobody reads it as 'before 1969 began'.

verdicts.reason: p6 states as a general design fact that C's types are 'the byte and the processor's own word'. K&R's own phrase is 'the natural size of integers on the host machine'.
verdicts.fix: p6: "Its types are the byte and an integer of the machine's natural size, its `if` statements and loops become conditional jumps, ..." Leave p7 unchanged.

verdicts.reason: p9 says 'every intended modification is written first', but Fig 4.13's strip and UNDER.md §4g (Pass 28 row) say ext4 data=ordered and NTFS journal metadata only. The prose brings back the corrected error and contradicts the figure two screens later.

verdicts.reason: 'the kernel runs until the machine shuts down' repeats the error §4g corrected in the glossary 'kernel' entry (resident, not running, while a user process runs; OSTEP 6.3). ch1-kernel-p4 now says 'stays loaded'. verdicts.reason: Checked docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html: EEVDF aims for equal sharing among equal-priority tasks, picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, and favours tasks that request shorter slices. verdicts.fix: p5 end: '...Linux's default is CFS's successor *EEVDF* (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First), which keeps the same bookkeeping but gives every task a virtual deadline set by the slice it asks for, so a task that asks for short slices gets the CPU sooner without taking more than its share.' Fig 4.4 strip: '...picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, so tasks that ask for short slices are served sooner.' Source: docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html.

verdicts.reason: 1/(mu - lambda) is the M/M/1 result and needs random service times as well as random arrivals. With fixed service times (M/D/1) the time at 95% load is about 10.5 service times, not 20. The figure strip names 'M/M/1' but does not say service times are random.
verdicts.fix: p10: 'For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals and random service times, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).' Fig 4.6 strip: '(random arrivals and service times, one server, called M/M/1)'.

verdicts.reason: Little's Law gives an average. 'At any moment' says the count is constant at 20, and the sentences right after discuss bursts and backlog, which contradict that. It costs one word to fix. Low severity.

verdicts.reason: 'This is how databases and search engines handle large data' overgeneralises. LMDB and Lucene map files, but PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB and Oracle deliberately use their own buffer pools (Crotty, Leis and Pavlo, CIDR 2022). The shared-library half is correct.

The 'entry marked not present' picture matches p3 and the book's teaching level, and law 4 says never close a gap with expert detail. Not something the baseline reader needs.

The italic 'Every' is a flat overclaim. Network interfaces have no /dev node on Linux, and System V message queues and semaphores in this chapter's own IPC table are not files. The bullets that follow are true, so softening the lead-in is enough.

verdicts.reason: Dijkstra invented the semaphore in 1962 or 1963 (EWD-35, for the Electrologica X8 OS). EWD123, 'Cooperating Sequential Processes' (1965), is the best-known exposition, not the origin. 'The idea is Dijkstra's, from 1965' (the Fig 4.18 strip) says the idea dates from 1965. Source: Wikipedia, Semaphore_(programming).
verdicts.fix: p12 last sentence: 'The idea is Edsger Dijkstra's, set out in his 1965 note "Cooperating Sequential Processes".' Fig 4.18 strip: 'The idea is Dijkstra's, set out in 1965.'

verdicts.reason: 'Namespaces are translation tables, not copies' is true of PID namespaces, which the sentence illustrates, but is false as a general statement. A new mount namespace starts as a copy of the caller's mount list, and a network namespace is a separate instance of the network stack (mount_namespaces(7), network_namespaces(7)). The caption sits under a figure that shows hostname, network and root too.
verdicts.fix: ch4-security-p12 caption: '...A PID namespace is a translation table, not a copy: to the host, A's PID 1 is just process 8472.'

verdicts.reason: Per unshare(2), unshare() moves the calling process into the new namespace and creates no new process. For CLONE_NEWPID only the caller's next children enter it. clone() starts a new process in the new namespace. The strip's sentence blends the two calls.
verdicts.fix: fig-4-20 strip 'Making one': '`clone()` with a flag such as `CLONE_NEWPID` starts a new process in a fresh namespace; `unshare()` moves the caller itself into one (for PID, only its next children). Children inherit the namespace.' Source: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unshare.2.html.

verdicts.reason: Checked Phoronix and The Register for Linux 6.16 (2025): the tree is about 38.4M lines in total, with 28.9M lines of code. Heise reported 40M at 6.14-rc1. verdicts.reason: The two rules do not collide. p4's 'always the most specific' is longest-prefix matching, which compares routes of different sizes. The finding's premise, that no 2025 measure gives 35 to 45%, does not hold. Measures differ: Cloudflare's Year-in-Review dual-stack metric is about 29%, but Cloudflare Radar's HTTP-request share, APNIC's capability measure and Google's user share sit at roughly 35 to 49% in 2025 and 2026 reporting. The sentence opens with 'Depending on how you count', which covers the spread, and the Fig 9.8 strip gives the Google user figure explicitly. A taste-level refinement at most, not something the owner will stop on.

Real internal contradiction. ch10-attacks tells how Mitnick held a blind, spoofed TCP session on Christmas Day 1994 by predicting the ISN, after Morris described it in 1985. Fig 9.10's strip says a forger 'cannot hold a TCP conversation', and a reader meets the opposite one chapter later.
verdicts.fix: Fig 9.10 strip, 'One way only': "A forger never sees the reply, so spoofing suits single packets, as in Chapter 10's SYN flood; holding a whole TCP conversation blind means guessing sequence numbers, which Mitnick managed in 1994."

verdicts.reason: Low severity. verdicts.fix: '...TCP's three-message setup (Section 03) would add a full round trip before the question could even go out, doubling the time the lookup takes, for nothing.'

verdicts.reason: ch10-why-p1 says 'Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals', yet p3 lists congestion-control state and Section 04 presents congestion control as a separate, deeper problem. Factually, the 1974 Cerf and Kahn design had no congestion control; Jacobson and Karels added it in 1988, which Section 04 itself says. So p1's universal claim is false as written, and the TCB list then contradicts it.
verdicts.fix: p1 last sentence: 'Everything in the 1974 design serves one of those four goals; the one large later addition, congestion control, is the subject of Section 04.' p3: 'the congestion-control state (Section 04), and a few dozen other values.'

verdicts.reason: The book never says an acknowledgement names the next byte expected until Fig 10.4 (ch10-aimd), after the handshake. The 'Plus one' strip says SYN counts as a byte but leaves the reader expecting ack 4170, the number they received. A single clause closes it.
verdicts.fix: Fig 10.2 strip, 'Plus one': 'An acknowledgement names the next byte expected, and SYN counts as one byte of sequence space, so the acknowledgements are 4171 and 9013.'

verdicts.reason: p3 gives the client path as 'the' well-trodden path and then calls the remaining states 'off-path' for simultaneous opens, closes and lost FINs. SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK are the server's ordinary path, shown in Fig 10.3 and in Fig 10.2 (LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED), so the text contradicts the figures until the Fig 10.3 caption sorts it out. The count works: 6 client states + LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK + CLOSING = 11.
verdicts.fix: Replace the two sentences after 'by fixed rules: a state machine covering setup, data transfer and teardown.' with: 'Most connections take one of two well-trodden paths. The side that connects and closes first goes CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the other goes CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The one remaining state, CLOSING, and the side routes exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send), and the dozen other partial-failure modes the protocol was designed to survive.'

verdicts.reason: p5 already gives the mechanism in sequence: queues filled, packets dropped, TCP retransmitted, the retransmits piled into the same queues, which overflowed again. That is the answer to why useful throughput collapsed. Adding 'the wires were full of repeats' would restate it, against law 2. The depth is right for the baseline reader.

p6 uses cwnd as the central variable and never says it is the sender's own cap, nor how it relates to the receive window just defined in p2. That is stated only in the closed Fig 10.4 strip ('The sender obeys the smaller'), which the reader may never open. The prose should carry the relation at first use.
verdicts.fix: p6: 'Slow start begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment: the sender's own cap on bytes in flight, its guess at what the network can carry. The sender obeys the smaller of this and the receive window, and cwnd _doubles_ on every successful round trip: ...' (rest unchanged).

verdicts.reason: ch10-why-p3 says a Linux server holds a million TCBs, and p2 then says the table fills at a few thousand SYNs a second (about 100,000 slots at ~30 s). The reader cannot reconcile the two. Half-open connections actually wait in a small, separate queue, the SYN backlog, which Fig 10.11 (kept-original) names without introduction. One clause in p2 fixes both. The Fig 10.10 and 10.11 captions stay untouched.
verdicts.fix: p2: 'Each half-open connection holds a slot in the SYN backlog, a short queue kept apart from established connections, for tens of seconds (the SYN_RCVD timeout); at a high enough SYN rate the backlog fills and legitimate clients cannot connect.'

verdicts.reason: I grepped Parts I to III: 'hash' is not explained before this point (SHA-256 hashing comes in Ch12, later), and the cookie mechanism rests on 'recompute the hash and compare'. verdicts.fix: See the combined p4 rewrite in #10.

verdicts.reason: p4 says the server 'encodes the necessary state' into a 32-bit keyed hash, which cannot hold addresses, ports and sequence numbers. In reality the returning ACK carries those, and the cookie only proves they answer a real SYN-ACK (plus a few bits of MSS). The Fig 10.11 text (kept-original, 'all state derived from the cookie') is loose, but the prose can be made exact without touching it.
verdicts.fix: Replace p4 from 'Instead, it encodes' with: 'Instead, it hides what it needs in the Initial Sequence Number (ISN) it returns in the SYN-ACK: a keyed hash (a fixed-size scramble of the values with the server's secret key: the same inputs give the same number) of the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and a time bucket, with a few bits for the MSS (the largest segment the client said it accepts, the one setting the server would otherwise have to remember). The whole fits in 32 bits and is hard to forge without the key. The third ACK repeats the addresses, ports and sequence numbers and carries the cookie back (its acknowledgement number is the cookie plus one); the server recomputes the hash from them, and a match proves the ACK answers a SYN-ACK it really sent. Only then does it rebuild the connection and allocate a TCB. Legitimate clients pass; the flood's spoofed connections never send an ACK at all.'

verdicts.reason: MSS is never expanded or explained in Parts I to III (only appears in the kept-original Fig 10.11 and its caption). The caption itself cannot be changed, so the prose must define it; the combined p4 rewrite under #10 does so.

verdicts.fix: 'Mitnick SYN-flooded a trusted host on Shimomura's network so that it could not answer with a RST to the SYN-ACK it had never asked for (which would have torn the forged connection down), then opened a TCP connection...'

Checked against the section: the listed path is the client's. LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK are the server's ordinary states, and the Fig 10.3 caption and strip draw them that way. CLOSING is the only state kept for a simultaneous close. No state exists for lost FINs; timers handle those. As written, a reader learns the server's normal states are failure handlers.
verdicts.fix: Replace the last two sentences of ch10-handshake-p3 with: "A client usually walks CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the server it talks to walks LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. Each side closes by sending a FIN (the segment that says I have nothing more to send). The remaining rules handle simultaneous opens and closes and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive." The "Most connections take one well-trodden path" sentence is dropped, since the two-path wording replaces it. The FIN gloss stays, so the first-use definition is kept.
